en: The Noble Mañjuśrī Nāmasaṅgīti: The Request Oṃ. Homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Now, the glorious Vajradhara, the supreme tamer of the difficult to tame, the hero who conquers the three worlds, the king of secrets, the lord of the vajra—1.

Oṃ, homage to Mañjunātha! I bow to the Lord of the Śabaras, who is the source of the cause for the union of the object, the subject, and space; who, by enveloping the paths of the sun, moon, and darkness, brings about the movement of the immovable mountains and the like;

who is the radiance of vast, shimmering wisdom; who is seated upon a gem-studded stone, hidden, and whose state is free from affliction; who appears as a drop of nectar, attained through the grace of the feet of the true Guru—may that [Lord] shine forth within me from the *Nāmasaṅgīti* for my own remembrance.

In this very place, at the site of the Great Caitya in Śrī Dhānyakaṭaka, the Blessed Buddha named Śrī Śākyasiṃha, having been requested by those desiring to hear various tantras, on the full moon day of Caitra, manifested the mandala of the glorious Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara and above that the glorious Ādibuddha, the mandala of the constellations; and having bestowed the Buddha-consecration there on that very day, he taught all the systems of mantra to the gods and others through the divisions of the great and small tantras.

And it is said in the *Śrī-bṛhad-ādi-buddha*: "Just as the Teacher taught the *Prajñāpāramitā* according to the system of the *Mantranaya* on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), so too was the teaching of the Dharma proclaimed by the Blessed One in the illustrious Dhānyakaṭaka.
In that regard, this very *Nāmasaṅgīti*, being the locus for the extraction of the ultimate truth that is most difficult to fathom, is the preeminent among all systems of mantra;
and herein lies the supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*) of the Blessed Lord Vajradhara, which is the feast of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
To Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
O Bharā!
There is no method for the *kaṇikas* in the treatise.

The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti* is the awakening through its nature as the locus of the *rasas*; it was perfectly revealed by the Tathāgata as the very heart. Through the purification of the cessation of the one hundred and sixty-two channels established within the six wheels (*cakras*) endowed with the six family channels (*kulanaḍī*), there are one hundred and sixty-two verses; the remainder consists of the benefits (*anuśaṃsā*) and so forth.

In that regard, first, by means of sixteen verses beginning with "Then the glorious Vastradhara," he speaks of that very same supreme syllable under the guise of a request: The word *atha* (then) here, by way of establishing selflessness (*nairātmya*), expresses emptiness (*śūnyatā*) endowed with the excellence of all aspects;
the word *tha*, moreover, by way of establishing the nature of Akṣobhya, expresses non-referential compassion (*nirālambakaruṇā*).

And this has been explained very clearly and lucidly in the *Hevajra-ṭīkā* (*Saṃpuṭa*). Because of the non-duality of those two, it is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)—the semen itself—situated within the jewel and the calyx that is the referent of the word; thus it is called "Now" (*atha*). And it is said: "The syllable *Vaṃ* in the center is the abode of the bliss of all Buddhas. This Vajrasattva in the element of space (*khadhātu*) exists through the union of body, speech, and mind. Body is the drop (*bindu*), the point (*indu*), and the semen; speech is emission (*visarga*), the dust (*rajas*), and the sun (*ravi*). These are declared to be the forms of mind, established thus in the element."
For this very reason, he is called Vajradhara because he wears as his very self the garment of the knowledge of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion.
"Vajra" refers to indivisible knowledge, so called because it cannot be pierced by the enemies of the aggregates, afflictions, and death, which are established upon false conceptualizations.

Thus it has been said: "Māra is one’s own mind; there is no other Māra. For Tathāgatas, there is no Tathāgata [other than themselves]. The destruction of Māra and the victory of the Sage consist solely in the awakening of the mind by means of the mind."

Therefore, he is "Vajradhara" (the Holder of the Vajra) because he wears outside that five-pronged cloth which indicates it, or because he wears it for the purpose of indicating its reality; this is the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*). He is "Śrīmān" (the Glorious One) because of his eternal union with non-dual knowledge (*śrī*) through identity, as he consists of the experience of that [knowledge]; this is the meaning of the word *mayā* (by me). As it has been said: "Thus, she who holds the *bindu* stands within the cloth at the center of the lotus-cloth. She alone is the undifferentiated Self; this has been made manifest by me."
"I have heard and known that it is bliss, and it is like the self to the self," as stated in the *Śrīmad-Ādibuddha*: "Having negated [all phenomena], emptiness is proclaimed."
By the letter *tha*, the nature of the sense-organ is its own form.
From the reality that is free from stains and dualistic, there is the co-emergent infinity in space.
O Fire, this is my resolve.
The meaning is that it consists of the reality of that which is extended like a bristle.
That meaning which is indeed intermingled within the center and the end of the vajra.
And it is stated in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*: "The self has been made."

In the *Amṛtakaṇikā* as well, there is the statement: "Thus it was heard by me in the Tantra. This has been understood by me as follows: the liquid of the moon [semen] from the three women enters the Buddha-field through the three emissions of the drop (*bindu*)—first into the head, then into the lotus of the throat and the heart, then into the navel, and finally into the secret place, the vulva of the women, and the supreme lotus. There, that Blessed One is to be known by the yogis. And here, the Vajradhara is none other than Mahāvajradhara himself.

Because of the capacity to grasp the meaning of any one among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) all at once, it is said: "I am the Dharma that explains; I am the listener, joined with my own retinue. I am the goal to be accomplished; I am the Teacher of the world; I am the mundane, and I am also the supramundane. I am the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the ultimate limit beginning with the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*). I am existence, yet I am not existence; I am the Buddha because of awakening to reality. Those fools who do not know me, and those who are afflicted by sloth—[I remain] dwelling in Sukhāvatī, in the *bhaga* of the true Vajra-consort. This [description of] the Buddha’s drama, including the requester and the compiler, is for the purpose of introducing beings to the primordial state.

Because they cannot be subdued by Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others, they are "difficult to tame" (*durdāntāḥ*). There are twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations; because [the yogi] is pierced by the great nectar of the knowledge of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), he destroys their nature and is thus the "tamer of the difficult to tame. The supreme yogi performs the "destruction of breath" (*prāṇātipāta*) day and night; that is said to be the destruction of the vital breaths for the sake of attaining the state of omniscience, not the external destruction of life. That which is called the external destruction of life for the purpose of taming the difficult to tame is [in fact] drawn forth from them by the power of yoga.
Furthermore, the yogin must re-enter that very same body; thus,
by being pierced by the essence (*rasa*),
the external and other [elements] are [transformed].

Thus it is stated in the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*: "He is the subduer of the difficult-to-subdue, but not the destroyer of the difficult-to-subdue. The "three worlds" (*triloka*) refers to the three realms, or body, speech, and mind. He whose nature it is to conquer and bring under control those [three] by means of primordial wisdom, merging them into a single unity with that wisdom, is described as such. And it is said: "Seated upon the thrones of the four Buddhas, well-established upon the vajra-lotus; the characteristic of the four joys is experienced precisely in sequence. In this way, through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, and by way of the divisions of body, speech, mind, and wisdom, there are four types of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣara-sukha*).

And it is said: "Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should not emit the *bodhicitta*; rather, one should meditate upon the form of the Buddha throughout the three realms without exception.
Thus, he whose breath-wind is free from sound and whose form is steady is such [a person].

The "Secret" (*guhya*) refers to the Vajrayāna, which is superior to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, or it is the state of the total integration (*lolībhāva*) of body, speech, mind, and gnosis; it is the "King of Secrets" (*guhyarāj*) because it shines (*rājate*) there in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Alternatively, he is the King of Secrets because he is the king of the five secrets.

And it was said by the *Ādibuddha*: "The yogi performs the 'taking of life' day and night; that is declared to be the destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). That sound which arises in the heart, devoid of a mouth, is indeed false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). Furthermore, the seizing of the ground of omniscient knowledge by the yogi is called theft (*steya*). And the bliss that occurs upon the falling of the two drops (*bindu*) is the service of another’s wife (*paradāra-sevā*) due to non-detachment. The drinking of wine is the drinking of the melted moon by means of the fire of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). One's own mind proceeds from the joint of the thumb at the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*) according to the lunar dates until the end of the full moon."
From the crown of the head it moves to the fingers; at the end of the dark fortnight, this very practice—which bestows the desired accomplishment—belongs indeed to the yogin at every daily occasion.
In the *Vikalparāja*: "You must kill living beings, you must speak false words, you must take what is not given, and you must consort with the wives of others."
Since the single mind is considered the living being and the living being is considered the mind, I shall deliver all beings; thus, even what is called "false speech" is proclaimed.
The semen of a woman and the wife of another are considered one's own beautiful woman.
From the perspective of yoga,
[one considers] both the disciple and the disciple-like.
O King, when the wise man is at peace, when the mind is tranquil, or even when one has awakened.
By the power of the falling of the seminal point (*bindu*),
that which is bound by living beings [is liberated].
People call it an eclipse at the end of the full moon.

O, [he is] Kuliśeśvara because he possesses lordship by virtue of his stability in the city of Vañcaśikhara within the *kuliśa* (thunderbolt), accompanied by the drops of supreme nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*).
The literal meaning of the term is not stated here as it is easily understood elsewhere.

The lotus-eyed one has awakened, his face like a full-blown lotus,
repeatedly brandishing his excellent thunderbolt with his hand.

"Vibuddha" means that the white lotus (*puṇḭarīka*) has blossomed; it is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), and his eye is innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*).

Thus, he is "one whose white lotus has blossomed," being endowed with the quality of whiteness due to the fullness of semen (*śukra*); or alternatively, he is "one whose eye—the gnosis arising from the five eyes—is upon the lotus at the peak of the vajra."

The heart of the supreme beings among yogins is a fully blossomed white lotus (*vibuddhapuṇḍarīka*); he [the Buddha] is so called because the gnosis of immutable bliss (*akṣarasukhajñāna*) exists therein through identity (*tādātmya*).

Alternatively, it is a lotus that has opened wide and expanded through the friction of the superior *vajra*, which, by means of the union of the *rajas* and *śukra*, is endowed with the qualities of white and red; he is so called because his face—meaning his gnosis—is therein.

Thus, through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, the four drops (*bindu*) whose nature is body, speech, mind, and gnosis are established as the state of the gnosis of supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukhajñānatā*).

Thus, [the practitioner] brandishes with his own hand this kind of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) supreme unchanging bliss-knowledge (*paramākṣarasukhajñāna*), the supreme *vajra*, by means of the radiation of rays from his own non-dual knowledge for the sake of the world; or else, by means of the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), through self-signs (*ātmanimitta*) and expansion, he brandishes and raises it, making it ascend to the crown-wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*) by means of his own hand—namely, through the realization of the non-duality of compassion and emptiness, which is to be personally experienced in a non-conceptual state. This is because false conceptualization cannot possibly occur even for a moment.

[He is surrounded] by infinite Vajrapāṇis headed by Bhṛkuṭītaraṅga, who are heroes who subdue the difficult-to-tame, possessing heroic and loathsome forms. "Bhṛkuṭī" refers to the contraction of the forehead; by this, the descent of the *bodhicitta* into the *ūrṇā-cakra* is indicated. Its "wave" (*taraṅgī*) or surge is due to its being restless with innate desire (*sahajābhilāṣa*). Those for whom the "pre-eminent means" (*pramukha-upāya*) regarding that object consists of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), as follows: [The text continues: ...by those [Vajrapāṇis] who possess the six-limbed yoga characterized by the pre-eminent means in that regard. Because of the restlessness of innate desire, there is a wave or surge of that [semen]. By "Bhṛkuṭī," the contraction of the forehead is meant; through that, the arrival of the *bodhicitta* at the *ūrṇā-cakra* is signified. Its "wave" is the surge [of the *bindu*], due to its flickering with innate longing. Therefore, by the Tathāgatas—who are Vajrapāṇis because their hands possess the five cognitions, such as the mirror-like [wisdom] and so forth, through identity with those infinite, non-conceptual blisses that are free from the two extremes;

who are the tamers of the untamable because they bring all conceptual constructions to the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) by means of being the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; and who are therefore heroes established in the meditative absorption of great bliss—[the teaching was given].
Because their bodhicitta is undeviating, they are "heroic" (vīra);

because their form is inexhaustible like space, it is "disgusting" (bībhatsa) and its very nature is great passion (mahārāga). Through identity with that [passion], by virtue of being joined with it, they possess the forms of heroes and the disgusting.

Fully awakened and in full bloom,
brandishing the supreme vajra and brandishing the supreme garment.
The elemental space has awakened, O Bhūtvākāśa!
The lotus is said there to be his great primordial wisdom (*mahājñāna*).
The Vajra is the space-yogin.
In *jñāna*, there is no [other] supreme immutable bliss,
[only] that which causes [bliss] to manifest, causing it to shine forth intensely.
O friend, there is no emptiness in pleasure.
Wave upon wave of happiness.
O friend, like a hand.
Among the Tathāgatas, there is no further dispassion.
With their own hands brandishing vajras with flashing tips,
they are supreme in performing the welfare of the world through wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion.
By those who, with their own hands, bestow (*rānti*) that bliss (*kaṃ sukhaṃ*) which is not known by others,

while brandishing them; they are those whose tips (*koṭi*)— the foremost parts of the *vajra*, which is the locus of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)— are quivering and blossoming due to the seminal essence (*śukra*) of great bliss having reached the pericarp of the *vajra-lotus*.

Wisdom is the non-conceptual form of all phenomena; having abandoned this *karmamudrā* which is defiled in heart and imagined, one should meditate upon the *divyamudrā*— the mother of the supreme Victors of perfect enlightenment, the stainless, unchanging, pervasive, and primordial wisdom-light that is equal to space, accessible through yoga, immovable, the remover of the stains of existence, and permeated by the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*).

Thus, that very Great Compassion is practiced by him as a means; having the nature of great bliss, it performs the welfare of the world through its characteristic of radiating as the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*).
Therefore, they are "supreme" because they transcend the world by means of wisdom, skillful means, great compassion, and the performance of the world's welfare.
With those who were joyful, contented, delighted, and appearing in forms of wrathful bodies;
