Together with the Protectors who perform the deeds of a Buddha, their bodies bowed in prostration.

"Joyful" (*hṛṣṭa*) means joyful through immediate pleasure; "satisfied" (*tuṣṭa*) means satisfied through subsequent pleasure. "Intentions" (*āśaya*) refers to those whose intentions consist of the innate body (*sahajakāya*), which has become unified with body, speech, and mind. Therefore, they are "joyful and satisfied in their intentions. For this very reason, they are "delighted" (*mudita*) for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings. Through "wrath" (*krodha*), there is the manifestation of the emptiness of all phenomena. Regarding wrath, the *Pīṭhavivṛti* states: "Wrath is the limit of cessation" (*viramaparyanta*). Alternatively, it may mean that wrath is the limit of cessation.

Free from grasping and incapacity, possessing their very form and essential nature, and for that very reason performing the Buddha-activities; through the very radiation of non-conceptual bliss, they possess the capacity to accomplish the welfare of others; together with the Lords, the masters of yoga who are to be served, they have become one, their bodies bowed in prostration, their body, speech, and mind immersed in great bliss.
Having prostrated before the Lord, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Blessed Tathāgata,
he stood before him with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words.
In the *Kālacakra-anu0* [commentary] together with the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, it says "having prostrated":

having prostrated and made manifest the Lord, whose bodhicitta is undecaying, the Perfectly Awakened One, whose bliss is fully awakened; from the center of the forehead wheel (*lalāṭacakra*) of the Blessed One, the gnosis-drop (*jñānabindu*) has gone to the secret calyx (*guhyavaraṭaka*). The gnosis of luminosity arising from that—the Blessed One—having emerged in the form of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) from the calyx of the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) into the opening of the jewel of the vajra, and having been revealed from the jewel-calyx, has likewise returned to the crown wheel as the Tathāgata.
And it is said: "He has come and he has gone, pervading and remaining established throughout the universe."
And because he has brought to cessation both going and coming, he is known as the Tathāgata.

Thus, having joined his palms in reverence and remained without going outside, he— either by means of the power of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) or by effecting a union— experienced this bliss which is to be personally realized; standing before [the deity], through the attainment of meditative absorption (samādhi), he remained within the central cavity of the excellent jewel.
For my benefit, for my sake, and out of compassion for me, O Lord,
may I become one who attains the perfect awakening through the Net of Illusion (Māyājālābhisaṃbodhi).
"For my benefit" means for the sake of my own welfare, which is followed by the experience of bliss within the excellent calyx of a diamond-jewel;
for this very reason, "for my purpose" means for the production of that same bliss for all sentient beings.
My sole purpose is the production of that bliss through its non-differentiation from the nature of suchness;
the address "O Pervasive One" refers to one who, out of compassion, has washed away the false conceptualizations of self and others and whose nature is great bliss, pervading the three worlds.

Through the cessation of the drops (*bindu*) such as the bliss of the sixteen bodies, there occurs the cessation of the limited aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; thus, by means of unattached bliss like a net of illusion (*māyājāla*), there is the perfect awakening to and direct realization of the three worlds. Being the possessor of that [realization], one becomes identical with it. For this very reason, he says: "Just as I become of the nature of union (*yuganaddha*) through the encapsulation of the syllables *A* and *Haṃ*, so may the Perfectly Awakened One proclaim the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. This is the connection.
For the sake of all sentient beings whose minds are agitated by afflictions, so that they may attain the unsurpassed fruit.

"For the benefit of those submerged in the mire of ignorance"—here, "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) refers to the latent tendencies of nescience (*avidyā-vāsanā*); that itself is the "mire" because it is difficult to cross. For the benefit of those submerged therein—for the sake of the radiance of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*)—for those whose minds are agitated by the suffering of afflictions and death, and who are habituated to wandering through the six realms of existence; [the text says] "let it illuminate the unsurpassed, ineffable, naturally luminous Great Bliss as the fruit, for the sake of its attainment. This is the connection with what follows. (8)

May the Fully Awakened One, the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Guru of the World, who knows the reality of the great samaya and is supreme in knowing the faculties and inclinations [of beings], reveal [this].
"May he reveal! [Thus it is said].
He is the "Perfectly Awakened One" (*sambuddha*) because, through the radiance of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), he has realized all phenomena.
"Bhaga" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) endowed with all aspects yet devoid of all forms; by virtue of being joined with that, he is the "Blessed One" (*bhagavān*).

Because he teaches the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths (*śvāsa*) as being non-different from Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), he is the Teacher (*śāstṛ*). For this very reason, he is the Guru of the world—the winds of breath, or body, speech, and mind—and the instructor of reality (*tattva*).

He is the Great Pledge (*mahāsamaya*) and the Fourth Drop (*caturthabindu*); or rather, his reality is that very [Drop]. Thus, he is so called because he knows through identity with that [reality], which is the "knowledge of bliss" (*sukhajñāna*).

One who knows the intention—the pleasure or natural disposition—of the senses, such as the eyes and so forth, which have entered into the state of being the grasped and the grasper, without distinction, is a "knower of the intention of the senses" (*indriyāśayavit*); for this very reason, he is "supreme," transcending the world.
O Blessed One, [I bow] to the one whose body is gnosis, the Great Uṣṇīṣa, the Lord of Speech, Mañjuśrī the Knowledge-Being, the embodiment of gnosis, the Self-Existent. || 10 ||

"Bhagavan, Bhagavan" is the address; the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*) is the fourth body, the holder of sixteen half-and-half drops (*bindu*). Because his bodhicitta-drop has not fallen, it moves upward and reaches the location of the *uṣṇīṣa*; thus he is the Great *Uṣṇīṣa*. "Go" is the sound consisting of six syllables, the letter *E*, which is the nature of the support (*ādhāra*); its Lord is the sixth syllable *Vaṃ*, the Vajradhara, whose intrinsic nature is that which is supported (*ādheya*).

And so he will say: "The great void of five syllables, the void of the bindu of six syllables"—this means having the form of the letters *e* and *vaṃ*. Regarding Mañjuśrījñānasattva: by the convention of *dharmatā*, the word *mañju* refers to the excellent, fully blossomed lotus on the peak of the *vajra*; because that very [lotus] is the support for non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), it is *śrī* (glory). The non-dual gnosis arising from that is [the nature of] Mañjuśrījñānasattva.

Because it dwells in the hearts of all sentient beings, and because it is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*) that arises by itself through its own nature, independent of causes, it exists; it exists directly, thus [it is] "self-arisen" (*svayambhuva*). That gnosis is not created by anyone, nor is it given by anyone; it encompasses all aspects, possesses all forms, and, being unconditioned, is to be personally realized within oneself.
As it has been said: "That which is innate is given by no one, nor has it come from anywhere;
it is known by oneself through merit and service to the Guru during the sacred festivals."
The supreme Nāmasaṅgīti, which possesses profound meaning, noble meaning, great meaning, and is peerless and auspicious; it is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end. (11)

"Profound" means that because it is difficult to fathom for those who have not received the instructions, its meaning— the state of Vajradhara— is profound, as it is to be accomplished through the Mantra Mahāyāna;
and it is "of vast meaning" because, in its innate form (*sahajarūpa*), it is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

Because it is to be accomplished through the Mahāmudrā initiation, it is of "great purpose" (*mahārthā*). Because it is not common to the knowledge of the Śrāvakas and others, it is "unequaled" (*asamā*). Because it is changeless due to its equality with the three times, it is "auspicious" (*śivā*). It is "virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end": the beginning is the knowledge of *ānanda* (joy), the middle is the knowledge of *paramānanda* (supreme joy), and the end is the knowledge of *viramānanda* (cessation joy). It is "virtuous" (*kalyāṇī*) because its form is the innate knowledge (*sahajajñāna*), and for that very reason, its nature is the non-perception of the three supreme joys. Thus it has been said: "Bliss is knowledge; knowledge is the form. O Lord of Secrets, one should worship the form. One should worship the joints (*parvan*) together with the drop of nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*). By means of the division of the three joys, one should characterize the fourth by that [non-perception], because of the non-perception of the three. Therefore it is called 'innate' (*sahaja*). Everything attains auspiciousness through the illumination of the sun upon the lotus. Such is the detailed explanation. The name of the bliss of innate joy, which has the aspect of great bliss as characterized in various tantras, is the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. The connection is with what will be said: "I shall maintain it in its innate form; I shall effect the state of non-duality. "That which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, and those of the future will indeed speak it, and the perfectly awakened ones of the present speak it again and again in this [Nāmasaṅgīti]. Regarding "by the past ones": that *Nāmasaṅgīti* which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past who were endowed with hearing and reflection.

Those [teachings] attained in the form of echoes, which have not yet arrived but will be spoken at the ultimate limit of the excellence of cultivation, will be realized in that very same way; and those present ones, current and engaged in the yoga of cultivation, speak and realize in that very same way. By this, it is also indicated that the Mantra Mahāyāna was taught by all the Tathāgatas, because it has been taught by all of them with regard to fortunate beings. That which is celebrated here in the *Māyājāla-mahātantra* by the Great Vajradharas, the immeasurable holders of mantra who are joyful, is called the *Māyājāla*. "Māyājāla" refers to the *Māyājālābhisambodhi-lakṣaṇa* (the characteristic of awakening through the net of illusion). It is called a *tantra* because it is extended and explained. It is a *Mahātantra* because it is both great and a *tantra*; the meaning is the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*). And it is said: "A *tantra* is declared to be a continuous sequence; *saṃsāra* is intended as a *tantra*; a *tantra* is the secret known as the mystery; the *uttara-tantra* is so called. The *Nāmasaṅgīti*, which is thus celebrated, is understood by the Great Vajradharas themselves—the holders of the great mantra who consist of the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), who hold the bliss consisting of the five gnoses, who are immeasurable, beyond the sphere of conceptual construction, joyful, and of the nature of the co-emergent (*sahaja*). "I, with firm resolve, shall uphold this until final liberation (*niryāṇa*), O Lord, so that I may become a holder of the secrets of all the Perfect Buddhas. Because it has been obtained, they speak of it as having departed like an echo, and as being taught in the present. "O you who delight in the *Māyājāla-mahātantra*, there is for you no departure. This is the *Ārya-Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*. "I" (referring to myself) shall uphold this; the meaning is that I shall effect a state of non-duality (*advayībhāva*). For how long? Until final liberation. That is to say, until I become a lord of the twelve stages (*dvādaśabhūmīśvara*) by attaining the state of the sixteen hundred breath-syllables free from duality. One whose resolve is firm, solid, unchanging, and whose nature is bliss is described thus. "I," as defined above, "shall reveal" that which is the secret of all Buddhas—the supreme immutable fourth drop (*paramākṣara-caturthabindu*)—"to beings according to their specific dispositions, for the destruction of all afflictions without exception, and for the removal of all ignorance without exception. Thus, having become a holder of the drop, I shall reveal it to fortunate beings according to their specific dispositions and innate nature; let it be revealed accordingly. This is the connection with what precedes. "For the destruction of all afflictions" means for the shattering of all suffering of transmigration; "for the removal of all ignorance" means for the striking down of the latencies of conceptual construction. Having thus requested the Tathāgata, Guhyendra Vajrapāṇi, with palms joined and body bowed, stood before him. These are the sixteen verses of request. "Thus" (*evam*) means having made the Tathāgata—who is of the nature of the syllable *Evam* and is the expounder—the object of the request. "Guhyendra" means one who has obtained mastery over body, speech, and mind. "Bowed body" means one whose body, speech, and mind are immersed in the co-emergent. Furthermore, because the request was made with sixteen verses purified by the sixteen years residing in the *avadhūtī*, these are the sixteen verses of request. "O Sage, you shall reveal the drop of the Perfect Buddhas... for the removal of ignorance... The Tathāgata, the expounder, gives the reply: Then the Blessed Śākyamuni, the Perfect Buddha, the best of bipeds, extending his own broad and beautiful tongue from his mouth, spoke.

Immediately following the request, he provides the response in six verses, beginning with "atha" (now). Since those who have awakened for the sake of sentient beings are inconceivable to ordinary people, their teaching and so forth are not contradictory.

Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Awakened One, is Mahāvairocana, the Holder of the Vajra, as stated in the *Śrī-Ṛgibhara-llimahātantra*: "O King Śuddhodana, the Bhaga has been revealed; therein Ṛgi is Mahāmāyā. The world consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*); Vajrasattva is Siddhārtha, the supreme bliss, the great happiness. Thus, Mahāmudrā is the Great Wisdom. Through union with her, he is called the Blessed One (*Bhagavān*). As stated in the *Śrī-hevajra*: "The Bhaga is declared to be the 'breaker' (*bhañjana*), because it breaks the afflictions (*kleśa*), the Māras, and so forth. Those afflictions are bound by wisdom; therefore, wisdom is called Bhaga. Because of the realization of the Gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) within the six wheels beginning with the Uṣṇīṣa, he is the Fully Awakened One (*Saṃbuddha*). By means of the two feet—the two types of knowledge, conventional and ultimate—he is the best, the most excellent among bipeds, the "Supreme among Bipeds" (*Dvipadottama*). Alternatively, by means of the two feet—the non-abiding and abiding [realizations] at the peak of the Vajra-jewel and the Uṣṇīṣa—he is the Supreme, the Lord of the twelve stages (*bhūmi*).

As it is said in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Having bowed my head to the Lord, who is honored by the three worlds, I shall always place one foot upon the vajra-jewel in the sun (rajas) and the second upon the uṣṇīṣa-semen in the moon; [thus] it is desired as uncuttable and indivisible."

Having thus determined and stabilized one’s own tongue— which is of the nature of the *anāhata*, the long and infinitely pervasive *jñānāvadhūtī* that extends throughout endless world-systems, appearing as a black line and manifesting within its interior countless *saṃbhogakāyas* of immeasurable radiance—
one should [draw it] from one’s own mouth, which is the universal image (*viśvabimba*), in this very manner of expansion.

And so it has been said in the *Bṛhadādibuddha*: "Smoke, a mirage, a firefly, a lamp-flame, and the suns; darkness, the digit (kalā), the great bindu, and the reflection of the universe—therefore [one perceives] that auspicious [form] which bestows innate bliss. (1)
Luminous.
Thus ends the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*. Having displayed a smile that purifies the three lower realms for the worlds, it brings light to the three worlds and subdues the four Māras. (2)

Having visualized and expanded the light of the innate Caṇḍālī, which is the manifestation of the smile, it is the purifier that cleanses the three lower realms; it is the purifier by producing the state of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) through the transformation of the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind—namely, the joys of worldly existence (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), and the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*).

It causes the appearance of the three worlds through *āloka* (light), and its characteristic is the absence of appearances (*nirābhāsa*), because the perception of light and the light itself are non-apparent.

Having attained the state of non-conceptual form, which is the subduer of the four Māras and resides within the excellent jewel-pavilion, it is therefore said: "The Vajra-casket is within; the thief is great and sinful; one should meditate upon the crushing of all Māras in the Great Bliss."
Thus,
with her sweet voice, which filled the three worlds, she spoke these words of Brahmā.
He replied to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, who possesses great power: ||3||

"Having filled," that is, pervaded, the "three worlds"—characterized by body, speech, and mind—with his own voice: self-arisen (*svayaṃbhū*), consisting of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*); sweet, consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). He replied—that is, he experienced—Guhyendra, who possesses the great power of the gnosis of innate joy (*sahajānanda*) and the capacity to render all winds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) devoid of appearance. || 3 ||
Excellent, O glorious Vajradhara! Excellent to you, O Vajrapāṇi, who, endowed with great compassion, act for the benefit of the world. (4)
"Excellent, Vajradhara!"—

the word "excellent" is used because he acts for the benefit of the world; "Vajradhara" refers to the illustrious one previously mentioned, who, by virtue of being the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), extends as far as the realm of space.

Excellent! May it be well with you, O noble one, you who—out of great compassion that flows effortlessly for the sake of the world’s welfare, as previously described—are endowed with the wind of conceptualization for the purpose of bringing about happiness for the world. (4)
Together with the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, you are now prepared to hear from me the *Mañjuśrījñānakāya*. || 5 ||

"Of great significance" (*mahārthā*) means that it is of great significance because its non-conceptual bliss is great bliss; it possesses the true meaning. The *Nāmasaṅgīti* is pure because its essence is the experience of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) and it is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It is purifying because it destroys the density [of afflictions] through the departure of worldly ignorance, or because it is pure by virtue of having the nature of innate freedom from obscuration, which is the supramundane example for non-falling away from conceptualization.
I, from the Body of Gnosis, have set out and am engaged in the endeavor to hear and realize [it]. || 5 ||
"Therefore, please teach this well; I am your disciple, O Lord of Guhyakas.
Listen with a one-pointed mind. "Very well, Blessed One," he replied. (6)
Thus are the six verses of response;
"it is well for you" refers to that which is proclaimed as Sahajānanda and so forth.
I teach and I reveal:
with a one-pointed mind and non-conceptual intellect, listen to the experience of the bliss of the space within the central pericarp of the channels in the six wheels, beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa*. 6.
The response by the Illuminator consists of six verses; thus, there are six verses of response. (2)
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, together with the Kaṇikā, surveyed the six families, the entire great family of mantras,
the family of mantra-vidyādharas, and the three families.
Immediately following the response, he speaks of the observation of the six families: "Then," and so forth;
the connection with what follows is that "the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke this verse.

The entire family of mantras is the Mantra Mahāyāna, and that [family] consists of the Tathāgatas such as Vajrasattva within the six cakras. Because it is a refuge for the mind (*manasa*), the mantra is declared to be bliss (*sukha*).
Because it is non-dual, it is the *kula*.

And by the word "Great" (*mahat*), he describes the arrangement of this very [reality] according to the sequence of the six chakras: the *bodhicitta* residing in the pericarp of the six chakras, all-pervasive, having attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhūta*) with all phenomena, self-cognizable, and of the nature of primordial reality (*prakṛti*). The *Kula of the Mantra-Vidyādhara* is Akṣobhya, whose nature is vajra-consciousness, because he wears the garment of the form of seminal essence (*śukra*) which is immovable bliss.
The meaning is that its range is hidden within the pericarp of the lotus situated inside the excellent jewel (*maṇi*).
"Illumination of the mantra" means that which produces the light of the innate (*sahaja*); there is also a reading: "mantra is secret speech."

Therefore, he is called a *mantravidyādhara* because he maintains the *vidyā*—which takes the form of the sovereign of the entire mandala—through its radiation; the meaning is that he himself beholds and experiences it.

"The three families" refers to the wheels of body, speech, and mind. Thus, Vairocana, whose nature is the non-vajra (*avajra*), abides in the navel wheel as the father of the body, the seed-drop (*bindu*) situated within the channel of the pericarp. || 1 ||
The worldly and supramundane family, the great family that illuminates the world, the supreme Mahāmudrā family, and the great Mahoṣṇīṣa family. ||2||
Thus, regarding these two verses on the observation of the six families,
the term "worldly" (*loka*) in the phrase "worldly and supramundane families" refers to body, speech, and mind.
Beyond that is the Wheel of Dharma; therein resides Amitābha, characterized by great bliss (*mahāsukha*), whose intrinsic nature is the designation "the co-emergent" (*sahaja*).
"The Great Family of the Illuminator of the World" (*lokālokakula*) means that the world consists of the worlds and so forth.

Their light is *prabhāsvara* (luminosity); its family (*kula*) is the location situated in the throat-cakra, which has the nature of a jewel. Because it experiences great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it has the nature of the sensation of silk (*vastra*).

Its greatness consists in non-duality due to the flow of the *bodhicitta* within the pericarp of the five cakras; thus, the family of Mahāmudrā is the "unfailing" (*amoghasiddhi*). He is situated in the forehead-cakra, having the nature of self-awareness and the nature of the vajra-conditioning (*vajrasaṃskāra*).

"The great family of Mahoṣṇīṣa" refers to Vajrasattva, who is established in the Uṣṇīṣa-cakra. Because he is of the nature of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), his intrinsic nature is that of the coemergent (*sahaja*). And it is said in the *Śrī Kālacakra*: "The semen (*śukra*) of unfluctuating bliss is the *vajra*; because he holds that, he is the "Bearer of the Vajra" (*vajradhṛk*). The seed of the body is the semen; 'Jinajik' is the Father, the bliss which is at the navel-cakra. That which is the object of perception (*lakṣya*) being perceived in the heart is supreme bliss; the Lord is *Ārolika* himself, by whom that is to be known. That which is held in the throat as immovable bliss is the experiencer; he is the "Bearer of the Jewel" (*ratnadhṛk*)."

He who holds wisdom—that which is held upon the head in this tantra—is the bliss of the purity of semen; the unchanging supreme bliss at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), full of the sixteen joys.

That wisdom which is without intrinsic nature, the sixteenth digit of the supreme moon at the end of the full moon, she who is infinite—she who is his knowledge upon the head, he is the sixth Vajrasattva in the *vajra*. (2)

The two verses on the observation of the six families demonstrate that the six families, through the purification of the relative and ultimate truths, are established as non-dual gnosis within the six cakras; thus, these are the two verses on the observation of the six families. || 3 ||

In the *Māyājālābhisambodhi*, the Lord of Speech spoke this verse concerning non-dual compassion, which possesses the nature of non-arising and is joined with these six mantra-kings: 1. Māyājālābhisambodhiḥ imāṃ ṣaṇmantrarājānaṃ saṃyuktām advayodayām anutpādadharmiṇīṃ gāthāṃ bhāṣate sma girāṃpatiḥ.
Now, with three verses, he explains the sequence of the awakening through the *Māyājāla*: "This" (*imām*), etc.

Although there are two stanzas, the word "stanza" (*gāthām*) is used in the singular to demonstrate that the *āli*, which consists of the digit of the *bodhicitta*, is the primary object to be accomplished; thus, it is said to be "conjoined with the six kings of mantras."

In the Mantra system (*mantranīti*), [the state] endowed with the six mantras beginning with *oṃ vajratīkṣṇa* is non-dual—the non-duality of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*) inseparable from emptiness and compassion, which arises from meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and has the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

In the Pāramitā system, however, it is the mind whose essence is the *svābhāvikakāya*, consisting of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*) and devoid of all mental fluctuations such as "self" and "mine," or "grasped" and "grasper. It is called "the arising of non-duality" (*advayodayā*) because it emerges by way of its object.
It is called the "Jewel of Non-arising" because non-arising phenomena exist within it as its objects of expression.

Furthermore, that nature of non-arising is established through reasoning and certainty; for instance: "The cause of that non-dual gnosis, which is the fruit, is precisely the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), because anything else, by its very nature of error, is a cause of *saṃsāra*.
And that knowledge of reality is of the nature of non-arising, as taught in the Pāramitāyāna and the Mantra Mahāyāna through the relationship of cause and fruit."

This is declared as it has come down through the lineage of the Guru’s instructions: "The Middle Way wisdom is neither real, nor unreal, nor both, nor neither; it is ineffable and consists of the excellence of all forms.

The Victor, the Teacher, is that very [wisdom]; she is also the reality of the stable and moving world. Victorious is the Goddess Svasaṃvitti (Self-Awareness), who is devoted to the garment of bliss. Thus, it is established that "Middle Way wisdom" (*madhyamakadhī*) is indeed the Middle Way itself, the path to enlightenment.
The Middle Way wisdom (*madhyamaka-dhī*) is the intellect of all Mahāyāna followers that does not abide in the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
That wisdom is neither true, nor false, nor both, nor neither;
for it has as its object and aspect a nature free from the four extremes, because its very nature is free from the four extremes.
Indeed, whatever makes something its object takes on the form of that object, just as the cognition of blue takes on the form of blue.
For this very reason, it is "without description," because every description whatsoever necessarily relies upon the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).

Now, if the Middle Way wisdom (*madhyamaka-dhī*)—the intellect that does not rest upon the two extremes of existence and non-existence—is indeed such, then how does a bodhisattva fulfill all the accumulations for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), such as generosity and ethical discipline, in every aspect? Furthermore, if the bodhisattva realizes those [accumulations] by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and if the Middle Way wisdom is itself of the nature of intrinsic nature, yet that [wisdom] is not of the nature of an entity while generosity and the others are of the nature of entities because they possess the property of becoming (*bhavanadharmakatā*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Consisting of the excellence of all forms. This means that the excellence of all forms consists of generosity and the other perfections; "consisting of that" (*tanmayī*) means having that as its intrinsic nature.
This is the meaning: even [virtues] such as generosity (*dāna*), being non-abiding in the form of existence or non-existence, have the very nature of Madhyamaka wisdom.
For instance, generosity and the others consist of both existence and non-existence because they are not subject to arising in the form of being or non-being;
furthermore, this is because all things characterized by coming into being are dependent upon causes.
Nor is the seed and so forth, which is considered the cause, [the cause];

for it does not become the cause when already ceased, nor when unceased, nor do entities possessing the nature of coming into being arise without a cause, because that would entail the absurdity of everything arising at all times and in all places due to the impossibility of any restriction regarding place and time.
Thus, giving and the other perfections are neither entities nor non-entities.

For instance, how could those things that never at any time exist as positive entities (*bhāva*) by their own nature become non-existent (*abhāva*), given that non-existence consists in the cessation of existence? Therefore,

whether they be qualities to be adopted such as generosity and the like, or qualities to be abandoned such as passion and the like, or even their results— namely, specific or non-specific bodies, enjoyments, and dwellings— all these phenomena are established neither in existence nor in non-existence.
However, the conceptual construction of existence and so forth regarding those [objects] is their unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Therefore, it remains established that the Middle Way wisdom, which consists of the excellence of all forms, is non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Now, it is said how one practicing these very [perfections] such as generosity, while adhering to this very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and intent upon the welfare of sentient beings, may swiftly accomplish the purification of the external and internal through the yoga of the deity: The Blessed Lady Nairātmyā—the wisdom of the Middle Way—is the intellect whose nature is the primordial vowel (*ādisvara*), abiding in the space between the lower goddess Bhava and the upper goddess Nirvāṇa. She is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both, nor neither; she is the utterly pure form of the *adhidharmadhātu*. This is because, by virtue of being the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), her essential nature consists of all phenomena liberated from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*).
She consists of the excellence of all forms; she is the excellence of all forms. The four goddesses have the nature of the pure aggregates (*skandha*) such as form and so forth;

the four goddesses have the nature of the perfectly pure elements such as earth and so forth; the four goddesses have the nature of the perfectly pure sense objects such as form and so forth. She consists of these—that is, she has their nature—because the wisdom of the Middle Way is the nature of all of them, being free from the four extremes.

That Blessed Lady is without delineation (*nirullekhā*), being the nature of the unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*) of all sentient beings regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth. Precisely by cutting off all delineations, she gives rise to the ego-identity (*ahaṅkāra*) of the perfectly pure aggregates, elements, and sense-bases in the form of the deity, thereby removing the ego-identity of the ordinary aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. It is explained how one should abide in the non-conceptual yoga of the deity: "The mind that does not dwell in either cyclic existence or nirvāṇa is the Middle Way wisdom. That very [wisdom] is the Blessed Lady, free from eternalism and nihilism, consisting of mere appearance (*ābhāsamātra*), devoid of subject and object, who is called *avadhūtī*.

That very intellect (*dhī*) has the nature of the primordial vowel (*ādisvara*), because it realizes the threefold world (*tridhātu*)—which is by nature unarisen—as being of a single flavor (*samarasībhāva*). That Blessed Lady is liberated from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭimuktā*), because, as before, she does not abide in the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

She consists of the excellence of all forms (*sarvākṛtivaramayī*), because she radiates all excellent forms, such as the four goddesses who have the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, which are themselves liberated from the four extremes.
And thus it is said in the *Siddhas*: "Together with the entire retinue, [she is] the *veṭila*, the *nāca*, the *cīā*, and the *rāareṃ*."
By this it is meant: the circle of Yoginīs exists exactly as it is; only adventitious ignorance is to be removed.
"The Jina, the Teacher, she herself"—this describes the fruit of the Pāramitā-naya.
"She who is fond of the garment of bliss"—she is also the reality of the moving and unmoving world according to the Mantra-naya; thus she belongs to both systems.

"Self-cognition" (*svasaṃvitti*) means that which has its own cognition or experience; such is [the name] *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*. It is the supreme intention, that Middle Way wisdom which is neither spoken by a teacher nor produced, but is experienced by oneself alone.
Self-arisen gnosis is inconceivable gnosis. || 1 ||
A Ā I Ī U Ū E AI O AU AṂ AḤ—abiding in the heart, I am the embodiment of wisdom, awakened as the Buddhas who exist throughout the three times. (2)
Oṃ, homage to you, Arapacana, the Lord of Speech, the embodiment of the wisdom-knowledge that cuts through suffering with the vajra-sharp sword, the body of gnosis. ||3||
Thus are the three verses on the sequence of awakening through the *Māyājāla*: "A Ā.
Here, only twelve vowels beginning with 'A' are taught, because the four beginning with 'Ṛ' are excluded due to their neuter nature.

It pervades the body through the twelve locations, such as the *pīṭha* and *upapīṭha*, because it consists of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—the twelve syllables beginning with *a* and the twelve digits (*kalā*) that indicate the digits of the *bodhicitta*.
As it has been said: "In the letter *a* is the designation of the *pīṭha*; in the letter *ā* is the *upapīṭha*.

In the letter *i* is the name of the *kṣetra*, and in the letter *ī* is the *upakṣetra*. By the letter *u* is the *chandoha*, and by the letter *ū* is the *upacchandoha*. In the letter *e* is the *melāpaka*, and in the letter *ai* is the *upamelāpaka*. In the letter *o* is the *śmaśāna*, and in the letter *au* is the *upaśmaśāna*."
"Pīlava in Aṃkāra, and Upapīlaka in Akāra.

Thus, by the cessation of three thousand six hundred breaths in each of the six secret cakras, one attains the mastery of the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) through the union of pairs of stages, indicated by the manifestation of great bliss in the form of the six syllables beginning with *A*, which function as a "seal" (*sampuṭa*).
These stages are known as: Samantaprabhā, Amitaprabhā, Gaganaprabhā, Vajraprabhā, Ratnaprabhā, Padmaprabhā, Karmaprabhā, Anupamā, Nirupamā, Prajñāprabhā, Sarvajñatā, and Pratyātmavedyā.

Alternatively, the triad *a*, *i*, and *u* is bliss (*ānanda*) by virtue of the non-duality of body, speech, and mind. The triad *ā*, *ī*, and *ū* is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) due to its dual nature.
The triad *e*, *o*, and *aṃ* is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), consisting of both vowels and possessing three garments.
The triad *ai*, *o*, and *aḥ* is inseparable from the cloth; the fourth is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
By this, the Blessed One, whose nature consists of the four joys and whose form is non-arising (*anutpāda*), is explained.

*Oṃ*: because of the single fusion (*ekalolībhāva*) of vajra body, speech, and mind, it is *oṃ*; that very [fusion] is the vajra, which is innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*). By means of that, he is "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*), the one who withdraws all winds of conceptual construction.
And he, situated within the excellent jewel (maṇivaraṭaka), is motionless and unshakeable because, as the vajra-body of all Tathāgatas, he is free from the suffering of death.
Vairocana, who abides at the navel, is the severer of suffering.
Amitābha, who resides in the heart, is "one whose form and body are wisdom and gnosis" (prajñājñānamūrti).
Knowledge itself, which is the mind of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is the body because it is of the nature of accumulation; he who possesses this is Ratnasambhava, the wheel-turner of the throat.
Speech, consisting of vowels and consonants, is the sovereign of which; its unstruck (*anāhata*) nature is Amoghasiddhi, the wheel-turner of the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft.
He for whom there is the manifestation of the five [families] through the two spokes of wisdom and means is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, Vajrasattva.

Thus, "Salutation to you," who possess the nature of the Six Chakravartins, because of your own direct manifestation of the gnosis of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); this is the reflective realization (*parāmarṣa*) through [the process of] transformation.
In this way, the fourth [body], the Gnosis-Vajra (*jñānavajra*), which is innate bliss, remains pervading the universe in both external and internal forms.

That very [Gnosis-Vajra], consisting of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), abiding within the centers of the navel and so forth, is said to be situated in the heart.

And it is said: "That which is the body of all Buddhas, free from appearance and stainless, unknown, uncreated, pure, and devoid of non-existence and the like; just as a reflection in a mirror, complete with all its limbs, appears as a form most translucent, so too, O God, is the body of the Vajra-holder, enriched with the eighty minor marks and the [thirty-two] major signs. Just as a rainbow seen in the sky displays various colors through the auspicious karma of the world, so too does the body, though pervaded by garments of black and other colors, truly accomplish its activity without deficiency. (2-3)

( *Svādhiṣṭhānaprabheda*, verses 54–55) It is so called because, through these three verses which summarize the great yoga (*mahāyoga*) consisting of the essential nature of body, speech, and mind, they indicate the previously mentioned sequence of awakening according to the *Māyājāla*. 4.
The Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu is as follows: The Blessed Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is born from the syllable A;
the syllable A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the supreme syllable. (1)

Now, by way of the mandala of the Vajra Realm (vajradhātumaṇḍala), which is the wheel of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases free from obscuration, he describes the radiation of the Bodhicitta-vajra—the holder of the illusion of the immutable drop (bindu) in all its forms—through all modes.
Thus: because he possesses the non-dual form of Mahāmudrā, he is the Blessed One (bhagavān); because he possesses the intellect (*buddhi*) of innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*), he is the Buddha;
and because he abides as semen within the excellent jewel (maṇivaraṭaka) and is eternally awakened speech, he is the Perfectly Awakened One (sambuddha).

Here, by the syllable *A*, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*)—which is naturally luminous, whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), and which is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—is expressed. She transcends the nature of atoms, is like a reflection in a mirror, and from her arises [the syllable]. Thus, the Perfectly Awakened One arising from the syllable *A* is Vajrasattva, whose essence is wisdom and method; he is called the "neuter state" and the "innate body" (*sahajakāya*).

Furthermore, that syllable *A* is the source of all phonemes because it is unstruck (*anāhata*); due to its being free from obscuration, it is the state of total integration (*ekalolībhāva*) of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and objects.
And it is said: "The supreme Lord, the imperishable, most subtle, and great light, blazing like a lamp within the heart at the center of the *anāhata*."
Mahāmudrā resides at the navel, holding a blazing lamp-flame;
she is of the nature of the primordial vowel (A) and is proclaimed as *dhīti*, the intelligence of the Buddha.
Thus, because she bestows all the qualities of a Buddha, she is of great significance (*mahārtha*).
Therefore, the supreme syllable is devoid of arising and cessation. || 1 ||
For it is the Great Vital Breath, indeed non-arising, devoid of verbal expression; it is the foremost cause of all discourse, and all speech is its radiant clarity. || 2 ||

"Mahāprāṇa" means that, through the radiation of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) or by way of the natural state (*prakṛtidharma*), because there is no movement of the ten mandalas through the left and right nostrils, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has entered the *avadhūtī*; thus, he is Mahāprāṇa— the reflection-body of Vajradhara, meaning his body is like an illusion (*māyopama*).
Therefore, non-arising (*anutpāda*) consists of non-conceptual and objectless knowledge;
for the word "hi" (because) has the sense of a reason or an emphasis, and there is also a reading of "pravyāhāraḥ" (utterance).

Because it is devoid of that [duality], it is free from the utterance and articulation of speech; because it pervades all things by way of being neither masculine nor feminine, it takes the form of the wind entering into all configurations.

Because it is the cause for grasping all expressions consisting of vowels and consonants, it is the source of all expression. Since those [expressions] arise from the mantra of the bodhicitta, which is non-different from ultimate emptiness and compassion, that Blessed One himself is the support for all cognitions of apprehension; thus, the meaning is that his nature is the experience of the bliss of the Middle Way.
Because he realizes all speech through its luminosity, he is the supreme syllable, the nature of the letter *A*, whose speech is perfectly radiant. || 2 ||
The great passion for the vast earth, the great hatred for the vast [world], he who brings delight to all sentient beings, the great enemy of all afflictions. ||3||
"Mahāmahā" means "great";
"mahā" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), and "mahāmudrā" is that which is great; he who possesses that is thus [described].
He whose passion (*rāga*) is great—[a passion] consisting of non-referential compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*)—is likewise [described].
Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound: he whose great festival (*maha*), which transcends the world, is a great joy (*mahotsava*)— that is, his natural radiance—

and who is such a one of "great passion" (*mahārāga*), is Vajrānaṅga, meaning Vajrasattva, because of the fullness of "supreme unchanging bliss" (*paramākṣarasukha*) and because of having filled the stages (*bhūmi*).
For this very reason, he who brings joy to all sentient beings is "Greatly Venerated" (Mahāmaha), as before;
[he] is Great Hatred (Mahādveṣa), Akṣobhya.

He is the slayer of the great enemy—the twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations of all the afflictions—and he is "immovable" (acala) by virtue of being the experiencer of great bliss; such is the meaning. || 3 ||
The great festival of great delusion, the great festival, the great wrath, the one of deluded intellect, the destroyer of the great light, the great enemy of great anger.
"Mahāmaha, mahāmoha,
mahāmaha"— this has been explained;
it is called *mahāmoha* because it transcends delusion (*moha*).

For this very reason, he is "the Destroyer of Delusion" (*mohasūdana*): one whose intellect is non-conceptual and thus deluded, yet who destroys—that is, consumes—the delusion that is the emission of semen;
he is "Great Wrath" (*mahākrodha*) because he shatters all conceptual constructions and afflictions.
Because he has transcended anger, he is Mahākrodha; he is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) that is the cessation of the joy of withdrawal (*viramānanda*).
He is the great enemy of Mahākrodha because he unifies the vajras of body, speech, and mind into one. || 4 ||
The great festival, possessing great greed, the destroyer of all greed;
he is great desire, great bliss, great joy, and great delight. || 5 ||
"Great festival,

great greed" means that because he transcends the greed for death, it is a "great festival"; and because he does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings through skillful means, it is "great greed."

The meaning is that he is the destroyer of all greed and the destroyer of the perishable limbs of pleasure; [thus ends] the *Paramākṣara-āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*. Regarding "Mahākāma": according to the view of some, because of reaching the ultimate limit of the excellence of desire for the Sahaja-body, he is Mahākāma at the root of the jewel in the *ūrṇā*-lotus; the meaning is that he is the bliss of the body (*kāyānanda*).
In that very place, in that very manner, by virtue of the desire for innate speech (*sahaja-vāk*), there is great bliss; the meaning is that its intrinsic nature is the bliss of speech.
Likewise, in that very place, in that very manner, by virtue of the desire for innate mind (*sahaja-citta*), there is great joy; the meaning is that it is the bliss of mind.

He who possesses great delight is "Great Delight" (*mahārati*); likewise, in that very place, in that very manner, by virtue of the desire for innate gnosis (*sahaja-jñāna*), it is the bliss of gnosis.

By means of the destruction of the waking state (*jāgrad-avasthā*), the four divisions of the bliss of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) have been shown; and it is said: "This non-conceptual great bliss is the bliss characterized by longing, comparable to the threshold at the door of the house of happiness."
"Oh, what happiness! What great happiness! Oh, how, how can I enjoy it?"—such is the supreme longing of the mind; that bliss is as if the foremost [of all joys]. Thus [it is said]. (5)
Of great form, of great body, of great color,
of great physique, of great name, of great nobility, and of a very vast mandala.
(6) "Of great form" means:
Now the divisions of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) are shown.

Regarding that, "of great form" (*mahārūpa*): according to the opinion of some, it refers to one whose "great form" is within the heart—that is, within the jewel (*maṇi*)—and who consists of the manifold conceptualization of bliss;
this is because, by virtue of being the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he possesses the form of the consecration as the Dharma King who pervades the realms of existence (*dhātu*).
For this very reason, he has a "great body" (*mahākāya*) because, through its luminosity, it is the *saṃbhogakāya*.
By these two words, the supreme bliss of the body (*kāyaparamānanda*) is described;
and because it brings light to the *saṃbhoga*, it has a "great color" (*mahāvarṇa*), meaning it possesses a supramundane color.
The meaning is that his great body is a manifestation due to its intrinsic luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*).
By these two words, the supreme bliss of speech (*vākparamānanda*) is expressed;
because it transcends even the mere name due to its supreme secret nature, he is "Great-Name" (*Mahānāman*); and because of the vastness of his bliss, he is "Greatly Generous" (*Mahodāra*).
And by these two words, the supreme bliss of the mind (*cittaparamānanda*) is expressed;
because he takes (*lāti*) the vast (*mahāvipula*),
extensive (*vistīrṇa*), essential (*maṇḍa*), and blissful (*sukha*) essence (*sāra*), he is the "One of the Great Vast Mandala" (*Mahāvipulamaṇḍala*).
Because it pervades the world through the bliss that is luminous like an illusion, this is "the supreme bliss of gnosis" (*jñāna-paramānanda*);

thus, by the destruction of the dream state, the four supreme blisses of the *saṃbhogakāya* are described. And it is said: "By crushing [all things] through the emptiness that consists in the removal of the superimposition of conceptualization regarding entities."
"Consisting of the nature of the union with the absence of intrinsic existence, its form is supreme bliss. Thus [it is said]. (6)
He who wields the great weapon of knowledge, the foremost leader with the great hook that subdues the afflictions, possessed of great glory, great fame, great light, and great splendor. ||7||

Accompanied by the *amṛtakaṇikā* (drops of nectar), through the exhaustion of the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*), [the nature of the *dharmakāya* arises]. Now, he describes the four divisions of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*) by way of its illusory-like self-mastery (*māyopama-svādhiṣṭhāna*). Regarding "bearing the weapon of great wisdom" (*mahāprajñāyudha*): Great wisdom is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), characterized as the *dharmadhātu*. Its "weapon" is the bliss of cessation of the body (*kāyaviramānanda*). He "bears" this at the tip of the jewel (*maṇiśikhara*) or in the navel-lotus (*nābhyabja*), thus he is the "bearer of the weapon of great wisdom. By this, the bliss of cessation of the body is expressed. The "great afflictions" (*mahākaleśāḥ*) are ordinary passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
Because it serves as a goad for them, it is the "Great Affliction Goad" (*mahākleśāṅkuśa*); and that is the bliss of the cessation of speech (*vāgvirāmānanda*).
For this very reason, it is the foremost, because it has attained the cause of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*);
and it is of great renown because it awakens the world through the sound of the unstruck, innate radiance.
He is of great fame (*mahākīrti*) because he generates joy for all through great bliss;
by these two terms, the mental stage of *viramānanda* (the joy of cessation) is described.
He is the great light (*mahājyotiḥ*) because all phenomena are of the nature of stainless primordial luminosity, which is beyond arising and ceasing.
Because he illuminates the experience of bliss free from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the grasped and the grasper, he is "of great splendor" (*mahādyuti*).
By these two feet, the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) of gnosis is demonstrated.

By this it is meant: that bliss which is perceived at the moment of the antidote to ignorance from the mouth of the Vajra Guru—by means of that very bliss as an illustration resembling a slight shadow [of the ultimate], he is the bearer of the thirty-two marks and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics.
Just as a painted cloth is perceived within a mirror, in that very same way the enjoyment body (*sambhogadeha*), which has a pleasant form, is to be known.
And it is said: "The Teacher, endowed with the thirty-two marks and the Lord possessing the eighty secondary characteristics, resides in the womb of a woman in Sukhāvatī under the name of Śukra."
"Aha! Knowledge! Aha! Knowledge! Aha! This is clearly known!"—thus the mind, intent on such expansion, consists of nothing more than the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*). (7)

The wise one who possesses the great illusion, the accomplisher of the purpose of the great illusion, who delights in the passion for the great illusion, and who is a master of the great illusion and sorcery. || 8 ||

Regarding "Mahāmāyā": because she is devoid of both passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*), Mahāmāyā is the form of Great Passion (*mahārāga*), the divine seal (*divyamudrā*). He who bears that ineffable [seal] through identity with it is "Mahāmāyādhara.

For this very reason, he is "the Knower" (*vidvān*); from the experience of bliss flowing forth from within the excellent jewel-cavity (*maṇivaraṭaka*), the innate joy of the body (*kāyasahajānanda*) is illuminated by this term.

Mahāmāyā is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā); because she accomplishes the welfare of the world through her emanation, she is the "accomplisher of the purpose of Mahāmāyā. By this, the innate bliss of speech is demonstrated. Mahāmāyā is the revealed object; "delight" in her is the experience of innate bliss. The meaning is that one who is delighted therein—immersed in it—becomes unified with great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
By this, the bliss co-emergent with the mind (*cittasahajānanda*) is indicated.

Through the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), which is the illusion of the Buddha’s emanation (*buddhanirmāṇamāyā*), he is a supreme magician (*aindrajālika*), a great master of illusion. By bringing the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths to the state of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣaratva*), and through the sequence of attaining two stages (*bhūmi*) at each wheel (*cakra*), he returns from the peak of the jewel (*vajramaṇiśikhara*) and abides in the pericarp (*varaṭaka*) of the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*). He is the Great Magician of Indra (*mahāmāyendra*), because he dwells non-dually within the space between the jewel and the pericarp of the crown. By this, the Blessed One in the form of the sixteen joys (*ṣoḍaśānanda*) is established.

And so it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The single [unity] of the emanation body, speech, mind, and gnosis; the single [unity] of the enjoyment body, speech, mind, and gnosis; the single [unity] of the glorious dharma body, speech, mind, and gnosis; the single [unity] of the innate body, speech, mind, and gnosis—this is the yoga-vow (*yoga-saṃvara*). Yoga-vow. Yoga-vow. Yoga-vow."

Neither waking, nor dreaming, nor deep sleep, nor the fourth state; not the pleasure born of two organs; not existing in the four stations of knowledge, mind, speech, or body; abandoned by the *karmamudrā* and devoid of the *jñānamudrā*; that which has arisen from the *mahāmudrā* is the innate (*sahaja*), and not with another. Thus, where one shines by oneself, free from the distinction between existence and non-existence, there is the majesty of awakening, consisting of intense bliss, pervading the interior of space.
With its vast and stainless manifestation in various forms, like the shimmering orb of a mirror, that innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), generally the abode of all happiness, is known as the fourth.

May that which is agitated by innate longing within the lotus of the *ūrṇā*, variegated and most excellent as it is coiled upon the bed of manifold conceptualizations in the interior of the heart-lotus; which shines with the destruction of all attachments upon grasping the navel-lotus; and which is auspicious through union with the diamond-lotus—may that tranquil self triumph in the night.
The mind, consisting of mere bliss, spreads forth at the base of the jewel; then again, in the middle of the jewel, it is restless with all its volitions.
Above that, within the peak, it extends something born of the innate nature—tranquil, free from delusion, and seated upon a lotus.
Another alternative view. || 8 ||
The supreme great lord of donors, the foremost upholder of great ethical discipline, the steadfast possessor of great patience, and one whose prowess is great vigor. ||9||

"Accompanied by Amṛtakaṇikā, the Great Lord of Generosity. Great generosity (*mahādāna*) is the relinquishing of all external and internal things, as well as the avoidance of the mind’s conceptual proliferation (*vikalpaprapañca*). He is its lord (*pati*), its master, because he is dependent upon the Blessed One of Innate Bliss (*sahajānanda*);
for this very reason, he is "supreme," since he is not equal to worldly lords of generosity.

Because he maintains the vow (*śīla*)—which is the non-emission of the *bodhicitta* during contact with an external woman—through identity with that [bliss], he is the "Foremost Upholder of the Great Vow" (*mahāśīladhara*), residing within the excellent jewel-pavilion (*maṇivaraṭaka*).
Non-attachment to external sounds and so forth is "great patience" (*mahākṣānti*); one who maintains that is "possessor of great patience" (*mahākṣāntidhara*).
For this very reason, he is "steadfast" (*dhīra*), because his nature is supreme fortitude.
Furthermore, through the dissolution of the ten mandalas in the left and right nostrils, the entry of the vital wind (*vāsavāta*) into the *avadhūtī* is "great heroism" (*mahāvīrya*).
In that context, "one who possesses valor" refers to one whose great exertion is such.
Abiding in the samādhi of great meditative concentration, possessing great power and great skillful means, he maintains a body of great wisdom; he is the ocean of aspiration and knowledge. || 10 ||

"Great meditation" (*mahādhyāna*): the mind that has entered into innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) is "great meditation"; that itself is "concentration" (*samādhi*) because of the absence of external distraction. He is so called because he abides therein by means of the yoga of non-abiding. "Great wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) is the unstruck (*anāhata*), all-pervading, and all-encompassing; she herself is the body, because of the attainment of the body of great enjoyment (*mahāsambhogakāya*) which is like an echo. He is so called because he sustains [reality] through identity with that.

And this meaning was stated by the illustrious Ādibuddha: "Generosity is the renunciation of wealth; discipline is the non-falling away of the mind from attachment to women; patience is the non-entry into [the perception of] sound and so forth; vigor is the destruction of both states of movement, like the wind;

meditation and wisdom are the mind that has attained innate bliss; and [the result] is all-pervading and expressed in all languages. Thus, it is said: "The six-armed Heruka," according to the *Bṛhatkāśmīrapañjikā*.

He who possesses that great non-dual power of knowledge which brings about the destruction of existence and is inseparable from emptiness and compassion is thus [described]. Great means (mahopāya) refers to compassion through the quality of seminal essence (*śukra*), because it is joined with the welfare of the world;

for by directly realizing the collection of phenomena as being without intrinsic nature, and by being established solely in great bliss, he radiates for the sake of the world throughout the duration of *saṃsāra*.

Through the realization that all phenomena are by nature unborn, like an illusion, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas; through the teaching of the Buddha-dharma which is like an echo; and as a source for the ocean of vows, knowledges, and states free from egoism—by this, the four perfections of skillful means, power, aspiration, and knowledge are described.
And it is said: "For the sake of sentient beings, his supernatural power brings about the destruction of existence; the others are the four [perfections] that have attained the unborn."
In this context, "for the sake of sentient beings" refers to skillful means;
"supernatural power" refers to the vow;
and "the destruction of existence" refers to power.

The knowledge that "this is the attainment of the Unborn" constitutes these four perfections; they are distinct from that very perfection itself, meaning they take on a specific form. Otherwise, the composition of the verse is due to its being of sacred (ārṣa) origin. || 10 ||

The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti: Consisting of great loving-kindness, immeasurable, possessing great compassion, supreme in intellect; possessing great wisdom, of great intelligence, possessing great skillful means, and of great form. (11)

"Consisting of great loving-kindness" (*mahāmaitrīmaya*) means that because he radiates the world endowed with supramundane bliss by way of the aspect of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) which is the entire mandala of all objects of knowledge, he consists of great loving-kindness; for this very reason, he is immeasurable (*ameya*).
Because he accomplishes the separation of the world from suffering through his own mastery of constant and uninterrupted great bliss, he is the Great Compassionate One (*mahākāruṇika*);
for this very reason, he possesses supreme intelligence (*agradhī*), due to the experience of great bliss upon the crest of the excellent jewel-pavilion.

"The Māras, afflictions, meditative attainments, and the cognitive obscurations have indeed been incinerated by the Great Wrathful Ones; only the power [of the innate] has been preserved. Thus it is said. One who possesses wisdom (*prajñā*) through identity with the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) by virtue of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] is "wise" (*prājña*). He who is both great and wise is "greatly wise" (*mahāprājña*); the meaning is that he dwells in the heart of the union (*yuganaddha*).
He is "possessed of great majesty" (*mahāśrīmān*) because he does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings, precisely through the form of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

My *upāya* is the Great Form (*mahākṛti*) because it pervades all limbs through the bliss of the movement and departure from the twenty-four locations; for this very reason, it is the knower of the ten states of passion (*kāma-avasthā*),
and the ten states of passion are the forms of the limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), namely the ten signs beginning with smoke (*dhūma*).

And so it is said in the *Śrī Kālacakra*: "Thought, longing, fever in the limbs, the pearl-oyster [of desire] in the lotus of excellent bliss, lack of engagement in other activities, trembling, madness, dizziness, mental delusion, intense fainting, and [the states beginning with] smoke—these ten manifest conditions of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (*vajrin*) arise within the limbs of living beings. In the world, these are manifested as the fixed states of the God of Love (*manmatha*). Who is the Victor (*jina*) and who is Desire (*kāma*)? (11)
Endowed with the power of great supernormal faculties, possessing great speed and great velocity; of great psychic power, of great renown, and of great strength and prowess. || 12 ||

"Great supernatural power" (*mahārddhi*) means that, through the manifestation of the factors of meditative absorption (*samādhy-aṅga*) and by pervading the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths with the essence of the innate bliss of bodhicitta, one is endowed with the power of great supernatural power.
"Great speed" (*mahāvega*) refers to the movement through all the channels (*nāḍī*) by means of the non-emission of bodhicitta.
He possesses great speed because he pervades all limbs through the sequence of contraction and expansion.
He possesses great supernatural power (*mahaddhika*) because he fulfills the mundane and supramundane accumulations of merit and wisdom by means of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
For this very reason, he is called "the Great Lord" (*maheśākhya*).
He is the Lord (*īśa*) because he rules and has power through the awakening to all things as they truly are; he is called Maheśa because his name is "Maheśa," meaning a Great Lord (*mahān īśaḥ*).
This signifies the omniscient wisdom that is inseparable from emptiness and compassion, accompanied by the *amṛtakaṇikā*.

Because it brings even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) and other evil deeds to the singular culmination of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it possesses great power and prowess.

And it has been said: "Even outcastes (*caṇḍāla*), bamboo-workers (*veṇukāra*), and others who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution shall become Buddhas in this very life if they follow the Mantra Vehicle. (12)
The shatterer of the great mountain of existence, the dense wielder of the great vajra;
the great cruel one, the great fierce one, the instiller of fear in those who cause great fear. ||13||

*Mahābhavānī*: "Great Bhava" refers to *bhava*—the afflictions such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth—which is "great" because it is difficult to sever. That very *bhava* is a mountain because it has twenty peaks, namely the [twenty] types of ignorance. She is the "crusher" (*samabhetā*) of that mountain; the meaning is that she has attained the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) through the attainment of correct, non-erroneous knowledge by means of her intense passion (*mahārāgānurāga*). She is so called because she wears the "great garment" characterized by *āloka*, *ālokābhāsa*, *ālokopalabdhi*, and *nirābhāsa*.
For this very reason, he is *ghana* because of his dense bliss;
he is *krūra* (cruel) because the vital winds (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) are difficult to subdue, and because he transcends them, he is *mahākrūra* (greatly cruel).

Because all breaths have been pierced by the great nectar of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), and because he has merged into the singular state of great bliss through the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the objects, senses, and so forth—which otherwise bestow the suffering of saṃsāra—he is *mahāraudra* (greatly fierce).

"Great fear" refers to the fear of falling into either of the two extremes—eternalism or nihilism. He who causes that [fear] to cease is thus called "the dispeller of great fear," which means he is one whose nirvāṇa is non-abiding. || 13 ||
The Lord is the supreme among great vidyās, the Guru is the supreme among great mantras;
he is established in the way of the Mahāyāna, the supreme among those of the Mahāyāna way. || 14 ||
Thus end the fourteen verses of the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu.
Regarding the term *mahāvidyottama*: it is the great vidyā, which is the Mahāmudrā; it is "supreme" (*uttama*) because it is eternally present.
The Lord (nātha) is the Master (svāmī).

He is "supreme" (uttama), meaning faultless, because of his Great Mantra—which is the knowledge of great bliss—and because he possesses that very nature. For this reason, he is the Guru of others, due to his instruction in the knowledge consisting of bliss.

The Mahāyāna is that by which the knowledge of great bliss (*mahāsukhajñāna*) is led to—that is, attained. "The method" (*naya*) means having ascended to the peak of the excellent *vajra* and *padma* calyx; the meaning is that one has reached the form of innate joy (*sahajānanda*). In the system of the Mahāyāna, this refers to the aforementioned supreme limit of the fourth dhyāna. || 14 ||

Thus, by means of the gateway of Śrī Vajrasattva, the presentation of the garment of bodhicitta has been made through these fourteen verses indicating the movement and non-movement at the crown, forehead, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and the tip of the jewel. ||5||
The wisdom of the utterly pure realm of phenomena, the Buddha Mahāvairocana, the Great Sage, the Great Muni;
arisen from the system of the Great Mantra, he is the very essence of the system of the Great Mantra. (1)

Regarding "Mahāvairocana": by the term Mahāvairocana, there is the wisdom that is naturally luminous (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*); because this [wisdom] is great, he is so called, meaning he possesses a body consisting of wisdom (*jñānamayakāya*).
He is a Buddha because of the awakening to great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
He is the Great Silent One (*mahāmaunī*) because he is joined with the silence of body, speech, and mind through the nature of ineffable bliss.
For this very reason, he is the Great Sage (*mahāmuni*) because he correctly contemplates the essential nature of great bliss.
As it is said, "Mantra is declared to be bliss because it is the protection of the mind"; thus, the Great Mantra is none other than the gnosis of great bliss itself.
"Leading" (*naya*) means that one is led or attained; "arisen from that" refers to being arisen from the Great Mantra Way (*mahāmantranaya*).
Although he has arisen from great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is stated that he is "of the nature of the Great Mantra Way" in order to demonstrate that his very essence is great bliss.
For this very reason, it is said—and furthermore stated: "This reality of mantra is manifest as the accomplishment of Vāgvajra."
"One should apply the mind to *cittamātra* by means of the distinction of the three knowledges.
And: "The yogi should abandon external recitation, which is an obstacle to meditative cultivation;
for how could the Blessed One, the Vajrī who is the essence of the vajra, recite the meaning of the mantra?"
And it is said in the *Śrī-buddha*: "The nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of this [reality] is expressed by the word 'full' (*pūrṇa*);
everything else, consisting of other states, is the cause of creation and dissolution. (1)
He has attained the ten perfections; he is the locus of the ten perfections. ||2||

The purity of the ten perfections, the method of the ten perfections, and the ten perfections themselves are as follows: generosity consists in the bestowing of the worldly and supramundane consecrations, beginning with that of water and so forth;
ethical discipline consists in the preservation of the *bodhicitta* during the union of the lotus and the vajra.

"Since all phenomena do not abide anywhere," this is the protection from attachment to all phenomena. "Patience" (*kṣānti*) is so called because it is capable of enduring the dissolution of the eon, being accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*.
"Vigor" (*vīrya*) arises from the exertion toward the manifestation of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
Dhyāna arises from immersion in the fourth dhyāna.
Prajñā is the divine mudrā, obtainable solely from the mouth of the Guru.
Haṭhayoga is also the means (upāya) for the purpose of making the limbs of samādhi manifest.

And such is Haṭhayoga: when the reflected image has been perceived through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs], it arises by means of the imperishable moment (*akṣarakṣaṇa*).

By virtue of the uncontrolled vital breath (*prāṇa*), through the practice based on the cause of sound (*nāda*) and the practice of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), one should, by force (*haṭhena*), cause the vital breath to flow through the central channel (*madhyamā*) by means of the *hūṃ* sound.

Thus, having properly inserted the *bola* (male organ) into the *kakkola* (female organ) of a well-trained, low-caste woman who possesses the qualities described in the Tantras and is full of passion, one should rest without trembling. Then, pressing the vajra-jewel into the opening of her filaments (*kiñjalka*) with the intense flavor of joy, one should not move for a moment. When the ten [drops] are about to flow from those two, preceded by the utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should cause the *bodhicitta*-drop—granted by the grace of the true guru—to manifest; through the experience of the fourth, innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), there is the cessation of the drop, and from that, the attainment of the immutable moment (*akṣarakṣaṇa*).
This is the meaning: the limbs of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) become clearly manifest.

Through the manifestation of the factors of meditative absorption (*samādhy-aṅga*), at the arising of the moment of awakening in a single instant (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi-kṣaṇa*), there is the fulfillment of all aims for oneself and others; this is the *praṇidhi*.
*Bala* is the power of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
*Jñāna* is the gnosis of great bliss, which proceeds from within the central channel of the jewel (*maṇi-varaṭaka*) up to the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣa-cakra*).

"One who has attained the ten perfections" (*daśapāramitāprāpta*) means one who has directly realized these ten perfections. "One whose basis is the ten perfections" (*daśapāramitāśraya*) means that the ten perfections themselves are his support; the meaning is that his essential nature is the bodhicitta which is solely intent upon bliss. [The compound] *daśapāramitāśraya* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the basis of the ten perfections."

The purity of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) arises through their identity (*tādātmya*) by way of the relationship between the support and the supported (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). And it is said: "The relationship of support and supported persists as long as the state of the imperishable (*akṣaratā*) is not reached; when the mind has attained the state of the imperishable, it no longer possesses the characteristics of support and supported. For this very reason, he is one for whom the system of the ten perfections exists according to the divisions of the path.
The Lord is the master of the ten stages, his self purified by the ten knowledges; he is established in the ten stages and maintains the purity of the ten knowledges.

"Lord of the ten stages" (*daśabhūmīśvara*): he is the lord, the principal one, of the ten stages beginning with *pramuditā*, which are characterized by the twenty-four seats (*pīṭha*), sub-seats (*upapīṭha*), and so forth, because he pervades them in the form of innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*).
This is its meaning: through generosity the yogi becomes joyful (*pramudita*); through ethical discipline he becomes pure (*vimala*).

"Through patience one becomes *Prabhākarī*; through vigor, *Arciṣmatī*; through merit, one becomes *Sudurjayā*. Through meditation, one is drawn toward *Abhimukhī*; but through wisdom, one becomes *Dūraṅgamā*. Through great skillful means, one becomes *Acalā*; through power, *Sādhumatī*; and through aspiration, *Dharmameghā*. But the eleventh is the possessor of gnosis, the Victor, the Tathāgata, to be realized within oneself. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Amṛtakaṇikā* and elsewhere in the *Śrīsarvarahasyatantra*, as well as in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "The own-mind is the entirety of all Buddhas; it is the compendium of the Dharma."
Through the yoga of the selflessness of phenomena, Māra dies by himself.
One's own mind alone must die, and one's own mind alone should be slain;
one's own mind alone is the perfectly awakened Buddha, and it is the mind alone that is to be awakened.
Thus it is said:
"Having transcended the ten stages (daśabhūmi), one then becomes one whose sexual organ is motionless (stabdhaliṅga). Having himself become one with a motionless organ, he sits upon his own lap."
Having empowered the liṅga-vajra, this Vajrasattva is the primordial being.
Thus,
because he follows meditative absorption, the Protector,
through effortless empowerment for the sake of all sentient beings, is established upon the ten stages.
The ten stages are the integration of the ten elements;
these are wind, mind, bodhicitta, blood, marrow, bone, sinew, flesh, the sense faculties, and skin.
Their integration is the state of becoming of one flavor (*samarasībhāva*).
Established therein, he remains as far as space exists in the form of non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Regarding this, the teacher’s instruction is the cause; he states it as: "The self purified by the ten knowledges.
These are the ten knowledges of the signs, beginning with smoke.

And it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*: "By those whose minds are unattached to space and whose eyes are unblinking, having entered the path of the vajra—there arises from the void smoke, a mirage, a manifest and stainless firefly, and a lamp; then flame, moon, sun, and garments, as well as the supreme digit (*paramakalā*) and the drop (*bindu*). In the midst of that, the image of the Buddha is seen—the manifold *saṃbhogakāya* devoid of sense objects."
Thus it is said.
In that regard, one should first practice the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) in a leak-proof house or a cave.
And here, the six limbs are: withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
Mindfulness and meditative concentration are held to constitute the six-limbed yoga.

Thus: "He whose self (*ātman*) is pure through those [means] accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā* is such [a one]. Because of the manifestation of the universal image (*viśvabimba*), the grasping of objects such as form by the senses such as the eyes is the food of transmigrating beings; the renunciation of that is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).”

By means of the objects of emptiness, the apprehension of other forms and so forth by the five eyes, beginning with the fleshly eye, up to the limit of the drop (*bindu*)— which is unconstructed through the distinction of vision— is what is meant by the aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*).

Because it bears that which is the purity, the oneness resulting from the purification, of the ten gnoses consisting of the objects and their subjects within the universal image (*viśvabimba*), it is called the "bearer of the purity of the ten gnoses" (*daśajñānaviśuddhadhṛk*).

The meaning is that when the *bimba* is perceived through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), there occurs the continuous flow of the yogi’s own mind—which is personally experienced and consists of the manifestations of the three times and the three realms—by means of the branch of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Thus, the venerable Āryadeva and Saraha have said: "When the Lord, the master of the vital breaths, has dissolved into the self; when the collection of inhalations and exhalations has ceased and the life-wind (*jīvānila*) has been restrained;
then that most radiant expansion of light belonging to the lords of yogins, having emerged from his very own body, pervades the three worlds, its darkness destroyed."
The forest-dwelling maiden, a messenger of unprecedented spring,
is scattering flowers from the sky.
She is not touched by the hand nor kissed during separation, even though he is playful.
With eyes unblinking and the flow of speech suppressed,
he remained motionless through the grace of the venerable Guru.
It is said that those of dull intellect imagine the destruction of the intellect following the destruction of the eon;
however, for the wise, there arises from this very [destruction] something indescribable that transcends even the sky.
Thus, by this, the factors of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga) have been stated.
And it has been said: "Discernment (vitarka), investigation (vicāra), joy (rati), unshakable bliss (acalasukha), and one-pointedness of mind (ekacitta) constitute meditative absorption."
Thus it is said.
In that regard, the ten [objects] beginning with smoke are stated to be the limb of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Meditation (dhyāna) is Akṣobhya, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
