That by which these are sought after—that is, desired—through their respective locations in the lotus-filaments of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown, is thus described.
By this, the limb of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) has been described.

And so it has been said: "The entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the point (*bindu*), which is devoid of both [upward and downward] movements, as well as one-pointedness of mind, is indeed concentration."
Thus it is said.
And that aggregate of sensation is Ratnapāṇi;
he himself is the Lord of Sages.
Because he has attained the capacity for the illumination of the innate Caṇḍālī;

because of his capacity for the practice of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*); and because he possesses the characteristics of the state of the non-existence of *kā* as previously described—he is the "Ten-Powered One" (*daśabala*).
Because he pervades the three worlds through the light of the innate Caṇḍālī, he is the All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*).

For this very reason, he effects the welfare of all the manifold aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth—whose nature is the manifestation of innate bliss—therefore he is the "Benefactor of the Welfare of the Entire Universe" (*aśeṣaviśvārthakara*).

he whose forms are characterized by the ten previously mentioned types of breath-restraint (*vāyunirodha*) is so described.

Thus it is said.

Even that which is preceded by the worldly consecrations (*laukikābhiṣeka*), when accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, has as its cause precisely the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

And that six-limbed yoga is to be cultivated through the sequence beginning with smoke (*dhūma*) and so forth. As it is said: "One should perform the practice of this very [yoga], and then [the goal] will appear even without being thought of."
By means of those signs such as smoke and so forth, which are reflections of wisdom and equal to the sky.
Having transcended existence and non-existence through the objects of cognition of one's own mind,
and being entirely devoid of the accumulation of atoms and particles;
Smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, sun, darkness, the digit [of the moon], the great bindu, the universal image, and the radiant light.
That reflection which is seen like a dream in the void, by eyes that are both closed and open, and which is not mentally constructed— always meditate upon that reflection.
Thus it is said.

And it has been explained that the yogin should, by means of smoke and so forth, bring about the accomplishment—that is, the manifestation—of the fire of omniscient wisdom through the complete removal of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
By what kind of [means] does he do so?
Because it is established in all the Root Tantras, the Condensed Tantras, and the Noble Prajñāpāramitā Vinītārtha Sūtras; and because it appears spontaneously within emptiness.

The manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) is free from all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) because it is the prior form of the fruit of reality (*tattvaphala*), which is beyond thought. It is wisdom (*prajñā*), a cognition empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnya*) devoid of the grasped and the grasper. Its reflection appears as the direct perception (*yogipratyakṣa*) of the yogi; because it is unstained by external or internal impurities, it is like the sky. Since it is not marked by the stains of conceptual constructions such as "existence" and "non-existence," it transcends being and non-being. It is the object of experience for one's own mind through its cognitive aspects.

Because it is in every respect an uncreated, arisen state devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is a manifestation of emptiness (*śūnyābhāsa*) appearing as white smoke, pervading all external and internal realms, and entirely free from the mass of atoms and dust. This arises immediately after the manifestation of clouds, as it has been said: "The first appears like a cloud; the second is similar to smoke.
And for the yogi, it is likewise like the shimmering of water.

these four are the emanations. first, in the form of a mirage; second, resembling smoke."
The third has the appearance of a firefly; the fourth is a blazing lamp;
