Peace.
O Tārā, at that moment when your eyes, moist with the vibration of vast compassion, gaze deeply from your resolute intention upon the stainless sky—

[a sky] which is otherwise impenetrable by the conceptualization of existence, non-existence, both, or neither— how is it that the entire logical concomitance of smoke and other signs suddenly arises from emptiness?
That which is free from beginning and end, situated only in the middle— whatever one avoids therein, that is his light; it is like the full moon,
resting upon the ten-fold self.
The eyes were closed and became motionless.
With intense compassion, he immediately began playing the hand-drum;
the king was left without a protector.
The entire universe is in the left; the Ārya Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti is in the right; someone says there is a path of the Guru in the middle, between them.
The manifestation of power is well-concealed;
the fool is attached to external things.
The blossoming flowers have fallen away; the five-fold clusters have withered and been cast out by the wind.
Likewise: "Why, having bound the moon and the sun, does Śānti laugh? Why has she lit lamps in the sky and the quarters? [She says] to herself, "O friend!
Again, others said: "It is wonderful! (abbhuā).
Having seen [him],
he was greatly delighted upon hearing the profound Dharma;
yet in the dark night, he could not see anything at all.
If one speaks of peace from the peak of the sky, then the mind and the wind in the intermediate space blossom;
the eyes are deluded and broken.
If one who is skillful in the Dharma attains it at a single time,
they will surely attain the state that delights in the qualities of the Jina;
such are the stainless words of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore: Free from various conceptual constructions,
the mind,
having been made into an internal eye by the ascetic, clearly perceives the path of the ten directions.
Likewise, O Lord of Yoga,
all are attached; thus— free from wandering and devoid of all characteristics, he has been realized.
At that very moment it arises;
at that very moment it stands up.

With half-open eyes, the wind blows in the middle, and the lightning-fire flashes. Therefore, one who desires Buddhahood should meditate upon the path beginning with smoke, which arises from that state of doubt.

Accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*: The self is beginningless, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), pure, and of the nature of suchness (*tathatā*). He speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, acts accordingly, and his speech is not otherwise. Everywhere, every fruit is seen to be dissimilar to its cause.
For indeed, a rice sprout does not arise from kodrava seeds.
A fruit accompanied by conceptual construction arises from seeds of conceptual construction;
a fruit free from conceptual construction arises from that which is free from conceptual construction.
Virtuous in the beginning through non-conceptual meditation, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end—just as the seed is, so is the tree; just as the tree is, so is the fruit.
This very principle of dependent origination is seen throughout this entire world.
Thus:
He is non-dual and proponent of non-duality, established at the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
he is the lion of selflessness, whose roar terrifies the deer that are the false teachers.
Regarding the term *advaya*: "non-dual" refers to the nature of bliss (*sukha*) and semen (*śukra*) being non-distinct; he is a proponent of non-duality because he reveals that very form.

"Reality" (*bhūta*) means knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); the "peak" or summit of the excellent jewel-pedestal (*maṇivaraṭaka*), which is the locus for experiencing that [reality], is where he is established—well-situated through the yoga of non-abiding (*asthāna-yoga*).
The selflessness of all phenomena, characterized by the absence of appearance and having the form of the universal image— that alone is the Lion, the union of thousands,
the beginningless,
and the source of all.
Then follows the *Ārya-mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, because it is unassailable.
Therefore, he whose roar is the sound of selflessness (*nairātmya*)— an outburst of an ungrasped resonance— is the "Roar of the Lion of Selflessness."

A "bad ford" (*kutīrtha*) is that which serves as a means for knowing what is not the reality; the knowledge of the self and so forth is such a bad ford, and those who speak therein are called "heretics" (*kutīrthya*).

The conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of subject and object is itself the "deer," because it is fixed within [the mind]. Through that very unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*), fear arises; he causes their disappearance by that very means, and thus he is the "terrorizer of the deer of heretics.
As it has been said: "All proponents of doctrines have been terrified by the lion's roar of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
"Wherever these enter, there indeed is emptiness. Thus it is said:
"The Victor is all-pervading, his movement is unfailing, he possesses the speed of the Tathāgata's mind; he is the conqueror who has triumphed over his enemies, a universal monarch of great power."

Regarding "everywhere": because he pervades all aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth by virtue of having great bliss (*mahāsukha*) as his intrinsic nature, he goes everywhere; thus he is so called.
For this very reason, he whose movement (*gati*) is unfailing and unimpeded is "Amoghagati" (of Unfailing Movement).
The meaning is that his nature consists of the continuous and unimpeded movement and return of the seminal essence (*śukra*) of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Just as he came to the *vastra*, *maṇi*, and *varaṭaka* [the three cakras], so too has he gone to the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra; thus he is the "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone).
By means of the surge of great bliss, his speed in traversing the constituents (*dhātu*) is like that of the mind; because of that union, he is "Mind-Swift" (*manojava*).
Subsequently, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound:

he is a *Jina* (Victor) because of his victory over passion (*rāga*), dispassion (*virāga*), and intermediate passion (*madhyarāga*); he is a *jitāri* (Conqueror of Enemies) because of his cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*).

He is the "Vajraratna" because he has conquered the winds of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) upon the peak; he is the "Vinaya" (the Disciplined One) because his nature is to circulate through the six wheels (*cakra*) in the form of the seminal essence (*śukra*) as great bliss (*mahāsukha*); thus, he is the "Universal Monarch" (*cakravartin*).
He is the "Greatly Powerful" (*mahābala*) because he has conquered the fourfold and sixfold armies.
The leader of the hosts, the teacher of the hosts, the lord of the hosts, the master of the hosts, the flute-player,
the one of great majesty, the wise one, the one who follows no other path, the one of great conduct. Regarding "the leader of the hosts":
He is the pervader of the host of seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) by virtue of being their sovereign, and his essential nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) and semen (*śukra*).

He is the teacher (*ācārya*) of the hosts—namely, the states of bliss (*ānanda*), supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*)—and he reveals the form of innate reality (*sahajarūpa*).
Because he is the Supreme Lord through the induction of the innate state into the "hosts," such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), he is the Lord of the Hosts (*Gaṇeśa*).

The *gaṇa* is that which has the nature of objects resembling illusion, such as the Tathāgatas, the Vidyās, and so forth; their lord (*pati*) is the *Gaṇapati*, the master, because his essential nature is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
For this very reason, he is the "subduer" (*vaśī*), because by manifesting each respective essential nature, he illuminates all forms.
He is "of great power" (*mahānubhāvaḥ*), meaning he possesses power (*prabhāva*) or majesty (*anubhāva*) due to his immutability (*acyuta*).
Because the vital winds (*prāṇa*) and so forth follow the great sequence;

*llālo*, *0lāsya*; the reality (*tattva*); indeed unstable; this river, both [aspects]; right there; in sequence; with peaks; the wheel (*cakra*); the leader (*dhaureya*); blissful; by means of accomplishment; the essential natures (*svarūpa*); by way of the preeminence of knowledge (*vidyā*); O, the luminous (*prabhāsvara*)—thus it is added.

Accompanied by drops of nectar, he is one who immerses [others] in bliss; because he bears the burden of the instruments of action, he is a leader (*dhura-ya*); because he cannot be led by others due to his nature as innate bliss, he is not to be led by another (*ananya-neya*).
He is such because the Great Way (mahānaya) in which he resides has the manifestation of smoke and so forth, being without support and without appearance. || 8 ||
Lord of speech, master of words, eloquent, lord of eloquence, one whose song is infinite, truthful in speech, speaker of truth, and teacher of the four truths. ||9||
"Vāgīśa" means the lord of speech; by the manifestation of the limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), he possesses the power of granting boons and so forth through his infallible speech.

By this, the attainment of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) is indicated. Furthermore, because his semen is undiminished (*acyutaśukra*), he is the master of speech in the form of the unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*), as he has abandoned external utterance.

By this, the attainment of the analytical knowledge of sounds (*śabdapratisaṃvid*) is stated through the illumination of the selflessness of all phenomena; and by this, the attainment of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) is stated through [the practice of] vajra-recitation and so forth, whereby one becomes a master of speech upon attaining true bliss.
By this, the attainment of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) has been stated.
Thus, through the attainment of the four analytical knowledges, he possesses infinite speech (*anantagīḥ*).

Because he turns the wheel of Dharma—beginning with the nature of intrinsic luminosity—for all sentient beings according to their spiritual capacity, and because he reveals the Dharma without contradicting conventional truth, he is one whose speech is truthful (*satyavāk*).

Conventional truth is the illusory body (*māyopama-śarīra*) through its own empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), and ultimate truth is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), which is the cause for its purification. Thus, he is a proponent of the two truths because he reveals the self-cognized gnosis in which emptiness and compassion are indivisible; he is a teacher of the four truths because he demonstrates the four innate joys (*sahajānanda*) and so forth. || 9 ||
For he is irreversible, a non-returner, a rhinoceros-like solitary leader who has emerged through various modes of departure; he is the great element, the cause of the letter *ka*. || 10 ||

The term *avairvātika* means that by means of the cessation of fourteen thousand four hundred breaths through the process of coming and going within the four wheels (*cakras*) and the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), one becomes a master of the immovable stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
He is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) because, no longer under the sway of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he does not return to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Like a sword, he is a *khaḍga* because he radiates through all the channels by virtue of being unshakable (*acyuta*).

Because he brings about the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) in each and every channel, he is the individual leader. Those from which conceptual constructions, afflictions, and sufferings emerge—that is, depart—are the "exits" (*niryāṇa*); these are various (*nānā*) and they are exits, thus "various exits" (*nānāniryāṇa*). The centers of the lotuses of the six wheels are those [exits]; having definitely emerged from them in the form of great bliss, he is "one who has emerged from the various exits" (*nānāniryāṇaniryāta*).
The singular, peerless cause of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) is "having the great elements as its sole cause" (*mahābhūtaikakāraṇa*).
The masculine gender is used due to Vedic usage (*ārṣatvāt*).
Thus it was said by the venerable Kṛṣṇapāda (*Dai.*): "O wise one, the five great elements arise from a combination."
The earth is perfumed with sandalwood paste, and the sky is adorned with incense smoke.
"In the sky, fragrant with breezes, filled with the five [senses], all gods and asuras have departed; it has become empty. Thus, in the *Okaraṇa*.
Having investigated sluggishness and so forth, as well as dullness and so forth,
[one should apply] the fourth [remedy].
And by means of truth,
he is the one who reveals joy.
The sword is the nature of great bliss;
thus it is said in the *Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*: "Likewise, it is stated in the *Śrī-hevajra-tantra*: 'By means of the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, the practitioner performs the *kunduru*.'"
From the quality of hardness arising from contact, earth is born therein.
From the liquid form of the bodhicitta, the water element arises;
from friction, fire is born; and from movement, wind is proclaimed.
Bliss is the space element, encircled by these five. Thus [ends verse 10].

The Arhat is a monk whose taints are exhausted, free from passion, with senses conquered; he has attained peace, attained fearlessness, become cooled, and is indeed undisturbed. (HeTa 1.10.38–40) 1.1.

"Arhat" means one for whom the outflows (*āsravas*) are exhausted; by the power of perfect meditative concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), he has slain all enemies that are conceptual constructions and afflictions (*kleśas*).

Through the application of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), because he possesses the complete fulfillment of all aims by virtue of the bliss of the reality that is inexpressible as either the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) or the illustrated meaning (*dārṣṭāntika*), and by the power of the instruction of a true guru at the moment of the fourth consecration—due to the transcendence of the fourth moment (*turyakṣaṇa*)—the disciple, through the immediate application of intense faith, abandons all ignorance. Thus, he is so called because his outflows are exhausted, or from which [exhaustion] he proceeds.

Even while enjoying the five sensory pleasures, he is a *bhikṣu* because his afflictions have been destroyed; he is free from passion (*vītarāga*) because, through entering the luminous state, his ordinary passion has vanished due to the experience of great bliss (*mahāsukha*);

and he is one who has conquered the senses (*jitendriya*) because, by abiding in the crest-jewel of the *uṣṇīṣa*, he cannot be overwhelmed by the objects of any sense, or because he does not arise from the union of the two organs.

He has attained security (*kṣemaprāpta*) because he has obtained a previously unprecedented and marvelous bliss through the non-performance of the five sensual pleasures; he has attained fearlessness (*abhayaprāpta*) because, by virtue of his bliss being unshakable, there is no longer any terror regarding that bliss;

and he has become cooled (*śītībhūta*) because, being pierced by the great nectar of innate joy (*sahajānanda*), the fire of all disturbances of body, speech, and mind has been extinguished—the particle *hi* here serves the sense of "because."
Because it is unstained by passion, dispassion, and so forth, the body of gnosis is untroubled. ||11||
Endowed with perfect knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the supreme knower of the world, free from "mine-ness" and egoism, abides in the method of the two truths. || 12 ||
Regarding "Vidyācaraṇa":

*vidyā* is great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) and knowledge; its *ācaraṇa* is the immersion in the fourth consecration (*caturthābhiṣeka*). One who is perfected in that is one whose nature is non-dual—this is the meaning.
Because of the bliss of non-attachment, he is superior to the bliss of *saṃsāra*. Because he has gone to the state from which there is no returning until the goal is reached, he is the *Sugata*.
He knows the world, consisting of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, as great bliss; thus he is "the other.

He is supreme because of being the highest among the joys—namely, Ānanda, Paramānanda, Viramānanda, and Uttamānanda—and because he has abandoned all conceptual constructions of self and mine, he is "without possessiveness," meaning his nature is suchness (*tathatā*).
Thinking "I have enjoyed happiness," and thus through the certainty of happiness and the disappearance of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), one becomes free from egoism;
that is to say, even the egoism of "I am Vajrasattva" should not be maintained.

Conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is like an illusion and has the characteristic of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*); ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is the thorough knowledge of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). These two constitute the two truths.
And so it has been said: "Self-consecration is the vision of the triple world within emptiness"; that is [attained] by means of the hand of the outflow (*āśrava*).
And the sciences are born of form; he is understood through that form.

"Viramānanda" means that which is accompanied by the drop of nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*); that very thing is the method (*naya*), the path (*mārga*). One who abides therein and realizes it is the "seizer of all breaths" (*sakala-śvāsahartṛ*)—this is the meaning. || 12 ||

Standing on the far shore of saṃsāra, having accomplished what was to be done, established on firm ground, overflowing with the knowledge of absolute liberation (kaivalya), he is the one who rends [ignorance] with the weapon of wisdom. || 13 ||

"Sāṃsārapārakoṭistha" means one who stands at the limit of the further shore of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Here, *saṃsāra* refers to the essence (*sāra*) that is bliss (*ānanda*), the supreme bliss (*paramānanda-sukha*). Its "further shore" (*pāra*) is the gnosis of the joy of cessation (*viramānanda-jñāna*). Its "limit" (*koṭi*) is the gnosis of the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda-sukha*). One who abides therein is "standing at the limit of the further shore of cyclic existence," which means one who holds the limit of the fourth meditative absorption (*caturtha-dhyāna*).
"One by whom what was to be done has been done" (*kṛtakṛtya*) refers to one by whom the bestowal of the gnosis of the fourth initiation has been accomplished.

The state of the bliss of nirvāṇa is accomplished through the enjoyment of the five sensory pleasures because it is the most secure place; "one who abides there" means the *jñānakāya* (body of gnosis) which is imperishable.
"Isolated gnosis" (*kaivalyajñāna*) refers to that which is characterized by the pure non-dual nature of reality (*dharmatā*), consisting of the *dharmakāya*.
"Emerging from that" means having issued forth, possessing the nature of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).
Wisdom has the characteristic of perceiving the images of all things; that very wisdom is a weapon because it eradicates all afflictions, and he who possesses it is thus [described].
For this very reason, he is the "Tearer," for he rends asunder the web of conceptual constructions regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. || 13 ||

The True Dharma is the King of Dharma, the radiant one, the supreme illuminator of the world; it is the Lord of Dharma, the Sovereign of Dharma, and the teacher of the path to the highest good. || 14 ||

"Sad-dharma" means that which is both real and the teaching of a true guru; because it is difficult to obtain, it is the Dharma itself in the form of the syllable *Eṃ*. And elsewhere: "Of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, I have declared the two syllables, the father and mother, to be the support of them all."
The letter *e* is the mother, and the letter *va* is remembered as the father; the *bindu* therein is their union, and that union is most wonderful.
The letter E is said to be the lotus, and the letter VA is the vajra;
the bindu therein is the seed-syllable, from which the three worlds are produced.
The letter *e* is indeed wisdom (*prajñā*), the letter *va* is the Lord of Bliss (*suratādhipa*), and the *bindu* is the reality of the Unstruck (*anāhata*); from these are born those syllables.
He who, knowing reality, understands the two syllables of the Dharma-seal,
shall become a turner of the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings.
The syllable EKA is proclaimed in the world as the sky, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
the syllable VAM, the array of the Sugatas, is perfectly established within the syllable EKA.
Regarding the withdrawal of inhalation and exhalation according to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
and elsewhere, in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*:
And this secret [is to be found] in the space-element, or in the bhaga, the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), or the lotus;
seated upon the lion-throne, the Vajrin was thus described by me in another tantra.
Vam; he is Vajrī, Vajrasattva, Vajrabhairava, Īśvara, Heruka, Kālacakra, and by such names as Ādibuddha.
He who awakened to the syllable *Evaṃ* has awakened to everything without exception;
he alone is the casket of Dharma, O Lord, wearing the guise of a mendicant.
Thus:

*dharma* is the *dharmadhātu*; he reigns therein or by means of it, thus he is the *Dharmarāja*. Because his nature is the light of innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*), he is radiant (*bhāsvat*), having the quality of shining.

Through the cultivation of uninterrupted non-appearance, he creates light for the worlds shrouded in the darkness of ignorance by means of the ten signs beginning with smoke and the image of the Buddha; thus, he is the "Light-Maker of the World" (*lokālokakara*).

He is supreme (*para*) and excellent, for although his nature is intrinsically luminous (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*), he takes the form of rays of supreme great bliss (*paramamahāsukha*) within, being superior to the light of the sun and other celestial bodies.

By means of the *Dharma*—the fourfold innate joy (*sahajānanda*)—he is the Lord (*īśvara*), the sovereign of the three worlds, due to his mastery over the constant tasting of the essence of bodhicitta.
He is the Dharmarāja because he delights the worlds with the rain of the Dharma of great bliss;
he is the one who causes entry into and reveals the path to excellence characterized by self-consecration. 14.
He whose purpose is accomplished, whose resolve is fulfilled, who is free from all conceptual constructions;
he is beyond thought-constructs, imperishable, the primordial element, the supreme element, and immutable.

Regarding "Siddhārtha": he is so called because the object (*artha*)—namely, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—is accomplished (*siddha*) or perfected (*niṣpanna*) through the manifestation of all phenomena in the form of gnosis (*jñānākāra*), or because that [gnosis] from which or for whom that [object] exists is thus.

He is one who has eternally accomplished [the goal] by making it manifest before his own eyes through the practice of meditation brought about by the Vajradhara of the Buddhas; he is so called because his conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*)—that is, the dualistic discrimination between subject and object (*grāhyagrāhakavikalpa*)—has ceased.
For this very reason, he is free from and has abandoned all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*), as well as the dogmatic attachment to the notions of "self" and "mine.
He is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) because he acts through a mind free of conceptualization at the time of consecration, the observance of commitments (*samaya*), and so forth.
He is imperishable (*akṣaya*) because, by being established in luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), there is no exhaustion.
The *dharmadhātu* is so called because it is the nature of all phenomena;
it is the *dharmadhātu* because its sole form is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), consisting of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*);
and it is imperishable because it is immutable.
Because it is called the "self-arisen" and the "innate," it is supreme;
by this, it is stated that non-conceptual meditative cultivation alone is the cause for the attainment of Mahāmudrā. || 15 ||
He is meritorious, possessing the accumulation of merit; he is wisdom, the great source of wisdom;
he possesses wisdom, knowing the real and the unreal, and is fully endowed with the two accumulations. || 16 ||
"Fortunate" (puṇyavān):

merit (*puṇya*) is the bliss (*sukha*) consisting in the turning toward the limbs of meditative absorption (*samādhyaṅga*) by means of the mind colored with the passion of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-rāga*). One is "fortunate" through identity with that [merit], due to being joined with it.
And it has been said: "There is no sin greater than dispassion (*virāga*), nor is there any merit greater than bliss."
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the pleasure of emission.
Thus, because it is the knowledge of bliss that is the means for attaining the siddhi of Mahāmudrā, it constitutes the accumulation of merit.
And it has been said: "Even if someone were to fall from the summit of the king of mountains, he would not desire to fall; yet even so, he falls."
One who has received instruction through the grace of the Guru does not desire liberation; he is thus liberated.
Thus [it is said] (Pañcakrama 2.69).
It is "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it fulfills the equipment of knowledge (*jñānasaṃbhāra*).
It is the "mine of knowledge" (*jñānākara*) because its nature is the blissful knowledge of non-apprehension within the jewel, and because it is a source of manifold bliss.
As it has been said: "With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands pervading all."

( *Gītā* 13.13) It is called "Great" (*mahat*) because it consists of the sixteen digits (*ṣoḍaśakalā*). He is "possessed of knowledge" (*jñānavān*) due to his eternal union with non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*), which burns away the fuel of all conceptual constructions through the yoga of Caṇḍālī; for he appears as one who has mastered the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, which are like an illusion.

And it is said: "I do not perceive within this supreme knowledge the assembly of the glorious maṇḍala and its deities, nor the reflection of that [divine] knowledge, nor the entire world consisting of Māyā and the rest."
That which is the state of the Indian drop within the expanse of the sky is seen as all-pervasive by those who are pure; it dispels the darkness of the world and brings about illumination.
And because of the departure of all false delusions, he is the knower of the existent and non-existent;
this means that his nature is self-cognized innate bliss.
Because he is endowed with the two accumulations just mentioned, he is "one who has gathered the two accumulations. (16)

Eternal, the sovereign of the universe, the yogi, meditation, the object of meditation, and the lord of intellects; indeed, he is to be realized within oneself, immovable, the supreme primordial one, and the sustainer of the three bodies. ||17||

44. *Māyājālamahātantrarāja-mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*: [He is] "Eternal" (*śāśvata*). He is eternal because he takes the form of the consecration of the Buddhas and others, pervading the space within the tips of all the pores of the skin; he is eternal because of the bliss of non-falling, being grounded in the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
He is the "Sovereign of the Universe" (*viśvarāṭ*) because he shines as the nature of bliss within the universe of seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*).
A yogin is so called because of the unification of body, speech, and mind;
meditation (*dhyāna*) is so called because of the oneness of the four joys;
and it is the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) because it is to be experienced by the lords of yogins within the *uṣṇīṣa* at the crown of the head.
Because he is the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas, he is the Lord of Intelligence (*dhīpati*).
The sixth is Vajradhara; because his bliss is like that of a maiden’s sexual union and is not to be known by another, it is to be personally realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedya*).
And it has been said: "Bliss cannot be described without the sexual union of a maiden."
Having attained sexual union in youth, one experiences great bliss by oneself.
Thus, it cannot be said that there is happiness devoid of meditative concentration;
having attained the imperishable within concentration, yogins experience it of their own accord.

He is immovable due to the cessation of the winds of conceptual construction; he is the Primordial Supreme because his nature is that of Vajrasattva; and he is the bearer of the three bodies because he is speech and mind. || 17 ||
The Buddha consists of the five bodies; the pervasive Lord consists of the five gnoses;
he has the five Buddhas as his crown and possesses the five eyes free from attachment. || 18 ||
He is called "Buddha" because his nature is the realization of the bliss of the self.

By virtue of consisting of the five families (*pañcakula*) and having the nature of the five cognitions (*pañcajñāna*), such as the mirror-like cognition (*ādarśajñāna*), through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, there arises the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of hardness from contact.
Since hardness is of the nature of delusion (*moha*), delusion is considered to be Vairocana.
Since the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is fluid, and fluidity is considered to belong to the water element,
and because the nature of water is Akṣobhya, hatred has Akṣobhya as its leader.
It is always produced:
from the friction and conjunction of the two, fire arises; passion is Amitavajra, and passion is born from fire.
That which is mind is of the nature of wind;
envy is Amoghasiddhi, for the unfailing arises from wind.
Pleasure becomes passion; the one who is impassioned has attachment as his characteristic, which is like space. Space is the betrayer (piśuna), and the betrayer is born from space.

Accompanied by the *amṛtakaṇikā*, or else: through the union of mother and father, the father’s seed of bodhicitta is the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) because of its lunar and Akṣobhya-like fluidity;
the mother’s self-arisen flower is the nature of equanimity (*samatājñāna*) because of its solar and Ratnasambhava-like passion;
and through the entry of the vajra into the lotus, it is the nature of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) because of the bliss of Amitābha arising from the seed of great passion.
The experience of moving and vibrating is the performance of activity (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*), because it has the nature of Amoghasiddhi.

Through the entry of the intermediate state consciousness, there is growth; from that, Vairocana is the emergence from the mother’s womb, the perfection of the image (*bimba*), which is the perfectly pure sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*).
This is because [he] pervades the stages beginning with childhood by means of the form of mental bliss.
Through the direct realization of the previously mentioned *bimba*, there is the radiation of the five unobscured aggregates (*skandha*), and thus he possesses a crown consisting of the five Buddhas.

Through the manifestation of the limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), retention (*dhāraṇā*), and recollection (*anusmṛti*), he possesses the five eyes.
Through union with the limb of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he is the holder of non-attachment. (18)
The progenitor of all Buddhas, the supreme and most excellent son of the Buddha; born from the source of wisdom, the womb, the source of Dharma, and the bringer of an end to existence. || 19 ||
Regarding "Janaka":
he is called Janaka because he generates eighty-four thousand moments of consciousness as the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) for the Buddhas;
that is to say, he is the mass of the mind of bliss contained within the vajra-jewel.
One is a *buddha* due to the awakening of the mind of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) as described;

his son (*putra*), his own offspring (*ātmaja*), is the innate (*sahaja*). This means that because it is directly perceived, it is the ultimate basis of valid cognition, and thus one has emerged through the negation of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa-pratiṣedha*).
Because it transcends the three joys (*ānanda-traya*), it is the supreme innate (*para-sahaja*).
The "excellent" (vara) is wisdom (*prajñā*) because it possesses self-experience;
that very wisdom, being the universal image, is the place of origin (*utpattisthāna*). Because he arises therein, he is "born from the existence of wisdom" (*prajñābhavodbhava*).
He is the *saṃbhogakāya* whose form is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and he is the "womb" (*yoni*) because he is the place of origin for all sentient beings.
Because he is the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), he is the source of the Dharma (*dharmayoni*);

because he brings about innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)—the end and conclusion of existence, which culminates in the threefold bliss—he is the "one who has brought an end to existence" (*bhavāntakṛt*). || 19 ||
The essence of the house, whose nature is vajra, the newly born Lord of the World, arisen from space, the self-existent one, the great fire of wisdom-knowledge. ||20||

*Dharmakāya* is "solid" (*ghana*) because it is dense, being unique and non-dual; it is "essential" (*sāra*) because, as innate bliss, it is free from the stains of all conceptual constructions and afflictions; and it is "of the nature of a vajra" (*vajrātmā*) because it is indivisible due to its being the *jñānakāya*.
Because the instruction of the Guru arises in the hearts of those possessed of extreme faith in the form of the Buddha in a mere instant, he is "Sadyojāta" (the Newly Born).
As it has been said: "That [Reality] itself gradually establishes its own station in the heart of those possessed of faith, purified by qualities such as compassion.

He is the Lord of the World; the meaning is that he is the Master of the World who stands in the place of mother and father for all people, and whose nature is the *vastusattva* (the reality of things).

"Space" (*gagana*)—now he speaks of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). And that is the vision of emptiness according to the conventional truth, known as the sign of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); it is an appearance like clouds, smoke, and so forth. That is first seen up to the end of the lamp. Furthermore, those four signs are mentioned in the *Samāja*, while the other six signs are from the flame up to the drop (*bindu*).
Regarding this, it is stated in two verses:
that which arises as a manifestation from the previously mentioned cloudless sky is the "sky-born" self-existent one (*svayaṃbhū*), because his mind is free from all conceptual constructions.
Therefore, "the fire of the wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñānānala*) is the appearance of flame;

"Vairocana, the great radiance, the self-arisen" (*vairocano mahādīptiḥ svayambhūḥ*) is the appearance of the moon; and "this *Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*" is the appearance of the sun, as it is said: "He is the light of knowledge, the illuminator (*jñānajyotirvirocana*), the lamp of the world."
The appearance of Rāhu is the torch of gnosis (*jñānolka*),
which is the great brilliance (*mahātejas*) and the luminous (*prabhāsvara*);

the appearance of lightning is the King of Vidyās (*vidyārāja*), the Lord of Supreme Mantras (*agramantreśa*), which is the appearance of the drop (*bindu*), and it has the form of a blue-colored lunar disc.

"The King of Mantras who accomplishes the great purpose" means that the manifestation of the entities of the three realms in all their aspects is seen by the yogin as being like an illusion, a dream, or a reflection (*pratisenā*).
As for the etymology: "the sky" is the Buddha-image; because he arises therein, he is so called.

[He is] "Self-Arisen" (*svayambhū*) because he exists by himself, through his own nature. "Wisdom-Knowledge" (*prajñājñāna*) is the knowledge of the innate *caṇḍālī*; he whose fire is like that very [knowledge], which is like a flame, is so described.
It is "Great" because it pervades everything. || 20 ||
Vairocana, the great illuminator, the radiance of his own light; the lamp of the world, the fire against the darkness of ignorance, possessed of great splendor, and self-luminous. ||21||
[Vairocana] means that Virocana is the wisdom of natural luminosity; he himself is Vairocana.
He is Mahādīpti because he possesses great radiance;
he is Jñānajyotis because his very light is wisdom.
He shines and blazes, thus he is Virocana;
because he illuminates the world like a lamp, he is the Lamp of the World (Jagatpradīpa); he whose torch is knowledge is Jñānolkā.
He who possesses the radiance of great splendor is "Mahātejāḥ";
for that very reason, he is "Prabhāsvaraḥ" (effulgent). || 21 ||
King of vidyās, supreme lord of mantras, king of mantras who accomplishes the great purpose;
arisen from the Great Uṣṇīṣa, the Uṣṇīṣa himself, the all-seeing Lord of the Sky. ||22||
[Regarding "Vidyārāja"]: He is the king, the master, of *vidyā*, which is *mahāmudrā*; thus he is the Vidyārāja.
Because he is preeminent in great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he is the foremost lord of mantras;
because he is the ultimate king of mantras, he is the Great King of Mantras (*mahāmantrarāja*).
Because he pervades the three worlds in the form of great bliss, he is the "performer of the great purpose" (*mahārthakṛt*).

Furthermore, because he is both "great" (*mahān*) and the "uṣṇīṣa," he is the "Great Uṣṇīṣa" (*mahoṣṇīṣa*). He is the drop (*bindu*) of all Tathāgatas, established in the sky in the form of an uṣṇīṣa, having become a mass [of light].

The Great Uṣṇīṣa is the *jñānabindu* arisen from the Uṣṇīṣa; it is the Uṣṇīṣa arisen from the Great Uṣṇīṣa. That Blessed One, the Wisdom Being (*jñānasattva*) of all Tathāgatas, who emerges from all the Uṣṇīṣas of the Tathāgatas through the path of the *ūrṇā* by way of a mass of radiance, stands upon the head in the form of a vajra.

And it is said: "By whom the Mind-born [Kāmadeva] was drawn from his own *vajra* and led to his own forehead by Śākyamuni through the power of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), so that the vajra reached the Great Uṣṇīṣa—homage to that Guru of gods, humans, and asuras, the sole teacher of the universe, for whom emptiness with compassion is indeed with an object, yet [for whom] it is without an object."

He whose nature is to manifest the universe in its various forms through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the self-abiding (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), thereby demonstrating the awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*), is the "Beholder of the Universe" (*viśvadarśī*).
He is the Lord of the Sky (*viyatpati*), that is, the Lord of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the meaning is the Lord of Bliss (*sukha*).
And it has been said: "The state of the non-manifesting mind (*nirābhāsasya cittasya*) is characterized by space (*ākāśa*)."
This very cultivation of space is considered the cultivation of emptiness for the sake of the embodiments of all Buddhas. Thus [it is said].
The eye of the world’s bliss,
possessing universal form, the creator, worthy of worship and honor, the great seer.

“Sarvabuddha”: the embodiment (*ātmabhāva*) of all Buddhas, such as Śāśvata and the others, is the self-cognized innate bliss-wisdom (*sahajasukhajñāna*); by that, he is "foremost" (*agrya*), meaning "supreme" (*śreṣṭha*), the "body of wisdom of all Tathāgatas. He is "Jagadānandalocana" because he looks upon, sees, and experiences the world through bliss in the form of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). He is "Viśvarūpī" because he perceives stable and moving entities through bliss in various forms according to their capacity for maturation (*yathābhavyatayā*). He is the "Creator" (*vidhātā*) because he brings about the realization of all mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and the embrace (*utsaṅga*), and so forth.
He is "Worshipful" because he is to be honored by virtue of being co-emergent;
he is "Venerable" because he is not to be transgressed through the constant practice of external and internal mudrās; and he is the "Great Sage" because of his knowledge of the supreme unchanging.
The mantra-practitioner upholds the three families, maintains the mantra of the great samaya,
bears the Three Jewels, and is the most excellent teacher of the supreme triple vehicle.
"Of the three families" refers to this triad of body, speech, and mind; he is so called because he upholds great bliss by virtue of belonging to those families.
Furthermore, he is a "mantrin" because he possesses supramundane gnosis.

He is called "Tathā" because he holds the mantra of the great assembly (*mahāsamaya*), which is the samādhi of the perfect awakening to true bliss; likewise, he is so called because he holds the jewels known as the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies, which are of a single nature with the innate (*sahaja*).
For this very reason, he is supreme, being without beginning or end.
The teacher of the supreme among the three vehicles, who reveals the fourth bliss, has said:

"Abiding in the center of the space-vajra-realm, one should meditate on the visualization of the vajra-maṇḍala; having contemplated the ego-identity of body, speech, and mind, one remains for an eon. Thus it is stated.
Amoghapāśa, the Victorious One, Vajrapāśa, the Great Seizer;
Vajrāṅkuśa, the Great Noose—these are twenty-four and a quarter verses on the Wisdom of the Perfectly Pure Dharmadhātu.
This is the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "The Unfailing Noose."
He is "Amoghapāśa" because his noose— characterized by the six-limbed yoga— is unfailing and unerring; he is thus because,
by means of the manifestation of the [deity] image, he causes the appearance of suchness for those beings who are to be disciplined by the Vajra of Bodhicitta,
or because he is victorious through the suppression of the vital winds via the diamond-like samādhi of the three worlds.
He is so called because he possesses a "lasso" (*pāśa*)—like a lasso for the diamond-mind-cloth (*vajra-cittavastra*)—since by binding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within, even the mind-cloth is bound;

and he is so called because he possesses a "great grasp" (*mahāgraha*) through non-conceptual yoga (*avikalpayoga*) that does not relinquish the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); and he is the "cloth-hook" (*vastrāṅkuśa*) because, like a hook attached to a cloth, he draws forth all blissful meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).

By the word "noose" (pāśa) is meant the specific channel named Vāsuki, which is situated below the navel in the form of a serpent coiled like a ring; having gone to the abode of Brahmā by way of the *avadhūtī*, it is called the "great noose" because it pervades the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases through the extraction of the *bodhicitta*.

Pervading the heart, the channels, the head, the top-knot (*śikhā*), the right ear, the backbone, the left ear, the eyes, the space between the eyebrows, the two shoulders, the two armpits, the pair of breasts, the navel, the tip of the nose, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the genitals, the secret parts, the anus, the thighs, the shanks, the feet, the back, the toes, the thumbs, and the knees—by means of these twenty-five forms of the *bodhicitta* moon, which purify the stages of the *bodhicitta* and convey innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), an exposition has been shown through twenty-four and a half verses concerning the supramundane aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) in its nature as Akṣobhya, the perfectly pure wisdom of the sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*).
The mirror-like wisdom is Vajra Bhairava, the terrifier.
The King of Wrath, six-faced and terrifying, with six eyes, six arms, and powerful; formidable with fangs, skeletal, Halāhala, and hundred-faced.

Now, with the verse beginning "Vastrabhairavabhīkara" and so forth, he provides an exposition of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) in ten and a half verses: *vajra* is *avadhūtī*; within its interior (*anantare*) is *bhairambha*, the wind. Because it arises from the *anāhata* [cakra] as the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) in the form of the aggregates (*skandha*) such as visible form, it produces the destruction—that is, the non-existence—of the conceptualizations of vision; thus, it is *vajrabhairavabhīkara*.

"Krodharāja" means the King of Wrath; he is called Krodharāja because he shines immediately after the bliss of cessation (viramānanda). He is Mañjuśrī in form, whose intrinsic nature is great bliss (mahāsukha).
He whose six faces consist of the means, such as withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and so forth, is thus [described]; he is Bhīma because of his quality of severing all suffering.

Because the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and action-faculties have ceased, he is like space in his clarity; thus, he whose six eyes are of the nature of the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*) is "Six-Eyed" (*Ṣaṇnetra*).
Because he enjoys the six objects as being of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he is "Six-Armed" (*Ṣaḍbhuja*).
By means of the knowledge whose nature is great passion (*mahārāga*), which has the power to pierce the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, he is "powerful" (*balī*);

and because he is the "beholder" (*draṣṭṛ*), he is *Caṇḍālī*. Through the teacher’s instruction, when she has been ignited, he is "fearful with fangs" (*daṃṣṭrākarālaḥ*) because he is her "peak" (*śikhara*).
He is a "skeleton" (*kaṅkālaḥ*) because he measures (*kalayati*) bliss (*kaṃ*).

Halāhala is so called because of his knowledge of space (*ākāśajñānatā*); the binding of the vital breath within the hem of his garment results in the bliss that pervades all the channels (*nāḍī*). He whose faces—the cognitions of bliss—are a hundred, or rather infinite, is Halāhala-śatānana.
Yamāntaka, Vighnarāja, Vajravega, Bhayaṅkara, Vighuṣṭavajra, Hṛdvajra, Māyāvajra, and Mahodara.
"Yamāntaka" means the ender of the pair of "yamas," namely, the dualistic clinging to self and other; the meaning is that he flows as the union of the two.
"Vighna" (obstacle) refers to Māra; Māra is the proliferation of one’s own mind, for there is no Māra other than one’s own mind.
He is called Vighnarāja because he shines by means of the destruction of those obstacles;

he is the "impetus" (vega) or expansion of the "thunderbolt" (vajra), which is perfect knowledge, because he possesses that nature; and he is "terrifying" because, through the unification of *nāda* and *bindu*, he swallows up (or dissolves) all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

By the sequence just described, through the non-differentiation of emptiness and compassion, he is the Great Sound proclaimed as the nature of the unstruck (*anāhata*) dharmadhātu; he is the Vajra because it is indivisible, or because he himself is indivisible by means of it.
He is the Heart-Vajra because he is the Sahajakāya.
He is such because his garment—which is the object of the mind’s illusion—is indivisible.
Because he encompasses all phenomena by virtue of being the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, he is Mahodara; he is the Lord of the Vajra, the Vajra-source, the Vajra-maṇḍala, and like the sky.
He possesses the majestic mass of a single unmoving matted lock of hair and wears a fresh elephant hide as a garment.

"Kuliśeśa" means that because he is the Lord (*īśvara*) by virtue of his nature as great bliss within the "thunderbolt" (*kuliśa*)— that is, inside the two vajra-apertures known as Oḍḍiyāna and Jālandhara— and because he is the "womb" (*yoni*),
the place of origin for all "thunderbolts"— namely, the body, speech, mind, and gnosis-thunderbolts of all the Tathāgatas— due to being the source of the arising of innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
Because it has the nature of the taste of divine bliss, it is the "Vajra-essence" (*vajramaṇḍa*), whose core is indivisible;
because it possesses the nature of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects through its state of being unobscured, it is like the sky;

because its vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been rendered motionless, it is immovable (*acala*); and because all things have attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*), it possesses the "majesty" (*āṭopa*) or grandeur of a single braid of hair (*ekajaṭā*). Such is he.

By means of the application of the divine mudrā, the semen—having reached the limit of the *dharmadhātu* by way of the nature of great bliss—is worn as a white elephant hide garment; because he maintains it through identity with the innate self-nature (*sahajasvābhāvatattva*), he is thus [described].
He is the one of great terror who utters "hā hā," the fearsome one who utters "ahi hi," the one of loud laughter, the one of great laughter, the one of vajra-laughter, and the one of the great roar.

"Hāhākāra" refers to the sound "hā hā," which arises from the outpouring of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); it is called "Hāhākāra" because it produces that sound and because it takes the form of a specific resonance. It is "Mahāghora" (the Great Terrible) because it transcends even the terrible.
Because it is, as before, of the nature of the sound of bliss, it is the syllable *ho-hī*; because it is valorous and terrifying within the aperture of great bliss (*mahāsukha*),
it is "laughter" (*aṭṭahāsa*) due to its form as the eightfold *ha* syllable through the application of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).

Because of the bliss of the vajra-dance in the embrace of divine women, there is great laughter; because it is self-experienced, it is the "laughter of the garment" (*vastra-hāsa*), which is the laughter of gnosis (*jñāna-hāsa*);
and the great roar is the sound of the great bliss of the three worlds.
Vajrasattva, the Great Being; Vajrarāja, the Great Bliss; Vajracaṇḍa, the Great Joy; Vajrahūṃkāra, the Utterer of Hūṃ.
"Vajrasattva" means Vajrasattva because his nature is the indivisible bodhicitta.
Having filled the body with the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), because he is in the form of a drop (*bindu*) whose flow is uninterrupted, he is a Great Being (*mahāsattva*).
He shines as the nature of great bliss within the *vajra*; therefore, he is the "Vajra King" (*vajrarāja*), and for that very reason, he is Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Because of the speed of proceeding toward the state of non-abiding bliss and nirvāṇa, he is Vajracaṇḍa, the Vajra-impulse;
because of the joy of the undecaying nectar through the absence of the positions of existence and non-existence, he is Mahāmoda, the Great Joy.

Because of the movement through Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pullīramalaya, and Maru in the form of the four *hūṃ*s—consisting of the four joys (*caturānanda*) and the fourth state (*turya*)—along with the drop of nectar of the King of Bodhicitta, which is the syllable *vaṃ*, he is *Vahaṃkāra-hūṃkṛti*.
He who bears the weapon of the vajra-arrow, the vajra-sword that cuts through all,
the wielder of the universal vajra, the Vajrin, the sole vajra-holder, who abandons all strife.
Regarding "vajrabāṇa" (diamond arrow):

because the two nostril apertures are blocked by the diamond-arrow of the *avadhūtī*, the *avadhūtī* itself is the "garment" (*vastra*). That very thing is the weapon of the arrow; because he bears that, he is the "bearer of the diamond-arrow weapon."
Because it is the support of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the *vajra* is non-dual gnosis itself; it is a "sword" (*khaṅga*) because it eradicates all afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus it is so described.
For this very reason, it is the "reaper" (*nikṛntana*) because it cuts through the supreme latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
It is the "universal *vajra*" (*viśvavajra*) consisting of the five-colored vital winds (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

As it has been said: "Having expelled the breath, which consists of the five cognitions and has the nature of the five elements, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose in the form of a mass as a great jewel of five colors; this is known as *prāṇāyāma*."

Having meditated on one's own mantra within the heart, one should place the mind upon the drop (*bindu*); at the tip of the nose, there is that which is called the mustard seed—this is the visualization for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). It is taught by the Buddhas that five rays abide within this breath control.
The wise practitioner of yoga should always diligently contemplate the five-colored breath at the tip of the nose as the visualization for *prāṇāyāma*.

He is the Holder of the Universal Vajra (*viśvavajradhara*) because he holds—that is, renders motionless—the movement of the five Tathāgatas, such as Akṣobhya, and the five goddesses, such as Locanā, which circulate through the left and right nostrils. He is the Vajrin because he maintains indivisible gnosis in the form of smoke, mirages, and radiant appearances.
He is the Single Vajrin (*ekavajrī*) because of his non-dual gnosis through the yoga of union (*dvandvayoga*).
He is the Vanquisher of Strife (*raṇañjaha*) because he abandons the "strife" (*raṇa*) of sporting in the pleasure of conceptualization within the lap of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*).
6. Fierce-eyed with vajra-flames, with hair like vajra-flames,
the vajra-penetration, the great penetration, hundred-eyed, with eyes like vajras.
Regarding "Vajrajvālā" (Blazing Vajra):

because of the blazing of the Wisdom Caṇḍālī, there is a "vajra-flame" equal to a mirror-image reflection (*ādarśa-pratisenā*); he is thus described as one whose formidable, jagged [form] consists of the vision of great bliss through the eyes, such as the flesh of the eyes and so forth.

Because it is indivisible like a vajra-flame, it grows upon the head; thus, he is "Vajrajvālāśiroruha" (He Whose Head-Hair is Vajra-Flame). Because of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the vajra enters the *uṣṇīṣa*. Through the cessation of the vital and downward-moving breaths (*prāṇāpāna*), there is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of resonance, vibration, and so forth; through union with that, there is "Vajrāveśa" (Vajra-Possession), meaning the bestower of the initiation of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the three realms. Because of great bliss, he is the nature of all phenomena; thus, he is "Mahāveśa" (Great Possession).
He is "Hundred-eyed" (Śatākṣa) because he possesses the knowledge that experiences divine tactile bliss, being free from all [wrong] views;
he is "Vajra-eyed" (Vajralocana) because his vision is unimpeded in seeing the universe, transcending the eyes of flesh and so forth.

His body consists of hair-tips as hard as adamant; his form is composed of a single hair as firm as adamant; he has the onset of adamantine tips on his nails; and his skin is dense with the essence of adamant.
*Vajra-roma* (Adamantine Hair).

The sprout of the channels that carry semen within the three and a half million body hairs is the natural radiance (*prakṛtyābhāsa*); that itself is the body by its pervasiveness (*tanurābhogena*). His body is of adamant hair (*vajromā*), a beautiful body (*suratanu*).

"Adamant" (*vajra*) is indivisible gnosis; that very gnosis is like a hair (*roma*) because it emerges continuously, and he whose single, non-dual body or form (*vigraha*) is thus, is one whose body is the innate space (*sahajākāśatanu*). This is the meaning.

The "Vajrakoṭinakhārambha" (the beginning of the diamond-point nails) refers to the fact that it is commenced by means of the nails—which, like diamond points, possess the qualities of red and white, being the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) drops—from which [the practice] begins; this is the meaning of the *jñānakāya*.

He is one whose skin is of diamond essence (*vajrasārā*), unchanging (*nirvikārā*), dense (*ghanā*), and uninterrupted (*nirantarā*), hanging down as bliss, and whose tongue is the *vastra* channel, consisting of the bliss of touch.
The glorious one who dwells in a garland of vajras, adorned with vajra ornaments,
whose roar is the great laugh "Hā hā," the sound of the vajra, the six-syllabled one.

"O wearer of the vajra-garland" (*vajramālādhara*): the garment refers to the locations on the body such as the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*. The innate arising (*sahajotpatti*) through the sequence of dissolution, enjoyment, and so forth—namely, the garland of vajras and the garland of innate drops (*bindus*)—is that which he wears; thus he is the "wearer of the vajra-garland," the glorious possessor of non-dual knowledge.
Adorned with vajra ornaments by virtue of being the nature of the semen (*śukra*) of supreme unchanging bliss pervading all limbs;

possessing the "loud laughter" (*aṭṭahāsa*)—the expansion (*vikāsa*) consisting of the sound "hā hā" produced from the bliss of embracing a divine maiden; he is called *Nirghoṣa* because he has gone beyond external sounds; the meaning is that he is the self-arisen bliss within, the sound of bliss.

And it has been said: Victorious is that Conqueror, the Sambhogakāya, whose body is the nature of gnosis; he who dwells between the sun and moon on the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā; by a mere fragment of whose command the two winds perform their respective functions in union; for those who take delight in the taste of the bliss experienced through the mind and other faculties, he appears as an indescribable sound of bliss within; his intellect is bound to the Great Twilight (mahāsaṃdhyā), variegated by the luster of the sun and moon; he attains identity with the world cherished in the time beyond the unsurpassed; he shines as the beloved woman, the singular resonance of the bliss of play in the state of equal flavor (samarasa); victorious is that Jina.

The drops of nectar together with those consonants and those sixteen vowels—both of which flash forth and withdraw; and from whom, even as they dissolve, there arises a clamor surging up from the depths of the netherworld—the Lord of the Realm of Enjoyment, manifested throughout the entire pillar of the universe, the Thunderbolt-Wielder whose celestial drum resounds, is victorious! Thus, because his body pervades all space and is the source of great bliss, it is the "Thunderbolt-Sound" (Vajraghoṣa).
Because he experiences the bliss of the imperishable (*akṣara-sukha*) within the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), he is the "Six-Syllabled One" (*Ṣaḍakṣara*).
Mañjughoṣa is the Great Sound, the single roar of the three worlds, the great one whose resonance extends to the limits of the realm of space, the best among those who possess voice. (9–10)
Thus are the verses on the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*): "Mañjughoṣa [is] with ten [syllables] plus one quarter.

Because the *nāda* has become integrated within the gnosis and consciousness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the drop (*bindu*) that have arrived at all the wheels (*cakras*), he is Mañjughoṣa, Mañjuśrī.
He is the Great Sound (*mahānāda*) because he has the nature of non-sound, abiding in the space at the center of the vajra-lotus.

He is "Sound" (*rava*) whose essence is the total luminosity of universal emptiness; he is one and without a second through the *āsphānaka* samādhi, which unifies the three appearances—such as the light of the three worlds—within the emptiness beyond emptiness (*śūnyātiśūnya*). Thus he is so described.
For this very reason, he is the Great One;

his voice is a pleasant sound whose culmination extends to the limit of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) through the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the eyes and other faculties, as well as of all phenomena.

Thus, he is the supreme among those possessing a voice regarding the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena. The Blessed One, who resides within the uṣṇīṣa at the center of the jewel, is the Drop of Bliss (*sukhabindu*). || 10 ||

The commentary on the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which takes the form of the supramundane truth-sphere (*lokottarasatyarūpa*) and the Buddha Vairocana, is provided by means of the ten and a quarter verses that establish the unobstructed state of the heart-pervading life-channel (*prāṇavāhināḍī*), the seven channels, and the four channels carrying feces, urine, semen, and blood.

[Verse 1: The Wisdom of Discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is suchness, the reality of selflessness, the limit of existence (*bhūtakoṭi*), the syllable-less, emptiness, the Bull among Speakers, and the one whose roar is profound and vast.

With the forty-two and a half verses beginning with “Suchness” (*tathatā*) and ending with “the flame of gnosis is most radiant” (*suprabhāsvara*), he expresses praise for the discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) by way of the Amitābha Buddha, who is the perfectly pure aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). “Suchness”:
suchness is the flow of the *avadhūti* through the reversal of the left and right channels.
And it is said: “By virtue of the nature of the channels and so forth, and through union with the reality (*tattva*) of the deity,”
This is their supreme, pure essential nature: the absence of intrinsic existence.
That which is the unity of wisdom and means, the single vow of all aspects, is the Avadhūtī; having shaken off the self, it is considered the Middle Way.
"Due to the lack of discernment regarding the connection with conceptualizations of beginning, middle, and end, that pure, crystal-like radiance is the Avadhūtīka."

The "reality" (*bhūta*) of the elements (*bhūta*), such as earth and so forth, is their selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is the non-apprehension of a self or anything belonging to a self (*ātmātmīya*).

That very reality is the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*), the ultimate state of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-niṣṭhā*); he who possesses that is "established therein. The meaning is that his nature is bliss.
He is "indestructible" (*anakṣara*) because he is filled with the essence of unfailing compassion (*acyuta-karuṇā-rasa*).
Through the cessation of body, speech, and mind, the attainment of self-cognized bliss is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); because he reveals that, he is a proponent of emptiness (*śūnyatāvādī*).
Because he is the preeminent leader in destroying all the enemies that are the Māras, he is a bull (*vṛṣabha*), or [alternatively], a single step (*ekapada*).
He is one whose roar and exultation is the bliss inseparable from emptiness and compassion, which is profound and vast;

and likewise, Vimalaprabhā [explains] that the state of being empty is "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*): the knowable, whether past or future, is empty; the vision of that is its state, emptiness, which is profound and vast because of the absence of past and future.
He is sublime because he perceives the past and the future.
He is the great-sounding conch of Dharma, the great drum of Dharma,
the nirvana of non-abiding, and the drum of Dharma in the ten directions.

It is the Dharma-conch (dharmaśaṅkha) because it is accompanied by pure drops of nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*), because it has arisen from the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), because the teaching of the Dharma is like an echo, and because, like a conch, it is stainless.

The king of thought, consisting of the drops of great bliss (*mahāsukha-bindu*), passes through the interior of the lotus into the nose; there, I know Śrī Heruka—the nature of all the world—as the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) arisen from the *vajra* in the form of the ocean of milk, according to the statement that he is the "great ocean.
He is called the "Great Sound" because he is the form of the sound of selfless bliss (*niḥsvabhāva-sukha*) which bestows the state of Buddhahood.

Because he is the nature of the light of Dharma that illuminates all phenomena, expanded through the samādhi of the Vajra of Speech consisting of all happiness, he is the "Gong of Dharma" (*gharmagaṇḍī*). Because he is the sound of the Dharma with the resonance of incomparable bliss, he is the "Great Drum" (*mahāraṇa*). He is the Joy of Cessation (*viramānanda*), yet because he is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he is not established [in a fixed state].

Since there is no Nirvana from falling from the tip of the jewel, and because that [fall] does not exist for him, he is one for whom both non-establishment and Nirvana are present. Thus he is described.

Because he reveals the auspicious bliss of the Dharma of unsurpassed joy, he is the drum of Dharma in the ten directions. || 2 || Formless yet possessing form, unchanging, manifold in form, and mind-made;
he is the glory that illuminates all forms, the bearer of every reflection. || 3 ||

"Formless" (*arūpa*) means that because all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*), as well as ignorance (*avidyā*), have ceased to appear due to being grounded in space, there exists no form (*rūpa*) distinct from its essential nature (*prakṛti-svarūpa*); thus, through the state of total integration with the Dharma-body and the Form-body (*rūpakāya*), it possesses form by virtue of having a non-turbid nature.
He is *Agra* (Foremost) because he has the nature of crushing all Māras by virtue of being the support for the solar disk that brings joy to the heart;
he is *Nānārūpa* (Multiform) because, within the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*), he exists in the form of the natural outflow (*nisyanda*) of the blissful sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
and he is *Manomaya* (Mind-made) because his nature is the perfect awakening in a single instant (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodhi*).

Because of being free from attachment, and because earth, water, fire, air, space, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind appear as objects of individual self-awareness, there is the manifestation of all forms.

Through the vision of the universal image (*viśvabimba*), the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*)—which is non-different from the infinite-infinite gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*)—appears within the black line; thus, he is said to "hold all reflections.
And it is said: "That which is situated within gold, silver, jewels, conch, stone, coral, lapis lazuli, copper, silver, and so forth..."
For in that regard, it is just as the single moon alone appears with its form pervading the interior of the sky.
Thus, that Lord indeed, whose nature is the vajra of mind, abides in manifold ways among the multitudes of living beings;
he is imperishable, possessing the form of the universe within his own self, consisting of illusion, and pervading all worlds. Thus [ends the section].
The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti: Invincible, of great majesty, the Great Lord of the three realms.
This great and exalted banner of Dharma, established upon the Path, is raised high;
it is "unassailable" because it cannot be carried away by any conceptual constructions.
Because he is the embodiment of the ultimate fulfillment of the two accumulations of non-dual merit and wisdom, he is called the Great Lord (*maheśākhya*).

Within the three realms—known as the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies—he is the Great Sovereign (*maheśvara*), the Gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*), who is most exalted and lofty because he is free from conceptual construction; thus, he is Noble (*ārya*).

They are called *mārga* (paths) because they are sought after (*mṛgyante*). Because he abides there in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) within the pericarp (*kaṇikā*) of the lotuses of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), he stands upon the elevated path.

Because he has conquered all afflictions (*kleśa*) in the jewel-center (*varaṭaka*), he is the banner (*ketu*) of the Dharma—the jewel of reality (*tattva-ratna*)—and because his bliss is inexpressible, he is the flag (*dhvaja*); thus, he is the "Dharma-banner" (*dharmaketu*). Because of the non-duality of Dharma and bliss, and because he manifests as infinite reflections of the immeasurable Buddha-forms abiding in the expanse of space (*ākāśadhātu*), he is the "Great Arising. He is thus described as one "in whom there is the full blossoming of bliss. 4.
He whose body is the sole youth of the three worlds, the elder, the ancient, the Lord of Creatures,
the bearer of the thirty-two marks, the beloved, the beauty of the three worlds.
(5) Regarding the phrase "he whose body is the sole youth of the three worlds":

The "three worlds" (*trailokya*) refers to the three bodies (*kāyatraya*); that which is one with them is the non-dual body of great bliss (*mahāsukhakāya*). That itself is the "youth" (*kumāra*), because, in the form of the *dharmadhātu*, it is devoid of transformation. He whose "limb" (*aṅga*)—the cause of all origination—is that very youth is called "one whose limb is the unique youth of the three worlds. This means he is the embodiment of bliss arisen from the divine seal (*divyamudrā*). Because he has reached the excellence of the seals mentioned previously and because he is the eldest among all accomplishments (*siddhi*), he is called the "Elder" (*sthavira*), according to the sequence of the *Mahārāja-samādhi*.
He is the "Elder" (*vṛddha*) because he consists of the wisdom of a Buddha;

he is the "Lord of Creatures" (*prajāpati*) because, through the awakening of gnosis, he brings forth all beings as the image of gnosis consisting of the luminosity that transcends the fourth state (*turyātīta*). Because his form is characterized by the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) which transcends the fifteen digits beginning with the first day of the waxing moon, he possesses the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*); thus, he is the "Bearer of the Thirty-two Marks."

He is "the Beloved" (*kānta*) because he maintains the two types of sixteen joys through the sequence of concealment and revelation, and because he is desired by all people due to the single flavor of all phenomena; he is "the Beautiful One" (*sundara*) because, through the manifestation of self-consecration, he is like a wish-granting tree for the three worlds in his capacity as the three worlds.
And it is said: "The Teacher, endowed with the thirty-two marks and the Lord possessing the eighty secondary characteristics, dwells in Sukhāvatī within the womb of a woman under the name Śukra."
Then, O Body, out of compassion for all sentient beings, you manifested a great emanation-body endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks.

One hundred thousand words regarding the path of pride have been spoken, and furthermore, it has been stated in the *Lakṣaṇīya*: "Without that which is accompanied by the drop of nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*), there can be no bliss; and having abandoned bliss, he would not exist.
The Blessed One takes the form of semen (*śukra*); that bliss is known as the beloved woman (*kāminī*)."
This is not the domain of the Pratyekabuddhas nor of the Śrāvakas;
it is the domain of the Sons of the Buddha, the state arisen from the Vajra-lotus.
Thus, may this entire world behold the divine drama whose nature consists of the five Buddhas.
"Behold! He, named Supreme Great Bliss, dances as one with manifold flavors.

Thus [is he] the Teacher of the qualities of worldly knowledge, the Teacher of the world, the fearless one, the Lord, the Protector from the three worlds, the Refuge, the Savior, and the unsurpassed one.

The knowledge of the worlds, such as the eyes and so forth, is the unobscured manifestation; its quality is the lack of defilement by the faults of saṃsāra despite the enjoyment of the five objects of desire. The teacher of that is the *lokajñānaguṇācārya*.
Because he bestows [initiations] up to the fourth consecration according to the disciple's capacity, he is the *lokācārya*.
Because he performs the welfare of the world through the radiation of various forms without cessation, he is *viśārada*, meaning fearless; the sense is that his knowledge of bliss is indivisible.
Because he is well-established through non-dual yoga, he is the *Nātha* (Lord);

because he protects according to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he is the protector; because he is eternally of an undecaying nature by virtue of having a single form within conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), he is the *Trātā* (Savior). Because he is of the nature of the manifestation of emptiness in all its aspects, he is the *Āpta* (Attainer) of the three worlds, even while standing as a teacher of stainless knowledge for those seized by the demons of the bliss of transmigration. Even while enjoying the five objects of desire, his defects are exhausted; thus he is the *Trailokāpta* (Attainer of the Three Worlds).
Because he brings the five elements to the culmination of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he is the Protector (*tāyin*);

he is one whose continuum of knowledge consists of bliss. He is called the "Protector" because of his union with that [bliss] without interruption; and he is "eternal," meaning he is of the nature of the fourth moment.
Because he is of the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) pervading the three worlds, he is unsurpassed (*niruttara*).
The enjoyment that fills the expanse of space, an ocean of omniscient wisdom,
the shatterer of the shell of the egg of ignorance, and the breaker of the cage of existence.

The sky (*gagana*) is the central pericarp (*varaṭaka*) resulting from the union of the lotus and the vajra; its expanse (*ābhoga*) is its width. He whose perfect enjoyment (*samyagbhoga*) therein consists of partaking in non-dual bliss is thus "one who enjoys the expanse of the sky" (*gaganābhogasambhoga*).
Because he is a mine of the jewels of the wisdom of the Great Vajradhara, which consists of the abandonment of body, speech, and mind, he is the ocean of omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñānasāgara*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the shell of the egg (*aṇḍakoṣa*), being the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence and the cause for the arising of the world.
The destroyer of that [bondage] is existence (*bhava*), which brings about the state of oneness with great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and pierces the body and speech.

Its shell is ignorance (*avidyā*); the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti* is the means for this, as it is the non-recognition of the mind's own nature, which is itself a cage because it is the cause of not escaping.
Because it tears that [bond] apart, it is the "Tearer of the Cage of Existence."
He who has pacified all afflictions, whose crown is the consecration of primordial wisdom, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra,
and who is adorned as a perfectly awakened Buddha.

*Śamita* means "pacified," referring to one by whom all afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), including the twelve links beginning with ignorance, have been brought to a state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*). He has mastered the five objects of desire;

the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) constitute *saṃsāra*, which is itself an ocean because it is agitated by passion and other defilements. One who goes to its further shore—the attainment of the unobscured aggregates and so forth—is thus called a "crosser to the far shore of the ocean of *saṃsāra*" (*saṃsārārṇavapāraga*).

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is of the nature of the fourth bliss; it is that which is consecrated (*abhiṣicyate*), made free from obscurations (*nirāvaraṇī kriyate*), by means of which the aggregates, elements, and so forth are [purified]—thus it is the "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*). It is the fourth drop (*bindu*), and he who has that very drop as his ornament is "such" (*tathā*). Alternatively, he is "such" because he ornaments the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*samyaksambuddhas*).

By this, the Blessed One in the form of the fourth consecration is described. And it is said: "Even in the context of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the Great Bliss must be protected for one who is devoted to the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*)."
The awakening mind [is attained] by those of firm vows.

By protecting this [mind] as if it were [the seed of] Buddhahood in this very life, the Lord of Yogis must protect the fourfold mind of living beings—which, together with the drops of nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*), resides within the three types of existence—within the center of the drop, for the sake of liberation, so that it may bestow the fruit of true bliss and be all-pervasive.

If the drop is liberated, where is there liberation for yogis in that seed of birth which has attained supreme bliss? Therefore, the happiness of cyclic existence in this world must always be avoided by ascetics, even for a moment. Thus.

And it is said in the *Samāja*: "When the bodhicitta, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen, and when the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, from where could blameless accomplishment arise?"

And in the *Vimalaprabhā*, as well as in the *Śrījñānavajrasamuccayayogatantra*: "One who is complete in the equipment of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and endowed with merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñāna*)."
The perfectly awakened ones existing in the three times have attained the ten perfections; by this, the wheel of Dharma has been set in motion by all the perfectly awakened ones.

When the lightning-flames of fire, struck by the winds, melt the moon at the crown of the head, each drop that falls from it and is restrained at the throat, heart, navel, and secret place—whatever vibration and fluidity of the drop reaches the diamond-jewel (kuliśamaṇi) and is firmly restrained at the tip of the banner (dhvajāgra), if that wisdom-moment of ignorance bestows bliss through the non-emission of the stream of drops; [then one attains the state].

Furthermore, this [wind], which has the nature of waking and dreaming, and the nature of deep sleep and the fourth state (*turya*), resides in the body and moves through the objects of the senses while merged with the breath; it moves while remaining motionless, merged in the mind, and established in gnosis. Through attachment to women, even for a moment, when the *bodhicitta* is melted, the mind—controlled by the wind—certainly arises in four ways in succession, beginning with the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
