"O Ka, Kha, Ga! For one whose white [semen] flows rapidly through attachment to wisdom, by what means can there be an increase in happiness?
When does the flower fall during the springtime, and by what means does the fruit of the mango tree appear? Thus it is said.
"Of all illusions, the illusion of woman alone is praised;

for this very distinction of the three types of knowledge is clearly perceived right here. Thus, the portion of night is the light, while the brilliance of the sun's rays is the light of day; the twilight is the perception of light, which is repeatedly joined with its own inherent natures.
There is neither night, nor twilight, nor day for him who is by nature liberated; this is the moment of awakening described by the supreme Guru, accessible only to yogis.

The darkness of night has perished and the entire twilight radiance has vanished; when the sun does not yet rise, during this pure moment, may the preeminent teacher reveal the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) to his disciple through the vision of external awakening that destroys the cataracts [of ignorance]. By means of the moment of a Buddha’s awakening, he attains some indescribable supreme state, the bliss of the inner self. Thus ends the *Yogācārābhisambodhi*, the jewel-like means for achieving happiness.
The middle way is perfect awakening, and at the end of death it is devoid of characteristics; thus,
there is no fear of the three realms of existence,
and there is happiness.
And indeed, in the *Gītākośa*,
the portion [of the text] in manuscript *kha* is distinguished from that in manuscript *ca*.
Just as the moment of the goal to be accomplished is beneficial.

ka. kha. Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgītiḥ. Thus, that which is mutually inseparable and has become unified as one, characterized by the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), is called the fourth.
O, from the perspective of form (*rūpa*):
the Master [Guhyasamāja], the Secret [Wisdom] (*guhya-prajñā*), and the Fourth Fruit are "formless" (*arūpatā*).
Therefore, how indeed can these great ones—who recognize the objective field (*lakṣya*) as being between the Great Joy (*mahāsukha*) and the Cessation of Emission (*paramavirama*)—be otherwise?
Even if they were to exert effort to establish a connection with the word,
this fourth sprinkling of theirs would not be applicable here;
for if [the result] has already been accomplished in its own nature as the third [moment], it exists in the form of a fruit.

Since the effect is already established at the outset, what is the use of a cause hereafter? This watering has been demonstrated for the sake of its accomplishment, not by means of any other cause; for if its establishment were already present beforehand, why would it need to come into being again?

If it is argued that the watering [of the cause] is mentioned later for the sake of the production of the fruit, then how can there be a distinction in the sequence of the breaths (*āśvāsa*) between the Buddha and Vajradhara? If the breath of Vajradhara comes first and that of the Buddha later, then by what means is the relationship of cause and fruit made manifest? It cannot be by following the order of the verse, because the subject matter (*lakṣya*) is not otherwise than its true meaning; rather, the meaning of the verse must be construed in accordance with the subject matter itself, as is appropriate.
It is refuted:
if it were [existent] in reality.
Furthermore:
"Indeed, the defined object is not led elsewhere simply out of deference to a verse;
for in reality, there is no difference here between the Śrīsamāja and the Hevajra."

The distinctions therein have been described according to the different types of means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). If it is argued that "the initiations (*seka*) therein are said to be threefold," that refers to the worldly [initiation]. However, although the supramundane initiation (*lokottarābhiṣeka*) has also been mentioned, it has not been made explicit.
"That fourth [empowerment] is to be known through the empowerment of the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna).
Thus, in order to understand this skillfully, one must indeed serve a true guru.
Therefore, those who, by some fortunate encounter, speak of the target within [the center], [should be served].

Accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, it is nevertheless established by both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*); there is no doubt that this is so.
If it is asked, "How is the connection of the verse established since the *sahaja* is included within [the others]?"—
there is no such fault, for there is a connection with the meaning of the verse.

When, between *paramānanda* and *viramānanda*, the *parama* and *virama* occur in the middle relative to *ānanda* and *sahajānanda*, then, by the rule of employing the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of disregard (*anādara*) in the phrase "between *parama* and *virama*" and so forth.
Alternatively, having observed that "the goal is through the practice of cultivation" (bhāvanādṛtyā), make it firm;
for there is the statement in the eighth chapter of the *Śrīhevajra*: "Again, likewise, up to the end of the *virama*" (1.8.24).

Since it is clearly understood that the "end of the *virama*" (*viramānta*) is the *sahaja*, and since it is said, "All this bliss of sexual union is the means to happiness for the All-Knowing One," it is indeed perfectly consistent.

These three joys (*ānanda*) have the nature of the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) that serves as their cause; thus, the nature of the pleasure of those three joys is the means (*upāya*) and the cause. Through this [means], whether directly or indirectly, one becomes all-knowing (*sarvavit*), having the nature of innate joy. By means of the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), there is detachment (*virāga*), and from the remainder, innate joy remains.
Thus, because bliss is the nature of the universal,
the meaning is that the innate fruit (*sahaja*) is devoid of these three [lower] joys.
Likewise: "Neither passion nor dispassion, nor even the middle, is perceived.
Passion (*rāga*) is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because its characteristic is attachment.
Because it is distinguished by the conceptualization of bliss, detachment (*virāga*) is the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*).
The mere middling bliss of the middle channel is the first joy (*prathamānanda*).
It is said that "it is not perceived."
The meaning is that these three are not perceived as being innate (*sahaja*).
As stated in the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*: "One should perceive [the state] beginning with the Cessation (*virama*), and that is devoid of the three joys (*ānanda*)."
The meaning is that one should perceive the innate (*sahaja*) within that [state] which has "cessation" (*virama*) as its beginning.
Likewise: "The supreme end, the middle, cessation, and the void-non-void are Heruka.
Here, the "supreme end" itself is the "middle," and it is called the "cause" in relation to the innate.
The meaning is that the fruit is the innate (*sahaja*), which is both empty and non-empty, and indivisible from emptiness and compassion.

However, as for those who, having described *virama* as dispassion characterized by detachment, maintain that the innate (*sahaja*) is the very object of focus between the supreme (*parama*) and *virama*, according to their opinion, the verses on the four joys arranged in sequence are as follows: "The first is mere joy (*ānanda*); supreme joy (*paramānanda*) is the second;
the third is called *virama*; and the fourth is remembered as the innate (*sahaja*)."
The Joy of Variety (*vicitra*) is the first joy; the Supreme Joy (*paramānanda*) is in the maturation (*vipākaka*);

the Joy of Cessation (*viramānanda*) is in the dissolution (*vimarda*); and the Innate Joy (*sahajānanda*) is in the signless (*vilakṣaṇa*). The joys of the Master (*ācārya*), the Secret (*guhya*), the Wisdom (*prajñā*), and the Fourth should be known in their respective order; those four are likewise [to be understood].
By way of counting the sprinklings (*secanasaṃkhyā*):

the bliss of desire (*kāmānanda*), accompanied by trembling and the loss of syllables, constitutes the first union; the full arising of power (*śaktyudbhava*) is indeed the second, which is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); the flame-point (*jvālābindu*) and dizziness (*ghūrma*) constitute the third, which is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*); and the awakening-sound (*bodhānāda*) and sleep constitute the fourth, which is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
How, then, is the meaning of such passages explained?
Likewise: "The first is mere bliss (*ānandamātra*); the second is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*);

the third is called the cessation (*virama*); and the fourth is known as the innate (*sahaja*). It must be maintained that the *Caturmudrānvaya-grantha*, together with the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, was not composed by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
The Kumbha is the secret initiation; the Prajñā is the wisdom initiation. Furthermore, Mahāmudrā is designated as its wisdom.
From that comes the mutable, then the immutable, then vibration, and after that, the non-vibration.
The three consecrations correspond respectively to the purification of body, speech, and mind;
the fourth is the purification of gnosis, which purifies body, speech, and mind.
It is the mature, the aged, and the fourth is Prajāpati.
The touch of the breasts and limbs of a young woman and the bliss of the emission of the bodhicitta—
because he experiences such bliss, he is called a "child" (bāla), having been consecrated by the breasts (payodhara).
From the prolonged striking of the secret place, knowledge arises and the bliss of the emission of the bodhicitta occurs.
He is the mature one, consecrated in the secret; for from that secret he has attained bliss.
The bliss produced after a long time from the striking of the secret [place], which throbs at the tip of the vajra—
that is the "consecration of the wisdom-knowledge" (prajñājñānābhiṣeka), because that elder has attained throbbing.

That which is born from passion for Mahāmudrā is the one consecrated by Great Wisdom; since he is the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*), he is to be known as Vajrasattva, the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), who is the Samayasattva. Through non-vibration, he is bliss;
he has attained the state of non-vibration.
Thus Janaka is the Bodhisattva of all Protectors, non-dual and immutable.
The application of the Vaṣṭra [mantra] may be of four kinds.
Thus, there is also the rule regarding the co-emergent (*sahaja*): the co-emergent bliss is called the fourth.
And it has been said: "What is the designation for that which is the fourth co-emergent bliss?"
Thus, the venerable Saraha has taught the knowledge that arises from the observation of the four moments of innate bliss.
Thus ends the section on "the shifting garment."
The Void, the Great Void, and the Great-Great Void as the third;
the fourth is distinguished by the division of fruit and cause.

All-empty, the alleviator of the suffering of the three types of suffering, the limit of the three, the infinite, attained to the three liberations, liberated from all obscurations, and having reached equality with space.

The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "Triduḥkha" refers to the three—body, speech, and mind—which are suffering due to being dependent on the one hundred and sixty innate [afflictions]. The "going" (*gamana*) toward their suffering—that is, the lack of realization of their true nature—is by means of the power of the knowledge of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*); he is the "goer" (*gamaka*). For this very reason, he is the "end of the three" (*tryanta*), the fourth, the infinite (*ananta*), who flows as the union (*yuganaddha*), because, upon the cessation of all winds of conceptualization, he is non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).

He is called "one who has attained the threefold liberation" because he goes to liberation from the three—attachment, aversion, and delusion; and being liberated from all obscurations, by virtue of his natural luminosity, he has attained equality with space.
Transcending the stains of all afflictions, having gone beyond the path of the three times, he is the great elephant among all beings, the crest-jewel upon the crests of all virtues. ||10||
By beholding the reflections of the entire universe, he has transcended all stains of affliction (*kleśa*) through the removal of every defilement;
because the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is inexhaustible, he is free from the movement of the past, future, and present times, having reached that which is beyond the three times;
and by perceiving the non-duality of all aspects, he is a great elephant among all sentient beings due to his victory in the battle against infinite afflictions.
The Blessed Buddhas—those who have attained the desired goal, who have obtained the Dharma, and who are the crest-jewels and crown-gems of virtue—their crown is the illustrious Sahaja-bindu.
Completely liberated from all substrates of existence, firmly established on the path of space,
he is the bearer of the great wish-fulfilling gem, the sovereign lord, the most excellent of all jewels.

"Free from all substrates" (*sarvopadhivinirmukta*) means being unconstructed by the conceptualizations of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; through the manifestation of the limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), one sees the universal image (*viśvabimba*) as the emptiness of all aspects with the eyes of flesh and so forth. For other sentient beings, seeing emptiness is like being born blind.
Therefore, "liberated from all substrates," he is "well-established in the path of space," which is emptiness, abiding by means of non-conceptual yoga.
And it has been said: "This cultivation of space is, namely, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."

Thus, he is the bearer of the great *cintāmaṇi* because he grants the accomplishment of all desired aims; he is the bearer of the innate (*sahaja*) drop (*bindu*), meaning that his nature is the innate *prajñāpāramitā* which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); for he bestows the unsurpassed bliss that is supreme among the drops of body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings.
For this very reason, He is all-pervasive and omnipresent.
He is a vast and flourishing great wish-fulfilling tree, the supreme and most auspicious jar;
he is the performer of the welfare of all sentient beings, a benefactor who desires their well-being and is affectionate toward them. ||12||
Because it grants the accomplishment of the supramundane goals desired [by beings], it is a great kalpa-tree;
it is flourishing and abundant.
Because it surpasses the auspicious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*), it is the supreme great vase of fortune (*mahābhadrakalaśa*);

for this very reason, it accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings effortlessly. Together with the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, it is the agent that brings happiness to all sentient beings through the gift of Dharma.
One whose nature it is to seek what is beneficial and conducive to future happiness is a "seeker of welfare" (hitaiṣī);
because he possesses love for all beings as if they were his only son, he is "affectionate toward sentient beings" (sattvavatsala).
He knows the auspicious and the inauspicious; he knows the time, he knows the occasion, and he is the master of the occasion.
He is the pervasive lord who knows the faculties of sentient beings, he knows the proper moment, and he is skilled in the three liberations.
"Pure" (śubhā) means that he knows both the pure and the impure in the form of great bliss; thus, he is "the knower of the pure and impure.
He knows the time—the moment of awakening to great bliss—thus he is "the knower of time" (kāla-jña).
One who knows the fourfold commitment (*samaya*) consisting of body, speech, mind, and gnosis is "thus" [described].
This was stated by Vajrapāṇipāda: "Through the kiss of wisdom (*prajñā*), the moment of bliss (*ānanda-kṣaṇa*) occurs; that is the commitment of the body (*kāya-samaya*).
By the entry of the cloth into the lotus, the moment of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-kṣaṇa*) occurs; that is the commitment of speech (*vāk-samaya*)."
In the lotus, through the expansion of the cloth, is the moment of *viramānanda*, the commitment of mind (*cittasamaya*).
When the *bodhicitta* has entered the *vajramaṇi*, there is the moment of *sahajānanda*, the fourth, the commitment of gnosis (*jñānasamaya*);
for this very reason, one is a possessor of commitments (*samayin*).
He is "all-pervading" (*vibhu*) because he possesses the nature of that [reality], which consists in the pervasion of both mundane and supramundane objects.

He is the "knower of the faculties of beings" (*sattvendriyajña*) because he fully understands the faculties of all sentient beings who have been consumed by the moments of the four joys (*caturānandakṣaṇa*).
Likewise, he is so called because he knows the time for the gift of Dharma and other such acts effortlessly (*anābhogenaiva*).
Due to its archaic nature, there is a short vowel;

through the gateway of the divine mudrās of the resolution of action, the knower—the wise one—attains the triad of liberations consisting of the accomplishments of the *bhūcarī*, *khecarī*, and *mahāmudrā*.
He is the possessor of virtues, the knower of virtues, the knower of dharma, the praised one, the source of auspiciousness,
the most auspicious among all auspicious things, and he is glory, fortune, fame, and goodness.
He is "possessed of qualities" (*guṇin*) because of his connection with the inseparable, innate qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;
he is a "knower of qualities" (*guṇajña*) through the thorough knowledge of the true nature of body, speech, and mind.
"Knower of Dharma" (dharmajña) means one who tastes the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of supramundane phenomena (*lokottaradharma*).
"Praiseworthy" (*praśasta*) means that by the sequence of the arising of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), he brings peace to the entire world; thus, the meaning is "Gnosis-Body" (*jñānakāya*).
"Source of Auspiciousness" (*maṅgalodaya*) means that from him arises the emergence of non-worldly auspiciousness.

Among the three types of bliss, the fourth, innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), is auspicious; it is *kīrti* (fame) because it is luminous and is proclaimed to be the form of indestructible bliss at all times,
and it is *lakṣmī* (fortune) because it is the basis of all prosperity.

Your fame is stainless because it arises from the abandonment of conceptual construction; it is radiant because of its nature as splendor; and it is auspicious because it consists of a collection of all happiness.
He is the great festival, the great relief, the great bliss, and the great delight;
he is honor, hospitality, prosperity, joy, glory, and the lord of fame.

It is called "Great Festival" (*mahotsava*) because it consists of uninterrupted festivals of bliss; it is called "Great Breath" (*mahāśvāsa*) because, through the manifestation of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the breath has entered the *avadhūtī* and thus transcends the world.
He is *Mahānanda* because he is the nature of the bliss of the world through the manifestation of the ineffable, non-dual Dharma-bliss;
he is *Mahārati* because he nourishes all sentient beings with great bliss;
he is *Satkāra* because he is worthy of honor as the very essence of great bliss; and the meaning is that he fills all the channels (*nāḍī*) of the body with the fluid of the bodhicitta.
It is *satkṛti* (honoring) because it consists of the honor of the ultimate consecration (*paramārthābhiṣeka*);
it is *bhūti* (prosperity) because it is uninterrupted bliss;
and it is *pramodaśrī* (the glory of joy) because of its association with the exhilaration of body, speech, and mind.
The meaning is: one who possesses happiness, mental well-being, fame, sovereignty, and so forth; that is, a lord of glory.

The most excellent, the giver of boons, the supreme, the worthy refuge, the best of shelters, the embodiment of wisdom, the great enemy of fear, the most eminent, the destroyer of all fears without exception. ||16||
"Vareṇya" means he is most excellent (*pravara*) because his form consists of wisdom purified in all its aspects;
"Varada" means the giver of boons, because he fulfills one's own intentions through non-conceptualization— that is to say, because he bestows the supreme radiance.
He is supreme because he is foremost in the inseparability of emptiness and compassion;
he is the refuge for the wretched who are dependent on conceptual constructions, for he protects them by teaching the knowledge of luminosity;
and he is the highest refuge because he brings about the form of the Great Mouth through the arising of great passion (*mahārāga*) that overcomes passion and the like.
Because it destroys the fear of the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of *saṃsāra*, it is the "Great Destroyer of Fear" (*mahābhayāri*);

for this very reason, it is the most excellent, as it completely eliminates all fear through the proliferation of conceptual constructs (*prapañca*) by means of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects (*sarvākāravaropeta-śūnyatā*), thereby destroying fear without remainder.

The emanation of various forms from the pure body occurs by the power of the inclinations of sentient beings; as it has been said: "Therefore, born yet not destroyed, having traversed even the three realms, the pure body of the Victor never abandons the welfare of sentient beings. The Lord of Victors is never constrained by karma;

likewise, I, Lokeśvara, am established in the field of karma within the abode of the three worlds like the sun, the giver of the path to sentient beings and the remover of the fear of hell—never any other god."
(Kāvyālaṅkāra-taraṅga 5.194)
He has a crest, wears a topknot, possesses matted locks, is shaven-headed, or wears a crown;
he is five-faced, has five tufts of hair, and is adorned with a crest of five rags. ||17||
"Śikhī" (the crested one):
through the manifestation of the factor of mindfulness, the innate Caṇḍālī blazes; because of that union, he is Śikhī.
Skin, flesh, and blood are connected to the mother-sun;

bone, sinew, and semen are connected to the father-moon. The union of these two is the *śikhaṇḍa* (crest); because he possesses this through the yoga of non-obstruction (*nirāvaraṇa-yoga*), he is Śikhaṇḍin.
Because he is bound by all phenomena—which, though appearing crooked and manifold, possess a single flavor—through yoga, he is Jaṭila (the one with matted hair).

He has a single form in all things by way of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*); he is *jaṭin* (having matted hair) because his hair is bound together; he is *mauṇḍa* (shaven-headed) due to the shaving away of all conceptual constructions and afflictions;
and he possesses a crown (*kirīṭin*) because of his connection with that great cranial protuberance (*mahauṣṇīṣa*).

He is "five-faced" (*pañcānana*) because he is the embodiment of the Dharmakūṭa consisting of the five Tathāgatas, and because the five winds—prāṇa and the rest—have been rendered free from obscuration; this means he has the nature of the five families (*pañcakula*).

He is likewise one whose "five crests" (*pañcaśikha*) consist of the characteristics of light (*āloka*), the manifestation of light (*ālokābhāsa*), the perception of light (*ālokopalabdhi*), luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), and the dharmadhātu.

He is "one whose crest is adorned with five locks of hair" (*pañcacīrakaśekhara*) because his form consists of the five states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (*turīya*), and that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*). || 17 ||

phīroṭi; kha.: prāṇāti.
Ka. [is] *svasupta*, Da. *susupta*.

Accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, he is a bearer of the great vow (*mahāvratadhara*), a wearer of matted hair (*mauñjī*), a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), and one whose vow is supreme (*vratottama*).
He is established in great austerity and penance (*mahātapastaponiṣṭha*), a graduate (*snātaka*), a descendant of Gautama (*gautama*), and a leader (*agraṇī*). (18)
Regarding "mahāvrata": it is so called; muñja is a type of grass, and from its connection with that [grass], it is called mauñjī.
Precisely because his bodhicitta is unfallen, he is a celibate (*brahmacārī*).
For that very reason, he is the supreme observer of vows (*vratottama*). He is such because he possesses that *bindu* through the process of absorption (*layīkaraṇa*).

He whose steadfastness in austerity is filled with supreme bliss is thus [described]. Because he has constantly bathed in the sky through great bliss, he is a *snātaka* (one who has performed the ritual ablution). He is Gautama because of that very supreme, imperishable bliss; he is Siddhārtha (one who has accomplished his purpose).
He is the foremost because he is innate bliss. || 18 ||

The knower of Brahman is the Brāhmaṇa; he is Brahmā, having attained the nirvāṇa of Brahman. He is liberation, the state of being liberated, the limb of liberation, emancipation, tranquility, and auspiciousness. || 19 ||
"Knower of Brahman" (brahmavid):
he is a knower of Brahman because he experiences [it] through identity with that (tattādātmyena).
"Brāhmaṇa": the syllable *haṃ* is the Brāhmaṇa; he is called a Brāhmaṇa because he carries away (*vahati*) the entire wind of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
He is Brahmā because his nature is that of the fourth face, which dwells unattached in space (*ākāśāsakta-vihāra*).
He is the bliss of Brahmā’s nirvāṇa (*brahmanirvāṇa*), according to the statement: "The bliss of Brahmā is nirvāṇa."
He has attained that;
liberation is due to its inseparability from emptiness.
Because it leads to indestructible bliss as far as space extends, it is the fourth meaning: liberation (*mokṣa*).
He for whom liberation itself is the constituent factor is "such" (tathā).
Through the removal of the bonds of passion and so forth, and by attaining the perfect thorough knowledge of great passion (*mahārāga*), the Blessed One is liberated.
And it has been said: "By passion the world is bound; by passion alone it is liberated."
For this is a perverted meditation, not understood by the Buddhist heretics.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, this *Nāmasaṅgīti* is such that by the very same portion of poison by which all living beings die, one who knows the reality of poison may dispel that poison with poison itself.
Just as those burned by fire are purified again by fire,
so too those burned by the fire of passion are purified by the fire of passion.
For by whatever fierce karma living beings are bound,
by that very same means they are generally released from the bondage of existence.
If the very tender sprout of the mind is not watered with the juices of sense-objects for the sake of purification,
how can it attain the state of a wish-fulfilling tree that pervades the sky and bestows fruits?
Some abandon sense-objects, while others make sense-objects non-obstructive.
"Some bulls among men, however, achieve awakening through sense objects alone.
Thus, tranquility (*śāntatā*) arises from the pacification of the mental disturbances such as the grasped and the grasper.
And it has been said: "The realm of nirvāṇa is tranquil [through] the practice of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*)."
Whatever happiness was attained by one's father, that very happiness one enjoys for oneself;
the happiness by which death occurs in this world is called meditative absorption (dhyāna).

Because its intrinsic nature is the gnosis of emptiness, the Gnosis-being of all Tathāgatas is auspicious (*śiva*); since it is always perfectly auspicious, the "semen" (*śukra*) is unbroken and auspicious. || 19 ||
Nirvāṇa, cessation, peace, the supreme good, the way out, the end; the ender of pleasure and pain, the ultimate goal, dispassion, and the state of tranquility. ||20||
Regarding "nirvāṇa":
it is called *nirvāṇa* because it is empty of the conceptual grasping of existence and non-existence.

It is "without support" (*nirālamba*) due to the absence of external objects; it is "cessation" (*nirvṛti*) because it has only that [inner reality] as its support; and it is "peace" (*śānti*) because its nature is the light of wisdom (*prajñā*) of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is uncontrived and self-cognizable.
Therefore, it is the supreme good (*śreyaḥ*).

It is called "departure" (*niryāṇa*) because all the perfectly awakened ones depart within it; it is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and it is the "end" (*antaka*) because it is ultimate bliss through the disappearance of all conceptual constructions.

Due to the absence of the emission of the seminal essence (*śukra-rajas*), and because pleasure and pain have become non-dual through wisdom and means, it is the culmination that brings an end to both pleasure and pain.
And it is said: "Indeed, having become weary of the accumulation of sins and merits, one should make the mind empty. Thus [it is said].
Where? In the *Dhāraṇī*.
Wherein? In the *Katarā*.
[The text] has been understood;
however, [in some versions], it is not.
kha. ga. ga. kurute | ka. kha. sukhaṃ | ka. kha. ṅa. antagaḥ |
kha. uncreated; ka. ga. the word "great" is absent; kha. da. departure.
O friend, there is no "great" [state] apart from this.

Because it consists of the nature of undecaying, great passion (*acyuta-mahārāga*) through the departure of ordinary dispassion (*prākṛta-vairāgya*), the Lord himself is dispassion (*vairāgya*) accompanied by the *amṛtakaṇikā*.

Through the disappearance of latent impressions (vāsanā) and by way of the manifestation of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is the destruction of the substratum (upadhikṣaya), because it consists of the perfectly pure gnosis of the realm of phenomena (suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna). || 20 ||
Unconquerable, incomparable, unmanifest, without appearance, stainless, partless, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, the seed, and free from outflows. || 21 ||
"Unconquerable" (ajaya): because of its luminosity (*prabhāsvaratva*), it is not conquered by conceptual constructions and the like; thus, it is unconquerable.
Because it does not fall away from great passion (*mahārāga*), it is devoid of any comparison with all other pleasures; thus, it is incomparable (*anupama*).
Because it is devoid of duality, the unmanifest is not of the nature of the manifest;
because it is luminous, it is without appearance;
and because it is untainted like space, it is stainless.
Because he has transcended the fifteen digits beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*), he is partless and without components.
Because his nature is the space of consciousness (*jñānākāśa*), he is all-pervading.
Because his nature is both stable and moving, he is omnipresent.
It is subtle because it is beyond the range of even the mind;
it is the seed, the gnosis of the dharmadhātu, because it generates all happiness through effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*);
and it is untainted (*anāsrava*) because it is to be personally realized within oneself. || 21 ||
Free from dust, stainless, immaculate, with faults expelled and free from affliction;
perfectly awakened, one whose self is enlightened, the omniscient, the all-knowing, the supreme.

"Arajara": because of the absence of the dust of passion (*rāga*), dispassion (*virāga*), and intermediate passion (*madhyarāga*), it is "dustless" (*araja*); it is the fourth, the Great Passion (*mahārāga*).
Because its nature is the purity of suchness (*tathatā-viśuddhi*), it is "stainless" (*viraja*).
It is stainless because of the absence of adventitious defilements;
it has expelled its faults because of the departure of all intrinsic natures;
and it is free from disease because of the destruction of the affliction of external distraction.
He is "perfectly awakened" (*suprabuddha*) because of his non-erroneous realization of the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
This means that he has transcended form and so forth, and is characterized by emptiness as awakened by compassion.
Because his nature is the luminosity that transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the Blessed One himself is primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
Because its nature is sublime and profound, it alone maintains the form of non-duality.
It is non-conceptual because even conceptualization regarding the knowledge of ultimate reality is absent.
And it has been said: "A wise person should not become attached even to conceptualization of the ultimate reality."
"For what difference is there in conceptual construction, whether it be toward the auspicious or even the inauspicious? [Thus it is said].

"ka" is the beginning.
ka. *gharmato'ti*, ga. *dharmatāmatīto'ti*. da.

The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti* is so called because it has emerged from the bliss of enjoying the five objects of desire without effort (*anābhoga*); he for whom there is no effort—that is, no activity of conceptual construction—is thus [described].
And it has been said: "The activity for the sake of others proceeds spontaneously (*anābhoga*) and continuously, sustained by former vows.

Thus, the Buddhas—known as the Nirmāṇakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Dharmakāya—who have arisen throughout the three times (past, present, and future) through the divisions of the three meditative absorptions during day, night, and the junctions of dawn, perform the activity of benefiting sentient beings, which consists of the experience of great bliss. Such is the meaning.
The Buddha is without beginning or end, the primordial Buddha, without causal succession;
he is the stainless single eye of gnosis, the embodiment of gnosis, the Tathāgata.

"Beginningless" means that, by virtue of being the nature of the gnosis of the *dharmadhātu*, it has no beginning or end— neither arising nor cessation, nor the moment of cessation nor the moment of death. One who is thus [designated] is a "Buddha," because of the realization of the equality of all phenomena.

Since the phenomena of affliction (*saṃkleśika*) and purification (*vaiyavadānika*) do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the term "aspect" (*ākāra*) has a negating sense.

Therefore, *Ādibuddha* means the primordial Buddha characterized by the bliss of the awakening through the net of illusion (*māyājālābhisambodhi*) consisting of one moment, five aspects, and twenty aspects.
He is such because he has cast away all phenomena characterized by subject and object, which consist of wisdom and means and follow after conceptual succession;
his knowledge is non-dual knowledge, which alone is the singular, peerless eye, for it bestows happiness upon all phenomena;
and he is stainless because he has abandoned all conceptual constructions.
Knowledge is the knowledge of emptiness; that very thing is *bhūti*, which is the manifestation of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*). One who possesses such [knowledge] is thus described.
Likewise, *tathatā* refers to the seals (*mudrā*) of action and so forth; one in whom the knowledge of bliss beginning with joy (*ānanda*) has reached that state is a *Tathāgata*.
Master of speech, great debater, king of speakers, bull among disputants, the best of those who speak, most excellent, lion of speakers, unconquered. || 25 ||
"Vāgīśvara" means that,

through the manifestation of the unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*), he nourishes all Buddhas who are the nature of every moment of consciousness; because he constantly manifests the letter *Ā* through the yoga of the churner and the churning, and because he is highly venerable among speakers, he is the "Great Speaker" (*Mahāvādī*).

By means of the application of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) in the form of the *manyanī* within all the channels (*nāḍī*), through the stream of *bodhicitta*, he nourishes all the sense-faculties and elements; thus,

by the application of the divine consort (*divyamudrā*), because he rejects the nirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas and others, he is the King of Speech (*vādirāṭ*), and because he proclaims non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), he is the Bull among Orators (*vādipuṅgava*).
He is the best of those who enter [the path] because of his perfect awakening to all phenomena;
he is the most excellent because he consists of the experience of innate bliss;
and he is the lion of speakers because he accomplishes the welfare of the world through the radiation of the realm of innate gnosis.

Because the bodhicitta is undecaying through the unity of all body, speech, and mind, one is not overcome by the waves of conceptualization belonging to others; thus, it is "unconquered" (*aparājita*).
Alternatively, the first half [of the verse] has stated the cause, while the second half has stated the result, which consists of the four joys. || 25 ||
kha. 'dvayaḥ • kha. hitaḥ kha. vigamād
ka. ga. Therefore, beginningless;
kha. knowledge; ka. ga. invincible.
Ga. Vādirāja; Ga. Vāriśreṣṭha;
Ka. Vācāmīśvara.
O, by means of retention (*dhāraṇā*),
[there arise] the forms (*rūpaka*) of Kāgapa,
Amṛtakaṇika, Sahitā, Samantadarśin, Prāmodya, Tejomālī, and Sudarśana.
Śrīvatsa, Suprabha, Dīpti, Bhā, and Bhāsurakaradyuti;
"Samanta" means one whose nature it is to see everywhere; such a one is a "Samantadarśin" (All-Seeing One).
He has attained that [state] by means of the form of Samantabhadra, out of regard for sentient beings who must be disciplined from passion.

Because great passion (*mahārāga*) radiates therein in the form of the non-dual realm of phenomena (*advayadharmadhātu*), and because one attains supreme joy through the maintenance of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is "Joy" (*prāmodya*). Because of the identity with the continuous stream of light— the radiance of the innate *caṇḍālī*— it is "Crowned with Light" (*tejobhālī*).

One whose vision is beautiful (*śobhana-darśana*) is one who has the direct realization of innate bliss (*sahaja-sukha*); thus, because he is filled with the nectar of the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*), which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion, he is a "Gnosis-Ocean" (*jñāna-sāgara*).

Because he possesses the characteristics of a Tathāgata, which have become the sprout of the seed of omniscience—unique and not shared by others—that is the cause for the arising of the entire world, he is the "Śrīvatsa."

He is thus because his beautiful radiance consists of the expansion of innate wisdom (*sahajajñāna*); he is "luminous" because he causes the illumination of the Buddhas and others residing in infinite world-systems; he is "splendid" because he shines with rays of light in the form of a mass; and he is "resplendent" because his brilliance takes the form of the wrathful deities such as Yamāntaka, for the sake of disciplining those beings who require such wrathful means.
26. ||| Thus ends the twenty-sixth [verse]. ||| 26 |||
The supreme and most excellent great physician, the peerless remover of the arrow [of suffering], the tree of all medicines, and the great enemy of the disease of the afflictions. || 27 ||

He is the "Great Physician" because he destroys all diseases, such as passion and dispassion; he is the "Supreme Physician" because he administers the medicine of unerring instruction; and he is "Excellent" because he establishes others in the nature of his own supreme great bliss.
He is the Extractor of Arrows because he removes the thorns of all winds of conceptual construction;

he is the Unsurpassed because his own nature is ineffable bliss; he is the Tree of All Medicines because, like a wish-fulfilling tree, he radiates grace toward the entire world through non-conceptuality;

and he is the Great Enemy and Destroyer of the diseases of the afflictions—those characterized by passion, dispassion, and so forth—because he directly realizes the form of great bliss, which is the natural luminosity that serves as the antidote to all afflictions.
The beloved Tilaka of the three worlds, glorious, a circle of stars,
extending to the limits of the sky in the ten directions, he is the great, lofty banner of Dharma. ||28||
Regarding "Trailokya":

the three worlds (*trailokya*) are the unity of body, speech, and mind; because they are adorned with great bliss (*mahāsukha*), they take the form of a *tilaka* (forehead mark), and thus he is the "Forehead Mark of the Three Worlds" (*Trailokyatilaka*).
Because he is the nature of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), he is beautiful and lovely.

The illustrious one is called *nakṣatramaṇḍala* because, through union with the glorious accomplishment of the ultimate reality whose nature is non-dual, he radiates as the great bliss that is self-cognizable and luminous, like a constellation-cluster in the sky;
[the masculine gender] is used due to Vedic usage (*ārṣatva*).
Alternatively, there are four channels in the *uṣṇīṣa* and sixteen on the forehead; these twenty channels provoke the *śleṣman* constituent.
There are thirty-two in the throat and eight in the heart; these forty [channels] are the causes [of disease], O Bhāskara.
ka. *bhāsurakarādīptiḥ*, ga. *bhāsurakarādīpta*, kha. *savikalpa*, bho. "sarva" is absent;
ka. ga. *svasvarūpa*; ga. *kāratvāt*; pha.
*trailokyaṃ*, kha. *kānta*.

Ka. Ga. The *Advayarūpāryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "The sixty-four channels at the navel are those that cause the bile constituent (*pittadhātu*) to flow; there are sixteen [channels] on the outer circumference of the secret lotus."
These eighty dances are provoked by the wind element (*vāyudhātu*);

specifically, ten are located in its middle circumference and six in its inner circumference. Correspondingly, they provoke the [three] humors (*sannipāta*) and have the nature of obstructing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*).
Thus, there are one hundred and fifty-six channels that bring death to the ignorant but grant bliss to yogins;
these consist of one hundred and sixty-two channels together with the channels of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*).
And within these channels, each individual channel becomes tenfold through the movement of the ten winds and the presence of the ten aggregates and elements;
thus, everything multiplied by ten results in a total number of sixteen hundred and twenty,
which are the carriers of the ghaṭikās of the twenty-seven lunar mansions.

Through the cessation of this, the glorious one—known as the "Circle of Stars"—is the luminosity of the sky pervading the ten directions; by its manifestation, it reaches the limit which is the nature of the ultimate point (*paramārthabindu*). He is thus described as one whose great banner of Dharma (*dharmadhvaja*) is exceedingly lofty, having reached the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*).
The vast umbrella of the world, the mandala of loving-kindness and compassion,
the glorious Padmanṛtyeśvara, the great sovereign Ratnacchatra. || 29 ||

Regarding the term *jagacchatra*: because it removes all the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the world itself—having become one with his body, speech, and mind—is the sole, non-dual parasol. It is "vast" and "extensive" because it reaches from the *uṣṇīṣa* down to the pores of the skin, being raised upon the golden staff of the *caṇḍālī* who is established in the stream of uninterrupted great bliss; he is thus described as such.

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has light as its intrinsic nature, and compassion (*karuṇā*) has the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) as its nature; he who "takes" (*lāti*) their essence (*maṇḍa*), the core, is thus [named].

Because he is the mind of awakening of ineffable bliss, he is the Lord of the Dance (*Padmanarteśvara*). The meaning is that his garment is the radiance of the blooming lotus. For this very reason, he is "Glorious" (*śrīmān*);

because he abides on the peak of the vajra-jewel through the application of the blazing *caṇḍālī*, and because he cools all limbs by obstructing the heat of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), he is like a parasol—a "jewel-parasol" (*ratnacchatra*).
Because he is the form of all existents, he is the Great Pervader.
The Great King of all Buddhas, who maintains the nature of the essence of all Buddhas; the Great Yoga of all Buddhas, the sovereign command over all Buddhas. ||30||

"Of all Buddhas" (*sarvabuddha*) means that Vajrasattva is the great king of all Buddhas, such as Vairocana and others; because his intrinsic nature is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he is the self of all Buddhas. That which is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*) is his very being (*bhāva*); since he possesses that form of existence (*sadrūpa*), he is "he who holds that" (*taddharatīti sa tathā*). This is because he dwells in the heart of all Tathāgatas in the form of the aggregates, elements, and so forth.
The Great Yoga of all Buddhas is the form of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by the aspect of supreme bliss;
it is so called because it brings about and establishes the oneness of each and every aggregate (*skandha*) and so forth of all Buddhas through bliss.
Possessing the glory of the vajra-jewel consecration together with the drops of nectar, he is the sovereign lord of all jewels,
the lord of the masters of all worlds, and the king of all vajra-holders. || 31 ||

"Vajraratna" refers to the Vajraratna initiation, which is the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*). Because his nature is that very [bliss], he is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). Furthermore, because he is held upon the head of the Buddha, the Lord of all jewels, he is the Sovereign (*īśvara*) of all worlds, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas; that very one is Vajrasattva, the Lord (*pati*), because he consists of all phenomena (*sarvabhāvamayatvāt*).
Those who uphold the three drops of body and so forth are the holders of all vajras; their sovereign is the fourth drop, which is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.
The great mind of all Buddhas, the great body of all Buddhas, the mental range of all Buddhas, and the eloquence of all Buddhas. ||32||
Regarding "Sarvabuddha":

because all Buddhas possess the nature of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) due to their non-obstructive state of mind (*apratighacitta*), it is so called. He is described as such because he has "gati"—meaning dissolution or identity—with the "mindless mind" (*acittacitta*) within the minds of all Buddhas.

Because he pervades all phenomena by virtue of being the Dharmadhātu-rūpa-jñāna-kāya, he is the Great Body of all Buddhas (*sarvabuddhamahākāya*). Because he is the form of inconceivable bliss, full of great bliss, which serves as the support for immersing the body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas in the flowing stream of the nectar of great bliss, he is the Sarasvatī of all Buddhas (*sarvabuddhasarasvatī*). [The change in gender] is due to Vedic usage (*ārṣatvāt*). He is one whose Sarasvatī consists of all Buddhas—an inconceivable river of bliss—and thus [the name] has a short vowel. || 32 ||
Vajrasūrya, the great light, possessing the great passion beginning with dispassion, with the stainless radiance of the vajra-moon, blazing with light of universal colors. ||33||
Regarding "Vajrasūrya":

he is so called because he possesses the great light of the Vajrasūrya gnosis-mandala, which illuminates the entire triple world and is characterized by the momentary state of mind (cittakṣaṇa) abiding within the excellent jewel-pedestal (maṇivaraṭaka). As it is said: "And one should behold that mind which is the Vajrasūrya, situated within the jewel, in the form of the gnosis-mandala, through its illumination of the [three] realms."
This means "the non-dual mind characterized by effortlessness.
*Bandhujñānendu* is "Excellent Moon" (*Sucandra*); he is "thus" because his stainless radiance—free from all conceptual constructions—is the illumination of the three worlds.
The meaning is that the single yoga of the moon, sun, Rāhu, fire, dust, semen, mind, and gnosis is expressed by these two lines.

He is such because the beginning of detachment—which is characterized by dispassion—is the Great Passion (*mahārāga*), consisting of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), with which he is identical as his fourth state.
He is such because his radiant splendor, possessing all colors—that is, various hues—dispels the terror of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
And this is the "mouth of the Guru."

And it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "When the image [of the deity] has been seen, one should perform the restraint of the vital winds (*prāṇavāyu*) at every daily session, until a wheel of light rays, revolving and encircling one's own body, is perceived. Within six months, for the practitioners, the path-consciousness—which is devoid of touch—attains equal bliss. O Lord, from the beginning, at the end of passion and dispassion, it increases even for a moment by the number of breaths. In the interval between the flames, in the midst of gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is the innate (*sahaja*) joy of cessation; in the union of the sleep and the whirl, there is that bliss arising from the conjunction of the two, the vajra and the lotus. One should cause its increase through the power of the guru’s instructions; that it increases in this way is no wonder."
"Having slain the afflictions and the Māras, the Lord of Victors enters [the state] through the yoga of the year, O excellent yogin.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Passion (*rāga*) consists of the fifteen digits (*kalā*) of the white half of the lunar cycle of the bodhicitta; dispassion (*virāga*) consists of the fifteen digits of the black half. In the middle of those is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the sixteenth digit, which is the sixteenth digit of all the elements (*dhātu*). The gathering together (*samāhāra*) of all the elements is the assembly (*samāja*) and the vow (*saṃvara*). (33)

The Perfectly Awakened One, seated in the vajra posture, who upholds the Dharma of the Buddha’s assembly; the glorious one born from the lotus of the Buddhas, who holds the treasury of omniscient wisdom. || 34 ||
Regarding "Sambuddha":

he is so called because his seat is the *sambuddhavaṃ*—the awakened tip of the *vajra*, or the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged posture) formed by the bending of the flow of the left and right channels (*puṭa*).

He is the "Upholder of the Dharma of the Buddha’s Chant" (*buddhasaṃgītidharmadhṛk*) because he maintains that Dharma which is the unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*) pervading the three realms, which is itself the Buddha’s chant.

Because of the statement: "One should behold the mind as the drop (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind-knowledge, or as the vajra-posture; and that mind which is the vajra-sun within the jewel. "Buddha" refers to non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); because it is unstained by the impurities of afflictions and habitual tendencies (*kleśavāsanā*), and because its nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is a "lotus" (*padma*), namely the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Since he arises from that, he is "born from the Buddha-lotus" (*buddhapadmodbhava*). For this very reason, he is "Glorious" (*śrīmān*).

The knowledge that is self-cognizable and consists of all aspects is the knowledge of the Omniscient One; that very thing is the treasury (*kośa*) of all phenomena because they are contained within it and because it sustains them—thus, [it is called] the "Treasury of the Knowledge of the Omniscient One. (34)
The King who holds the universal illusion, the great master of the knowledge of the Buddhas; the one with the sharp vajra, the great sword, utterly pure, and the supreme syllable. ||35||

"Viśvamāyā" means that which sustains the entire world of illusion. Above the letter *va* is the pure *rajaḥ* (passion); above the half-moon in the form of the syllable *va* is the nature of the *bindu*, which is bliss, the *bodhicitta* in the form of the *anāhata*, accompanied by *nāda*. It is so called because it sustains (*dhārayati*) the "entire world of illusion" (*viśvamāyā*), which consists of the enjoyment of the five objects of desire and so forth.
It is a "King" (*rāja*) because it shines (*rājate*) as the form of the light of primordial wisdom (*jñānajyotis*).
He is a *buddhavidyādhara* because he holds the Buddha-knowledge characterized by the four drops;
for this very reason, he is great.
He is the "Vajra-sharp" because his nature is innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*), being of a stainless form located in the *ūrṇā*.
Accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, he is the Great Sword (*mahākhaṅga*) because he cuts through conceptual construction by virtue of his motionless nature;
he is the Pure One (*viśuddha*) because of his form as a Puruṣa;
and he is the Supreme Immutable (*paramākṣara*) because all phenomena are of one taste within the form of the poison-remover (*vipāva*). || 35 ||
The cutter of suffering, the Mahāyāna, the great weapon of Vajradharma; the Victor, the Conqueror, the profound Vajra, the Vajra-intellect who knows things as they truly are. (36)
"Duḥkhaccheda" means that which cuts through suffering; thus, it refers to that Mahāyāna which is the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
"Vajradharma" is the dharma of gnosis (*jñānadharmma*).
He who possesses that very great weapon is thus [described].

By etymological derivation (*nairuktya*), he is called *Jinajig* because he gives birth to the Victors (*jinān*) such as Akṣobhya and others; the meaning is that his nature is the realization of a mind that is stainless and free from appearances.
He is likewise one whose nature is the profundity of the vajra—of perfect gnosis—which is wisdom (*prajñā*) devoid of conceptual constructions regarding an object of apprehension and so forth.
He is Vajrabuddhi because his mind is unshakable on the adamantine path;
he is a knower of reality as it is because the nature of the fruit has become manifest. (36)
He who fulfills all the perfections, whose pure nature is selflessness, who adorns all the stages, and whose heart radiates the light of the moon of perfect knowledge. (37)
He is the "Fulfiller of All Perfections" because he fulfills the perfections such as generosity (*dāna*).
He is the "Ornament of All Stages" because he possesses the previously mentioned mandala of the stages.

He is so called because he possesses the light of the fire of the moon of perfect gnosis (*samyagjñāna*), which is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); this moon has arisen from that nature-luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*) which is the reality (*dharmatā*) consisting of the non-appearance of selflessness (*nairātmya*)—the characteristic of the mind that penetrates the pure Dharma. || 37 ||

The Great Exertion of the Net of Illusion, the supreme sovereign of all tantras; he who sits in the vajra posture upon the entirety [of reality], and who sustains the body of inexhaustible gnosis. (38)

He who possesses such yoga is thus [described]. Because he alone is the subject to be propounded by all tantras—the great tantras beginning with Yoga—he is the Lord of All Tantras (*sarvatantreśvara*), and he is supreme (*para*).

Having become non-dual through the cessation of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, his cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) consists of the vajra of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*); thus, he is "one whose cross-legged posture is composed of the entirety of vajras" (*aśeṣavajraparyaṅka*).
He is called the "Bearer of the Entire Body of Wisdom" because he maintains the activity of the wisdom of all Buddhas without exception, which has become supremely non-dual. || 38 ||

The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti: Samantabhadra, the one of excellent intelligence, Kṣitigarbha, the sustainer of the world, the great womb of all Buddhas, the bearer of the wheel of manifold emanations. (39)
Regarding "Samanta":
he is so called because his innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which is knowledge, is auspicious (*bhadra*) on all sides (*samantataḥ*) due to the manifestation of signs such as smoke;
and he is so called because his intellect is adorned with the aspect of emptiness due to the absence of all conceptual constructions and the attainment of perfect awakening (*sambodhi*).

Since the word "earth" (*kṣiti*) indicates the five elements, *Kṣitigarbha* is the cause; *Kṣitigarbha* is the drop of innate bliss (*sahajānandabindu*). For this very reason, he is the sustainer of the world (*jagaddhṛti*), the support of the entire universe.

Because he is the cause of the arising of all Buddhas—those existing in the three times who cultivate the six-limbed yoga—he is the great womb of all Buddhas (*sarvabuddhamahāgarbha*), the vessel of the innate bodhicitta.

The pervasion of worldly and supramundane deities is the universal emanation; that itself is the wheel (*cakra*) or mandala. One who holds that is "the holder of the wheel of universal emanation" (*viśvanirmāṇacakradhṛk*). This means one who maintains the external and internal body, speech, and mind as they have become unified through the blending of the two—semen (*śukra*) and passion (*rajas*). || 39 ||

The foremost of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, the upholder of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; he whose nature is non-arising, whose purpose is the universe, the upholder of the intrinsic nature of all dharmas. || 40 ||
Regarding the term *sarvabhāva*:

the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*bhāva*) is the pure body of the Tathāgata’s gnosis (*tathāgatajñānakāya*). That which is both that [nature] and supreme is called the "intrinsic nature of all phenomena. It is called the "upholder of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" because it upholds (*dhṛk*) selflessness (*nairātmya*), the intrinsic nature of all phenomena characterized as the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, the non-dual [Reality-body], and the Emanation-body.

"Non-arising" (*anutpāda*) means being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). He whose reality (*tattva*) is such a phenomenon (*dharma*) is [described as] "thus" (*tathā*). The "object of all" (*viśveṣām arthaḥ*) is that which is to be accomplished and is desirable.

Because he maintains the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—exactly as they are, he is called "the upholder of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmasvabhāvadhṛk*). || 40 ||

Possessing great wisdom in a single moment, he maintains the awakening to all phenomena; he is the realization of all phenomena, the Sage who has reached the limit of reality, and possesses supreme intelligence. (41)

"Ekakṣaṇa" means the single, non-dual moment that transcends the fourth state (*turyātīta*), which is the singular embodiment of the four joys and characterized by innate awakening (*sahajasambodhi*). In that state, the one of great wisdom is one whose intellect has merged into the sole bliss of the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths; this is the meaning.

By this as well, Mañjuśrī, the Blessed One, spoke of the fourth [state] as the wave of bliss: "Purified by the washing of the seed-syllable of the thunderbolt, nourishing the sprout that has become the lotus-born, the fourth grain reaches full maturity; though hidden even from the wise, the fourth becomes manifest. Thus it is said.

Because he maintains the realization of the bliss of awakening to the names of all phenomena through every breath, he is the "Awakener of All Phenomena" (*sarvadharmāvabodhaka*). All phenomena—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are thoroughly perceived and directly realized by him as the innate moon;
thus, he is so called because he possesses the state of reality together with the *Amṛtakaṇikā*.

The Real (bhūta), the True (satya), and Suchness (tathatā)—the culmination of these is the state of fruition; because he contemplates that [state] exactly as it is, he is the Sage who has reached the limit of reality (bhūtāntamuni).
Because he awakens from the sleep of pleasure, he is one of supreme intelligence (agradhīrva). || 41 ||

Stable, with a perfectly serene self, upholding the awakening of the Perfectly Awakened One, manifest before all Buddhas, he is the brilliantly radiant flame of wisdom. (42) Thus end the forty-two verses on the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*).

"Stimite" means that because he is nourished by the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*), he is "stilled" (*stimita*); because his nature (*ātman*)—that is, his essential form (*svarūpa*)—is perfectly serene due to the clarity of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and its immovability, he is so described. He is one who holds the gnosis of the bliss of awakening belonging to the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*), whose mind is contained within the jewel of the *vañca*. Thus is he.

Through the love for the innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) that is self-cognizable, he is directly perceived by all Buddhas residing in the three times; by means of the flame of gnosis—the non-referential gnosis naturally luminous—he is supremely radiant, illuminating infinite and endless Buddha-fields. (42) Thus ends the explanation of the discerning gnosis (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) through forty-two verses concerning the purification of the six aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, objects, and the sixfold activity of the action-faculties within the seven locations beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa* and ending with the crest-jewel. 8.

Now, by means of the phrase "the knower of equality (*samatājñāna*) is the supreme accomplisher of desired aims," and so forth, he describes that very innate knowledge (*sahajajñāna*) through the gateway of the gnosis of equality in the form of Ratnasambhava, the jewel-like aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) free from obscuration: "The supreme accomplisher of desired aims, the protector who is the best of all beings, the purifier of all miserable states, and the liberator of all sentient beings. (1)
Regarding the term *iṣṭārthasādhaka* ("the accomplisher of the desired object"):

because it is of the nature of the supreme imperishable gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*) that fulfills all hopes, it is both "desired" (*iṣṭa*) and an "object" (*artha*), hence *iṣṭārtha*. Its "accomplisher" (*sādhaka*) or producer is "supreme" (*para*) because it transcends the three drops (*bindu*) experienced within the vajra and lotus;
it is the purifier of all misfortune and the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence, and the sole creator of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

He is the supreme body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*) of the body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings; for this very reason, he is the protector of the protectorless, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), who liberates all sentient beings by illuminating the lotus. ||1||

The sole hero in the battle against the afflictions, the destroyer of the pride of the enemy that is ignorance, the glorious lord who bears the ornament of wisdom, and the one who assumes both heroic and loathsome forms. (2)
In the battle against the afflictions, he is a solitary, peerless hero because he cuts down the afflictions of the conduct of all sentient beings with the weapon of perfect knowledge.
Due to its archaic nature (*ārṣatva*), there is a different arrangement of words:

ignorance (*ajñāna*) is *avidyā*; that very thing is the enemy (*ari*), because it causes one to fall away (*acyuti*) and bestows suffering. Its arrogance (*darpa*) is the scattering of feathers (*barhivikṣepa*). By making it appear as nothingness, the intellect (*dhīḥ*) destroys the arrogance of the enemy that is ignorance, because, through the rejection of even the "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), it is free from primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśopakleśa*).

By convention, *dharmatā* is *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment), because it is the seminal fluid (*śukra*) of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Likewise, by means of the stream of bodhicitta surging from the *uṣṇīṣa* and nourishing all limbs, he possesses the prosperity of both the mundane and supramundane; thus he is "Glorious" (*Śrīmān*). Since means (*upāya*) has compassion as its constituent, it is the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*); since wisdom (*prajñā*) has emptiness as its constituent, it is the loathsome sentiment (*bībhatsarasa*). He bears that form of great bliss which consists of the heroism and loathsomeness of that piercing (*vedha*); therefore, he is so called. || 2 ||
He dances with the casting of hundreds of staff-like arms and the planting of his feet; he dances across the expanse of the sky with the extension of his glorious hundred arms. ||3||

Regarding "the staff-like arms" (*bāhudaṇḍa*): the two staffs of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds are infinite due to the differentiation of the ten transitions (*saṃkrānti*) through the left and right nostrils; thus, there are one hundred [transitions]. Their "projection" (*ākṣepa*) is their drawing back (*ākṛṣṭi*), which occurs through entry into the central channel (*madhyamā*) and the state of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).
What is the desired object?
What is the essence (sattva)? Kha.
Then,
the object [is perceived] by means of the breath.
O, you who have become the essence of the lotus! Bho!
Kha!
And by that,
there is no cognition of us. Empty.

But compassion alone, when joined with the drops of nectar (*amṛtakarṇikā*), is the collection of breaths; its placement in the state of great bliss (*mahāsukhapada*) is its dissolution (*layīkaraṇa*). One who possesses the radiance of bliss through that dancing (*vānartana*) therein is thus described.

The supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*) is pierced by the horse; through its possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*), it enjoys the infinity of the manifestation of the glorious hundred-fold knowledge (*jñāna*). Thus he is the "Glorious Hundred-Armed One" (*Śrīmacchatabhuja*), the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*). His "expansion" (*ābhoga*) is his vastness and full development.
Because of his realization of all phenomena as having emptiness as their intrinsic nature, there is the "expansion of the sky," which is its pervasiveness.
He in whom dancing proceeds—that is, the movement—of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) therein is so described.
Standing with the surface of the earth beneath the sole of one foot, he stands with the tip of the Brahmāṇḍa resting upon the nail of his big toe.

"With one foot" means that with the sole of one foot, acting as a second support, he has firmly established his seat upon the surface of the earth's mandala; "he by whom the dust of the bodhicitta resides on the crest of the jewel-robe at the navel" refers to him in such a state.
Due to its archaic (ārṣa) nature, there is no mention of the elision of the letter *l*.

Alternatively, it should be construed as follows: "Mahī" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); because it holds the seed-syllable *śukra*, its "essence" (*maṇḍa*) is the core. The "summit of the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍaśikhara*) is the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*). That which is the toenail of the big toe which has ascended there, by way of the process of upward retention (*vighṛti*), is the mind connected to the vajra located at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*). Abiding there through non-dual yoga, one foot is on the "dust" (*rajas*) of the sun within the jewel-vajra, and the second is on the "moon" of the semen (*śukra*) at the crown.

Having bowed with his head to the one who is ever-indestructible, indivisible, beloved by his Lord, and honored throughout the three worlds—he by whom that state, the imperishable gnosis (*jñāna*), is reached and attained; which state is established within the *vajramaṇi* for the cessation of ignorance, on the ground of the non-abiding nirvāṇa, in the dust of the sun and the surface of the great mandala, as the single gnosis-element—the right foot, that single step, has been placed, having trodden upon it with the sole of the foot.

When the semen has become the moon that transcends the bliss born of the *uṣṇīṣa*, and when, through the arising of the primordial desire (*kāmakala*), it resides in the toenail, then the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) becomes non-dual; this is the "Left" (*vāma*), which, having transcended the peak of the Brahma-egg, always pervades the three times, and because it has transcended the veil of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it cannot be severed by the blade of ignorance-knowledge (*avidyājñāna*).
Because it has transcended the nature of consciousness, it is indivisible by the categories of subject and object;

because its nature is great bliss, it is desired; because it resides in the state of having accomplished all that was to be done like a jewel, and because it is free from worldly conduct, it is honored by the three worlds.

It is stated in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha* that [the bodhicitta] resides in the *uṣṇīṣa* at the far limit of saṃsāra: "By means of the fire of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), even the melted moon becomes a drink, the drinking of wine; it travels from the thumb-joint to the *uṣṇīṣa* by the power of the lunar days until the end of the full moon. One's own mind travels from the *uṣṇīṣa* to the fingers at the conclusion of the dark fortnight. This is the conduct of the yogin, which bestows the desired accomplishment at every moment of the day. Thus it is said.
And what is the deposit?
Who has not been overcome by him?
Kha Mahā Ka
ga vivṛtti kha
O Yoginī Kha-da!
Having placed [the hands] in the *kakha* mudrā.
The sky-ground prior to the arising of the lotus.
O Mañjuśrī, this *Tāmasaṅgīti* has a single meaning: it is the non-dual reality of the Dharma, the ultimate truth, which is imperishable.

The various forms of representation (*vijñapti*), means, mind (*citta*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the continuum (*saṃtati*) constitute "one meaning"; thus it is "single-meaning" because there is no differentiation due to its nature as the ultimate truth.
Upon entering the middle way between the moon and the sun, because of the non-existence of duality, there is the meaning of non-dual reality;
it is the meaning of the illumination of the moon of gnosis; it is the ultimate truth because it shatters all attachment;
and it is indestructible because it has the nature of the meditative drop (*dhyānabindu*) which is equal to space.

Like space, in the form of the *dharmatā*, the Blessed One is seen as having the nature of the *ālaya*, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), and the six evolving consciousnesses; thus, he is the object of incomparable Dharma. Because all conceptual darkness has set and he consists of a continuum of wisdom and compassion that is beyond mind, the continuum of mind and consciousness is [identical to] the object in the form of various representations (*vijñapti*).
Delight in the meaning of all phenomena without exception, transcending passion for existence and the like; delight in emptiness with supreme intelligence;
and great delight in the three realms of existence.
Regarding the phrase "all phenomena without exception" (*aśeṣabhāva*):

all phenomena without exception are themselves the objects (*artha*) because they have become manifest as the innate (*sahaja*). His delight (*rati*)—that is, his incomparable joy—is directed toward them.
And it has been said: "These very objects are the five moments of activity for the mind; they are the very powers of the senses that cause longing, and the wind that sows the seeds of agitation.
Blessed is the touch of the dust from the lotus feet of the true Guru, by whose power this nectar of reality—which is my very essence—throbs day after day."
Through the realization of the suchness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, there is delight in emptiness; through not falling into either extreme, there is supreme intelligence;
and through the departure from the nature of passion and aversion, one transcends the passion for existence and so forth.

He is so called because he possesses a great, natural delight in the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) which is free from conceptual elaboration (*kalola-bhāva*) regarding body, speech, and mind within the three states of existence.
Pure, white as a bright cloud, with the beautiful luster of the autumn moon's rays;
possessing the brilliance of the orb of the rising sun, and the radiance of great red-colored nails.
Regarding "pure and clean":
he is pure because of the removal of the stains of ignorance due to his essential nature as Vajrasattva;
he is white like an autumn cloud because of his utter purity, and possesses the brilliance of a bright cloud because all the elements have been liquefied.

Because even mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are absent, his radiance is as beautiful as the rays of the autumn moon; thus he is "one who possesses such radiance. Because he is followed by great passion (*mahārāga*), his own mind appears like the orb of the rising sun due to the power of the union of the upward and downward vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*). Thus, he is "one whose shadow—meaning his splendor—is like that of the rising sun's orb," because he is embraced by the light of the innate *caṇḍālī*. Alternatively, because great bliss pervades from the big toe to the tips of the nails, the shadow—the radiance and the pervasion of bliss—of this King of Bodhicitta extends to the tips of the nails of those [toes] of the great passion; thus he is so described.
|| [Thus ends] the Lord of Discipline (Vineśvara). || cha || ka ||
And the nature of space is the Buddha.
ga gha ṅa ghavala ka
It is so; there is no "self."
Gaḥ is pure, accompanied by the Amṛtakaṇikā;
Indranīla is the true crown, bearing the tips of the hair of Mahānīla.

The glory of the rays of the great jewel is the ornament of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa. Because of the radiance of the perfectly pure sahaja sapphire known as "Indranīla," the *bodhicitta* is the Indranīla; its peak is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Its excellent garment-like covering (*cīra*) is light; such is he who, by virtue of having rendered the crooked nature free from obscuration, flows from the tips of the great dark-blue hair—those who hold the non-dual mind-vajra—filling all limbs. Because it is blue due to being projected by the winds of the heart, it flows at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*); thus he is so named.
The meaning is that emptiness and compassion take as their objective support the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) as far as space extends.
Because he has emerged from the circle of the earth (*pṛthivīmaṇḍala*), although he possesses great passion (*mahārāga*), he is "yellow" (*pīta*);

thus, "of the world-system" (*lokadhātu*) means one whose nature it is to have compassion for hundreds of world-systems and infinite world-systems through the radiation of innate great bliss (*sahajamahāsukha*). Such is he.
Due to its archaic nature (*ārṣatva*), the word *nu* is not employed [here].

Because all aspirations are fulfilled through the radiation of body, speech, mind, and gnosis upon the cessation of passion and dispassion, there is the great stride of the bases of miraculous power (*ṛddhipāda*). Because he is immersed in emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects without interruption, there is great mindfulness; because he possesses that, he is the "Great Bearer of Mindfulness" (*mahāsmṛtidhara*).

Through union with the reality whose singular nature is both existence and non-existence, he is the Lord of the Fourfold Samādhi; by means of the four pairs—laughter, gazing, hand-holding, and embracing—he is the Sovereign of the Samādhi of the Fourfold Mindfulness.

He is the fragrance of the flowers of the factors of enlightenment, an ocean of the qualities of the Tathāgatas; he knows the method of the eightfold path and knows the path of the perfectly awakened ones. || 10 ||

*Bodhyaṅga* refers to the sevenfold revolution (*saptāvarta*) because the six Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the others, have become one with Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Alternatively, it refers to the sevenfold revolution because, through the digestion of the six tastes of food and drink—such as what is eaten and drunk—and through processes such as intoxication and alchemical transformation (*jāraṇā*), they take the form of chyle, blood, flesh, skin, channels, bone, and marrow. Thus, he is so called because he possesses the fragrance—the radiance of Great Bliss—of the seven drops (*bindu*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the flowers. Furthermore, the meaning is that this very [bliss] is consumed and made imperishable (*acyuta*) by means of the sevenfold revolution.

And it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "When the aggregates, elements, and so forth have been incinerated; when the flow of the five maṇḍalas has ceased; when the objects and sense faculties have been restrained; and when the [four] joys, beginning with *ānanda*, have been completely transcended..."
The moon-drops flow; I am the ego situated at the crown. From the moon at the forehead, [the flow goes] to the sun; from the throat, the fluid [descends] thence to the heart.
Possessed by Caṇḍālikā at the navel, it then moves to the secret wheel;
this "great beast" (mahāpaśu) is said to have descended into this secret wheel.
The moon of petals is shown at the base of the three channels;
it is the "beast" (paśu) born of seven lifetimes, which bestows the siddhi of Khecarī.

When swooned, it removes disease; when the aggregates and elements are removed, it bestows the state of a universal monarch. When the senses and objects have been slain, it bestows the qualities such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth.
When pursued by means of the destruction of old age and other afflictions, it swiftly bestows the state of Buddhahood.
Just as external nectar, when bound [within the body], bestows vast accomplishment that removes all suffering, so too does this essence of ignorance.
In this way, Brahmā is the sacrificial animal and Viṣṇu is struck down in the secret wheel;
he indeed bestows abundant life as long as the flood reaches the heart.
Rāhu above is declared to be the animal (paśu), while the Moon and Sun are the great animals (mahāpaśu);
when cast down through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), they bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Blood, sinews, as well as marrow—these must be diligently cast away;
these alone are to be known as the sacrificial animals for embodied beings, and not any others outside of this.
O Supreme Lord, [you are] the seven births of all living beings;
just as you are seven births within the body, so shall I describe that—listen to it.
All food and drink, once consumed or drunk, becomes sixfold in taste through digestion; that is its first birth.
Afterwards, it turns into blood; this second stage is clearly manifest.
The third becomes flesh, and the fourth turns into skin.

Accompanied by the Amṛtakaṇikā, it attains the state of a channel in the fifth [day]; it attains the state of bone in the sixth; it attains the state of marrow in the seventh; thus it becomes sevenfold.

Likewise, *tathatā* (suchness), *dharmodayā* (the source of phenomena), and *avadhūtī*— because all qualities arise by being situated therein— and because one has attained the fruit-stage culminating in the *Samantaprabhā* (All-Illuminating) tenth stage through the cessation of the tenfold vital winds (*prāṇa*) and so forth, he is the Tathāgata. He alone is the limit of qualities, for by virtue of being the support for all stages, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings.

Alternatively, because of the nature of the internal sphere of space (*antargatākāśamaṇḍala*), there are eight spheres of the flow of vital breath (*prāṇavāha*) in the left and right nostrils; their path is the entry into the central channel (*madhyamā*). One who knows that way—by means of the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth as taught by the Guru—is thus [described].
