He is the perfectly awakened one of the commitment (*samayaka-saṃbuddha*), the self-arisen (*svayaṃbhū*), the Knower (*jñānin*); his path is the gnosis of the *dharmadhātu*, and he is so called because of the direct realization of that. || 10 ||
He has great attachment for all beings, yet he is free from attachment like the sky; he is born from the minds of all beings and possesses the speed of the minds of all beings. ||11||

“Toward all sentient beings” means that because he does not abandon the welfare of all sentient beings through his emanation body (nirmāṇakāya), which is inseparable from the dharma body (dharmakāya), he possesses “great non-attachment” toward all sentient beings by means of ripening them and so forth;
yet, by his very nature of emptiness, he is free from attachment.
Because it is free from the stain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is like the sky;

because it has arisen in the minds of all sentient beings through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) to their natural luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*); and because, by the power of resolve (*adhimukti*) toward all sentient beings, it appears in the form of Vajradhara and others—it is "swift as the mind of all sentient beings. (11)

He knows the faculties and objects of all sentient beings; he captivates the minds of all sentient beings; he knows the reality of the meaning of the five aggregates; he maintains the purity of the five aggregates. ||12||
Regarding "the faculty of all beings" (*sarvasattvendriya*):

it refers to the faculties of all beings, which exist in the forms of weak, middling, and superior; he knows their objects through the unimpeded great bliss samādhi, which is both with and without conceptual proliferation (*saprapañca-niṣprapañca*). Thus, he strikes the minds—that is, the conceptualizing minds—of all beings and renders them devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvīkaroti*); therefore, he is "the captivator of the minds of all beings" (*sarvasattvamanohara*).

The meaning of the five aggregates is the entry into the *tathatā* (suchness) of the array of all Tathāgatas by means of the ultimate truth; through the knowledge of that, it is said as follows: "That which belongs to the aggregate of form—the mirror-like [wisdom], the earth element, the eye faculty, and form as the fifth—goes together with Krodha and Maitreya."
Thus, and so forth;

because it arises from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) and maintains the pure meaning of the five aggregates as being naturally luminous (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratā*), it is called the "Purifier of the Five Aggregates" (*pañcaskandhaviśuddhadhṛk*). 12.
The Noble Mañjuśrī Nāmasaṅgīti: Abiding at the limit of all deliverance, abiding on the path of all deliverance, skilled in all deliverance, and the teacher of all deliverance. || 13 ||
Regarding "all deliverances":
because he abides in the yuganaddha-samādhi at the limit of all deliverances,
he is thus "skilled in all deliverances" because he experiences bliss through the ineffable selflessness.

Because he abides on the path of all vehicles—such as that of the Śrāvakas—through the power of great compassion despite being free from attachment by virtue of being the jewel of great bliss, he stands upon all paths of deliverance.
Since the sphere of reality (dharmadhātu) is the nature of the body of great bliss, it is "all deliverance"; he who reveals it through non-conceptualization is its teacher.
He has uprooted existence with its twelve links, possesses the form of the method of the four truths, maintains the purity of the twelve aspects,
and maintains the realization of the eight knowledges.
Or, it is called "twelve-limbed" because it has uprooted existence with its twelve limbs.
And it has been said: "The seat of another (parapīṭha) is called wisdom (prajñā), and the seat of oneself (ātmapīṭha) is skillful means (upāya).
The non-dual state of these two is known as the yoga-seat (yogapīṭha).
That which arises from that is one's own seat (svapīṭha), and that which is devoid of it is likewise."
It is declared to be "innate" (sahaja), a domain beyond the path of speech.

Thus, the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) arises as the secret lotus of the woman; in the same way, the secondary seat (*upapīṭha*), the field (*kṣetra*), the grove (*chandoha*), the meeting place (*melāpaka*), and the cremation ground (*citibhuvana*)—all these are likewise.

The *pīṭha* is the left limb first, and likewise the other [limb] is the *upapīṭha*, the right; in this way, all the *kṣetra*s and so forth are located in the hands and feet, as well as the fingers and knees, up to the boundary.
Thus, because he maintains the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) which are devoid of the forms of subject and object, he is the "bearer of the twelvefold purity."
Ordinary, conceptually constructed happiness is suffering;
the origin is characterized by the fourth state (turyā);
and the cessation of the nature of body, speech, and mind within the sphere of gnosis is the truth of cessation.

The path is the vision of the world as the reflection of one’s own mind, free from objective support, and as the image of the Buddha. That which has this state of total non-duality as its form is such [a path]. By maintaining the eight cognitions—the four beginning with the "variegated" (*vicitra*) and the four beginning with the "motionless" (*niḥspanda*), along with great bliss—it is the bearer of the realization of the eight cognitions.

Possessing the essence of nectar, he is the knower of the meaning of the truths in twelve aspects, the knower of reality in sixteen aspects, fully awakened to enlightenment in twenty aspects— the supreme omniscient one. (15)

"Twelve aspects" means that because each of the characteristics of outflow (*niḥsyanda*), maturation (*vipāka*), human form (*puruṣākāra*), and purity (*vaimalya*) possesses a threefold quality, there are twelve aspects; the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) are the "twelve-aspected meaning of truth" through their connection with the non-duality of the conventional and ultimate truths.
Among these, the first triad—distinguished by the outflows of the isolation of body, speech, and mind—belongs to the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The second triad—distinguished by the maturation of the appearance, reflection, and natural absence of appearance—belongs to the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The third triad belongs to the *dharmakāya* through the distinctions of the purity and maturation of the forms of the person (*puruṣa*) consisting of mind, mental factors, and ignorance;
the fourth triad belongs to the *jñānakāya* through the distinctions of the two joys (*ānanda*), the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), and innate joy (*sahajānanda*).

By the exhaustion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the cessation of passion (*rajas*), or by the attainment of the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) through the twelve signs beginning with Aries and Taurus, the meaning of the Truth (*satya*) is twelvefold.

By means of the cessation of semen (*śukra*), one knows the sixteen-fold reality of the sixteen blissful digits (*kalā*); thus, because it is imperishable due to the exhaustion of the sixteen worldly digits, one is a knower of the sixteen-fold reality.

Through the cultivation of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-bhāvanā*) and the purification of the *avadhūtī*, there is the awakening to the twenty-fold enlightenment through the purification of the five aggregates, the five elements, the five sense faculties, and the five sense bases.
Through the cessation of ignorance he is awakened;
through the realization of the entire multitude of existences as being composed of all Buddhas, he is the All-Knowing One. 15.
He manifests millions of bodies as the emanations of immeasurable Buddhas; he has realized the direct intuition of all moments and knows the meaning of every moment of mind.

"Immeasurable" (*ameya*) refers to the visualization in a single moment of the entire collection of breaths— which has become a wave of all nirvāṇas— as the manifestation of the multitude of forms of immeasurable Buddha-emanations through the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*);
thus, by this, the middle sign (*madhyanimitta*) is described.
Because all breaths are realized through great bliss with every inhalation, there is the realization of all moments;
thus, one knows the mental moments of all sentient beings precisely as great bliss—such is the nature of reality. (16)
He manifests the welfare of the world through the means of the various vehicles; having emerged from the three vehicles, he abides in the fruit of the single vehicle.

"By means of various vehicles" (*nānāyāna*) refers to the methods and skillful means (*upāya*) of the four-limbed, six-limbed, and *bindu*-yoga practices and so forth; by these, he causes this world to be visualized and expanded as great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Thus, because he has emerged from body, speech, and mind as the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*), he is "one who has emerged from the three vehicles."
The vehicle is one and without a second; the fruit is the state of being established therein as the "I-maker.
The self whose realm of afflictions is purified has crossed over the ocean of floods; he brings about the exhaustion of the realm of karma and has emerged from the wilderness of yoga. ||18||
The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "The one whose nature is the purification of the elements of affliction (*kleśadhātu*).
Because ignorance has been destroyed, he is thus [described] as one whose self is the purification of the elements of affliction.

And those elements of affliction are eighteen, known as: bone, skin, flesh, blood, sinew, marrow, fat, semen, phlegm, feces, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, liver, spleen, raw meat, impurities, and body hair.
Due to the absence of conceptualization regarding sin and merit, he brings about the destruction of the elements of karma;
by the cessation of all intrinsic natures and having reached the further shore of gnosis, he has successfully crossed the ocean of the floods.

And those innate dispositions (*prakṛti*) are: detachment (*virāga*), moderate detachment, and extreme detachment; that which pertains to the mind’s coming and going; sorrow (*śoka*), moderate sorrow, and extreme sorrow; gentleness (*saumya*); conceptualization (*vikalpa*); fear (*bhīta*); craving (*tṛṣṇā*), moderate craving, and extreme craving; grasping (*upādāna*); lack of purity (*niḥśubhra*); hunger and thirst (*kṣuttṛṣā*); feeling (*vedanā*), equal feeling, and excessive feeling; knowledge (*vidavid*); retention (*dhāraṇā*); the state (*pada*); discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇa*); shame (*lajjā*); compassion (*kāruṇya*); affection (*sneha*), moderate affection, and excessive affection; trepidation (*cakita*); accumulation (*sañcaya*); and stinginess (*mātsarya*). These are the thirty-three moments (*kṣaṇa*) of the wisdom of primordial gnosis (*prajñājñāna*).

Passion (*rāga*), the impassioned (*rakta*), contentment (*tuṣṭa*), moderate contentment (*madhyamatuṣṭa*), extreme contentment (*atituṣṭa*), exhilaration (*harṣaṇa*), joy (*prāmodya*), wonder (*vismaya*), laughter (*hasita*), gladdening (*āhlādana*), embracing (*āliṅgana*), kissing (*cumbana*), sucking (*cūṣaṇa*), steadiness (*stheya*), vigor (*vīrya*), pride (*māna*), making (*karaṇa*), seizing (*haraṇa*), strength (*bala*), enthusiasm (*utsāha*), daring (*sāhasa*), moderate daring (*madhyamasāhasa*), supreme daring (*uttamasāhasa*), ferocity (*raudra*), gracefulness (*vilāsa*), enmity (*vaira*), auspiciousness (*śubha*), clear speech (*vāksphuṭa*), truth (*satya*), falsehood (*asatya*), certainty (*niścaya*), lack of grasping (*nirupādāna*), burning nature (*dāhatva*), incitement (*codana*), heroism (*śaurya*), shamelessness (*alajjā*), roguery (*ghūrtatva*), wickedness (*duṣṭatva*), and crookedness (*śaṭha-koṭilya*)—these are the forty moments of the knowledge of means (*upāyajñāna*).
Moderate passion, forgetfulness, delusion, silence, weariness, laziness, and dullness—these are the seven moments of the knowledge of the attainment of light (*ālokopalabdhi-jñāna*).
These occur in one hundred and sixty varieties due to the distinctions of their occurrence during the day and night.

Having departed from the wilderness of yoga by consuming all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), the yogi [perceives] that the "wilderness" is merely the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of gnosis, because it is difficult to comprehend.

Having thoroughly abandoned the afflictions, secondary afflictions, and all defilements along with their latent tendencies, he accomplishes the welfare of the world through wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion—never in vain. ||19||
Regarding the phrase *kleśopakleśa*:

he is one in whom the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and defilements (*saṃkleśa*), such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, have been thoroughly and completely eradicated.

Through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), he has realized Mahāmudrā-Prajñā; having become non-dual with that, through Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he performs the welfare of the world with unfailing, fruitful, and unimpeded bliss; thus he is so described.
He has abandoned all conceptualizations for the sake of [others], he possesses the meaning of consciousness, and he maintains cessation;
he is the object of the minds of all sentient beings and the movement of the minds of all sentient beings. ||20||

"Free from all perceptions" means that because of the absence of perceptions such as those of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), it has the sense of having abandoned all perceptions; he is "thus" because his cognition, grasping, object, and external world have departed.
Precisely because it consists solely of the untainted nature (*anāsravadharmatā*), it sustains cessation;

because it has arisen through non-conceptual union within the minds of all sentient beings, it is the object of the minds of all sentient beings, yet it is not an object nor a sphere of activity [for them]. For this very reason, it is the movement of the minds of all sentient beings.
Abiding within the minds of all sentient beings, gladdening the minds of all sentient beings, having attained equality with their minds, he brings delight to the minds of all sentient beings. ||21||
The purpose of abandonment is the abandonment by all Buddhas.

In the section on *vāgha*, together with the *Amṛtakaṇikā*: "Of all beings" (*sarvasattva*) means that within the minds of all beings, the nature of the light exists as the form of the *dharmadhātu*; thus it is so.

He has gone to— that is, attained— the equality of mind of all those sentient beings in the form of suchness (*tathatā*); because there is no distinction in the form of the *dharmatā* of all things, and because of the arising of the knowledge of great bliss through the reversal of cognitive distortions, he gladdens the minds of all sentient beings and delights the minds of all sentient beings, as his nature consists of the delight of untainted bliss.

The established doctrine is free from delusion, devoid of all error, characterized by a mind beyond doubt, possessing three purposes, encompassing all objects, and consisting of the three qualities. ||22||
Regarding the term *siddhānta*:

it is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) because it consists of the ultimate culmination through the departure from the positions of existence and non-existence. It is "free from delusion" (*vibhramāpagata*) because it is devoid of the misconceptions concerning the person (*pudgala*) and so forth.
Because it is free from the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected [natures], it is devoid of all delusion.
Through the thorough knowledge of mundane and supramundane tenets, he possesses a mind free from doubt due to his teaching of non-perverted reality to sentient beings.
It has three purposes: the purpose of wisdom is that which is to be accomplished, and it has three purposes because its nature is that of all happiness.

It is "all objects" because it takes the form of all stable and moving entities; it is "consisting of the three qualities" because its sole inherent nature is the unobscured qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. || 22 ||

He who realizes the meaning of the five aggregates throughout the three times, who discerns every moment, who is perfectly awakened in a single moment, and who upholds the essential nature of all Buddhas. (23)

Regarding "the meaning of the five aggregates": through the manifestation of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) by means of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), the Buddha is the meaning of the five aggregates; thus, he is "the meaning of the five aggregates.
By virtue of his permanence, he is the three times.
He is "thus" (tathā) because he cultivates and pierces every moment of the breath of conceptual construction with great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Furthermore, in that very single fourth moment, he is the knower who has awakened to that which is called Samantabhadra, which is non-different from all phenomena; for this very reason, he is the "upholder of the nature of all Buddhas," meaning he is the bearer of the Innate Body (*sahajakāya*). || 23 ||
Bodyless-body, the body within the body, the one who manifests millions of bodies;
he who displays all forms, the great jewel Ratnaketu. || 24 ||
Thus are the twenty-four verses on the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). Regarding "Anaṅga":

because it resides within the *cūḍāmaṇi*-wheel, the *dharmadhātu*—the vajra-wisdom limb—is the "body of Anaṅga" (*anaṅgakāya*). Since that very [dharmadhātu] consists of the accumulation of bliss, it is "one whose body is the limbs" (*kāyāṅga*); thus, by means of great bliss, he "manifests the limit of the body," and is therefore called the "Manifestor of the Limit of the Body" (*kāyakoṭivibhāvaka*).

For this very reason, he is the "Displayer of All Forms" according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*vineya*). He is the "Jewel Banner" (*Ratnaketu*) because his banner is marked with the jewel of bliss for the purpose of pleasing all people.
He is the "Great Jewel" (*Mahāmaṇi*) because he abides as a great gem. (24)

Thus, there are twenty-four verses on the knowledge of equality, concerning the purity attained through the realization of the twelve stages via the cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination]. 9.
There is nothing attained.
This is the established tenet;
it is free from delusion.
Now, because it is its own nature:
[the verse] "In the three times, in the three times, the bodiless body.
Verses in praise of gnosis.

"He cultivates and expands"—thus, the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (the wisdom of accomplishing activities) is now described as that very same supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*) in the form of Amoghasiddhi, the aggregate of unobstructed formations (*anāvaraṇasaṃskāraskandha*), by means of the verse concerning the fifteen accomplishments of activity: "The All-Buddha who is to be awakened, the syllable-less, the Buddha-awakening, the unsurpassed;
the source of mantra, the great mantra, the three families. (1)

"By all the perfectly awakened ones" means that he whose nature is perfect knowledge is to be understood and directly realized by all the perfectly awakened ones existing in the three times; he alone is Mañjuśrī, the Body of Knowledge (*jñānakāya*).
And it has been said: "Perfect awakening depends upon you; you are the father of all embodied beings."
The Tathāgatas who have arisen and those who will arise have all come into being by relying upon you.
Because its nature consists in the realization of the true essence of body, speech, and mind, it is the non-dual Śrī herself, the awakening of the Buddhas.
Because it is the nature of the fourth perfect enlightenment, it is unsurpassed.

Since it is devoid of the relationship between signifier and signified, and because it is the self-nature of the union with the supreme syllable of the *dharmadhātu*, it is "without syllables" (*anakṣara*).

The meaning is that he is "not transcended" by qualities such as form and so forth. Because he is the source—the cause of the arising—of worldly and other mantras through his innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*), the Blessed One is thus [described]. Since the three families (*kulatraya*)—consisting of body, speech, and mind, and characterized by bliss, supreme bliss, and the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*)—are his own self-realized domain by way of the states of exhaling (*recaka*), inhaling (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*), he is one who possesses that great system of mantra (*mahāmantranaya*). || 1 ||
The great bindu, which is without syllables, gives birth to the meaning of all mantras;
it is the five-syllabled great void, the bindu-void, and the six-syllabled. || 2 ||

Regarding "the meaning of all mantras": the worldly mantra is characterized by rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and by withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); the supramundane mantra consists of the *bindu* and *nāda* through union with the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
That very object, because it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is the meaning of all mantras; it is the meaning of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Its progenitor is its producer.

Through the forms of the syllables *oṃ* (and *ha*) together with *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa kṣa*, the ten groups [of consonants] and the ten vital winds (*prāṇa*) and so forth become unified as a single mass by way of flowing through the central channel (*madhyamā*), and because they dissolve into all bodies, the Blessed One is the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*).
Because it is of the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is syllable-less (*anakṣara*).
Vajrasattva is the knowledge of the bliss of the ultimate truth.
And it is said in the *Mūlatantra*: "Since he is the protector (*trāṇa*) of the elements of body, speech, and mind, therefore..."
"The meaning of mantra is the syllable that is the gnosis of emptiness;
mantra consists of merit and gnosis, and has the nature of emptiness and compassion. Thus [it is said]. *Bodhāṅgayo*.
The imperishable;
not born from a womb;
the sahaja syllable *oṃ*.
By virtue of being a potter. Regarding the rites for pacification and prosperity:
[the word] "from oneself" does not exist.
The hundred-syllabled;
the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*).

Accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*: the state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*) regarding the aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*), the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), mind, ear, sound, the dharma-element, the divine faculties, and the forms of the flow of the female secretions and the emission of semen; each of these being devoid of grasping its own respective object, having become of one flavor (*samarasa*) and unified as a single whole, [this is] the supreme (the first syllable, emptiness), to be personally realized by the yogi, and not characterized by the total non-existence of all things.

He says that very thing: in the center, the form of the letter *ka* (the agent), which is the void of the letter *ta* and consists of a mere line, is the state of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), the nose, touch, the organ of speech, and the emission of feces having become unified; it is to the east of the central unstruck mark (*anāhata-cihna*). The second syllable is the void of the letter *i*, having the form of a staff; it is the state of the absence of obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*) of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), the eye, taste, the hand, and movement, located to the south of the central unstruck mark. The third syllable is the void of the letter *kā*, consisting of two points (*bindu*).

The state of being free from obscuration regarding the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the water element (*toyadhātu*), the tongue, form (*rūpa*), the foot, the faculty (*indriya*), grasping (*ādāna*), and so forth, is [symbolized] by the left side of the central unstruck sign (*anāhata-cihna*); it is the single drop-form (*bindu-rūpa*), the unutterable, the void *m*, the fourth syllable, the great void (*mahāśūnya*).

The state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*) and the state of becoming one mass (*ekalolībhūtatva*) regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), odor (*gandha*), the anus, and speech (*ālāpa*), is [symbolized] to the west of the central unstruck sign; that is the shape of the letter *ha*, the void *e*, the fifth-syllable void (*pañcākṣara-śūnya*).

Thus, the syllable *vaṃ* consists of five letters; it is the great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), supportless, and of the nature of compassion. It transcends the reality of atoms, is comparable to a reflected image (*pratisenā*), and is accessible only to yogis. Its support is the letter *e*, which has the form of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), whose intrinsic nature is the emptiness of all aspects, and which is the six-syllabled "emptiness of the drop" (*binduśūnya*). To explain: it is the unobstructed emptiness of the aggregate of consciousness, the element of space, the auditory faculty, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the female organ, semen, and emission. Above the previously mentioned central unstruck sign (*anāhatacinha*) is the consonant *ka*, the essence of the *ka*-group, which is not to be articulated; this is first the "emptiness of the drop."

The unobstructed emptiness in all aspects of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), touch (*sparśa*), speech (*vāk*), excrement (*viṭ*), and urine (*srāva*).
Regarding the previously mentioned sign, one should not pronounce the consonant *ca*, which consists of the *ca*-group and is the second [element] empty of the bindu.

This is the unobstructed emptiness in all aspects of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), taste (*rasa*), the hand faculty (*pāṇi-indriya*), and movement (*gati*).
To the south of the southern symbol is the syllable *ṭa*, the essence of the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*), which is unutterable, the third [vowel] *i*, and empty of the bindu;
it is the emptiness free from obscuration of perception, the aggregate of formations, the water element, the tongue, form, the foot-faculty, and the faculty of appropriation.
To the north of the northern symbol is the syllable *pa*, the essence of the *pa*-group (*pavarga*), which is unutterable, the fourth [vowel] *u*, and empty of the bindu.

The emptiness that is free from obscuration regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), odor (*gandha*), the anus (*pāyu*), and speech (*ālāpa*).
At the western position of the western sign, the consonant *ta*, which consists of the *tavarga* group, is not to be uttered; it is the fifth, the emptiness of the bindu.

The emptiness that is free from obscuration in all aspects regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*jñānaskandha*), the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*), the mind faculty (*manaḥ*), sound (*śabda*), the divine faculty (*divyendriya*), and the emission of urine (*mūtrasrāva*).
Below the sign of the *anāhata* [cakra] is the consonant *śa*, which constitutes the *śa*-group; it is unutterable, the sixth, and the void of the *bindu*.
Thus, the six-syllabled *dharmodaya* is the void of the *bindu*.
The wielder of the vajra is the syllable *e*; emptiness is with support, having the nature of a reflected image (*pratisenā*).
By this, the great void consisting of five syllables—
the collection of vowels— is called the Moon;
the void with a bindu consisting of six syllables— the collection of consonants— is called Passion, the Sun.

In this context, *śukra* (semen) is the moon, the syllable *vaṃ*, and the *vajra*; *rajas* (ovum) is the sun, the syllable *e*, and the *padma*. The unification of these two, the *vajra* and the *padma*, is *vastra-sattva*.
*Vastra* is supreme bliss; *jñāna* is *śukra*; and *sattva* is the image of wisdom (*prajñā*) in all its aspects, which is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Established in both primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), being free from obscuration and having attained a state of single integration, it is the *vastra-sattva* that acts for the benefit of the world.
And this should be understood as stated in the Vimalaprabhā. || 2 ||
The object is the grasping;
it has not gone [to the object], yet it has the form of the fruit.
Mind.
It is real;
[it is] that of the faculties and so forth.
Being! Being!
The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti is endowed with all forms yet is formless, bearing sixteen half-moons and half-bindus.
He is timeless, transcending all time, the upholder of the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna. || 3 ||
"Of all forms" means that the cause of both having form and being formless has been explained.
That entity, such as a jar or the like, which is perceived through sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra)—
The appearance is equal to a *pratisenā* (divinatory mirror-image), possessing all aspects (*sarvākāra*).

It is formless (*nirākāra*) because it is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and devoid of error; it transcends the nature of atoms (*paramāṇudharmatātīta*) because it is devoid of conceptualization. It is accessible to those with eyes both closed and open. Thus, the cause—both possessing all aspects and yet formless—is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) endowed with all aspects. The fruit arising therefrom is the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), which possesses sixteen half-moons and drops (*bindu*); this is called the "Great Wisdom-Knowledge" (*mahāprajñājñāna*) by the Tathāgatas.

And it is said: "Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is shown to be the cause; subsequently, non-referential compassion, which effects the welfare of the world, is the fruit. Thus, of the sixteen digits (*kalā*), half is eight, and half of that is four drops (*bindu*), characterized by body, speech, mind, and gnosis. These are the generators of the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turyā*);
he who sustains them is the "sustainer of the four half-and-half drops" (*ṣoḍaśārdhārdhabindudhṛk*).
The meaning is that he is Vajrasattva, the Great Passion, who observes the four commitments (*samaya*).

He is "without parts" (*akala*), being devoid of the fifteen parts of the bright fortnight; he abides at their end, at the conclusion of the full moon of the bright fortnight, as one who has transcended conceptualization (*kalanātīta*). Here, "conceptualization" refers to the first day of the dark fortnight; not abiding therein means he is the Innate (*sahaja*) who has transcended conceptualization.

The "holder of the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna" (caturthadhyānakoṭighṛk) refers to this: first, the dhyāna of the bliss of joy; second, the dhyāna of the bliss of supreme joy; third, the dhyāna of the bliss of the cessation of joy; and fourth, the dhyāna of the bliss of innate joy. The fifth, which is the tenth, is the full [state];

at the end of the full, the dhyāna of the bliss of the supreme immutable syllable (paramākṣara-sukha) resides within the drop (bindu). Its "pinnacle" (koṭi) is its foremost part, the state of being completely filled with bliss; he who holds that is the "holder of the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna. || 3 ||
He is the master of all the arts of meditation, the knower of the lineage and family of meditative absorptions;
he is the body of absorption, the supreme body, and the sovereign of all enjoyment bodies.
It should be known that through the application of investigation, there arises the knowledge of all meditations;
the third is characterized by joy, and the fourth is the gathering of bliss.

The fifth, however, is constant light, cloudless, and resembling the sky. Thus, because he possesses mastery over the five branches of meditation (*pañcadhyānakalā*), he is "one who knows all branches" (*sarvakalābhijña*); and because he possesses the power of the collection of meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharmasamatā*), he is "one who knows the lineage of the family of meditative absorptions" (*samādhikulagotravit*).
The body of concentration (*samādhikāya*) is this very *dharmakāya*; he who possesses it as the foremost of both the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya* is thus [described].
Because he shines in the midst of all assemblies by means of the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is non-different from the *dharmakāya*, he is the "King of all *saṃbhogakāyas*" (*sarvasaṃbhogakāyarāṭ*). 4.
Deluded,
having planted [the seeds], he weeps for the fruit; he is the upholder of the lineage.
The one who manifests ten million bodies,
the secret, the arising of reasoning, the investigation of reasoning,
together with the seed-syllable of the deceased, is the Nirmāṇakāya; the supreme body, the lineage-bearer of the Buddha's emanations.
He who fashions the universe throughout the ten directions and acts for the benefit of the world as is appropriate. ||5||
Regarding the *nirmāṇakāya*:

the *nirmāṇakāya* itself—which possesses the nature of effortless benefit for external beings—is the foremost among all other emanations; it is worthy of being called the body of the *nirmāṇakāya* because it maintains the lineage of the three families, five families, and so forth, together with all phenomena, by means of its luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). Thus it is.

He is thus because he is the one whose emanation of the universe spreads throughout the ten directions; as he acts for the benefit of his own world, he is the one who truly accomplishes the welfare of the world. (5)
The god beyond gods, the lord of gods, the lord of the Suras, the sovereign of the Dānavas, the lord of the immortals, the preceptor of the gods, the destroyer, and the lord of the destroyers. ||6||
He is the god beyond gods because, as the embodiment of great passion (*mahārāga*), he has the nature of Brahmā;
he is the lord of gods because, as the garment of the luminous mind (*prabhāsvara-citta*), he has the nature of Viṣṇu.
He is the Lord of the Gods (*surendra*) because, by entering the *uṣṇīṣa* within the jewel, he possesses the form of *bali*;
he is the Lord of the Dānavas (*dānavādhipa*) because, by attaining the incomparable, non-dual glory of the nectar of Dharma, he possesses the nature of *rāhu*;
and he is the Lord of Men (*amarendra*) because, through the gait of Airāvata within selflessness (*nairātmya*), he possesses the nature of Purandara.

He is Bṛhaspati because he possesses the nature of Bṛhaspati through the revelation that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). He is the Teacher of the Gods (*suraguru*) for the same reason. He is Pramatha because he is the lord of obstacles (*vighnādhipati*), having subdued the hosts of obstructing deities such as the Prādeśika and Kṣaṇa through the semen of great bliss (*mahāsukha-śukra*).
He is the Lord of Destruction (*pramayeśvara*) because he possesses the nature of Tryambaka (the Three-Eyed One) in the form of liberation from body, speech, and mind. || 6 ||
Having crossed the wilderness of existence, he is the sole Teacher, the Guru of the world,
renowned throughout the ten directions, and the great Lord of the Gift of Dharma.
Having crossed over existence, he is one without a second, having crossed the wilderness of existence by means of setting forth the correct knowledge for all sentient beings.

The Teacher is the Guru of the World because he teaches the Dharma that gives rise to great happiness for those suffering from various forms of misery; because he dwells in unshakable blissful gnosis through the pacification of all conceptual proliferation (prapañca); and because he is renowned throughout the ten directions as the Lord of the Gift of Dharma, appearing to Bodhisattvas and others—those who are famous and have become "Awakened" through the accumulation of merit and so forth—in the form of the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) and other manifestations.
It is great, pervading all things by virtue of its nature as both the stable and the moving. || 7 ||

Girt with the armor of loving-kindness, mounted on the elephant of compassion, and armed with the sword and bow of wisdom, he abandons the battle against the afflictions and their objects of cognition. ||8||

"Loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) is the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*); it is "loving-kindness" because it pervades all limbs. One is "armed with that armor," meaning one is fully equipped and fortified by removing mental distraction through the previously mentioned armor of compassion (*karuṇā-varma*), and is thus protected.

He is one who possesses the sword of wisdom—that great seal (mahāmudrā) which has attained stainlessness—and likewise the bow, the sound, and the arrow, because they are of that very nature; and through the union with the samādhi of great passion, he abandons the battle of afflictions and knowledge by consuming the latent tendencies of emission. || 8 ||
The Lord of Gods, the Lord of Asuras,
the teacher of non-self, the unique instructor.
The world is renowned as the source of happiness.
The rhinoceros [attains] consumption through the latent impression of union.

The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti: The enemy of Māra, the conqueror of Māra, the hero who brings an end to the fear of the four Māras, the vanquisher of all the armies of Māra, the perfectly awakened one, the leader of the world. ||9||
"Mārāri" means the enemy of Māra;

because his body, speech, and mind are characterized by passion that is pervaded by the luminous jewel, he is Vajrasattva. Through the cessation of the vital winds (prāṇa) and downward-flowing winds (apāna), there is victory over the life-force of Māra; for this very reason, he is "Bhīra" (the Hero).

Because his nature consists of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], and because he has brought to an end the waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and fourth states, he is the destroyer of the fear of the four Māras.
By virtue of his naturally stainless self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), he is the conqueror of all the hosts of Māras;
and because he is the sovereign of the six maṇḍalas, he is the Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddha*).
Because he has abandoned the impurity of craving for existence, he is the Leader of the World. || 9 ||
He is to be saluted, worshiped, and greeted; he is to be honored perpetually—the most worthy of adoration, the venerable one, the supreme teacher to be bowed down to. || 10 ||

He is "to be venerated" because, by entering into the knowledge of the auspicious sacred ford (tīrtha) and thereby washing away the impurities of ignorance and so forth, he is the supreme teacher of all the worlds, including the gods. || 10 ||

He whose gait traverses the three worlds, whose prowess extends to the limits of space, who possesses the three types of knowledge, who is learned in the Vedas, who is pure, who has the six supernormal powers, and who possesses the six recollections. || 11 ||

*Trailokyeka* means that whose movement (*gati*)—that is, experience (*anubhava*)—is the peerless innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) of the *trailokyaka* stage; or, by that movement, its pervasion (*vyāpti*) in space (*vyoman*) is such that its stride (*vikrama*) reaches the limit, and its play (*krīḍana*) consists in its innate nature (*sahajarūpatā*). Thus he is so described.
Because the non-manifest (*nirābhāsa*) has the nature of radiating, it is "form" (*rūpa*); thus,
he who possesses the three sciences (*traividya*)— namely, the three sciences that accomplish the *mahāmudrā-siddhi* of the desire realm and the form realm—
is a *śrotriya* because he is utterly pure due to his capacity to produce supreme bliss even through mere hearing.
Because he rises eternally in his fourth form, he is pure and sanctified;
because he possesses non-dual knowledge through the unity of the grasped and the grasper, he possesses the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijña*);

and because he consists of the retention and recollection of the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity, which have entered into the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the six chakras, he is the one who possesses the six recollections (*ṣaḍanusmṛti*). || 11 ||
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has transcended the world, possesses great supernatural power, is established in the perfection of wisdom, and has attained the true nature of wisdom. || 12 ||
He is called a *bodhisattva* because he awakens to the meaning of the Mahāyāna through non-attachment to all phenomena;
he is a *mahāsattva* because he satisfies sentient beings with immeasurable happiness.
Because he is free from worldly conceptualization, he has transcended the world (*lokātīta*).
Because of his great power in uplifting sentient beings through the bliss of enjoying sensual pleasures—which is inconceivable—he possesses great supernatural might (*maharddhika*).
Through his state as "Fine Moon" (*Sucandra*), due to the disappearance of all objective perception, he has reached the culmination of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Through wisdom, you have attained and reached the true nature of Mahāmudrā. || 12 ||
He knows himself and knows others; he is all, the most excellent, the foremost of persons.
Having transcended all comparisons, he is the supreme Lord of Knowledge, the object of knowledge. 13.
One who knows the self (*ātmavit*) is so called because, by virtue of transcending all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they possess the nature of space;
and because of the realization of the non-duality of self and other, they are one who knows the supreme (*paravit*).
He is "all" because he manifests the intrinsic nature of all phenomena without exception;
he is "belonging to all" because of his realization of the non-duality of existence and non-existence;
and he is "without person" because he is the gnosis-body whose essence is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Because his form is the incomparable *dharmakāya*, he has transcended all worldly analogies; thus, he is "transcending all analogies.
He is to be known as "innate" because it is to be personally realized within oneself, and as the "Lord of Gnosis" because he is easily grasped through the sovereignty of gnosis.
For this very reason, it is supreme. || 13 ||
The supreme lord of the gift of Dharma, who teaches the meaning of the four mudrās, is the most worthy of veneration by the worlds of those traveling toward the three vehicles of liberation. (14)
"Dharma-dāna" means giving the Dharma according to one's capacity; because he gives the Dharma without error, he is a master of the gift of Dharma.

Because he practices renunciation even of his own mind, he is preeminent as a master of the gift of Dharma, and he is the teacher of the meaning of the action-seal (karmamudrā), the great seal (mahāmudrā), the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā), and the commitment-seal (samayamudrā).

The Illuminator is worthy of veneration by the worlds of those traveling toward the three types of liberation—those who proceed toward the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the *mahāmudrā* of the earth-dwellers and sky-goers—precisely because he illuminates the meaning of the four *mudrās*.
And it is said in the *Caturmudropadeśa*: "The luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) is known as the *karmamudrā*, the *jñānamudrā*, and the *samayamudrā*."
The cause is that which is to be cultivated and likewise attained; the fourth is indestructible.

Regarding "the cause," it is first the innate, non-emitting bliss arising from the *karmamudrā*, which was spoken by the Blessed One and is indeed true; however, it is [true] only conventionally through worldly analogy, like a reflection, and not in the ultimate sense.
Therefore, one of sharp faculties should not grasp the action-seal (*karmamudrā*).

The action-seal—characterized by breasts and hair—is the cause of pleasure in the desire realm; "action" (*karman*) consists of activities such as kissing, embracing, touching the secret parts, and pulling at garments, and the seal (*mudrā*) defined by that which produces a [sensory] condition.
In this context, "pratyaya" (condition) is characterized by perishable pleasure (*kṣarasukha*).

It is called a *mudrā* because it bestows (*rāti*) joy (*mudaṃ*), that is, a specific kind of bliss. This is to be meditated upon as the *jñānamudrā*. She is mentally constructed by one's own mind, has the nature of goddesses such as Viśvamātā, and was previously experienced as the cause of the bliss of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is characterized by the cultivation of previous laughter, amorous play, and so forth; the condition (*pratyaya*) here is characterized by the bliss of vibration (*spanda*).

Having purified the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases in the form of deities, one should clearly manifest the nature of the mandala-circle according to the ritual procedure. By means of the union of the churner and the churned, one kindles the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*); once [the fuel] is burned, the moon flows from the tips of the lotuses at the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the vajra.

The *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*: having entered into a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that has become one with the ocean of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—which consists of the totality of objects and sense-faculties in the form of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—one should remain until the glorious Mahāmudrā becomes manifest.

Since the Mahāmudrā is obtained as being like a dream, a magical illusion, or a mental creation, and because it is both "great" (*mahatī*) and a "seal" (*mudrā*), it is called Mahāmudrā; furthermore, its greatness consists in its being endowed with all supreme aspects (*sarvākāravara-upeta*) and not being merely partial.
That by which one is sealed is the *mudrā*, namely the vajra of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Here, "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to that which is devoid of the phenomena imagined by one's own mind, preceded by signs such as smoke, and is the manifestation of one's own mind accessible to the yogi, like a reflected image (*pratisenā*). Embracing that [the *samayamudrā*], one proceeds until the *samayamudrā* is directly realized.

She is imperishable and has the nature of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*). Furthermore, she is the *mahāmudrā* in the form of the fruit; she bestows (*rāti*) joy characterized by supreme unchanging bliss and maintains it at all times through the yoga of immobility in the state of perfection—thus she is called *mudrā*.
Moreover, her greatness consists in the greatness of her abandonment and the greatness of her realization.

In this regard, the greatness of abandonment consists in the realization of the luminosity known as the *svabhāvakāya*, characterized by the abandonment of all obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*). The greatness of attainment, however, is the realization of the body known as the "united pair" (*yuganaddha*), which has the nature of all the perfectly pure qualities of a Buddha.

Furthermore, the very direct realization of the luminosity that is emptiness—resembling the cloudless midday sky—is itself the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha in the form of accomplishing the welfare of the entire world without exception.
In that regard, because all the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma) are reflected therein,
for this very reason the body which is the support of those qualities is called the *dharmakāya*. Furthermore,

if realization were established even by way of a mere appearance (*pratibhāsa*), then the undesirable consequence would be unavoidable that the realization of a jar and so forth would occur upon the appearance of a jar.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya system would be faultless;

moreover, the perception of the entire collection of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as being like an illusion, a dream, a city of Gandharvas, or a reflected image is called the vision of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).

This very conventional truth is said to be the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), which is luminously pure and takes the form of a mirror and so forth, including the host of deities to be supported such as Vairocana, and the maṇḍala of the supporting celestial palace and so on. And that very same [truth] is proclaimed in all the *tantrarāja*s as the supramundane maṇḍala.

And because it has the nature of all the qualities of a Buddha, that very same reality, which possesses the nature of the non-duality of the two truths, is called "yoked together" (*yuganaddha*); therefore, the *dharmakāya* is precisely the *yuganaddhakāya*,
distinct from both the *sāmbhogikakāya* and the *svābhāvikakāya*, and directly perceivable by yogins.
And it was said by the venerable Nāgārjuna: "That which is neither one nor many," and so forth, [describes] the characteristic of the *dharmakāya*;
"supramundane and inconceivable," and so forth, [describes] the *sambhogakāya*;
and "that which, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, shines like fire in some places," and so forth, [describes] the *nirmāṇakāya*.
By the words "free from the conduct of the three worlds" and so forth, the body of great bliss (*mahāsukhakāya*) is described;
and it is also stated in the *Svadarśanamato-uddeśa*: "The infinite mass of forms is my supreme emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
the infinite mass of sounds is my supreme enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)."
"The infinite mass of Dharma is proclaimed by me as my Dharma-body; the infinite mass of bliss is my supreme, imperishable Bliss-body."

Thus, accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, the realization of the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśī-kalā*) has been explained as the nature of the four bodies (*catuḥ-kāya*), characterized by the knowledge of the minds of others, the comprehension of sounds resembling echoes, and the perception of all forms. And it is said in the *Śrī Kālacakra*: "This body of the Innate (*sahaja-tanu*) is neither wisdom (*prajñā*) nor means (*upāya*); it has become the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). Indeed, its nature is wisdom and means, free from darkness through the distinction between gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*);
this is the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*)."
Like an echo, this emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha acts for the benefit of many sentient beings and serves as the cause for their maturation;
thus, through the purification of body, speech, and mind, the four seals (*mudrā*) have been explained.

And it is said in the *Śrī-Ādibuddha*: "The entry of the vajra into the lotus, the descent of the wind into the fire, and thirdly, the falling of the drop—these three yogas are the manifest and fixed seals of body, speech, and mind."

"The end of passion and dispassion, a treasure-trove of supreme bliss, accessible through yoga—that fourth among the mudrās is the Mother; she is the one who bestows excellent fruit, and she resides in the mouth of the glorious Guru.
And it is said in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi Tantra* and elsewhere: "Having attained the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), one should meditate upon the dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*)."
In that regard, "above" refers to Mahāmudrā, and from her arises the *samaya*. Thus,
having abandoned that auspicious Goddess, the Fortune of Liberation who possesses imperishable bliss, they take pleasure with a young woman.

"Generally, because of their previously accumulated fierce karma, they abandon the nectar and drink poison"— thus it is said in the *Śrī-Āvibuddha*: "These four mudrās, which yield the fruit of imperishable bliss, should be meditated upon by yogins at all times in every situation, even when engaged in the worldly path of sexual union with celestial nymphs."

In villages, forests, cremation grounds, in impure or pure dwellings, in houses or temples, through the application of caste or non-caste, and through the application of physical strength, happiness, food, drink, and so forth— thus [ends] the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṃgīti*, the Great One, auspicious in the three worlds, whose glory is purified in the ultimate sense.

"Mañjuśrī, the glorious one who brings about all prosperity, the best among the glorious"— these are the fifteen verses on the gnosis of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). "In the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha*) means he whose intellect possesses the two-fold purity of the hero through gnosis in the ultimate sense.
Because he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings, he is the fortunate one of the three worlds;
because he is pervasive and great, being the foundation for the attainment of all happiness and prosperity, he brings about every success.
Because he is the unfallen precious jewel beloved by all yogins, he is the Glorious One (*Śrīmān*);
because his nature is the non-duality of all phenomena, he is Mañjuśrī, the Non-dual Glory (*Advayaśrī*);
and because he is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), he is the Best among the Glorious Ones.

The Commentary on the Verses of Knowledge Concerning the Performance of Duties Characterized by Cause and Effect as Attained through the Samādhis of All Tathāgatas, by way of the Purification of the Fifteen Unobscured Kalās;
the Praise of the Five Tathāgatas: Homage to you, O Giver of Boons, Supreme Vajra, Limit of Reality! Homage be to you!
Homage to you, whose womb is emptiness, the Awakening of the Buddhas! Homage be to you!
O Buddha-attachment, homage be to you; O Buddha-desire, homage again and again.
O Buddha-joy, homage be to you; O Buddha-delight, homage again and again. O Buddha-smile, homage be to you; O Buddha-laughter, homage again and again.
Homage to you, the speech of the Buddha; homage, repeated homage, to the nature of the Buddha. Homage to you, the source of non-becoming; homage to you, O Buddha, the source of manifestation.
Homage to you, the source from the sky; homage to you, the source of primordial wisdom.
"O Net of Illusion, homage to you! Homage to you, the Buddha’s drama!
Homage to you, all of all! O Body of Gnosis, let there be homage to you!
These are the five gnosis-verses of praise to the five Tathāgatas.
Thus, the instruction on the sequence of emanation is given by way of Vajrasattva and the others; however,
the occasional instructions on transposition are for the purpose of concealing the oral tradition (āmnāya),
or because such appearances arise through the vibration of the unstruck sound (anāhatanāda) according to the disposition of sentient beings, the compiler has written it down in that very manner.

Now, praising that very same Blessed One—who is revealed within the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu—by way of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*) through these five verses beginning with "Homage to you" (*namaste*), he says: therein, by way of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), [he says] "Homage to you, the Giver of Boons" (*namaste varada*) and so forth; by way of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), [he says] "O Buddha-Passion" (*buddharāga*) and so forth; by way of the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), [he says] "O Buddha-Smile" (*buddhasmita*) and so forth; by way of the nature of the all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), [he says] "Arising from the Non-arisen" (*abhavodbhava*) and so forth; and by way of the essence of the perfectly pure wisdom of the dharmadhātu (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*), [he says] "The Net of Illusion" (*māyājāla*) and so forth.
The meaning is that [it is] by way of the nature of the Tathāgatas Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya.
In this regard, the first verse states the cause, while the remaining verses state the effect;

thus, there is causal knowledge (*hetujñāna*), conditional knowledge (*pratyayajñāna*), knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*), and knowledge of liberation (*muktijñāna*).

The mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is the cause; the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is the condition; the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*); and the wisdom of liberation is the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*).
Thus, the cultivation of the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) has been indicated.

Therefore, in the *Mūlatantra*, within the *Praise of the Fivefold Wisdom*, the Blessed One taught the meditation on the five aspects through five verses, as follows: "This entire collection of phenomena is empty, devoid of the form of conceptual construction;
it is seen like a reflection in a mirror by a young girl. Thus, the supramundane truth (*lokottarasatya*) is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Having become equal to all phenomena (*sarvabhāva*), one phenomenon remains as the imperishable (*akṣara*);
born from the knowledge of the imperishable, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Thus is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) as the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
"All letters consist of conceptualization and arise from the family of the letter A;

having attained the state of the Great Syllable, they are neither conceptualization nor possessors of conceptualization. Thus ends the aggregate of conceptualization, which is the wisdom of discernment.

In phenomena that are unarisen and devoid of formative activity, there is no awakening, nor indeed Buddhahood, nor a sentient being, nor even a life-principle. Thus is the aggregate of formative activity; this is the gnosis of the performance of duties.

"Phenomena have transcended the nature of consciousness; they are indeed pure gnosis, untroubled, luminous by nature, and have reached the course of the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the gnosis of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*.

Likewise, it is stated in the *Laghutantra* through three verses beginning with "one hundred and one" that the characteristics of the aggregates of the Tathāgatas, starting with the wheel-sign, [are as follows].

That is to say: the wheel is the pure triple world; bliss is its jewel; passion is its lotus; the sword is the destruction of the afflictions; the vajra is the indestructible body of great gnosis; the excellent sixfold axe is the cutting away of ignorance. Those who have been produced by these [deities] of the six families should be understood in this way: like space, the aggregates, elements, and sense-faculties are of a single flavor.

That in which the form of birth reaches its end is called the Great Form; that in which the suffering of saṃsāra reaches its end is called Great Sensation; that in which the perception of saṃsāra reaches its end is the Great Vajra Perception; and that in which the increase of saṃsāra reaches its end is the formation of the Vajra itself.
That in which states such as sleep reach their end is called *vijñāna* (consciousness); that in which the state of ignorance reaches its end is indeed the *jñāna* (gnosis) of the Sage.

These Vairocana and others are the six supreme and excellent Victors, the six families; the others are the divisions of the six elements: earth, fire, water, wind, space, and peace. The meaning, however, is as follows: "O Supreme Vajra, Bestower of Boons," is an address [to the Buddha] because his nature consists of the four joys (*caturānanda*).
Because it is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) by its very nature,
it is the womb of emptiness through its blissful, empty, and non-dual character;
as the form of the illustrative example, it is the enlightenment of the Buddha and the entry into luminosity— this is the homage.
Because it is the nature of great passion (*mahārāga*), it is the passion of the Buddha (*buddharāga*);
because it is the *dharmakāya* by virtue of being the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), it is the body of the Buddha (*buddhakāya*);
or, according to another reading, it is "the desire of the Buddhas" (*buddhakāma*).
Buddha-joy (*buddhaprīti*) arises through the moment of innate bliss whose essence is emptiness;
Buddha-delight (*buddhamoda*) arises from the attainment of the joy of non-dual bliss through the abandonment of duality.
By this, the cognition of the condition (*pratyayajñāna*) is explained.
Because he manifests the primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) consisting of bliss through yoga, he is the "Smile of the Buddha" (*buddhasmita*);
because he pervades the entire mandala of all objects of knowledge by means of the light of the innate *caṇḍālī*, he is the "Laughter of the Buddha" (*buddhahāsa*);

and because, even by way of the Karmic Woman (*karmāṅganā*), the vital winds such as *prāṇa* have been brought to the state of the *avadhūtī*, he is the "Speech of the Buddha" (*buddhavāca*) in the form of the vibration of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*).
The state of Buddhahood arises from the non-dual enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) inseparable from the *dharmakāya*;
because it consists of the four bodies produced from emptiness, it arises from the ultimate realm (*aghabhava*); and because it is the essential nature itself, it is the birth of the Buddha.

Because it is the nature of the self-arisen (*svayambhū*), it is the "Arising of Gnosis" (*jñānasambhava*) due to being self-cognizable as transcending existence and non-existence beyond the fourth state, like the sky;
because it is supreme bliss arisen from Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), it is the "Net of Illusion" (*māyājāla*);
and because it is the nature of the steady and moving that flashes forth spontaneously, it is the "Buddha-Drama" (*buddhanāṭaka*).

The address "to all" (*sarvatra*) is used because of the plurality [of the Buddhas] due to their nature as the sixteen joys; "to all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*) [is used] because Samantabhadra is the foremost of the Great Bliss Knowledge Body (*mahāsukha-jñānakāya*), hence he is called the "Knowledge Body" (*jñānakāya*). This is the state of existence (*bhava*).

—Thus end the five verses of praise to the wisdom of the five Tathāgatas. O Vajrapāṇi, this *Nāmasaṅgīti*—the praise of Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, who is the wisdom-body of all Tathāgatas and the Blessed One Vajradhara—is uniquely pure. It has been taught, proclaimed, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and empowered by me for the sake of generating unsurpassed joy, palaces of delight, and great exultation; for the purification of the secrets of body, speech, and mind; for the fulfillment and purification of the accumulations of merit and wisdom on the stages and perfections that have not yet been fully purified; for the attainment of the unsurpassed goal not yet attained; for the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired; and, finally, for the purpose of upholding the guidance of all phenomena of all Tathāgatas. O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, it has been placed within your own mental continuum through my empowerment as the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all mantras.

Thus ends the eleventh section on the benefits of the first wheel. Furthermore, O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, this *Nāmasaṅgīti* is perfectly pure and completely refined; it is the secret of the body, speech, and mind of the omniscient wisdom-body (*sarvajñajñānakāya*); it is the awakening of all Tathāgatas, the realization of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the perfectly enlightened ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). It is the unsurpassed [teaching] of all Tathāgatas, the defeat of the forces of all Māras by the Sugatas, and the possession of the ten powers by all who possess the ten powers. It is omniscience for all forms of omniscient knowledge, the source (*āgama*) of all phenomena, and the full attainment (*samudāgama*) of all Buddha-qualities. It is the fulfillment of the accumulations of stainless and perfectly pure merit and wisdom for all great Bodhisattvas; the birthplace of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the field for the prosperity of all gods and humans; the foundation of the Mahāyāna; the origin of the Bodhisattva conduct; the culmination of the noble path; the touchstone for liberations; the source of the path to Nirvāṇa; the non-interruption of the lineage of the Tathāgatas; the growth of the family and clan of the great Bodhisattvas; the subjugation of all opposing disputants; the destruction of all heretics; the defeat of the army of the four Māras; the gathering of all sentient beings; the ripening of the noble path for all those traveling toward liberation; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for those dwelling in the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*); the meditation (*dhyāna*) for those with one-pointed minds; the yoga for those devoted to body, speech, and mind; the dissociation from all fetters (*saṃyojana*); the abandonment of all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*); the pacification of all obscurations; the liberation from all bonds; the release from all substrates of existence (*upadhi*); the peace of all mental disturbances; the mine of all prosperities; the prevention of all calamities; the closing of the doors to all miserable realms (*apāya*); the true path to the city of liberation; the cessation of the wheel of saṃsāra; the turning of the wheel of Dharma; the raising of the parasol, banner, and flag of the Tathāgata’s teaching; the empowerment for the teaching of all Dharmas; the swift accomplishment for Bodhisattvas practicing the mantra-path; the realization through cultivation for Bodhisattvas devoted to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); the penetration of emptiness for those devoted to the cultivation of the realization of non-duality; the completion of the accumulation of all perfections (*pāramitā*); the purification through the fulfillment of all stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections; the penetration of the four noble truths; the penetration of all phenomena within a single moment of mind; and the complete mastery of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—this *Nāmasaṅgīti* is the embodiment of all the qualities of the Buddhas.

Thus, these are the fifty-two words constituting the praise of the second wheel. Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, this *Nāmasaṅgīti* pacifies all the evils of the bodily, vocal, and mental conduct of all sentient beings; it purifies them, wards off all miserable rebirths, completely cuts through all karmic obscurations, prevents the arising of all eight inopportune conditions, and brings to rest the eight great fears. It destroys all bad dreams, dispels all ill omens, and pacifies all ill-omened portents and obstacles. It renders all Māras and enemies powerless, increases all roots of virtue and merit, and prevents the arising of all improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). [This is] the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*.

It is that which eradicates the syllable *ṅ*, which prevents the arising of all suffering and mental distress; it is the heart of all Tathāgatas, the secret of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the mystery of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and the essence of all mudrās and mantras. It generates mindfulness and clear comprehension for those who proclaim the ineffability of all phenomena; it produces unsurpassed wisdom and intelligence; it brings about health, strength, sovereignty, and prosperity; it increases glory, auspiciousness, peace, and welfare; it illuminates fame, renown, praise, and eulogy; it pacifies all diseases and great fears. It is the most pure among the pure, the most sanctifying among the sanctifying, the most blessed among the blessed, and the most auspicious among all that is auspicious. It is a refuge for those seeking refuge, a shelter for those seeking shelter, a protection for those seeking protection, and a final resort for those seeking a final resort. It is an island for those seeking an island, and for those without a destination, it is the unsurpassed destination. For those crossing the ocean of existence, it is a vessel; as the king of great medicines, it eradicates all diseases. As wisdom, it discerns what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. As the light of knowledge, it dispels all darkness, gloom, and false views. As a king of wish-fulfilling gems, it fulfills the intentions and aspirations of all sentient beings. It is the omniscient knowledge itself, for the sake of attaining the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*) of Mañjuśrī. It is a mirror of perfectly pure knowledge, for the sake of attaining the five eyes. It is the fulfillment of the six perfections through the relinquishing of material gifts, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of Dharma. It is the attainment of the ten stages through the fulfillment of the accumulations of merit and wisdom and the perfection of meditative concentration. It is the non-dual nature of reality because it is free from dualistic phenomena; it is the form of suchness because it is free from superimposition. It is the form of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), having the nature of the perfectly pure Wisdom Body of all Tathāgatas. It is the form of the great emptiness of all aspects, because it eradicates the thicket of all paths of false views. This *Nāmasaṃgīti* is the ineffable form of all phenomena, insofar as it reveals the collection of names for the purpose of entering into the non-dual nature of reality.
Thus, these are the benefits of the third wheel, consisting of fifty-two words.

Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, O Wielder of the Vajra, if any son of noble family or daughter of noble family who practices the conduct of the mantra-path should daily, at the three times of day, uphold, recite, master, and properly attend to this *Nāmasaṅgīti*—the crest-jewel of names accompanied by the *Kaṇikā*, complete in its entirety, neither deficient nor fragmented, consisting of these very verses, phrases, and syllables; and if they should meditate with one-pointed mind upon any particular name-meaning, taking it as the object of the wisdom-body of Mañjuśrī; and if, abiding in the *Samantamukha-vihāra* through both resolute faith and mental attention to reality, they are endowed with supreme, unclouded, and penetrating faith that penetrates all phenomena; then all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas bound to the three times will gather together and reveal to them the gateways of all phenomena and manifest their own forms. Furthermore, the empowerment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will correctly empower their continuum through all body, speech, and mind within the state of non-conceptualization (*acitta*), and they will favor them with the grace of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, bestowing upon them the eloquence and confidence regarding all phenomena. All Arhats, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas will also manifest their own forms as the standard of the Noble Dharma. And the Great Wrathful Kings, such as Mahāvajradhara and others—the subduers of the difficult-to-tame, who are the protectors of the world—will bestow upon them the power, splendor, and invincibility of various emanations, and they will bestow all the mantra-seals, realizations, and maṇḍalas. All the great queens of mantra-vidyā, the *Pratyaṅgirā* spells, and the great invincible ones who destroy all obstacles, impediments, Māras, and enemies, will provide protection, shelter, and defense day and night, at every moment and in all modes of conduct. And those such as Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, Nārāyaṇa, Sanatkumāra, Maheśvara, Kārtikeya, Mahākāla, Nandikeśvara, Yama, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Hārītī, and the World-Protectors of the ten directions—all of them will constantly and continuously, day and night, provide protection, shelter, and defense in every way: whether he is walking, standing, lying down, sitting, sleeping, waking, concentrated, or unconcentrated; whether he is alone or in the midst of a great crowd; whether he has gone to a village, city, town, district, kingdom, or capital; whether he is in the vicinity of a boundary pillar, a carriage road, a main street, a city gate, a royal highway, a crossroads, a junction, or the middle of a marketplace or a shop; even when he is in an empty house, a mountain cave, a river, or a thicket; whether he is defiled by food remnants or not, intoxicated, or heedless—they shall always and in every manner provide protection, shelter, and defense.

Day and night they will provide supreme auspiciousness; and all other gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as other planets, constellations, Gaṇapatis, the Seven Mothers, and the yakṣīs, rākṣasīs, and piśācīs—all of them together, united, with their armies and retinues—will provide supreme protection, defense, and concealment in all modes of conduct, and they will instill vigor and strength in his body and bestow health and long life.
Thus, these nineteen words constitute the praise of the fourth wheel.

Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, whoever shall daily recite this *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the crest-jewel of names, three times a day with unbroken concentration, whether from memory or while reading from a book; whoever, focusing on the form of the Blessed Mañjuśrī-Jñānasattva, contemplates that form and meditates upon that very form, will—by means of his emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—soon protect the lineage of those to be disciplined. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwelling in the expanse of space, accompanied by various emanated bodies, will also protect him. That being shall never, under any circumstances, fall into the miserable states or the lower realms; he shall not be reborn in a low family, nor in a border region, nor shall he have impaired faculties. He shall not be born into a family of wrong views, nor shall he arise in Buddha-fields where no Buddha resides. He shall not be turned away from the appearance of a Buddha, nor shall he be averse to or alienated from the Dharma taught by him. He shall not be reborn among the long-lived gods, nor during the intermediate aeons of famine, disease, and weapons, nor during the times of the five corruptions. He shall have no fear of kings, enemies, or thieves; no fear of poverty or lack of all necessities; and no fear of ill-repute, slander, blame, infamy, or dishonor. He shall be endowed with a noble birth, family, and lineage, and possessed of a form and complexion that is universally pleasing. He shall be dear and agreeable to others, living in supreme happiness, and a pleasant sight for the world. He shall be auspicious, fortunate, and his speech shall be persuasive to the world. Wherever he is reborn, he shall remember his past lives. He shall possess great wealth, a great retinue, and an inexhaustible following. He shall be a leader of all beings, endowed with the foremost virtues, and naturally possessed of the qualities of the six perfections. He shall dwell in the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāras*), and be endowed with mindfulness, alertness, skillful means, power, aspiration, and wisdom. He shall be proficient in all treatises, eloquent, clear-spoken, and free from dullness. He shall be capable, untiring, contented, highly purposeful, and free from craving. He shall be supremely trusted by all beings and honored as a teacher and a guru. All the sciences of arts and crafts, as well as the knowledge of their treatises, shall manifest to him in both their meaning and their textual expression. He shall practice with perfectly pure morality, livelihood, and conduct. He shall be a true renunciant and endowed with beauty. His mind of omniscience and awakening (*bodhicitta*) shall never be forgotten, and he shall never enter the fixed course of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Thus, these are the fifty-one quarter-verses of praise for the fifth wheel.

Thus, Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, that person who practices the conduct of the mantra-path will be endowed with immeasurable qualities; he will be endowed with other immeasurable multitudes of qualities of this kind. Before long, Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, that person who upholds the *Paramārthanāmasaṅgīti*—having well accumulated the equipment of merit and wisdom—will very swiftly perfect the qualities of a Buddha and realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. He will be the teacher of the unsurpassed Dharma for all sentient beings whose nature is not to pass into parinirvāṇa for many eons, their supporter, and the drum of the True Dharma in the ten directions, born from the sound of the Dharma.
Thus, the benefits of this sixth wheel are immeasurable. Now, even a small portion of the benefits of the words [of the *Nāmasaṃgīti*] shall be analyzed.

This very *Nāmasaṃgīti*—as the attainment of bliss being directly experienced as "this is it"—is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*) because its nature is luminosity; it is innate experience (*sahajānubhūti*) because, by virtue of having an eternally innate pure nature, it is uniquely purified even during the enjoyment of the five desires, being unmixed with afflictions (*kleśa*). It is unsurpassed and immeasurable.
This Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti is unsurpassed joy because it is the path.

Because of the manifestation (or production) of clarity through the experience of the causal signs (*nimitta*), there arises great agitation. The guidance of the non-existent Dharma (*asaddharmanetrī*)—which is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—is the secret nature of body, speech, and mind, having the essence of the garment of the *bodhicitta*. Its "upholding" (*sandhāraṇa*) consists in bringing it to the state of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). Through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), because of the revelation of the *bodhicitta-vajra* whose nature is both the conventional and the ultimate, it is taught by the six terms beginning with "deśitā. It is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the stabilization [of the mind], because of being the sovereign of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakravartin*); since the first wheel possesses the quality of natural luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*), it is the gnosis of the Omniscient One (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The awakening of a Buddha is the experience of the fourth gnosis;
it is the clear realization, the direct perception of the luminous and non-manifesting gnosis;
and because its intrinsic nature is the emptiness of all aspects, it is the realization of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Through the power of the ten kinds of signs, such as smoke and so forth, one possesses the strength of the ten powers;
it is an "āgama" (scriptural tradition) because it comes from great bliss,
and it is a "samudāgama" (attainment) because its nature is realization through effortless spontaneity.
It is "stainless" because it is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
it is "birth" because, through emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one perceives the reflection of the Buddha in the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
and it is the "field" because its nature consists of the completely pure network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*).
It is *pratiṣṭhā* because it exists in the form of the fruit; it is the *saṃvṛti-mahāyāna* and the *paramārtha-triyāna*.
It is the *bodhisattvacaryā* because its nature is the realization that is non-contradictory with practice;
it is the *niṣṭhā* because it is the cause for attaining the ultimate consummation.
