It is a touchstone because it is the locus for the examination of reality;
it is an arising because it is the distinguished means for deliverance;
and it is non-interruption because it performs the work of a Tathāgata without effort.
Through the empowerment of luminosity there is increase;
through pervasiveness there is inclusion; and through the inconceivable nature there is meditative absorption.
It is *dhyāna* because it consists of the fivefold meditations beginning with wisdom (*prajñā*);
it is *yoga* because it is the abode of pure knowledge alone;
and it is *prahāṇa* (abandonment) because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have become non-manifest.
It is liberation because it is the cause for the removal of the bonds of passion and so forth;
it is release because its intrinsic nature is correct knowledge;
it is peace because it consists in dwelling in innate bliss.

By virtue of its luminosity, it is the source of all calamities and all defects; because it has the nature of cutting them away, it is their abandonment, and it is the closing of the gates to the lower realms— the gates to the lower realms consisting of the states of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Because it is the path to perfect awakening, it is the "true path" (*satpatha*);
because it severs dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is "non-arising";
and because it is the cause for turning the wheel of Dharma according to one's capacity, there is "turning."

Because it is the Vajrayāna, it has the nature of victory over the Śrāvakas and others; because it is the cause for stabilizing the yoga through the raising of the parasol, banner, and flag, it is an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
and because swift accomplishment is attained by Bodhisattvas practicing the conduct of the mantra-path through the recitation of mantra-syllables and so forth, it is swift success.

Because it is of the nature of direct realization, it is the attainment of meditative cultivation; because it is of the nature of the established doctrine of the specific excellence of emptiness, it is the penetration of emptiness;
and because it consists of both fruit and cause, it is the perfectly pure form of non-conceptual penetration for those devoted to the penetration of non-duality.
Because it is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), there is the penetration of all phenomena into a single mind.
Bad omens, such as signs of death from gods and so forth, and the impure latencies (*vāsanā*) for birth in inferior wombs such as those of a sow and the like, constitute ill omens;
all these are to be removed by the practice of the meditation on the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm (*vajradhātumahāmaṇḍala*) and others, which dispels the activities of all Māras and enemies.

Arrogance (*mada*) is the exhaustion of an exalted mind through the attainment of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), which prevents the arising of all improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*);
pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind.
Excessive pride,
arrogance, egoism, and the conceit of "I"— these are physical suffering and mental distress;
because they have been brought forth by the Tathāgata, they constitute his very heart.
Because it is supremely secret, it is accompanied by the *Amṛtakaṇikā*;
because it is revealed in this manner through the sequence of the Mantra system, it is of a hidden nature;
and because it is the cause for accomplishing the service of the non-conceptual *karmamudrā* and so forth, all *mudrās* are of the nature of mantra.
Health is freedom from disease; strength is physical capacity; sovereignty is the possession of elephants and the like; wealth is riches, grain, and so forth;
glory is due to being non-dual; and auspiciousness is due to being preeminent in the ten wholesome paths of action.
Peace arises from the practice of yoga;
excellence because it is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end;
and glory because of the fulfillment of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
Fame arises from the manifestation of consecrations and so forth; "verse" (śloka) because it bestows Buddhahood;
and "praise" (stuti) because of the giving of the path.
The ninety-eight afflictions are all diseases;
they are most pure because they fulfill the equipment of merit and wisdom;

they are most sanctifying because they wash away the stains of all conceptual proliferation; they are most auspicious because, by accumulating the equipment of wisdom, they remove the coarseness of the heart and establish the Buddha-dharma among those who possess the knowledge of non-Buddhist sectarians and others.
He is the refuge because he provides shelter for the helpless; he is the abode because he is the cause of delight;
he is the protection because he guards those seeking nourishment according to their respective duties.
She is the ultimate refuge for those bereft of protection,
having become an island by leading them to the city of Nirvana;
she has become the light of primordial wisdom through the illumination of emptiness, which is both endowed with all aspects and devoid of all aspects.
The five eyes, beginning with the flesh-eye,

are the non-dual nature of phenomena due to the absence of grasped object and grasping subject; because they have entered the *avadhūtī* and are free from all superimpositions, they are the form of suchness,
being the ineffable form of all phenomena due to their lack of intrinsic nature.
Because he practices the conduct of hearing, reflection, meditation, and application by way of the mantra, he is thus named Cūḍāmaṇi. As for the name *Sarvatathāgatakulodbhavānām-cūḍāmaṇi*:

because of his possession of the complete qualities of a Buddha, he will uphold—in both text and meaning—a work that is fruitful, fully perfected, complete in the purpose of all dharmas, without deficiency, unimpaired, unsurpassed, and invincible.
He will recite it through speech as the precursor to the mandalas;
he will master it through reflection;
and he will attend to it fundamentally through cultivation.

The strength of *ojas* is common; the strength of *tejas* resounds as *tejas*. *Tejas* is the internal vibration, and the majesty of *tejas* is the five-fold afflictions (*pañcakleśa*), which are the adversaries of *Pratyaṅgirā* and are characterized by the expansion of the view of self-existence (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) and the lifespan.

The connection is as follows: he will become a sovereign over the King of Dharma (Dharmarāja), who is such that his drum of Dharma resounds in the ten directions for those who are beloved, pleasing to the mind, captivating to the heart, established, and obedient, even when preceded by rejection, defamation, slander, and censure.

The arrangement of the mantra: *Oṃ sarvadharmābhāvasvabhāvaviśuddhavajra a ā aṃ aḥ*. "All phenomena are pure by nature, because they partake in the purity of Mañjuśrī, the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas. *A āḥ sarvatathāgata hṛdaya hara hara oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ bhagavan jñānamūrtivāgīśvara mahāvāca sarvadharmagaganāmala supariśuddhadharmadhātujñānagarbha āḥ*. This is the arrangement of the mantra.

Oṃ! All phenomena are pure by nature, having the essence of the non-existence of all phenomena—A Ā AṂ AḤ—by virtue of the purity of Mañjuśrī, who is the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas. A ĀḤ! O heart of all Tathāgatas, take away, take away! Oṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ! O Blessed One, embodiment of wisdom! O Great Speech, Lord of Speech! O you whose womb is the wisdom of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*, stainless as the sky of all phenomena! ĀḤ! This mantra is empowered at the beginning, middle, and end.

For instance: the syllable *A* is the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*); the syllable *Aṃ* has the nature and form of the stages (*bhūmi*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), and the conduct (*caryā*), and it indicates Buddhahood;
the syllable *Aḥ* illuminates the great emanation (*mahānirmāṇa*).

The aspect characterized by the empowerment of the body of gnosis consists of the syllables *oṃ*, *hūṃ*, and *hrīṃ*, which are the empowerments of body, speech, mind, and passion. They are established as the Dharmakāya, whose nature is the Lord of Speech of the Dharmadhātu, abiding in the form of all phenomena, both stable and moving; this is the meaning of the mudrā. At the end is the syllable *āḥ*. Then the glorious Vajradhara, joyful and satisfied, with palms joined in reverence—
Having prostrated before the Lord, the Fully Awakened One, the Blessed Tathāgata,
along with many other lords of secrets and Vajrapāṇis.
Together with the kings of wrath, he spoke these words aloud:
"We rejoice, O Lord! Excellent, excellent is this well-spoken teaching!"
A great benefit has been wrought for us, which leads to the attainment of perfect enlightenment,
as well as for the world that is without a protector and yearns for the fruit of liberation.
This pure path to the higher good, proclaimed through the method of the Net of Illusion (Māyājāla),
is profound, vast, and extensive; it possesses great significance and accomplishes the welfare of the world.
"For this is the domain of the Buddhas, spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Thus are the five concluding verses.

The *Advaya-paramārtha-nāma-saṅgīti* (The Litany of Names of Ultimate Non-duality) of the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, spoken by the Blessed Lord Śrī Śākyamuni from the chapter on the Net of Samādhis within the Noble *Māyājāla* Sixteen-Thousand-Line Mahāyoga Tantra, is hereby completed.
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; thus speaks the Great Śramaṇa.
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: immediately after that (*atha*), he who was first requested by the heroic Vajradhara spoke these words aloud.

Delighted by the accomplishment of his own bliss, and satisfied by the accomplishment of future bliss, he is the one who brings about perfect enlightenment; he is the path to excellence, arisen through the system of the mantras of the *Māyājāla*.
It is called "great" because it has been established as the basis for the welfare of both oneself and others;
furthermore, it is settled that this path is the domain of the Buddhas alone, and not of others.
The commentary on the *Śrī-nāmasaṃgīti* entitled *Amṛtakaṇikā* is completed.
It is the work of Ācārya Raviśrībhikṣu; [the reading] "of the monk" (*bhikṣoḥ*) is not found.

The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti: "Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, and also their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. In the year [represented by] the sky, the void, and the six-faced one (1600), in the dark fortnight of Caitra, on the sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, under the asterism Anurādhā, on Thursday, and in the Yoga Śuddhi.
For the benefit of sentient beings, the glorious Rūparāja has transcribed this *Śrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, the collection of the essence of the Dharma spoken by the Buddha;
and in this great monastery named Śrī-Maṇisaṃgha where you reside,
he honors the lotus feet of the Blessed Lady, the illustrious Vajravilāsinī.

Born in the family of Vastrācārya, virtuous, a knower of Dharma and the scriptures, a teacher (or knower), and possessing the splendor of the feet of the illustrious Ravi and Candra, he is renowned throughout the circle of the earth;
it has been written exactly as it was seen—there is no fault on the part of the scribe.
May there be auspiciousness at all times.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

This is the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*. Having bowed my head to the venerable teacher Śabara, whose feet rest upon it and who possesses the splendor of the sun, Vibhūticandra composes this *Amṛtakaṇikodyota* as a response to the request [of the master].
Here, indeed, the master Raviśrī, bowing to the venerable Śabaracaraṇa—the best of yogins and knower of the jewel-path taught in the *Śrī-nāmasaṅgīti*—composes this verse beginning with "viṣaya...
The connection is as follows: "I bow to the Lord of the Śabaras," because he is the foremost among all other Śabaras.

Of what nature is he? He is one for whom there is a means (*nimitta*) or method by which the contact (*āśleṣa*) of the objects (*viṣaya*)—namely form and so forth—with the eyes and other senses occurs in the sky (*vyoman*). Thus it is.
For Śabarasvāmin has taught to those seeking liberation the means for attaining union with the sky;
therefore, because he acts for the sake of others and is compassionate, and because these [beings] have entered upon this path, I bow down to him.
And it has been said: "I pay homage to those bodies in which that excellent *bodhicitta* has arisen."

And [the phrase] beginning with "bo ca" means that he has revealed precisely the path as he himself experienced it for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Furthermore, regarding this Śabaraguru, the causes (*nimitta*) such as smoke and so forth—which will be described here—proceed from the "union of the sky of object and subject" (*viṣayaviṣayivyomāśleṣa*).
In this context, the etymological derivation is: "that whose cause proceeds from the union of the sky of object and subject.
Moreover, of what nature is it? [The text continues with] "ravī" and so forth.
O child, having occupied the path of the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu, expand with the radiance of knowledge, having covered [them]—

for "āśarārī" means arrows (*śara*) and spokes (*ara*), which are five; thus, the meaning is that the wheel of saṃsāra, which has five spokes— that is, five sections— is comprised of hundreds of asuras within the [six] classes of gods.
His activity, which performs the welfare of sentient beings, is pervasive on all sides and mobile in its manifesting form;
even the sun and other celestial bodies merely indicate the auspicious or inauspicious nature of days and nights for sentient beings, yet they are themselves subject to saṃsāra,
whereas this lord of the Śabaras possesses a supramundane efficacy for the sake of beings.

Furthermore, what form do they manifest? They are intensely radiant, exceedingly vast, and greater than the light of knowledge; for while the sun and moon possess light that has hearing as its range and extension, they do not possess the light of knowledge.

Therefore, the obscuring of the sun and other luminaries by this [power] is for the sake of such a name; for it is impossible for those possessed of egoism to attain [the state of] being "seized" (graha).
Thus it has been said: "The darkening by its rays is with respect to the fitness of the gods."
Furthermore, what is this *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti* like? Regarding the passage beginning with "maṇi":

"maṇi" refers to a particular kind of ray; that which consists of it is the "stone" (*śilā*) of reality (*tattva*). Upon that very mountain called the "resting place of the mind," he is seated, because this Śabara was disciplined there by the Lord of the World.

For this very reason, [the Buddha] is described as "hidden," having entered a most profound meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and consequently as being free from calamity, unassailable, and one who has accomplished what was to be done.

By means of this, his knowledge of the path, his performance of the welfare of others, his superiority over the sun and other luminaries, his possession of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), his being supported by a body that is a "heavy" [receptacle] characterized by a specific location, his abiding in the fruit, and his having gone beyond the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) are stated. Thus, by way of establishing this analogy, it is demonstrated that one should become free from doubt and attentive to one's own welfare and to that which brings about diligence.

Alternatively, desiring to explain the *Śrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, which is the witness to the *Śrī-kālacakra* commentary that illuminates the knowledge of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*), this master—who has realized the supreme *Ādibuddha* and aspires to Buddhahood—speaks while introducing the "Innate [State] with its Means," the sole practice of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). He says, beginning with "The object" (*viṣaya*), etc. Here too, the connection is: "I bow to the Lord of the Śabaras.
To the question "Of what nature is he?", he says, beginning with "The object" (*viṣaya*), etc.

The objects (*viṣaya*) are the five [senses] beginning with form, and the subjects (*viṣayin*) are the five beginning with the eye. Among these, when there is an attachment to the void (*vyoman*), knowledge arises; he for whom the causal signs such as smoke have thus proceeded is "one such as that.

This was stated [in the Kārikā]: "by those whose minds are attached to the ether" (*ākāśāsakta-cittaiḥ*), and so forth; by this, he speaks of the two limbs of yoga: withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditation (*dhyāna*).
As it has been said: "Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the non-engagement of the ten objects and their corresponding subjects within the body;
discernment (vicāra) is that which is well-known through wisdom; delight (rati) is immovable bliss; and meditation (dhyāna) is one-pointedness of mind."

Based on the statement, "Once the image has been seen, one should then perform *prāṇāyāma* continuously," he speaks again starting with "ravī" and so forth. *Ravi* is the *rasanā*, and *śaśin* is the *lalanā*; because there is no flow in their two channels (*vartman*), which are the apertures, and because there is a continuous flow in the middle channel (*madhyamā*)—that is, by way of a constant progression—it is called *prāṇāyāma*.
As it has been said: "Prāṇāyāma is the stumbling of the two paths and the entry of the vital breath into the middle [channel].
Regarding the term *śarāricakra*: *śara* means five, and *ari* refers to spokes; thus, through their conjunction, it is the "wheel of spokes" (*aricakra*).

In that wheel—consisting of the five centers of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown—the movement of coming and going constitutes its activity, meaning it performs the action of moving. This is what is described as *dhāraṇā*.
As it has been said by Ratnapāṇi: "Furthermore, *dhāraṇā* is tenfold:
'The entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the *bindu*, [an entry] in which both movements have ceased, and one-pointedness of mind—this is *dhāraṇā*'.
Following *dhāraṇā*, the *caṇḍālī* necessarily blazes; this is the instruction, and he says "sphurat" and so forth.

Because there is a continuous flow of hearing—that is, the light of gnosis—which is more vast than the [previous] light residing in the lamp and which has emptiness as its object due to its great expansion, that is called "recollection" (anusmṛti).
As it was said: 1. These [are] of the Lord;
2. [His] ascetic heat.
And what?
6. The innate.
7. middle; 8. non-existence; 10. wheel.

11. *Vighā!*—4. The state of *rabhāva*; 5. 9. The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* states that there is an additional ‘*a*’: “Indeed, when the vision of Caṇḍālī occurs within the body, there shall be *anusmṛti* in the sky.”
Thus (Kā0 Ta0 4.117): Śabara is the most excellent bliss; he alone is the sovereign lord (*adhipa*), the king of all phenomena, because he exercises sovereignty over them with ease.
As it has been said: "O bee, drink deeply from this vast net of desire."
"The incomparable Śabara play is performed by means of the quality of the mind"—
by this, the fruit of stainlessness, which is the imperishable bliss resulting from the state of oneness between knowledge and the object of knowledge, has been stated.
As it was said: "Samādhi is [attained] in the reflection of gnosis (*jñānabimba*) by virtue of the non-emission of bliss through the nature of wisdom and means" (Kālacakratantra 4.117).
Thus the limb of samādhi has been explained; that very point he states with the words beginning with *maṇi*: "The jewel (*maṇi*) is a gem;

that which consists of it, having that as its nature, is the stone (*śilā*) of the jewel-mountain Sumeru. Mounted upon that stone made of jewels is the skeleton, which has emerged through the cavity in the middle of the skeleton-frame and reached the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*)."
As it has been said: "By means of samādhi, one goes from the throat to the head, completely filled with the bliss of purity.
For this very reason, it is hidden, concealed, and beyond the reach of the Śrāvakas and others; and because it is imperishable (*akṣara*), it is free from calamity and free from obstacles.
As it has been said: "O Lord of Mountains, why does the Śabara not dwell upon your lofty peak?
For even the noble elephant does not disregard the high ground when a lion is nearby.
That very mountain is the ancient one; its peak is its summit, which is itself the support of great bliss, a lofty and vast plateau.

Where the Śabara Vajradhara has made his dwelling, that place is neither leaped over nor smelled by the lion of the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*), which consists of the five great maṇḍalas; therefore, the leaping over of the elephant-like mind is even more remote from there. Thus, he expresses his aspiration: "How may I become one who is inclined toward that, intent on that alone? beginning with the words *amṛta* and so forth.

In comparison with the nectar-treasure of the accomplishment of supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna-siddhi*), the gnosis that serves as even a minuscule drop of nectar— which was obtained from the feet of Dharmākaraśānti, the crown jewel of the circle of scholars and the guru of King Lakṣatilaka Goḍagopāla— is here briefly set down and written in summary for my own recollection, so that my dull-witted self may remember it; or rather, it is stated thus to prevent arrogance regarding who might grasp this [teaching], or because this path is supremely profound and difficult to fathom, and is thus spoken for those whose nature is difficult to restrain.
As it has been said: "First, by this [seeing the Buddha], my own impulse of serene confidence increases so that I may cultivate the wholesome;
furthermore, another person of a nature similar to mine might also see him. Therefore, for this reason as well, this [act] is purposeful."
1. Paṇa 2. Vaimalya 3. Nāsti
4. Prācitaḥ 5. Mārgaratnasya 6. Rodyataḥ

Regarding the question of where this *Mṛtakaṇikodyota-nibandha* on the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti* is to be applied, he says: In that *Nāmasaṅgīti*, which consists of the correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and the exposition of the meaning of names—that is, designations—of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), the innate (*sahaja*), and the means (*upāya*), which are differentiated by various distinct manifestations; [this work] provides an exposition of the title, the subject matter, and the connection of its own text.
It gladdens the minds of those who proceed with prior intelligence, and it tells the story of the illumination of generosity, enriched by the meanings of what precedes and follows.

According to this principle, he states the cause for the inspiration of those who follow the Dharma, beginning with the words "In this place" (*iha*) and so forth. Here, the word *iha* is used as a particle of emphasis (*vākyālaṅkāre*), signifying certainty. Since this teaching of the vehicle (*tadyānadeśanā*) constitutes a compendium of the meaning of all [Buddhist] scriptures, the description of the location, the assembly, the requester, the teacher, the time, and so forth, is provided as a necessary factor for its commencement. Because it is the primary grain and because it rains down grain, there exists a mountain ridge (*kaṭaka*) called Śrīdhānya, where four kings have attained accomplishment; or alternatively, it means "that which possesses a slope (*nitamba*) here."

Within twelve *yojanas* of Śrīparvata, in the valleys known as Śrīdhānya, he established a great *caitya* during his final nirvāṇa out of concern for ritual remains (*saṃskāra*), because it serves as a refuge for the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*) that exhausts all illness;
thus, the excellence of the location is described. It was there that those devoted to the study of various tantras, such as the *Māyājāla* and the *Kālacakra*, [attained realization].
As it is said: "The *samaya* named Trailokyavijaya is the crusher of Māra."
In that place, the Teacher sat upon a jeweled lion-throne, facing the east.
That Lord, filling the three worlds with arrays consisting of five rays of light, was worshipped by Bodhisattvas, the lords of the asuras, and the lords of the gods.
Having prostrated again and again with their five limbs touching the ground and their heads bowed, they sat down each upon their own seat, seeking to hear the meaning of the Mantrayāna.
Certain Bodhisattvas who have attained the superknowledges, as well as the gods and others, all with joyful and contented intentions, contemplate this in their minds.
The teaching of the Mantra Vehicle which was previously given by Dīpaṅkara must now be performed for us by the virtuous Gautama.
Now, therefore, Sucandra, the king known as Sambhala and emanated by Vajrapāṇi, arrived at his own heart-city, Śrīdharmadhātu.
Having first performed a circumambulation clockwise around the Teacher’s two lotus feet,
having honored them with jewel-flowers, and having prostrated again and again;
Having joined his palms in reverence, he stood before the Perfectly Awakened One;
that Candra was the requester of the Teacher and the compiler of the scripture.
Thus: 1. his 2. former.
3. The ultimate good;
4. The two assemblies, the requester, and that which was spoken.
By the words "Śrī Śākya" and so forth, the teacher is indicated;
by the words "in Ceta" and so forth, the specific time is indicated.
As it has been said: "On the great mountain Gṛdhrakūṭa, the system of the Prajñāpāramitā [was taught]."
Having instructed the bodhisattvas in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
Then the Tathāgata dwelt together with the Bodhisattvas and others at a certain great caitya, within the maṇḍala of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Thus, having first established the maṇḍala of the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśvara) and his retinue, and having guided those to be trained, he projected above them the maṇḍala of the Primordial Buddha (Ādibuddha), like a circle of stars in the sky. On that day, having consecrated [the assembly] according to the ritual of the Paramādibuddha, he taught the vehicle of the three gods and so forth. In that regard, the extensive Ādibuddha consists of twelve thousand [verses], while the concise version consists of two thousand five hundred verses in the Sragdharā meter;
the extensive Samāja consists of twenty-five thousand [verses], while the concise version consists of eighteen hundred.
The passage beginning with "the five-lakṣaṇa [system]" and so forth has already been explained; its meaning is understood.

Therein, by means of the words "and therein, the movement" (*tatrecepa*) and so forth, he states the summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*): "Those very objects are well-grasped as all... and so forth, according to the principle that "those whose characteristic is elaboration (*prapañca*)."
Since one who has mastered the meaning of the whole easily ascertains the meaning of the individual parts, [it is said:

"here, that which is difficult to fathom is the ultimate reality (paramārtha), namely emptiness (śūnyatā); its 'exudation' (niryāsa) is its essence (sāra), which is the innate (sahaja). The locus (adhikaraṇa) or support (ādhāra) of that is the *Nāmasaṅgīti*; by means of its state (bhāva), that is, its true nature (tattva)."
As it has been said: "With respect to the vision of emptiness, all ordinary beings are indeed like those born blind."

Thus, Vajradhara Vajrasattva [expounds] the supreme unchanging gnosis (paramākṣarajñāna) which is about to be described. Regarding the phrase "of all," and so forth: because Mañjuśrī is the heart-essence of the Buddhas, he is the gnosis-body (jñānakāya) of all Tathāgatas; and as for the Bodhisattvas, since their conceptual constructions (vikalpa) are afflictions, those conceptual constructions are ceased along with their latent predispositions (savāsanā) within the supreme unchanging.

Regarding "the six families" and so forth: in the six-spoked wheel consisting of the six channels, these [deities] such as Vajrasattva and the others are each of six types. Among them, in the spoke below which is the nature of the Śaṅkhinī channel, there is imperishable gnosis; in the right spoke which is the nature of the Rasanā channel, there is imperishable sensation.
The Avadhūta is the imperishable consciousness at the upper aperture of form;
the imperishable form is at the western aperture of the *ciṇ* channel; and the imperishable mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is at the front aperture of the urine channel.
Lalanā, Rūpottarā, and Rakṣasamjñā—these are the six aggregates (*ṣaṭ-skandha*), which are themselves the six families (*ṣaṭ-kula*). The summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:

Above is Avadhūtī, which is consciousness (*vijñāna*); knowledge (*jñāna*) is below in the west in Śaṅkhinī, which carries feces (*viḍ-vahā*); form (*rūpa*) is in the east; and Saṃskāra is in Mūtrādhṛk.

On the spoke of Saṃjñā there are six, namely lalanā, rasanā, and the three left sensations; four in Mahāsukha; sixteen on the forehead; thirty-two at the throat; eight in the heart; sixty-four at the navel; and thirty-two in the secret place—thus there are one hundred and sixty-two channels. As it has been said: "In the uṣṇīṣa there are four [channels], on the forehead forty, in the throat thirty-two which are the provokers of the phlegm constituent, in the heart-lotus twenty-eight which are the provokers of the bile constituent, and in the navel sixty-four. There is no [further mention] here.

In the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, at the navel and the secret place, there are likewise sixty-four lords; these are the disturbances of the wind element. At the secret place, another set of six directions is revealed as the fixed cessations of the humors (sannipāta).
Thus, there is this commentary on the *Vṛtti*; the commentary on the *Śrīmānnakṣatramaṇḍala* is being noted,

as are the sixteen verses of the request (*adhyeṣaṇā*), the six responses, the two observations of the families (*kula*), the three [verses on] awakening through the net of illusion (*māyājālābhisaṃbodhi*), the fourteen [verses on] the vajra-realm (*vajradhātu*), the twenty-four and a quarter [verses on] the utterly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*), the ten and three-quarters [verses on] the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), the four [verses on] discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), the two [verses on] the ocean of equality (*samatājñāna*), the fifteen [verses on] all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), the five [verses on] the praise of the five knowledges (*pañcajñānastuti*), and the one hundred and sixty-two *kārikās*.

The cessation of the channels (*nāḍī*) occurs through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the praise of the mantra, the joy of inspiration, and the concluding praise are to be understood.

Therein, with the words "tatra tāvat" and so forth, he begins the explanation of the meaning of the individual components; there, with the words "atha" and so forth, he explains the root [text] as having the sense of "thus by me" (*evaṃ mayā*) and so on.
Regarding the phrase "by the syllable *a*" and so forth: emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is Vajrasattva, which is wisdom (*prajñā*); compassion (*karuṇā*), Akṣobhya, is skillful means (*upāya*).
As it has been said: "What is that which obstructs pleasure? It is compassion, the supreme gnosis (*jñāna*).
Emptiness is the very mirror-image that perceives all phenomena."
This is the instruction here:

the universal image (*viśvabimba*)—which will be described as having the form of the threefold path of the three realms—is said to be emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects; the entry of the yogi’s mind into that [emptiness] by means of great bliss at the moment of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-kṣaṇa*) is what is expressed by the word "thus" (*iti*).

This is stated in the *Kālacakra*: "In the void, gnosis becomes thoroughly mixed, the equal taste, imperishable and eternal. This very point is expressed by the words "of those two," meaning that without the non-duality of emptiness and compassion, the arising of bliss would not occur; thus, its means—the yoga of the vajra and lotus—is taught by the passage beginning with "the jewel" (*maṇi*).
He explains the first half of the verse beginning with "in the syllable *E*":
"In the sky, in the universal image (*viśvabimba*), Vajrasattva is the mind."
"Equal flavor with the body and so forth" explains the yoga of body, speech, and mind. Body, *bindu*, moon, and semen are synonyms; likewise for speech and so forth. Mind is the quality of *tamas*;
because, through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) and by means of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is called "mind."
The union of these—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is established within the avadhūtī.

And it is said: "Therein, at first, one leaves behind the state of cessation (virama) and the path of passion (rāga) in the middle moment; he who, being absorbed in that, abandons the pleasure of women and grasps the other, the immutable pleasure (akṣara-sukha), is the illustrious one. Through the seal of camphor (ghanasāra-mudrā), the wise man, his mind reeling from drinking the wine of his own bliss by the command of the Guru, does not fall into delusion."

Thus ends the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*. Following this sequence, one who has practiced the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) perceives the ten signs through the yoga of night and day by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). Having seen the universal image (*viśvabimba*) within the tenth great drop (*mahābindu*), he stabilizes it through meditation (*dhyāna*). Having purified the center through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and stabilized the bodhicitta through concentration (*dhāraṇā*), he becomes one for whom Caṇḍālī blazes through recollection (*anusmṛti*). Through the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-samāpatti*), he shall directly realize the supreme immutable innate state (*paramākṣara-sahaja*) by means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Having thus explained the meaning of the word *atha*, he now explains the term *vastradhara* according to its intended sense (*mayārtha*), beginning with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The aforementioned *vajra* expressed by the word is [the non-existent]; the "unreal conceptualizations" (*asatsaṃkalpa*) are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) arising from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). When these exist, there arise the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as passion, which proceed from the notions of "I" and "mine" and are antagonistic to the cultivation of the Path. The "obstacles" (*vighna*) are the hosts of the *devaputramāra* and so forth; and because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has not been ceased, there is "death" at the end.
These four Māras in the world are called "unbreakable" because they cannot be destroyed;
furthermore, these are created by the mind,
for it is the mind alone that fashions the world of sentient beings as well as the receptacle world in its extreme variety.
For the entire world is said to be born of karma, and apart from karma, there is no mind.
Because of this statement, he says "from the perspective of the system" and so forth;
and therefore it is said: "One's own mind alone is to be killed, and one should kill the mind itself;
one's own mind alone is the perfectly awakened one, and the mind itself is that which is to be awakened."
Thus,
the meaning is that it is heard [in scripture] that the five-pronged vajra on the outer hand indeed indicates the attainment of the liberated gnosis; so he said,
"The Glorious One."
Regarding the passage beginning with *śrī*, because of the statement, “The syllable *śrī* is non-dual gnosis,” he speaks here of its piercing (*nidalana*): “In this way,” and so forth.

“In this way” means that the Vajrin, the Holder of the Vajra, whose nature is the syllable *evam*, who holds the innate drop (*sahaja-bindu*), and whose self is inseparable from bliss and emptiness—he himself has realized [it]. The meaning is that, having made bliss the object of knowledge (*śruta*) and realization (*jñāta*), he has known his very self by means of the self.

"In the tantras," such as the *Samāja* and others, the statement "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) has the same meaning as "Thus have I known" (*evaṃ mayā jñātam*). "The Vajra-holder" (*vajrī*) refers to the Blessed One situated within the semen. He reiterates [the phrase] "in the wombs of the Vajra-women" (*vajrayoṣidbhageṣu*), for the "wombs" (*bhaga*) of women are here the lotuses of the heads and so forth.

"At one time" means that following the release of the three drops (*bindu*) from the body and so forth, by means of the three releases of the drop, [the Buddha] proceeded through the stages and reached the tip of the jewel; "he dwelt" means he entered the Buddha-field.

This is the explanation according to the exclusive definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Alternatively, another [tradition] explains it as Vajrapāṇi and so forth; and "I," namely Śākyasiṃha, am the Dharma because of being the Dharmakāya.
And as for what was said regarding the sixfold Vajrapāṇi, he is none other than Mahāvajravara himself; thus,
by his own retinue such as Ānanda, Paramānanda, and so forth,
he is to be accomplished because he is of the nature of the Innate (*sahaja*).
I am the Teacher because I teach the subduing of the afflictions of the world;
I am worldly because the world is pure by nature; and I am of the form of coemergent bliss because the world has the nature of suchness, as it is said: "Bliss is the form of Brahman."
And that should be known as the cessation (*virama*) at the ultimate limit;

it is non-existence (*abhāva*), yet it is the universal image (*viśvabimba*). It is not existence, because its nature is the non-perception of external entities; he is called "Buddha" because of his awakening to the reality of things.
Therefore, those who are deluded and indolent do not know me;

[I am] Sukhāvatī because I dwell there in bliss (*sukham avati rakṣati*). There, in the lap of the divine Vajrayoṣit, I sport. In that very place is the supreme, primordial innate experience (*sahajānubhava*), wherein conceptualization and breath dissolve in bliss.
And it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "The innate is pervasive in the *kapara*; the innate is pure in the *vilehūra*."
"Like a royal swan [separating] milk from water mixed with wine.

Then, Vajradhara standing before the Tathāgata spoke these words, and so forth; this connection was stated for the purpose of introducing the uninitiated to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*): "The Teacher is the factor for the engagement of those possessed of faith, and the assembly is the witness."
The place and time have also been specified.
Thus, that which was said beginning with "Hari-Hara," namely: "O Hari, Hara, Brahmā, Purandara! O all you, flow into my heart! and so forth.

Even those whose vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are unrestrained are transmigrating beings; for them, there is the entry and exit of breaths occurring day and night. Because their innate knowledge (*sahajajñāna*) has been pierced, the obstruction of the form of breathing occurs.
Thus it is said: "By the very cessation of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the destruction of the twelve limbs (*dvādaśāṅga*) occurs.
Through the cessation of cause and effect, who would not become a Buddha?"

By means of the drops of the infallible *bodhicitta*, one fills and completes the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*). Regarding "of other living beings" (*paraprāṇinām*): the verbal root is *an* (to breathe) preceded by *pra*; *prāṇana* is breathing, and *prāṇa* is the act of breathing. Those who possess this [breath] are "living beings" (*prāṇinaḥ*), meaning those who have breath.

The obstruction of their movement is "slaying," which is called "the piercing of the enemy. That which is described as the "heroic conduct" (*vīrakrama*) externally is not what is taught here; rather, it is precisely the restraint of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within the body.

Regarding the passage beginning with "sa teṣām" and so forth: this was said concerning one who is capable of drawing in the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*) and causing it to enter by the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). As it is said: "A practitioner should perform everything, having abandoned the deception of self-interest.

Sentient beings are Buddhas; there is no other great being here in the world-system greater than them. By propitiating them, immeasurable existence is severed through non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*)."

A yogi who commits malice indeed goes to the great hells, such as Raurava; therefore, even when the mind is purified, one should not act in opposition to ignorant or wise people. Thus, regarding "body, speech, and mind": these are the drops (*bindus*) of the body and so forth, located in the forehead, throat, and heart. One whose discipline consists of making them merge into a single flavor with the wisdom-drop (*jñānabindu*) situated at the navel, through their innate single essence—[that yogi] is seated upon the four seats of the Buddhas, namely the forehead and other locations which are the abodes of Amoghasiddhi and the rest. There, he sequentially experiences the forms of bliss and so forth, residing in the *vajra*, the *padma*, and the central point (*varaṭaka*).

The three are the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and the pervasive (*vyāpaka*) is the fourfold innate (*sahaja*), beginning with the innate bliss of body and the innate bliss of speech. Regarding that, there is the *Amṛtaphaṇikodyota* commentary: "Due to differentiation, it is the Buddha-image; thus the universal image (*viśvabimba*) is non-different from the three times and the three realms."
The meaning is that by cultivating the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth, one should stabilize the *bodhicitta* and become capable of [visualizing] the image (*bimba*).
"Free from sound" (*vigatarava*) means motionless because it has entered the central channel; this is the method (*upāya*).
Thus, while explaining the verse beginning with "And thus living beings are to be slain by you" (*he0 ta0 2.3.29*), he speaks of the five secrets, starting with "the yogi," and so forth.

The taking of life is the rendering motionless [of the vital winds]; that which is devoid of a mouth and cannot be uttered even by the happy ones arises spontaneously as the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) within the heart.
Stealing is said to be the seizing of the twelve stages from the ground of knowledge of the Omniscient One within the body free of obscurations.
The bliss that occurs at the falling of the seminal drop (*śukrabindu*) is the service to the consort (*prajñā*) of Vajrasattva through immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).
When the *prāṇa* and *apāna* are restrained, that which blazes as the *caṇḍālī* is the fire of *prāṇāyāma*.
By means of that, the drinking from above of the melted moon of *bodhicitta* through the mouth of the *vajra* is called "the drinking of wine" (*madyapāna*), which generates the innate (*sahaja*).
He describes the natural accomplishment of the movement of the semen (*śukra*) with the words beginning with "uṣṇīṣa."

From the first day of the waxing moon onwards, as the lunar digits increase, the bodhicitta travels from the big toe of the left foot to the *uṣṇīṣa* at the end of the full moon; from the first day of the waning moon onwards, it travels from the *uṣṇīṣa* to the toes of the right foot.
Therein, on the first day of the waxing moon and so forth, [the bodhicitta resides] in the first joints of the toes of the left foot.

On the second [tithi], in the second; on the third, in the third; on the fourth, in the joint of the left foot; on the fifth, in the knee joint; on the sixth, in the hip joints; on the seventh, in the first phalangeal joint of the fingers of the left hand; on the eighth, in the middle joint; on the ninth, in the third joint; on the tenth, in the hand joints; on the eleventh, in the arm joints; on the twelfth, in the shoulder-arm joint; on the thirteenth, in the heart; on the fourteenth, in the throat; on the full moon day, in the forehead; and at its conclusion, in the crown of the head.

Furthermore, on the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*), [the practice is] on the forehead; on the second, on the throat; on the third, on the heart; and on the fourth, it should be at the joint of the left shoulder for the semen (*śukra*). The remainder is as on the left; that is the *caryā*.

For the semen that has moved according to the flow of the left and right channels, the upward movement from the secret place and the other six wheels (*cakras*) by means of the flow of the central channel (*madhyamā-vāha*)—that is the *caryā*. When practiced constantly, this Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) bestows accomplishment.
He explains that very same point otherwise, beginning with "one," and so forth.
Because the mind is the vehicle of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), when those [breaths] enter into the center, there is motionlessness below; consequently, due to non-duality, there is a single mind.

Since, in reality, there is an absence of a sentient being, it is false. By that equality of both [fluids], through the reversal of the two discharging [semen and blood], there is the grasping of the unreleased semen.
"Self-luminous beauty" refers to the Mahāmudrā, the universal image (*viśvabimba*), which is the mere radiance of one's own mind;
because it is sovereignty, that is, because of its stability and lordship.
As it has been said: "And by means of that sign, the yogi should always be one whose vital energy flows upward."
Regarding "yathā" and so forth:
the meaning according to the literal sound (*yathāruta*) has been easily found elsewhere as well, such as in the *Vilāsavañcā* and other works, and thus it is not stated here.
By this, the connection (*sambandha*) and other elements have already been accepted in the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*).

And therefore, whoever here— possessing the shaft of desire (*rāga-śalya*), with a mind full of conceit (*māna*), and ignorant of the truth of the scriptures— is indifferent [to this teaching], thinking "this [reality] is devoid of birth, death, and connection to the realms of existence," such a person is merely dear to the gods.

For it is said in the description of the benefits of the fourth wheel: "Taking as an object any one of the various names or meanings individually, one will meditate with a one-pointed mind through both the mental application of resolute faith (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) and the mental application of reality (*tattva-manasikāra*). Abiding in the dwelling of universal bliss, endowed with supreme, stainless wisdom that penetrates all phenomena, Ārya Mañjuśrī—who possesses the *Nāmasaṅgīti*—being thus endowed with faith, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas belonging to the three times and the time-less state will gather together and manifest all the gateways of the Dharma for him" (p. 103). Thus, since each word is said to be co-emergent (*sahaja*) and noble, what is the need for a connection with mantras and the like?

Indeed, in other contexts, distinctions in meaning are postulated for synonymous terms such as *mukti*, *mokṣa*, *vimokṣāṅga*, *vimukti*, *śāntatā*, and *śiva* (Nāmasaṃgīti 8.19). However, here, by way of a stylistic turn, the innate (*sahaja*) meaning is intended everywhere; thus, even "vulgarity" is not a fault at all, because this *Nāmasaṃgīti* belongs to Mañjuśrī, whose nature is exclusively innate. From the passage beginning with "Lord of Speech, Master of Speech, Eloquent One" (Nāmasaṃgīti 6.9) up to the point where the destruction of the three-fold assembly of the essence of qualities is described through beautiful words that are possible [to utter], the innate alone is the subject matter.

As for what was said regarding the words for qualities: "By whom these [qualities] and the collection of qualities in the world are designated with the name 'quality'—namely, the fourfold group beginning with *mārdava* (gentleness)," and so forth; and that which is the source of qualities, which is indeed innate—that has been stated: "In this world, *nirvāṇa* is indeed innate (*sahaja*)."

He has explained the supreme unity; furthermore, there is no other [reality] beyond that measure. Everything else is merely a secondary perception. That very [Reality] is established, it is multiplied, and it is indeed understood through the *Satya Purāṇa*. He is not seen who does not perceive Him.

"Look at the feet of the excellent Guru"—in such *dohās* and other verses, the *sahaja* alone is to be expressed. In the threefold *Jinajanani*, by such words as "form is empty; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty," the *sahaja* alone is to be expressed.

Up to the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma taught by the Great Sage, those who do not know that reality (*tattva*) are indeed all fruitless. Thus, let it be determined here that reality is the *sahaja* alone. (1) "It has become manifest"—this means it is realized through one's own merit and the instruction of the Guru.
By the word "that," the attainment of the co-emergent (*sahaja*) is not said to be through that which is called Mahāmudrā; rather,
by the words "blossomed" and so forth, the entry into the co-emergent through the Action Seal (*karmamudrā*) is stated.

Regarding the "five eyes"— the flesh eye, the divine eye, the deathless eye, the serpent eye, and the illuminating eye— there is a threefold explanation according to the divisions of the Buddha’s insight (*prajñā*) and gnosis (*jñāna*), or as the Lord (*nātha*) whose nature is the imperishable bliss within the hearts of yogins, like the moon reflected in many clear vessels of water; thus begins the passage starting with "firstly" (*prathamataḥ*).

That which adorns (*alaṅkaroti*) bliss (*kaṃ*) is *kamala*; thus, by means of the phrase "the luminous gnosis is thus" and so forth, the innate (*sahaja*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the three [states] beginning with bliss (*ānanda*), which are the pervaded (*vyāpya*). Through its connection with that [innate state], [it is so designated].
Through the four drops of the body and so forth, which are the synonyms for bliss and the rest, he is the enjoyer whose nature is the gnosis of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).

Regarding this, the characteristic of wisdom (*prajñā*) is stated in the *Kālacakra*: "Until the age of ten, she is one [type], being of ten kinds, fit to be seen and touched; therefore, those who are to be embraced are like oceans of nectar. After sixteen years, the mudrās are to be cultivated; they are terrifying, possessing the portions of the wrathful ones, spirits, and asuras, and bestow the fruit of equal bliss—six for the purpose of consecration (*sekārtha*), and four others for the purpose of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanārtha*)."
Starting from one year up to ten years, the single mudrā becomes the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in its tenfold form through the purification of the ten [perfections] such as generosity;
it is both to be seen and to be touched.
Therefore, from the tenth year onwards, the six flavors beginning with the eleventh year, as well as the four oceans—these ten mudrās, beginning with *calā*, are to be embraced and served.

Thus, purification is said to occur when they possess the nature of the wind element and so forth. Beyond the twentieth year, the mudrās become extremely terrifying; because they have the form of the ten wrathful goddesses beginning with *Atinīlā*, they are portions of the wrathful deities (*krodha-aṃśa*).
And from the twenty-first year onwards, the eight [mudrās] are portions of the elements (*bhūta-aṃśa*), because they have the form of the eight female messengers (*dūtī*) beginning with *Cañcikā*.

In that regard, for the purpose of meditation and for the purpose of initiation (*seka*), those who are thirty-nine years of age and so forth— the eight who possess portions of the asuras— because they have the forms of asura-females such as Śvānāsyā and others,
up to forty-six years of age; and likewise, those who are six, four, and eleven years of age and so forth, bestow the fruit of equal bliss according to their possibility.

It has been restated: the mudrā is taught for the sake of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) during the time of day and night, not for the sake of the destruction of passion; speech is for the sake of satiation, and indeed, intoxication is not taught for practitioners (*mantriṇām*).

Likewise, all food is for the sake of comfort at every daily occasion, and is not taught as a cause for indigestion. Wandering here is for the sake of the accomplishment of the glorious conduct (*śrī-caryā-siddhi*), not for the sake of mental play at night.

Regarding the consecration by the mudrā: that which is the first touch of the glorious Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*) upon the breast is the "consecration of the jar" (*kumbha-seka*); that very same [act] becomes the "secret-to-secret consecration" (*guhyābhiṣeka*). The tasting of the moon [nectar] in the navel is the "worldly" [consecration].

In the initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), having purified the limbs and faces of all the families of the Victors, the Guru, the Lord of the Victors, should bestow the mudrā upon the disciple after making [the deities] witnesses here. Its defects have also been stated in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "Terrified, distracted in mind, deceitful, under the sway of others, afflicted by disease, recently delivered, angry, stubborn, fickle, addicted to lies and quarrels, deficient in her own limbs, or impure—these should be avoided by a highly skilled Guru during the wisdom-initiation, O King. Those previously mentioned who are devoted to the Buddha and uphold the Guru’s commitments are to be saluted and worshipped."

The merit arising from the purity of mind through the mudrā has also been stated: "Whatever woman, for the sake of merit, offers Vajra-worship with the threefold purity to the Ācārya—she who is moon-faced, lotus-eyed, and anointed with divine perfumes—the entire merit she gains, O King, reaching as far as the sun and moon in the sky, is equal to the merit obtained from the gift of elephants, horses, chariots, many maidens, and the gift of land.
Thus it is said.

It is also stated in the *Dvikalparāja*: "The conduct that is proclaimed as having a terrifying form is not taught for the sake of enjoyment; rather, it is for the purpose of examining one's own mind: 'Is the mind stable or is it moving?
Such is the nature [of this practice]," and so forth.

Having thus explained the means for the benefit of others by causing the previously mentioned supreme *vajra*, which is the referent of the word, to arise within the mental continuum of those to be trained through the radiation of the rays of clear light (*prabhāsvara*), he explains the benefit for oneself, beginning with "Alternatively," and so forth.
He states that very point by means of the final sign: "Compassion" refers to the immersion of the mind of the yogin—formless in its nature—into the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*).

The bodhicitta is the *uṣṇīṣa*; "leading" it refers to the manual action of drawing it upward from its [usual] position. This is so that there may be no opportunity for false objects such as thoughts of sensual desire (*kāmavitarka*), because the path is continuous.
By the words beginning with "frowning" (*bhṛkuṭī*), the means of leading [the bodhicitta] is indicated.
Those who have stated that "the fold on the surface of the forehead" (lalāṭataṭabali) is [the sixth limb] are indeed ignorant of the secret;
for the six limbs will be explained below, beginning with pratyāhāra,
and the two extremes are existence and non-existence.

Since these two, when devoid of those [qualities], are extremely corrupt, the adoption of even a slight conceptual construction is like a seizing grip for the sake of devouring; this yoga, once abandoned, results in the mother having long since departed to the further shore.

This is because of the statement: "The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* [is that which abandons such yoga]," for [conceptual] investigation and experience are, by their very nature, erroneous (*viparyāsa*).

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*): "In this context as well, by means of the blisses that are like the negation of conceptual construction, [the four wisdoms]—namely, the mirror-like wisdom and so forth, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of discernment, and the wisdom of the performance of duties, as well as the wisdom of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*—are called 'Dharma' because they are luminous (*prabhāsvara*).
Since it is said that the mind is luminous by nature (*prakṛti-cittasya prabhāsvarā*), [it is stated]: 'Wherever the mind expands, there the Lord is manifest.'"

And from the statement, "What else is the hot wave? It is water; the ocean of existence is like space," it follows that for those established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), Mara is defeated solely by the power of the great bliss of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It is described as loathsome, deformed, and having the form of wrath.

As it has been said: "In the service [of the deity], the primary yoga consists of the tenfold wheel of Narbhasa; with the gaze of wrath, and with the gaze of Vighnāntaka directed toward the path of nectar, one attains the six-limbed [yoga] in the state of Upasādhya."

The inexhaustibility [of the hero and the repulsive] arises from their being of one flavor with space (*vyoma-samarasatva*); through the unity of compassion (*kṛpā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they take the form of supramundane great passion (*lokottara-mahārāga*).
Thus Saraha said: "Space," and so forth:
"Compassion without emptiness, or emptiness without compassion— he who clings to either does not attain the supreme state; or rather, the path consists of compassion alone."
Through such states, one does not attain liberation even in a thousand births.
If emptiness and compassion are practiced together, one remains neither in cyclic existence nor stuck in nirvana.
Emptiness, when wrongly perceived, destroys the person of dull intellect.
"Like a snake poorly grasped, or a spell poorly mastered"—
according to this statement,
[the teachings] are revealed only to those who are capable.
Regarding the passage beginning with "one's own" (*svam*): "The innate (*sahaja*) is not described by another; it is not found in anyone else.
It is known by oneself through merit, by serving the Guru during the sacred festivals. Thus it is said.

"Mahā" and so forth; as it is said: "By means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) characterized by smoke and other signs, by the flow through the central channel, by the vow of knowledge (vidyāvrata), and indeed by the descent of the vajra—that is, the upward-moving semen."

The *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti* states: "Having abandoned the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) because of its defiled nature, and having abandoned the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*) because it is conceptualized, one should meditate upon the divine seal (*divyamudrā*). It is great, immutable, and eternal. Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) remains constant—namely, suchness (*tathatā*).

Because of this statement, it is called "interpenetrated," meaning it is included within that [seal] and is liberated; that very thing is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), for it is accomplished by means of that, since without it there is falling away.
Regarding this, he says: "In meditation, he who does not enter into the emptiness of all phenomena—how can he accomplish great bliss?
Just as a thirsty deer runs toward a mirage and dies, for where can it find the water of the sky?

In other words: "In meditation—that is, in the state of contemplative cultivation—he who does not penetrate the emptiness of all phenomena through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), how can he achieve great bliss?"

Just as one who is thirsty runs toward a mirage and withers away due to the absence of water in the sky, so too the world, whose body is the Yoga of the Lord, goes to various states of existence; thus, they have transcended the world by departing from it through the upward turning [of the gaze].
"Delighted," and so forth:

with joy, [the Buddhas] spoke this path for the sake of sentient beings when the unity of the body and so forth— the drops, winds, and mind— is established in the flow of the central channel (*madhyamāvāha*).
Krodha is the vajra of hatred, Akṣobhya, who is pure emptiness because of the nature of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) and the form-element (*rūpadhātu*).
In that regard, he is called "Krodha" (Wrath) because he exerts himself through the vision of wrath, whether by means of its direct realization or by reaching its limit (*virama-paryanta*).
In both cases, it should be understood as being free from purity, due to the power of the non-conceptual object, just like a Buddha.

They are called *nātha*s because they are sought after and entreated by those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*s). O Lord of Yogins, they are served by those who have become one with compassion and wisdom.

As it has been said: "In the state that is without intrinsic nature, wisdom has entered into that which is without intrinsic nature; compassion, together with the intellect, has become of a single form, like space within space."
"Prostrate" means that, due to being delighted by great bliss, one's sole delight is in that [bliss] alone. || 5 ||
"Having prostrated" means having directly realized the bliss of awakening due to its imperishable nature (*acyutatva*).
"Possessing *bhaga*" refers to one who possesses that luminous gnosis (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*) which arises when the water emerging from the forehead enters the *jñānabindu* located in the secret place.
"So be it"—the meaning is that the eye, having opened from the *uṣṇīṣa* in the manner it had come, returned again to the *uṣṇīṣa* in that very same way.
Regarding "having come," and so forth:
the meaning is that he remained motionless, pervading the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) of the universe.
As it has been said: "One should not desire life, nor fear death; one should not bring anything from anywhere.
Even while killing, there is no meat—thus Bhusuku says, kill the wife.
This refers to the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* and so forth; its meaning is the union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths.

As it has been said: "When struck by the wind, the flame-tips of lightning melt the moon at the crown; whichever drop falls from that [moon] reaches the throat and heart, and being restrained, it goes to the navel and secret place.

That vibration and flow of the drop which has reached the *kuliśa-maṇi* (the jewel of the vajra) is completely restrained at the tip of the banner. If that moment of the wisdom of Prajñā bestows bliss through the non-emission of the stream of drops...
This very point he expresses with the words beginning "This" (*idam*) and so forth. (6)
Regarding the word "to be cultivated" (*bhāvayet*):

for whose sake is this previously mentioned goal to be accomplished? He says: "for myself and for others. How so? It is said that the referent of the word "myself" is [the same for others] because there is no distinction in the form of suchness (*tathatā*). Alternatively, it is because Buddhahood is desired through service for the sake of others. He states that the purpose of that [cultivation] is indeed for himself: "He nourishes the six elements; let them nourish him; he gives his own self," and so forth. Buddhahood arises precisely from the absence of false conceptualization (*asat-saṃkalpa*).

As it is said: "Luminous, free from conceptual construction, with the stains of passion and other impurities abandoned—neither grasped object nor grasping subject—that very state the Supreme Beings have declared to be the excellent Nirvāṇa.
It is called "great" because it pervades through bliss.
As it has been said: "The innate great tree has borne fruit throughout the three worlds;
in its nature, which is like space, there is no obstruction for even the liberated ones. Regarding the "sixteen":
[they are] the body of bliss (*kāyānanda*), the body of supreme joy (*paramānanda*), the body of cessation (*viramānanda*), and the innate (*sahaja*).
Thus, through four sets of four—of speech, mind, and gnosis—there are sixteen joys (*ānanda*).
These are localized and belong to the self.

The cessation and non-perception of the drops (*bindu*) and the aggregates (*skandha*), etc., following the arising of the innate (*sahaja*), is the state of being all goddesses (*sarvadevī*) at all times.

As it has been said: "The body is transparent, unimpaired by atoms, equal to space, and fully endowed with the [thirty-two] marks and so forth; the entire universe appears transparent, like a dream, devoid of obstructions.

Speech is uninterrupted on all sides, reaching the hearts of others through manifold languages; the mind is filled with true bliss and never wavers, embraced at all times by the Innate (*sahaja*). Thus the characteristics of accomplishment (*siddhi*) have been stated.
*A* is wisdom (*prajñā*) in the secret place; *HŪṂ* is method (*upāya*) in great bliss.
The meditative union (*samāpatti*) of these two occurs through the channel of the *avadhūtī*.
Where these two are bound together, that is "yoked in pairs" (*yuganaddha*).
This connects with the words beginning with "just as," and so forth. (7)

The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti* states "ignorance" (*ajñā*). Just as those sunk in mud cross over by clinging to another, so too the three worlds, shown through ignorance and being a place of attachment to nescience (*avidyā*), are crossed over by taking refuge in the Blessed One. The passage beginning with "the suffering of death" (*cyutiduḥkha*) is clear.

As it has been said: "From the destruction of passion arises sin; from that, hatred toward one's dearest is born; from hatred comes delusion; from this, there is constant fainting of the mind due to the falling away of its own garment.
Thereupon, the entire mind engages with other objects, such as unwholesome food and drink; thus mocked by that [delusion], the mind, robbed of its happiness, wanders through six births.
"Nature" (prakṛti) refers to the direct realization of natural luminosity through stainless purity. (8)
"Simultaneously born," and so forth. One who possesses awakened, blossomed intelligence (*sambuddha*) has what is called the pervasion of all that is to be known (*sarvajñeya*).
The yoga of space (*ākāśayoga*) is taught by the words beginning with "all" (*sarva*).
As it has been said: "By the entry of the garment of the mind into the space of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).
[The passage] beginning with "six," etc., follows.
Because it teaches the reality of those breaths that enter into great bliss (*mahāsukha*) through the guru’s instruction,
as it is said: "That which is like water in a level vessel becomes water of uneven flavor."
"Vyata" means for this very reason.
As it has been said: "He whose mind does not waver from the tip of the nose to the end of a mustard seed..."
"That excellent Guru said: 'When [the mind] wavers, perform *prāṇāyāma* for its sake.
Or [it may be through] the instruction on the principles (*tattva*) of the body and so forth, as it has been said:
'Form is like a mass of foam; sensation is like a bubble.'"

"Perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like the trunk of a plantain tree, and consciousness is like an illusion—thus it was said by the Kinsman of the Sun. Regarding the word "great" (*mahā*):
they are so called because they are fully realized (*samīyante*) or directly perceived.
The *samaya* itself is the reality (*tattva*);
or, it is the reality of those things that are to be guarded and so forth;
or, it is the reality because the sense faculties (*indriya*) are born from the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).

As it is said: "From the foul-smelling ocean of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the five waves of conceptual proliferation known as the aggregates arise together with their turbulence from the agitation of the wind of ignorance.
They dissolve along with that very ignorance when it has been driven far away; by those who have drunk this nectar of the Jina’s teaching, they are destroyed, whereas others have fallen far away.
Therefore, he is supreme precisely because he knows the ultimate truth. (9)
"Bhagavan," [he said].
Since its meaning has already been explained, it is not stated again.
Other instances should be understood in the same way.
The Gnosis Body is the collection of gnosis-bindus;
it is the fourth, the innate, which holds the four bindus within the four wheels.

[The commentary on the term *vivṛtyordhvagamanam* (ascending by unfolding): The support (*ādhāra*) is the *Anāhata*. It consists of the six syllables to be mentioned later—*ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, sa*—from which the letter *e* is produced. Its lord is *Vaṣṭrī*. The "Great Void" (*mahāśūnya*) consists of five syllables—*a, i, ṛ, u, l̥*—due to the addition of the *bindu*; however, the letter *e* is devoid of the *bindu*. In the terminology [of this system], that which adorns (*alaṅkaroti*) happiness (*kam*) is "the lotus" (*kamalam*). [It is called] "possessing happiness" (*sukhāvat*), because one may achieve awakening (*bodhi*) through happiness. For the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated (*samādhīyate*). As it is said: "There is no sin greater than dispassion (*virāga*), and no merit greater than happiness. By means of which [happiness], even those who have committed the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*) are gathered together. Because of such statements as: "By intense and difficult observances, the body of the suffering person withers; by suffering, the mind is distracted, and from distraction, success (*siddhi*) is otherwise [attained]," the intention [of the teaching] is as follows: having abandoned the middle and extremes of what is called the "drops of sensual pleasure," awakening is to be achieved through the practice free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-caryā*). This is its exposition. Regarding the phrase "because of dwelling in the heart": since the mind exists as a sense-faculty, its presence in the heart is direct. Thus, when it is established from the beginningless [time] and is free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*), it would become visible. It becomes the object of experience (*gocara*), but it does not arise [as something new]. Because emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is all-pervading, it is included within all forms. As it is said: "Every form would be emptiness itself, for it is an entity," and so forth. Like space, it is uncreated and is to be known by the yogin through the instruction of the Guru. (10)
*Artha* means that which is sought after or accomplished.
It is "noble in meaning" because of the statement: "A single entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities. Regarding *maha* and so forth:
"From the passion of Mahāmudrā, bliss is born from the state of motionlessness;
he is consecrated by Great Wisdom because he has attained that state of motionlessness," according to this statement.
[The phrase] "śrāvakas and so forth" refers to...

As it is said: "The Mahāyāna indeed hastens toward those who possess higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) as if with a superior vehicle; for those lost on the path, it is like a swift speed that brings about their rescue from afar.
Thus begins the section on the three times (*tryadhva*), and so forth.

Because it has been said that "whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this true nature (*dharmatā*) and suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena remains constant," and because [the term] "beginning with me" (*mādī*) establishes that Ānanda and the others are also co-emergent (*sahaja*),
and because of the phrase "by the sun," meaning by the sun of the wisdom of Caṇḍālī, which causes the unfolding of the navel-lotus and so forth.
The *Nāmasaṅgīti* is the perfect knowledge (*samyakjñāna*) characterized by names.
To the question "Of what [is this] name?", he says: "Name," and so forth; this is clear. (11)
Yeti:
because its nature is innate (*sahaja*), it is in reality unarisen, like an echo.
By this [it is meant]:

The Mantra Vehicle was taught in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. One might object: "Is there not a contradiction with the works of Dīpaṅkara and others? To this he says: "For those who are fit"—that is, for those alone who are fit for the profound [teachings] of others, and not for everyone in general. (12)

The *Māyājālābhisambodhi* has been described with its defining characteristics; it is the very non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*) of the mantra-great-bliss-knowledge (*mantramahāsukhajñāna*) of the *Uttaratantra*. This would indeed be the measure of the sphere of experience (*gocara*). The remainder is easily understood. Non-exhaustive existence is primarily ignorance (*ajñāna*), and that arises from the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) for conceptualizing existence. (13–16)
|| The Request || 1. kha.. la u | 2..kha.ga. – [The] range of activity arises; [the word] "does not exist" is absent. 3. ka. yadbhūte vā |
4. ka. nāśān | 5. ka. [the reading] "tathāgatānāṃ nāsti" is absent | 6. ka. veyantā |
7.kha. ga. *aśleṣam* | 8. pha. *tat*, ga. *tava* | i:
The reply: Whatever was previously dear to someone, that very thing one should perform for him.
"For one who is hostile is never a vessel for the True Dharma. Thus ends the recitation of the response preceded by praise.
Alternatively, *śāka* means "ability" (*śakana*) or "power" (*śakti*); that which arises from *bhaga* therein is *Śākya*, and the syllable *vaṃ* [is added].
The Sage is so called because of his contemplation on the non-existence of distinctions among the three bodies;
he is the Vajra-holder, the Vajrasattva;
the Goddess is Ṛgī, and the Blessed One is Aralli.
And these two are to be understood as having the forms of Lokeśvara and Mañjuśrī. Therefore, there is no contradiction. One does not speak without reflecting or without deliberating.
Since the Protector is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), how can there be teaching and so forth? To this he says: "Sentient beings... and so on.

Thus it is said, and it will be stated later: "But by the mere presence of that Person, as if he were a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), teachings issue forth according to desire from his mouth and other parts.
Empty, yet conceptualized as real, they are like imagined illusions.

In the systems of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), the states beginning with the fourth (*turya*) are to be abandoned. For it is said: "Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) apart from the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), and it is due to the afflictions that the world wanders here in the ocean of existence. [The term] *jñānakāya* refers to the drops of gnosis (*jñānabindu*).
Conventional knowledge is the awakening to phenomena as being like an illusion;
ultimate knowledge is the non-apprehension of all phenomena;
"non-abiding" is the state of remaining without attachment.
He will explain the verse beginning with "one" (*ekam*) in the commentary on [the verse] *Ekapādatalākrānta* (Nāmasaṃgīti 9.4).
Regarding the passage beginning with "having determined" (*nirṇamaya*), it is because of the statement:
"And therein is seen the drop (*binduka*), and within that, the Buddha-image, the manifold Saṃbhogakāya devoid of sense-objects" (Kālacakratantra 5.115).
Within the great bindu, the universal image (viśvabimba) is seen—
referring to what was just mentioned as "the universal image.
Having stabilized the Jñānāvadhūtī, which has the form of a black line, and so forth, such are its qualifiers.
As it has been said: "The yogi should gaze at the sky, free from clouds, with a fixed gaze, until a black line, shimmering with pure radiance, is seen in the dance of time," and so forth.
1. Ma. Śā. *kathaṃcana*. 2. Ga. *metanna*.
3. Kha. Ga. by means of the two truths;
4. Ka. Kha. Ga. and that. The commentary on the *Amṛtaphaṇika* states: regarding withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is space, characterized by emptiness.

"And wherever the mind is fixed upon the region of the nose—at the end of the *nimitta*, the moving and unmoving universe is within that line," so it is said. "The outcaste (*caṇḍāla*) is the light and the manifestation; he is the cause of *saṃsāra*.
Bhava is said to be supreme bliss, and Nirvāṇa arises from dispassion. || 1 ||

Because of the statement, "It is merely the bliss of the middle" (*madhyamānandamātram*) [Hevajra-tantra 1.8.34], the purifier is that which, by causing the drops (*bindu*) to enter the innate (*sahaja*)— which has the nature of bliss and so forth— and thereby bringing about their transformation into that very form,
purifies the three worlds, namely the triad beginning with the *māloka*.
The nature that effects the non-appearance of that [object] is the "jewel" (*maṇi*).
He explains the "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*) by means of the phrase "immediately after the request," because it teaches the cessation of conceptual constructions such as waking and so forth.
"Vajre," etc.

The very vajra is the door-panel of conceptualization. Within it, the thieves—the states of waking and so forth—were encountered by me; having dissolved all those "Māras," great bliss was attained. (2) Regarding "the body and so forth": this refers to the triad of channels, such as the lalanā and the others.
"Self-arisen" means that he experienced the innate (*sahaja*) through the unstruck sound (*anāhatagīrā*) acting as the instrument. Regarding "fruitful":
when one is liberated by means of the manifestation (*ābhāsa*), one attains the state of having the wind as a vehicle.

"Then one should set in motion all those [energies] belonging to that [state], though they may be disordered. Thus, [the state] is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) because, by making the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) devoid of appearance, it is stainless. Regarding the term "worldly":
it refers to attachment such as "I am the enjoyer," "these objects of enjoyment grant pleasure," and so forth.
By means of the path of the vision of mundane knowledge;
upon its destruction, because the afflictions caused by evil are destroyed.
As it is said: "Having brought about the complete exhaustion of all afflictions to be abandoned by vision..."
"One applies oneself to meditative cultivation for the sake of abandoning the cognitive obscurations.
Thus, the third initiation is the innate [wisdom] consisting of the nature of the non-conceptualization of all supramundane emptiness, which is the essence of the example.
The fourth is that which is free from obscurations even beyond that, namely the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*).
The remainder has its meaning already explained. || 4-6 || 1. *ga.* reads *māī*.

Regarding the "observation of the six families" (*ṣaṭkulāvalokana*), since it is precisely the wheels (*cakras*) of the six families that are to be taught, he speaks of their observation starting with "Śākya," etc.
Family (*kula*) means lineage (*gotra*) or element (*dhātu*).
"Everything," and so forth.
