The mind, having fallen away from the duality of awakening, is pervaded by the *śukra* (semen) throughout the wheels (*cakras*).
As it has been said: "Just as when a fish is cast into water, its brilliance cannot be enjoyed."
"In the three, the mind delights; in the sky, it attains the state of equal flavor.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the mantra-master Akṣobhya, whose secret domain is within the pericarp of the vajra and lotus—whence comes the "illumination" (*dīpana*) of the innate (*sahaja*) bliss? He says: there is also the reading *bhāsana* (shining).
The meaning is that the element of the mantra-master also serves the purpose of illumination.
In the maṇḍala—by means of such subtle yoga—one sustains the wheel through its radiation within the *dharmodaya*.
Regarding "body, speech," and so forth:
within the inner circle from the navel, there are four channels whose nature is gnosis (*jñāna*).
The world outside consists of sixty-four, within that twelve, and further within eight; these are known respectively as the wheels of body, speech, and mind—this is the worldly convention.
Regarding the scripture for the knowledge of the body and so forth, however, that which is to be known is the destruction of the self (*ātman*).
"Father" refers to the seminal drop (*bindu*), because it generates the body. [Regarding the phrase] "the world," etc.:
It is perceived by the world; through the phrase "light and so forth," there is the appearance of light and the perception thereof.
The meaning is that which has emerged from vibration (*spanda*) and is untainted (*anāsrava*).

The semen (*śukra*) is the bliss of non-vibration (*niḥspandānanda*), wherein the vajra, through its unfolding, [manifests] Vairocana and the others at the navel and other locations; this has already been explained previously by means of "non-vibration" and so forth.

In the *tantra*, "in the body" (*dehe*) means at the end of the full moon of wisdom (*prajñāpūrṇimānta*), that sixteenth [digit] which is infinite space by virtue of its infinity; he who is in the head, in the thunderbolt (*vajra*) endowed with half a garment, is the sixth—this is the meaning.

And it is said in the *Vajragarbha*: "Here, Vairocana is the leader in the earth-circle, Akṣobhya in space, Amitābha in water, Ratnasambhava in fire, Amoghasiddhi in wind, and Vajrasattva is the leader in the gnosis-circle.
Conventional truth and ultimate truth are the non-dual gnosis of bliss and emptiness. || 2 ||

**The Survey of the Six Families** It is known: "The sequence of awakening through the Net of Illusion (*māyājālābhisambodhikrama*). Because it is produced by the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is the awakening to—and the non-apprehension of—the three worlds as being like a net of illusion, O Subhūti!
There exists that mind which is no-mind (*acitta*) (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, p. 3); the nature of the mind is luminous (*prabhāsvara*).
"Neither beginning, nor end, nor middle"—then there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
"That is the supreme great bliss; neither other nor self," so it is said (*Dohakośa*, p.
21). This refers to the verse beginning with "imām" and so forth.
The mantras begin with "Oṃ, homage to you, the sharp vajra," and so on.
In the Mantranīti, non-duality is the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

As it is said: "I bow to that very non-dual Blessed One, the Paramādibuddha—the omniscient progenitor of the Buddhas, endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*), the knower of the three times—who is embraced by the Blessed Lady Prajñā, who is both with form and formless, who is free from arising and ceasing, whose bliss is imperishable, and who is devoid of the pleasures of laughter and the like."
"Neither wisdom nor means—this is the body of the co-emergent" (Kāyatrayastotra 589). Furthermore, according to the system of the *Pāramitānaya*, this is the *svābhāvikakāya* (essential body).
As it has been said:

"Those untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects—the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of the Sage is characterized by their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*). (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.1) This means that the intrinsic nature of those phenomena which have attained purity—such as the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and so forth—is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), that is to say, selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Therefore...
"Since reality is the fruit of the verse, and there is no means of realizing reality other than [the verse] itself, reality is that which is devoid of the four extremes.
As it has been said: "That which is conceptualized as the form of hair and so forth from the appearance of a cataract is indeed false."
"Know that whatever one with pure vision perceives through a particular nature, that very thing is its own [nature] here as well.

Just as one free from cataracts sees the hair and other things perceived by one with cataracts as not being reality, so too is the notion of "self" and "belonging to self" false, because it is a perversion.
As it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "A form perceived from a distance is seen clearly by those nearby.

If a mirage were water, why would it not be seen by those nearby? (Ratnāvalī 1.52) Just as a mirage resembles water but is neither water nor [water] in reality, so too the aggregates resemble a self but are neither selves nor [selves] in reality."
(Ratnāvalī 1.54): "The grasping at existence is an error due to apprehending that which is not [the self] as being that; and this error is the cause of saṃsāra," as it has been said:
"First there is the notion of 'I', followed by the notion of 'mine'; from the production of both these arises passion and so forth, and from that, the fire of hatred in one who holds a harmful view."
Therefore, the remainder is affliction; from the proliferation of karma arising therefrom, cyclic existence (saṃsāra) spreads out, devoid of refuge and characterized by extreme suffering—
thus it is of the nature of non-arising.

As for what was stated—that "non-arising is reality, and the intellect also arises from the *nayas*," meaning it consists of the *mantranaya*—this is because there is no distinction between these two vehicles (*yāna*) regarding non-arising.
For it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "He who [practices] in the *prajñāpāramitā* will enter into union with space," and so forth.
In this regard as well, [it is said]: "by those whose minds are unattached to space" (Kālacakratantra 5.115), and so forth;
the reason is non-arising (*anutpāda*), and the fruit is such that as the cause is, so is the fruit—for indeed, a rice sprout does not arise from *krodrava* grain.
That is said: he himself will explain [the passage] beginning with "not existing," etc.;
the Madhyamaka cognition arises in the interval between the two extremes.
The path of practice is awakening; it is the knowledge of the destruction and non-arising of impurities. It is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it is sought for that purpose.

It is established as the "vehicle" (*yāna*) because, according to the reasoning to be stated later, one goes by means of it; and it is "great" (*mahat*) because it is greater than the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvaka*) and others.
They conduct themselves by means of that; it is established in their being when he said:
"O deer, do not form an unequal attachment; bind me, die, speak, act."

"Behold the fish, the moth, the elephant, the bee, and the herd of deer, each joined to its object. (Dohākośa, p. 31) The fish is attached to taste in water; the moth to form in fire; the elephant to touch in the female elephant; the bee to smell in the lotus; and the herd of deer to sound in song. They are bound by constant attachment, not by the severance of emotion. For it is said that even for a person of right conduct, if they possess false vision (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), all their merit results in a most terrible ripening. As stated in the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*: "Emptiness, when wrongly perceived, destroys the person of dull intellect."

According to the statement, "Like a snake poorly grasped, or like a spell poorly mastered" (Mokṣaśāstra 24.11), the adoption of some [particular] doctrine is like a seizing grip for the sake of devouring; it is a clinging that, once abandoned, has been suddenly cast off, while the mother who has long since reached the further shore remains.

Thus, when the true path has been submerged, I ever and always salute that excellent Guru who points out the sky-like image beyond the mind, whose nature is the compassion of space. He who knows that there is first the warding off of demerit, in the middle the warding off of the self, and finally the warding off of everything—he is wise. Ask the world of the proponents of Sāṃkhya, Ulūka, the Nirgranthas, and those who speak of the person (pudgala) and the aggregates (skandha), whether they declare the transcendence of "is" and "is not. For these radiant words of the Tathāgata-sun are indeed the straight path leading to the city of Nirvāṇa.

The state of selflessness (*nirātmatā*), which has been traversed by thousands of noble ones (*ārya*), is not perceived even when revealed to those of dull vision. According to the logical principle that it cannot be a real entity (*vastu*) unless it transcends being either one or many, it must be either one or many;
yet that which is neither one nor many is not real. Thus, the entire universe (*viśva*), being devoid of both unity and plurality, is unreal in every respect.
For it is said: "Because of simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts. If it has parts—above, below, and in the four directions—a single entity cannot be established.

As long as the atom lacks parts, because the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be no larger than a single atom. Even a mountain would be a mere atom if atoms were to interpenetrate one another.
Thus, [the argument] is "like a flower in the sky" and more.

The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti* is indeed one, yet it is spoken of as many and manifold; though one, it is not accomplished, and those [many] are likewise unaccomplished— being neither real nor unreal, because its nature is radiant manifestation.

Even amidst hundreds of thousands of contradictions, where could that which is experienced as a manifest form go? It is not non-existent, because there is no experience of things that are absolutely non-existent, such as a rabbit’s horn in the sky; yet this [manifestation] is experienced because it consists of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Nor is it both real and unreal, for it is afflicted by the defects inherent in each of those respective positions.
Nor is it neither, due to the arguments already stated regarding the first two positions.
Thus it is said: "The Madhyamikas know reality to be free from the four extremes—neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither;
for them, there exists no position such as 'existent,' 'non-existent,' or 'both existent and non-existent.'"
"Even after a long time, no criticism can be leveled against it. Thus, in Sāṃkhya, Madhyamaka, Digambara, and Lokāyata, these four positions (koṭis) are to be known respectively.

Because it has as its object the opposite of the four positions mentioned, that cognition which is liberated is the "four-cornered" (catuṣkoṭi); whatever knowledge has a particular object, it is the awareness of that very form.

Just as the cognition of blue has the form of blue, so too the Madhyamaka intellect has an object free from the four extremes; yet, while this [ordinary] mental impression involves an adherence to reality, this [Madhyamaka] intellect is without such impression because it has realized the illusory nature of the world.

However, this does not mean that there would be no engagement in generosity and other virtues, for it is said that "with the ascent to the pinnacle of non-duality, there is both engagement and withdrawal."
If it is argued that one likewise attains [the fruits of] giving and so forth, let it be granted; however, how does the practice of giving and so forth come about? It is said:
because it is possible only when there is the perception of the object to be given, the giver, and the recipient.
Therefore, he says: "Consisting of the excellence of all forms. As it has been said: "Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is taught as the cause;

subsequently, non-referential compassion is the fruit that accomplishes the welfare of the world. The intention is this: the delusion regarding effects is not to be prevented, because without the accumulation of merit through generosity and so forth, there would be no accumulation of gnosis (*jñāna-sambhāra*). In its absence, enlightenment would not occur. Therefore, at the time of application, one does not cling to evil because one knows its falsity, yet one engages in merit just as one does in enlightenment—even in emptiness.

The fruit of the accumulation of merit consists of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while the fruit of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) is the truth body (*dharmakāya*) and the innate body (*sahajakāya*).

Therefore, the five practices beginning with generosity must be purified through the intellect of the Middle Way; otherwise, generosity and the other perfections would not even possess the status of being *pāramitās*.
Nor is it through the assistance of Mahāmudrā; as it is said:

"Just as a single person possessing sight, by means of a treatise illuminating the *amṛtakaṇikā*, can easily lead a whole multitude of blind people to their desired destination, so too here, having taken hold of those devoid of vision, one attains Buddhahood through the supreme qualities of vigor."
He says this very point with the words beginning "this," etc.:
that which exists, such as space, does not arise; yet giving and the other perfections do arise.
That which is non-existent does not arise, such as a tortoise’s hair; yet generosity and the like do arise.
Whatever possesses arising is dependent upon a cause, because things such as space, which lack a cause, do not possess arising.
Furthermore, if the cause were something already ceased—such as a seed—the cause would also have to be something that has been ceased for a long time.
If the sprout were to arise from a seed that is in a state where it has not ceased, such a thing does not exist; thus he says:
"The production of a sprout does not occur from a seed that has ceased, nor from one that has not ceased.
Furthermore, the claim that things are causeless is also untenable, because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby everything could arise from everything.
For instance, in the passage beginning with "tathāhi" and so forth:

for those things whose existence by way of their own nature does not occur without a cause, even their non-existence cannot be causeless, because non-existence consists in the cessation of existence. Therefore, it is said that generosity and the other perfections are neither existents nor non-existents, and thus they are like an illusion, having the nature of conventional truth. As it has been said: "Delusion is 'conventional' (saṃvṛti) because it conceals the true nature; that which it presents as true is merely artificial."
"That sage declared that to be conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya), and that a produced entity is a conventional reality.
By this it is meant: the web of illusion of the three worlds has been indicated as [the object of] perfect awakening;
therefore, [there exist] generosity and the other perfections.

And its fruit is the illusory body (*māyā-deha*), the divine fivefold objects of desire, and the Buddha-fields of gold and so forth; as for the distinguished [passions] such as attachment and their fruit—the ordinary body and the world of the vessel-receptacle—all these are entirely non-abiding and like an illusion. Thus, for the firm master, this does not cause any contradiction.
When [the object] has ceased, the cessation of existence occurs for the intellect, together with its receptacle; this is the accomplishment of non-duality—such is the benefit.
Therefore, conceptualization regarding existence and so forth is merely unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
By stating, "Unreal imagination exists; duality is not found there;
emptiness, however, exists here, and within that [emptiness] it [unreal imagination] also exists," he concludes the proposition with the words "thus it stands" and so forth.

With the words "Now" (*idānīm*) and so forth, he states the second limb: "Below and above the two goddesses" refers to Bhūcarī and Khecarī; "born from the first vowel" refers to the letter *A*; "of very pure form" means she whose body is inseparable [from that]; "the sphere of phenomena" (*dharmadhātu*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
All phenomena are factors conducive to enlightenment because they have that as their intrinsic nature; thus,
through the words "the noble one," "Gaurī," "the earth," and "the great solar disk," she is Samantaprabhā, Amitaprabhā, and Mahāvajraprabhāsvārā.
The light of space is well-established like space; the light of clothing is adorned with the sprinkling of radiance from the lake;
the light of the lotus is stainless through the nature of the pure Dharma;
the light of karma performs the deeds of a Buddha; it is incomparable and free from grasping.
Wisdom is incomparable, being the realization that transcends all comparisons; it is omniscience, immensely luminous,
to be personally realized, and the fulfillment of the knowledge of yogins.
Thus, the goddesses of the sense objects, such as Pukkasī and the others, and the external goddesses, such as Gaurī and the others, are described by the words "pari" and so forth.

Because they constitute the central form of all those residing within the *Nairātmyā* maṇḍala—which consists of fifteen deities—they are beyond description; they sever the conceptualization of unreal mental constructions for beings who are free from the proliferation of phenomena (*niṣprapañca*).
This explains the third meaning.
Regarding that very mind through the yoga of the deity, it says: "One's own mind is the entire possession of all Buddhas; it is the collection of phenomena.
Through the yoga of the selflessness of phenomena, one should slay [the mind]; it dies of its own accord. Thus.

Regarding what was said concerning the "first vowel": "That mind which abides in the heart—whether red, white, or yellow—is by nature the first vowel; it is called *dhī* (intellect), and thus proclaimed as the intellect (*buddhi*)."

Because one’s own mind and the [consort] *mattā* abide in a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within the universal reflection (*viśvabimba*) through non-arising and so forth, they are liberated from the four extremes.

As it has been said: “Wisdom (*prajñā*) and gnosis (*jñāna*) are the mind; its tenfold manifestation is the consecration (*seka*). Immersion therein is like a stainless moon, indeed comparable to a reflection in a mirror.

Within that, there is the bliss of nirvāṇa, the unchanging (*acyuta*), the innate (*sahaja*), and the fourth (*caturtha*), whose face is thus twofold. He in whose heart and mouth this resides is the glorious Guru. In this context, “wisdom” (*prajñā*) refers to the grasping mind (*grāhakacitta*).
"Knowledge" refers to the tenfold object of perception (*grāhya*), such as smoke and so forth, which appears like a mirror;
the entry of the subject (*grāhaka*) into that object is here called "immersion" (*majjana*) by means of the four [practices] beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
From that immersion, there arises the innate (*sahaja*), imperishable fourth state, which does not fall away from the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

This knowledge is the mouth of that teacher in whose heart it resides as personal experience; it has come to his mouth for the sake of imparting it to the disciple— Śrī Vastradhara is he— and that very [knowledge] is the radiance.
"Thus," and so forth: the King of Mind, standing surrounded by a shimmering retinue, dances.
Regarding this, he says "it is adventitious": that nature of the mind which is luminous never undergoes transformation, just as the sky does not.
"For this [mind] undergoes defilement through adventitious factors such as coming and so forth, which arise from unreal conceptualization.
Thus ends the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*. He explains the remainder with the words "The Victor," and so on:

"Thus, although the systems of the Perfections (*pāramitā*) and Mantra have the same objective, the system of Mantra is praised because it is free from confusion, possesses many skillful means, is not difficult to practice, and is intended for those with sharp faculties. (1) "Poṭha," and so forth...

The body, which consists of twelve locations, is pervaded by the twelve syllables beginning with *a*, which indicate the *bodhicitta-kalā*; because these very [syllables] have the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) consisting of twelve digits (*kalā*),
they are called "secret," and so forth.
Due to the cessation of eighteen hundred breaths for each stage (*bhūmi*),
or alternatively, because of the body and so forth, and because of the shortness of *ānanda*, there are short vowels;
and because of its twofold nature, due to its length, there are long vowels.

The nature of being the essence of both vowels and consonants, due to the imperishability of the qualities (*guṇa*), is non-different from the three vajras; thus, the fourth [empowerment], non-different from the third empowerment,
is "Oṃ" and so forth.
As it is said: "Brahmā is the body, Hara is speech, and Hari is the mind of living beings; they are the three Vedas;
Oṃkāra is their [three] syllables; the moon, sun, and fire are their [three] channels and the [three] qualities. Thus, in that context, [the reference is] to the body and so forth.
The meaning of the syllable *oṃ* consists of the three phonemes *a*, *u*, and *ma*; thus it is called *cyavana*.

"By whom the Imperishable has not been attained, yet who desires the bliss of the Imperishable; everyone seeks water even when thirsty, yet the *cātaka* bird does not suffer for the water that exists on the ground.
Thus, in this manner.
Because it pervades the three worlds through its state of being unobscured, because the innate (*sahaja*) arises,
because the *saṃbhoga* and other [bodies] are manifested through their respective garments, and because it resides in the centers of the wheels (*cakra*) starting from the navel.

By the three verses beginning with "That which is the root, situated in the heart" and "The body," the characteristics of the three bodies— the innate (*sahaja*), the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), and the emanation (*nirmāṇa*)— are stated.
The characteristic of the emanation body is stated as having various colors and so forth, because emanations are infinite.
The dissolution of the perception of the body and so forth occurs in the Great Yoga of Clear Light, as it is said: "Where the mind dies, there the wind is dissolved;

that is the reality of all observation. What fruit can be told by words? (2-3). [This is] the *Māyājālābhisambodhi*. Because it has the form of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, the Vajradhātu-maṇḍala is "possessing all forms" (*sarvākāra*); because its hands, feet, and so on are everywhere, and its eyes, heads, and faces are everywhere, it is "possessing all sense-faculties" (*sarvendriya*).

The Holder of Māyā (*māyādharah*), who—having ceased the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—is of the nature of the immutable drop (*akṣarabindu*), speaks through the gateway of the Vajradhātu-maṇḍala the wheel of the aggregates and so forth, which is the unobstructed universal image (*viśvabimba*) manifested from the radiation of the garment of bodhicitta. Regarding him, it is said: "Time is the means (*upāya*), the gnosis of immutable bliss; the wheel of the world, which is the form of the knowable, is the glorious wisdom (*prajñā*), whose nature is compassion and whose essence is emptiness.
Thus, "Now," and so forth.
With these three verses, the introduction concludes; he now states that this *Nāmasaṅgīti*, for whose sake it was composed, is being explained:
"Namely, because the universal image dissolves into the yogi’s mind, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) possesses a dual nature; the experience of that innate state is innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*).
He explains the means for that [gnosis] with the words beginning 'the jewel' (*maṇi*)."
By means of the word "with" (*akāreṇa*) and so forth, he states their synonymy through the elimination of the notion that they are distinct;
as it has been said: "This which is called the radiant and beautiful reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*)."
"That very perfection of wisdom is the shatterer of all Māras.
Thus, "from that" means from that great non-dual yoga.
For this very reason, he says "prajñā" and so forth, and "sa ca" and so forth; by these words, the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) residing within the secret cavity and other locations is expressed.
As it is stated in the *Ādibuddha*: "That which is designated by the name 'A' is the Great Immutable Dharmadhātu."

"The cause of the body, speech, and mind of the lords of men born from the vajra-womb" means that it is the cause of the nirmāṇakāya, sambhogakāya, and dharmakāya; [it refers to] the unity of the aggregates with the elements and of the sense faculties with their objects within the maṇḍala.
Because of the statement, "That very thing for her sake is the blazing Caṇḍālī in the navel," and so forth,
the phrase "blazing" and so on refers to the meaning already stated; [this is understood] by means of the heart.

Regarding what was stated [in the *Guhyasamāja*] concerning the heart-center of the wheel, starting with "the entire [mandala]" and so forth: "She who, through omniscience, leads the Śrāvakas seeking peace to tranquility..."

Homage to that Mother of the Buddha, who, together with the hosts of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, is endowed with the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and accomplishes the welfare of the world for those who act for the benefit of beings; she through whom the Munis, having attained union, declare this entire universe in all its aspects. Thus, [verse 1].
The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* states: "Light," and so forth.
At the arising of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), the movement through the ten maṇḍalas—which is the natural law (*prakṛtidharma*)—does not flow.

In that regard, it is said that the five maṇḍalas, beginning with space and the five aggregates of consciousness, and the five elements, beginning with earth, [flow] respectively in the left and the right. As for the sequence: "At the base, earth and water flow in the left; fire flows in the right; wind at the crown; and space flows in the center of both nostrils, [emerging] from the *vaṃ* [syllable], in succession. Thus it is said.
Here, "left" refers to the side of the nasal septum, because it is said that for all [channels], Meru is the northern one.
As for the sequence of dissolution: earth goes into water; water also goes into fire; fire goes into wind; wind goes into space; and the tenfold space with its causes goes into the causeless.
It proceeds into the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), which is the supreme bliss beyond the syllable and possesses all forms.
"O Lord of Men, through knowledge, the activity of knowledge, and the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), perfection (*siddhi*) arises for men even in this very life.
Thus, Vajradhara is the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*);
he is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) because of the absence of conceptualizations such as arising and so forth.
Because it has the nature of entry into the center, it is the neuter body (*napuṃsakakāya*).

Of those aforementioned desires, Mañjuśrī is the delightful cause because he is the cause for teaching the Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings; and precisely because he experiences the bliss of the middle way, his perception is based on another support through a continuous connection.
This is so even regarding speech, due to the realization that the universe itself is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
He states the reason for that: "Because of the direct realization of the Great Space of the supreme imperishable *ha*. (2)
The word *mahā* situated as the final member (*uttarapada*) expresses wisdom.

In the case of one for whom [the quality] is great (*mahatī*), it is a subordinate element by virtue of its state of being; thus, there is shortening of the vowel in the final member according to the rule *uttarapade hrasvatvam*, and lengthening of the vowel in the prior member according to the rule *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇe*.
This refers to the passage beginning with "mahā" and so forth.
He is the Great Passion (mahārāga) because of his passion for sentient beings.
"Of such a kind" means that,

by virtue of being the master of the twelve stages (bhūmi) through the subduing of passion and the fulfillment of the stages, he is the limb of enlightenment consisting of the diamond-like knowledge (vajrānaṅga) due to his victory over desire.

"For this very reason" means because of his affection for sentient beings (*sattvānurāga*). As it has been said: "Filled with the supreme immutable bliss, perfected by the stages (*bhūmi*), the Great Hero (*mahāsattva*) is the one who brings delight to all sentient beings."
"Akṣobhya" (the Immovable) is so called because of being unmoved at the ultimate limit;
for this very reason, he is "Acala" (the Motionless). As it has been said: "A sentient being established in enlightenment is a Bodhisattva; therefore, he is immovable."
"Among the multitudes of afflictions such as hatred and the rest, great hatred is the great enemy. (3)
The *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti* [states]: "Because of having transcended delusion (*moha*).
This means that by transcending the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), one enters the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*).

Through the teaching of "the deluded" as being without mind (*acittatā*), there is the Great Wrathful One (*mahākrodha*) at the ultimate limit, who is the vision of the *uṣṇīṣa* for one who has passed away while in a state of affection.
Regarding the passage beginning with "kāya" and so forth:
"When the winds of the drops (*bindu*) and the minds have been made of one flavor within the central channel, it is said:
'The secret commitment (*samaya*) is the nectar of the moon; its consumption is non-emission (*acyuti*').'"
For it has been said: "By this mode of existence, the deluded-minded one becomes the destroyer of delusion, with all [defilements] remaining entirely destroyed. (4)
Great greed arises from the attainment of supramundane bliss;
it is so called because, by teaching the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*), one destroys the greed even of sentient beings.
As it has been said: "The oneness of all mantras is with the syllables of the body of wisdom (*prajñākāya*)."
"Mahākrodha is the great Śakra among those who take the form of wrath. Thus:
"Through the means of great immutable bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*), one should never abandon the welfare of sentient beings;
to liberate sentient beings, he is the great passion (*mahālobha*), while the passion for the perishable (*kṣaralobha*) is his destroyer."
"O great fools, you do not obtain even the impermanent happiness of saṃsāra here;

yet the wise man, having obtained the happiness of sovereignty, renounces it for the sake of liberation. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the commentary on the sixteen joys (*ānanda*): there are four [joys], beginning with *ānanda*, which consist of the bodies of bliss (*sukhakāya*)—namely, the emanation (*nirmāṇa*), enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), and dharma [bodies].
Regarding the passage beginning with "there, waking," and so forth:
it is not innate (*sahaja*) in the same way as the waking state and the others.
It does not abide even in these locations of knowledge—the *nābhicakra* (navel-center), which is the locus of gnosis—and the loci of mind, speech, and body known as the heart, throat, and forehead.
Together with Mahāmudrā, there shall be the supreme innate [bliss].
Regarding the words "bhāva" and so forth:
it is because even existence (bhāva) is brought to the state of non-apprehension.
Devoid of the distinction between existence and non-existence, consisting of dense bliss, and shining by itself—such is the greatness of awakening, that is, of gnosis.
Of what nature is it? It pervades the interior of space because the collection of entities, which constitute the veil over the object of knowledge, is no longer perceived.

For this very reason, within the universal reflection containing various forms such as blue and yellow, it is a repository of all-pervading, supramundane bliss, like a shimmering orb in the mirror of the self through its own stainlessness—the radiance that spreads forth. This Sahajānanda is to be known by the single name "the Fourth."

By the words beginning with "O Karṇa," he describes the varieties of bliss (*ānanda*): Bliss (*ānanda*) is that which is great and tremulous arising from the experience of objects of pleasure. The lotus of the heart itself is the dwelling or house; within it, there is a bed (*talpa*) spread out, consisting of no small number of mental constructs (*vikalpa*). Therein the mind is turned and drawn in, and for that very reason, it is diverse due to its preoccupation with embracing, kissing, and so forth. Because it is devoid of anything graspable (*grāhya*), it is supreme; thus it is called "the highest" (*parama*).

When the mind possesses a single-pointed certainty (*niṣṭhā*) regarding the grasping of the navel-lotus, because even the state of being a grasper is absent, there is cessation (*virama*), which is a radiant binding of the illumination of drops of nectar through the breaking of all distractions.

Because even the conceptualization—"I have enjoyed auspicious, desirable happiness from contact with the tip of the thunderbolt"—is absent, the great duality of pleasure does not expand for the beginner during the sprinkling of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), as is clear from such statements.
The summit within the jewel-tip is peaceful due to the abandonment of external supports.
The mind, as if unerring and resting upon a lotus, expands some indescribable innate state. || 5-8 ||
Regarding "external sounds and so forth":

even within the universal image (*viśvabimba*), there exist sounds and the rest; thus, they are called "external. [This applies] to non-attachment toward worldly phenomena that have not been attained or seen. (9)

"Otherwise" means by way of the sequence of skillful means (*upāya*), aspiration (*praṇidhi*), and so forth; otherwise, [it would not be] "the one of great power and great skillful means" or "the world joined with happiness.
As it is said: "The blind see forms, the deaf hear," and so on.
Now, regarding "entry into the city," it begins with "Māra" and so forth.

Māra refers to death and its ilk; the obstructions of Māra consist of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), as well as those termed meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), according to the Conqueror Krodhejin.
"Merely a moment's delay":
one who has not awakened does not attain the supreme state, nor does one whose afflictions are intensely roused find the means to accomplish their own welfare.

Thus it is said: "Since you have attained awakening through the exertion of firm vigor, the afflictions have been rendered as light as a blade of grass by your instructions. This is according to that principle.

The twenty-four [sites] are as follows: on the head, the crest-lock, the left ear, the back of the head, and the pedestal (*pīṭha*); on the left ear, between the eyebrows, the eye, and the shoulder (*upapīṭha*); on the armpits and breasts, the field (*kṣetra*); on the navel and nose, the secondary field (*upakṣetra*); on the mouth and throat, the *chandoha*; on the heart, the penis, and its vicinity, the *melāpaka*; on the genitals and anus, the secondary *melāpaka* (*upamelāpaka*); on the thighs and shanks, the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*); on the fingers, the feet, and the back of the feet, the secondary cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*); and on the big toes and knees, the secondary secondary cremation ground (*tadupāṅga*). These correspond respectively to the going and coming [of the breath].
"Cintā" and so forth:
In the world, those ten states of Manmatha which are said to exist in the limbs of living beings are themselves the ten signs, such as smoke and so on, of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Vajrin).
What is the Victor (Jina) and what is Desire (Kāma)? They both exist in the form of the drops of the bliss of the two organs.
"Entering"— the state of that [ignorance] wherein it is as if entering a peak;
"pierced by the great aesthetic flavor" (mahārasa)—
this is the intended meaning.

"Just as a great elixir situated even in a single part of iron pierces the iron heated by a fierce fire on all sides, so too here, the imperishable bliss situated even within the entry [of the mind] pierces the mind heated by the fire of desire on all sides. Thus it is said.
The fourth dhyāna consists of mindfulness, equanimity, purity, and the two sensations of neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
it has four factors, and the fourth [dhyāna] is accompanied by one-pointedness of mind. || 10-14 ||
The Pervasion of Bodhicitta

"One whose mind is undisturbed by sufferings and free from longing for pleasures, who is devoid of passion, fear, and anger— the sage whose intellect is steady is called one of perfectly pure knowledge of the dharmadhātu.
Thus, the reality of mantra is the bodhicitta consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Speech itself is the vajra; its meaning is that which accomplishes it and restrains the breath.

The three knowledges are *āloka*, *ālokābhāsa*, and *ālokopalabdhi*. In the self-consecrated (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) realm consisting of illusion, which is the movement of the mind alone, external recitation and withdrawal of the senses [are abandoned] because they act as obstacles to the cultivation of vajra-recitation.

Since the Blessed One, whose nature is Vajradhara, is himself the meaning of the mantra and is to be accomplished through the mantra, how could there be an obstacle to the recitation? Just as the state of fullness is the very nature of bliss through the *syama* and other [mantras], so too other states of being, such as the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and so forth, are made accessible by the grace of the Guru; this is the "intermediate" [state], beginning with "without breath" (*anapavana*), and so on.
Regarding the passage beginning with "samādhi," etc.:
From the immutable bliss whose nature is wisdom and means, there is the accomplishment of the state of complete enlightenment in a single moment within the knowledge-image (*jñānabimba*).
The vow [is fulfilled] on the eighth stage.
Regarding the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*): [they are as follows].

Because the perfections (pāramitās) obtain their very self-nature from the Lord alone, they do not possess the characteristic of a support and its supported, due to the absence of conceptual construction regarding them. || 1-2 ||
From giving, there is the state of being joyful and so forth.
Upon the fulfillment of each individual perfection, such as giving, there is the attainment of each respective stage, beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*).
Through the garment-like meditative absorption (*vastrôpama-samādhi*), one attains the Victor’s stage of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā*).
"Te ca" refers to wind, mind, the bodhicitta, blood, marrow, bone, sinew, flesh, and the sense faculties;
"carma" (skin) makes ten elements.

By means of the supreme immutable accomplished elixir (*paramākṣarasiddharasa*) of these, the illusory body (*māyādeha*) arises, for through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), mastery (*vibhutva*) is attained.

By the statement "supreme," [it is meant] those whose minds have attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) with space, as indicated by the words "space" and so forth; by them, with eyes half-open, the *avadhūtī* has its breath stilled.
From emptiness, one perceives four signs through the practice of night: the earth, a mirage, fireflies, and a lamp;
then, through the practice of day, one perceives six signs in the cloudless sky: a flame, the moon, the sun, a black jewel, lightning, and the blue luster of the moon—thus making ten signs in total.

In the midst of that, within the great bindu, there is the vision of the Buddha’s form—the perception of all forms such as jars and cloths—which is empty of external objects; it is the vision of a form consisting of many non-conceptual enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), wherein all appearances manifest simultaneously like an illusion.
Thus, within the body of the yogin, consciousness no longer functions through the relationship of object and subject.

"In the Blessed One," and so forth: when the mind that grasps—the mind which perceives the universe as its own reflection—has dissolved into the mind that is the object of perception, and when the Lord, the master who impels the breaths, is present; *āram ityādi bhagavati grāhakacitte svātmani svapratibhāse viśvabimbe grāhyacitte vilayaṃ gate prāṇānām adhipe vāhake svāmini sati* (In the Blessed One, and so forth: when the mind that grasps—the mind which perceives the universe as its own reflection—has dissolved into the mind that is the object of perception, and when the Lord, the master who impels the breaths, is present).

When the cycle of inhalation, exhalation, and breath has become tranquil, the life-force wind (*jīvānila*)—the vital air—is restrained within the heart. This radiance of light, which is the manifestation of the drops of nectar, is more intense than sound; it is the continuous flow of the yogis through the limb of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Having emerged from one's own very body, this [light] dispels the darkness of ignorance in that state. Pervading the three worlds throughout the three times and three realms, it proceeds from the arising of the universal image (*viśvabimba*).
As he will say here: "And the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*)," and also "by the unprecedented," and so forth.
"O Lord of the Śabaras, this spring has arrived unprecedentedly; by your grace, it brings happiness"—this is the underlying intention.
For [the word] *ambara* yields the sense of "sky," while *phulla* bears the sense of "blossomed," and [the word] *kañca* yields the sense of "smoke" and so forth.

And even though the yogi sees them, he neither lifts them up nor touches them, because he abides in non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) samādhi; but when separated from that—that is, upon emerging from samādhi and no longer seeing them—he engages in play, being conceptual (*savikalpa*) due to the perception of the signs of liberation.
He speaks of the restraint of the vital winds (*pavana-nirodha*), beginning with "unblinking," and so forth.

Having withdrawn all thoughts from every side, with a mind stilled and eyes unblinking, one fixes the gaze upon that which was taught by the Guru and thereby arrests the mind; then the vital wind, having entered the central channel, is bound, and through the cessation of conceptual constructions such as "it is" and so forth, his intellect becomes tranquil— thus say the venerable Candrakīrti and others.

He refutes those of dull intellect because it is from this very [state] that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) perishes; for those of noble intellect, the ineffable reflection of the universe arises. Although it pervades even more than space, because it is devoid of the mind, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*), which is the beholding of the reflection.
The first dhyāna has five factors: applied thought, sustained thought, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind. ||3||
That by which the ten mandalas of Caṇḍālī are drawn forth and pulled into the center is thus [described]; "in the drop" refers to that which resides in the cakras of the navel and so forth;
"innate," etc., follows.

He whose powers are the ten stages of desire (*kāmāvasthā*) by virtue of the capacity for accomplishing the supreme immutable gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*), and whose state of being the means to the supreme immutable arises from the capacity of the smoke and other signs to illuminate the innate *caṇḍālī*— he is one for whom there is the "light" (*āloka*) which is the vision in the sky through the practice of recollection (*anusmṛti*).
"Prajñā" refers to the woman who is a limb of action;
[the fourfold meaning] beginning with "in the reflection of gnosis" and "in the universal reflection" is to be accomplished solely through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).
The passage beginning with "of this" (*asya*) and so forth refers to the limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*);
that beginning with "concealed" (*pihita*) and so forth refers to the limb of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Regarding the phrase "in the cessation" (*nirodhe*), it is precisely the cessation of the conceptualization of the winds that is the "vajra. When the mind has attained that [state], there arises the sign (*nimitta*) of smoke and so forth.

The "jewel-light" (*ratnāloka*) has an appearance like a black jewel; the "jewel-lamp" (*ratnapradīpa*) is indeed a lamp because it does not burn; the "moon-light" (*candrāloka*) has an appearance like the moon; the "sun-lamp" (*sūryapradīpa*) has an appearance like the sun and is blazing; the "all-aspect-seeing" (*sarvākāradarśin*) is the radiant universal image (*viśvabimba*);
the "object of realization" (*pratyayārtha*) is the yogi who is to be personally realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedya*);
[these] are the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), and so forth.
Just as smoke is a sign that is non-deviant from fire, so too are smoke and the others signs for the attainment of Mahāmudrā.

As it is said: "Having made the mind one-pointed on the void, one should examine it for one day. Because of this statement in the *Paramādibuddha*, the Vajra-word regarding the path of Mahāmudrā meditation—consisting of smoke and the rest—is manifest [in the scripture], and not something arrived through the lineage of the gurus' oral tradition.
And it has been said: "Having abandoned all doubt, one should test [this] for a single day;
if no conviction arises, then that word of mine is mere ornamentation.
Furthermore, there is no other means of accomplishing the mantra and so forth, apart from the signs such as smoke and the rest, if [the result] is not achieved in a single [day]."
It performs this as the primary cause, and so forth;

"stiffness" (*stabdhatā*) arises from the absence of blinking, and it is the creator of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That is the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*, which for yogins is stillness (*staimitya*) due to the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "vimala" and so forth: when the eye—half-opened and directed toward the object of a stainless sky free from obscurations such as clouds—is employed while hanging down from the neck, it consumes—that is, renders devoid of intrinsic nature—the support, which is the conceptualizing mind, from a heart-mind moistened by a vibrant and intense compassion. Therefore [the verse says this].
By this, the oral tradition has been stated;
and it has been taught that with the eight-syllable mantra one should not think of anything at all.
Having produced [the deity] and made the mind its root, one then performs the friction within the void.
Since that which is beyond [the senses] is the collyrium for the eyes blinded by the cataract of ignorance, one should take up the root of the mind and rub it against the friction of emptiness;
for it has been said: "Without an object of support, it becomes tranquil."
Because of this saying, one should make all sounds there equal to space;
by the very nature of being equal to space, the mind itself is held within.
Thus, he is both with mind and without mind by his innate nature; he is made manifest and rejoices through this [state].
By this, the cause—both with form and without form, existing and non-existing, and so forth—is declared.

The remainder [of the verse] refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*): it is that which is devoid of the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), which arises unexpectedly without depending on the causes of conceptual construction, and which, being hidden from the difficult-to-perceive, is born as a self-experience accompanied by signs such as smoke;
this is what is connected to emptiness.

"Beginning," and so forth: the beginning is the support (*āśraya*), the end is the object (*ālambana*); liberated from these two, one relies solely on the middle (*madhyamātra*) and remains steady therein. Gradually, even that middle is abandoned; for him, the ten signs of light (*jyotis*) will arise.
"In this world," and so forth.
The realization of the intermediate state occurs only for those who possess the lineage (*gotra*) and are endowed with merit and wisdom through the great grace of the Guru;
and that [realization] is expressed by the term "the middle way.
For this realization of the lords of yogins is called the state of *nirvāṇa* for the conventional world of existence (*saṃvṛti-bhava*) in the *Vajragīti*, the *Caryā*, and other works.
He says that very thing: "O deluded ones," and so forth.
O deluded men, while you possess the desire for liberation, examine the characteristics of the intermediate lineage;
if you should ever come to know them, then this web of delusion will be destroyed.

If, at first, one perceives a cloth (*paṭa*) and so forth as an object of distraction— a ground of exertion that takes the three worlds as its support— and then purifies it through emptiness, then for one who investigates in this way, vision will gradually cease. For those who observe continuously in this manner,
[the mind] becomes clear, and so forth.
Let be; what is the use of much talk? Having half-opened your eyes at this moment of resting the vision, you shall know for yourself the authority of the Dharma—“O! and so forth.
O Bhusuku, behold the wonder arising in the midst of the sky!
The nature of emptiness is Bhusuku; it is a blossomed, incomparable flower, devoid of *ka* and *kha*. It is not perceived by *ga*, nor is it known through *ga*, *ma*, *ta*, *ka*, *kha*, or *na*.
Ka kha ga, all phenomena; ka kha ga, consciousness;
ka kha ga, Chinese and non-Chinese.
The connection between *ka* and *kha* is *ga*; there are nights, and since *ka* has no middle measure,
it abides in *kha*.

The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* on the *Kha-ga-antarāvagama*: "Take this flower of priceless value; this flower has various colors such as smoke, mirage, and so forth, and it blooms only in the empty forest of the sky. O Mother, the sky is in bloom! Alas, how profound is this groundless state, which arises from mere negligence!
"Citta," and so forth:
when the mind is in a state of non-mind (*acittatva*), the night of ignorance has not yet dawned;
therefore, Śāntipāda, having lit the lamp as a sign, reveals the path of vision and the rest.
Regarding the passage beginning with "u i maṃ" and so forth:
in the final watch of the night, Bhusuku says "the star has risen. There, at the end of the night of ignorance, the firefly is said to have risen in another context;
if the firefly has risen, Śānti declares that the final watch of the night remains—that is to say, it is nearly dawn.
Furthermore,
when the moon of the full moon of the signs and forms— such as the full moon of the month of Caitra (*caitra*) and so forth— has risen and the king of the mind has been purified,
then there is the wonder of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*).
"Karuṇā" (compassion) is so called because it obstructs "kaṃ" (pleasure);
the Lord Āryadeva, free from support, resounds like a hand-drum and shines forth.
"O Vāmā!

You two do not abide in the left [lalanā] nor in the right [rasanā]; O Kṛṣṇapāda, he says you are in the intermediate space, not by the path previously mentioned"—this is the jewel of awakening for experience and knowledge.
This self-awareness is profoundly deep;
for it is the wise man alone who is liberated,
while the fool is bound.
Having blossomed, the five signs are blue flowers right there in that very supportless state; the mind thus offered and dedicated yields great fruit—
so it is.
"What is this that has been done so wonderfully, that the two lamps of the moon and sun are blazing?
Thus Śānti laughed, being satisfied;
he himself is the witness in this matter.
Having seen that space is produced by causal conditions,
yet remaining satisfied merely by hearing the profound Dharma, such a person is deluded;
for in the darkness of night, he has not perceived any actual cause.
When smoke and the other signs arise at the summit of the sky, Śānti says that this alone is the supreme state; [otherwise] delusion persists until the end, and so forth.
Within the previously mentioned interval, if a skillful person simultaneously joins the mind, the vital breath, and the eyes, then [the signs] will necessarily arise.
The qualities of the Victorious One alone are the jewels;
this indeed is the secret of the Buddha's teaching throughout the ten directions and the three times—
this is "diverse."
If the mind were free from various conceptual constructions and the gaze were fixed within the space between the eyes, then the tenfold path beginning with smoke would clearly manifest.
If one's own mind (*ṇima*) were devoid of mental constructs and objective supports, accompanied by half-closed eyes, [the signs would appear].
When, for one practicing in this way, the wind enters the middle channel, then fire, smoke, and lightning arise; from such scriptural teachings, this pride should undoubtedly be cultivated. || 4 ||
"By this" refers to the universal image (*viśvabimba*) consisting of smoke and so forth; therefore, from the very beginning, the path for the yogi is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
As it has been said: "In the six-limbed [yoga], the path of smoke and so forth, the accomplishment of the image, the protection of the imperishable, and its attainment constitute the primary sign."
"Great passion," and so forth, refers to the middling [level of practice], which is the cultivation of the aggregates and so on through the bliss of the non-dual passion of wisdom and method.
As it has been said: "The attainment of the first bhūmi occurs through eighteen hundred moments of the supreme unchanging."
The five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) are the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) not previously seen; the attainment of worldly accomplishments is the "intermediate sign.
Thus, [emptiness] is "great" (*mahā*) and so forth because its nature is suchness (*tathatā*); emptiness is compassion (*karuṇā*) by virtue of being the immutable drop (*acyuta-bindu*).
Then, by virtue of the non-emission bliss consisting of wisdom and means, there is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the image of gnosis (*jñānabimba*). What is this? It is not "puṣpa" (flower).
It is *ga* for clarity (*prasāda*), *ka-kha* for power (*prabhāva*), and *ga-tta* for *ka-e*.
A: "There is no remainder"; Kha: "The remainder is Ka"; Pha:
"It is joined with Sa."
The *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, which consists of the syllables KA, YA, and GA, is said to be a limb of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

As it is stated: "Buddhahood is the wearing of the garment [of liberation] through twenty-one thousand six hundred supreme unchanging moments (*paramākṣara-kṣaṇa*); because of the attainment of the twelve stages (*bhūmi*), the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is the ultimate sign—this is non-perverted bliss."
Just as from the contact with what is unreal there is the pleasure of passing away, so it is because [the path] is free from outflows (*anāsrava*), like smoke.
Regarding "five," and so forth:
because the entire universe manifests as luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), it is said: "By which those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution are embraced through bliss."
"By means of the consecration of the Lords of Jinas in the tantra whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means"— thus,
other [statements] are "other words" because they constitute frivolous chatter (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
By this [phrase], "beginningless, endless, and middleless" is meant its state of being free from conceptual construction regarding beginning, end, and middle;
for this very reason it is said: "The supreme *Nāmasaṅgīti*, auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end. (Nāmasaṅgīti)
"By which," and so forth:
the meditation on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is a conceptual meditation for the purpose of bringing the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) to face one in the interim.
This was stated with reference to those for whom this constitutes the initial practice, as they have already attained the fruit; furthermore,
the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*) here is intended for those of superior capacity,
acting as the cause.
"Since it has been stated that there is no means of accomplishing reality other than this, the sprout arises from the rice seed alone; thus [the opponent] conceptualizes."
Just as from a mind of passion a mind of hatred arises non-conceptually,
so too does a mirage appear immediately after smoke.
"Like," and so forth:
from a cotton seed comes a cotton tree; from that, a cotton fruit arises in dependence upon its own cause. That is its birth. //5//
Bliss is bliss, emptiness is the white [element], and that is the means; thus,
for the sake of those to be trained, the universe appears in the form of non-duality.
"Real" (bhūta) means reality; by means of the yoga of non-abiding, one who stands at the limit of the locus of its experience [realizes] selflessness (nairātmya).
Immediately following the non-appearance of the source of phenomena and persons, the very image is the lion; when that is seen, the unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*) arises.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
[the mind] is unstable because it lacks a foundation due to being devoid of an object.
The term "proponents" refers only to the conceptual proliferations (prapañca) residing within the minds of others.
Regarding what was stated beginning with "mahā" and so forth: "The aggregate of the elements, the lord of immortality, is devoid of impurity by its innate nature."
The term "adhyāhṛtā" (brought forth) refers to the state of being one whose vital breaths have been restrained, by virtue of which there is the bliss of the Imperishable (acyuta-sukha),
just as it is.
Having experienced bliss and so forth, one "attains the elements"; the remainder is that the accomplishment of mind-velocity pertains to body, speech, and mind.
"Tathāgata" and "manojava" form a *karmadhāraya* compound;
"rāgādi" refers to the triad beginning with Ānanda,
while "avidyādi" refers to [the other triad].
Ka-ga arises from the touch of the elements;
ka-kha is the fruit of the cause,
O Viśvavineya.
This is the *Amṛtakanikodyotanibandha*, composed by Amṛtānanda. The formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to a previous state of affliction are the cause of previous karma.
Consciousness, however, consists of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking; from that point onward, it is name-and-form.

Prior to the arising of the six sense bases, there is contact resulting from the conjunction of the preceding three; this occurs prior to the capacity to discern the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Experience prior to sexual union belongs to one who is attached to the enjoyment and sexual union of craving.
But clinging (upādāna) is the acquisitions of enjoyments for those who run about [in pursuit of them].
That karma produces the fruit of future existence; that existence, in turn, consists of birth, old age, and death.
And by these factors—namely, through concealing, planting, leading, and grasping—[the cycle continues].
Because of filling, because of the threefold discernment, because of enjoyment, and because of drawing forth.
"Because of bondage, because of facing [objects], and because of suffering, the world is afflicted.

Thus, in the *Sahajodaya*, it is said that from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formative predispositions, up to the cessation of birth, from which comes the cessation of old age and death;
this is the "Vajra-jewel."
Through withdrawal (pratyāhāra), there is victory over conceptual construction by taking emptiness as the object;
through breath control (prāṇāyāma), there is victory over the vital winds within the six [centers], such as the uṣṇīṣa and others.
He is victorious by means of the four limbs consisting of service, near-attainment, and great attainment, as well as the six limbs beginning with withdrawal (pratyāhāra).

It is called a *gaṇa* because it is counted (*gaṇyate*) or enumerated; the master (*ācārya*), by means of the reversal [of the process], causes that drop (*bindu*)—which was obstructed at the tip of the cloth—to pervade it.

This is because he brings about the state of innate non-conceptuality even for those possessed of conceptual thought, and because he easily nourishes the five aggregates, elements, and sense-bases in the form of the Victors such as Vairocana.
Therefore it is said: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra, which is the passion of all Tathāgatas.

This is because the mantras (vidyās) of the Tathāgatas—such as Locanā and others who take the form of earth and the other elements—or the groups consisting of the eighty-four natures such as passion and so forth, are indeed the means (upāya) of the bodhicitta, and thus possess its lordship.

The term "tattad" (this and that) refers to the power consisting of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth, because by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), one manifests various forms for the sake of attracting those to be trained (*vineya*).
The power (*anubhāva*) of great bliss is that which causes the vital energies (*prāṇa*, etc. to dissolve into bliss; it is indeed the innate (*sahaja*) state, as it has been said:
"O Rāma, when the mind is motionless in the innate, what is not of a single flavor?"
"He is indeed established at that very moment, free from the distinction of old age and death.
Thus,
because of its supreme brilliance and clarity of self-awareness, it cannot be led away by ignorance, doubt, false knowledge, and the like.
The method consists of the perceptual path of smoke and so forth. || 8 ||
The *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*: "Discrimination regarding meaning" (*arthapratisaṃvid*) is so called because one causes others to attain the meaning through mere speech;
it is "discrimination regarding words" (*śabdapratisaṃvid*).
From the realization of the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*), there arises the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); thus,
the initial moisture becomes thoroughly condensed by the cloud, and that moisture remains undissolved within the form of water.
Even in the middle, there is no such variety as a rain-stone;

rather, that which consists of the naturally luminous nature shines forth as luminosity even between the two limits of beginning and end. Having thus perceived the three worlds as consisting of luminosity, and so forth, through the illumination of light and the restraint of the breath and speech, he is the Lord.
Because of the intuition that practices such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) alone are the cause of worldly prosperity, there is the analytical knowledge of intuition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*);
it is "infinite" because it awakens infinite sentient beings,
and it is "truthful speech" because it is based upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Because of the statement, "Illusion itself is the truth of the conventional," the purification of the illusory body is emptiness; since it is said that this alone is the cause, the ultimate truth,
and the means for realizing reality— and nothing else— he is a speaker of truth.

The fourfold coemergent consists of the coemergent body, speech, mind, and gnosis. Because it is non-conceptual and has the nature of the non-apprehension of all phenomena, it is inseparable from emptiness;
because it is the non-duality of bliss, it is inseparable from compassion. ||e||
Regarding the passage beginning with "four hundred," etc.:
because eighteen hundred breaths are ceased on each level, the eighth level is "Immovable" (*acalā*) in terms of being under the influence of afflictions;
however, by the power of compassion, they indeed continue to cycle through existence.
As it is said: "First I bow to you, the Awakened One; then to Great Compassion, by which alone you, knowing my faults, have long remained fixed upon me in saṃsāra. Thus, like a sword.
Just as a sword fallen from the hand of a hero flashes within the body,
so do Śakra and the other [deities] flash within each individual; because they have the nature of the drop of wisdom (*prajñā-bindu*), he is their leader.

"From which" refers to the apertures of the six cakras; when great bliss arises, the sufferings of conceptual construction and the afflictions perish. "Gone to them" means having entered into those [apertures] of the great elements known as earth, water, fire, and air.
Taking as its material cause the seed of the five great elements—the bodhicitta of great bliss—[the body] is born from the contact of the two organs. From this, the solid earth arises;
the fluidity of the bodhicitta is water;

from friction, fire is produced; from the hollow channels of space comes wind; and bliss is space. Through these five great elements, the complete manifestation of all beings, including gods and asuras, occurs.

O fool, know this to be empty, because from the seed—which is of the nature of space and bliss—the elements arise, and from them, embodied beings. For that which has no seed, how indeed could there be a sprout from reality? O clothed one, *bola* is the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and *kakkola* is the lotus (*padma*).
Their union is their meeting; from that contact, the earth element is born as the locus of solidity. Then, from the liquid form of the *bodhicitta*, the water element arises.
From the friction of the two organs, fire is produced. From movement, wind is said to arise.
With the five elements combined—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—the body comes into being. || 10 ||

The meaning is that the "enemies" are the afflictions (*kleśa*) which consist of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); they are so called because they "conceptualize," "defile," and "oppress" the mind.
Regarding the passage beginning with "bodhi," etc.:

That which cannot be expressed by way of examples and their correlates—that reality (tattva) which was generated through the application of the *bodhicitta* by the Teacher—its state (*bhāva*) is such that, because the Teacher’s purpose is fully accomplished, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is exhausted through the thorough knowledge of the nature of existence. [This results in] the light of the *Amṛtakaṇikā* commentary;
there is the bliss of the fourth state (*turyā*) beyond transmigration, and through the twofold vision of that which resembles the ocean of self-nature, the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) is ended.
He whose outflows of the view of a self-identity and so forth have been exhausted through the realization resulting from the fourth experience,
whether that refers to the Vajrī or to the world.
"Five," and so forth:
since it destroys the enemy of the afflictions, it is the *jalūṣā* [the water-born plant]; from where, for whom, and how could these vows to uplift the world be fulfilled without awakening (*bodhi*)?
That bodhicitta has been generated through practice by the Teacher, because the ordinary [nature] has been purified by means of luminosity; therefore,
attachment to sentient beings is indeed to be adopted.
When [the mind] remains pervading the space from the tip of the jewel up to the *uṣṇīṣa*, there is no overcoming [of the mind] because it does not function toward other objects;
by means of the yoga of the "two organs" (*dvindriya*), which is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), one attains accomplishment, according to the statement: "That is the imperishable."
"Five," and so forth;
by attaining untainted bliss, one becomes a recipient of happiness in the future and is "unfallen."

Like that of the śrāvakas and others, because there is no falling away from the fruit already attained, "innate" refers to the unserviceability of the body, which is the affliction of the body (kāyopaplava).
The affliction of the moon and other [planets] is the corruption of speech;
the unserviceability of the mind is the corruption of the mind.
By the phrase "dispassion and so forth," coldness and the like are included. || 11 ||
"Vidyā" means ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is its opposite. The third is practice; the fourth is immersion, which consists of respectful and uninterrupted cultivation.

As it has been said: "The wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) becomes a tenfold mind, and its very manifestation is the consecration (*seka*); immersion therein occurs when [the mind] is like the reflection in a mirror resembling a stainless moon."

"He is the glorious Guru in whom this fourth state—the bliss of Nirvāṇa, the unswerving, the innate (*sahaja*), and the imperishable (*akṣara*)—resides as the bound face, having entered the heart-bliss. Thus—(Kālacakra-tantra 5.11).

"In the object-consciousness (*grāhya-citte*), the entry of the subject-consciousness (*grāhaka-citta*) is 'immersion' (*majjana*); because it is untainted bliss (*anāsrava-sukha*), it is superior to worldly bliss; it has 'gone' (*gataḥ*) there, or rather, it does not return."

Regarding the welcome for one who has gone as far as he must go, it is said: "The non-Buddhist heretics have gone to a praiseworthy state; the trainees (śaikṣa) have a return once more; the adepts (aśaikṣa) have followed the path entirely; and the Sugata has gone in all three ways. Thus.
Because of the statement, "They are called the light of the aggregates and so forth," since they are characterized and perceived as the aggregates and so on,
[this] is superior to the three preceding joys.
"Self," and so forth,
refers to the abandonment of the view of a real body and other such views, in accordance with one's vow.
Having covered over the view of a self-identity and being free from desire for the source of all false views and for the enjoyments of existence,
when shall we [say],
"Happiness has been experienced by me"?
Subtle conceptualization, which persists even for one who has abandoned the grasped and the grasper, also does not arise through the fourth [dhyāna],
because it too is of the nature of conceptualization.

According to the maxim, "Is a golden chain not a chain?", since it is said that "only illusion is the truth of the conventional," this very form is the nature of that which is its own substratum, like an illusion.

As it is stated in the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*: "Illusion (*moha*) is the concealment of one's own nature; it is called 'conventional' (*saṃvṛti*). That which is artificial is what it reveals as 'truth'."
The Sage declared that "that which is produced as an entity is conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Therefore, because there is nothing beyond it, and because it is the ultimate object due to its initial correspondence with reality, it is the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*), which is luminous. As he said: "Just as the imagined darkness, appearing in the form of hair and so forth, is false when compared to light," so too [is the conventional].
"Understand that here too, that very nature by which one of pure vision perceives is reality (tattva). Thus,
the "method" (naya) is that by which the universal image of the elements (dhātuka-viśvabimba) is led— that is, attained— to Buddhahood.
"That" refers to the two truths; one who perceives them is, by the very fact of perceiving the truths, the restrainer of the wheel of breath. || 12 ||

The essence (*sāra*) is so called because it is the cause of the knowledge of yogins; the distinguished flavor (*rasa*) is the cessation of emission (*virama*), which is the limit of the peak (*koṭiparyanta*); and the gift (*dāna*) is the bestowing of the knowledge of consecration (*sekajñāna*) upon others through teaching.
The bliss of nirvāṇa arises from the equality of all phenomena; it is like a firm ground,
and for that very reason it becomes a secure and wholesome state,
being absolute liberation because it is free from all obscurations.
The reality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-tattva*) is that very form; the body is the *dharmakāya*, and that which is perfected from it is the *sahajakāya*.
The universal image is one's own mind as a reflection, as it is said: "The stainless, powerful nature is manifest when one delights in looking at the illusion."
"Having attained the taste of the equality of flavors, the Lord of Yoga sports in bliss.

Thus, because it is the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*), passion, hatred, and delusion are said to arise from conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*); for they indeed come into being in dependence upon the inversion of the beautiful and the ugly.

"Those things which arise dependently from the distortions of the beautiful and the ugly—do those entities truly exist? Therefore, the afflictions do not exist in reality. Since this has been stated, [the commentary begins with] "therefore," and so forth.

Because even the conceptualization of emptiness is flawed, as it has been said: "The dull-witted person who meditates on emptiness as 'non-arising,' 'empty,' 'objectless,' or 'without support' does not truly meditate upon it; rather, he causes its destruction. [Emptiness] is characterized by the severance of the continuity of conceptualizations of the beautiful and the ugly.
Emptiness has been taught as the nature of cognition; emptiness is not considered to be anything other than that. Thus [ends verse 13].
"In the void conjoined with the form of the syllable *evaṃ*, [and] in the *ekāra* which is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), because of the entry into the garment of the mind"— thus,
regarding the words "phenomena" (*dharma*) and so forth,
since the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are included within the Mahāyāna.

And it has been said: "The vehicle arising from the Mahāyāna is also called the second [vehicle], for the sake of providing rest to those exhausted by the path of existence, but not in reality. Thus ends the *Amṛtakaṇikodyota* commentary, which is the foundation of all because it summarizes the meaning of both vehicles, and is the grandfather and mother because it gives birth to all dharmas without exception.

That very [reality] has been described by another [author] as "she" (sā) because of its feminine gender, and as "he" (sa) because of its masculine gender; the "dot" (bindu) is "yoga" because it consists of the most wonderful and terrifying nature.
He states another formulation: "The lotus (padma) because of its quality of gladdening, but the thunderbolt (vajra) because of its quality of piercing and non-piercing."
That seed is its outflow;
the three yogas are body, speech, and mind; and the nāda resides in the secret place of wisdom.
The syllable *vaṃ* is the Lord of Delight (*suratādhipa*), because it is the field for the arising of ineffable gnosis;
it is the unstruck (*anāhata*), because it is not touched by conceptual construction.
The "syllables" (akṣara) are the cognitions of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).

According to the stated sequence, that which is the symbolic seal (*mudrā-saṃketa*) of the seeds possessing the nature of the two syllables—being of the nature of the entire range of speech, both vowels (*ali*) and consonants (*kāli*)—is the knower of reality (*tattvajña*); this is the stage of the path (*mārgāvasthā*).
"The Turner of the Wheel of Dharma" refers to the state of fruition;
the vision of the sky is the *dharmadhātu*, and the *vaṃ* is the array of the Sugatas; situated therein is the universal reflection (*viśvabimba*).
And so forth are the synonyms for the syllable *e*;
*vaṃ* and so forth are the synonyms for the syllable *vaṃ*;
and *evaṃ* and so forth [are the synonyms for the syllable *e*].
The syllable *Evaṃ*, which is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) embodied as emptiness and compassion—
by that lord of yogins who has realized it, even the fact that the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, have that very nature as their essence is realized;
for that same Great Seal is the form of the casket of the Dharma.
For the phenomena (dharmas) are indeed the Dharmakāya and so forth; their casket (karaṇḍaka) is the support (ādhāra).
That very thing is the address, the attire, and the supreme ornament of one's own Lord Vajradhara;
it is the Dharmadhātu, the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna).
"Emptiness is not other than phenomena, nor do phenomena exist without it"— thus, because there is no difference,
it is called "the innate."
The "Outcaste of Gnosis" (Jñānacaṇḍāla) speaks by means of the flame regarding the cause for the designation "jewel": "By nature, the jewel is luminous; it consists of rays of bliss within [itself].
Because it is superior to the light of the sun and so forth, which is devoid of bliss, it is 'supreme' (para).
Regarding the word *dharma*... and so on.
Through the mastery of tasting the essence of the innate drop (*sahaja-bindu*) by means of the mouth of the *vastra*, it is said:
"By this, one always possesses celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the fire of the *vajra*. This is the meaning.

By teaching the path seen by oneself and through the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one gladdens and delights the worlds by generating great bliss (*mahāsukha*). One is the instructor of the vision of the universal image (*viśvabimba*) within the emptiness of one's own empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). || 14 ||

By means of the Gaganagañja-samādhi, which has realized the reality of emptiness, one possesses the capacity for various visions; through mastery over all phenomena, whatever cultivation has been performed by the intellect and the vajra-body, by practicing therein, even the conceptual constructions of the grasped object and so forth are made to enter into the innate (*sahaja*).
As it is said: "Whatever manifests in the mind, O Lord, that very thing is the true nature."
The waves are one thing and the water another; yet the world is like this. Thus it is said:

"Wherever the mind goes, the object of knowledge follows by moving right there; where else could it go? For that which is equal to space is the supreme of all things. One should apply [this teaching] in this way.
"Consisting of that.

Thus ends the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*. By [reciting] "abhī" and so forth, one neutralizes poison; therefore, there is not even the slightest suspicion of any obstacle arising from eating [the poisoned food].
Regarding the passage beginning with "prabhā" and so forth:
because the heart of reality (*vastu-hṛdaya*) is not a property of a [conditioned] entity, it is neither born nor does it die; it is neither afflicted nor does it decay.
This is because it is stated that the element (*dhātu*), the lineage (*gotra*), and the nature (*prakṛti*) of the mind are luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
