Regarding the passage beginning with "kāya," because the three bodies (trikāya) manifest from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) itself, it is imperishable (*avyaya*) since no emission is possible in the arising of the innate (*sahaja*).
Independent of anything else, the object of the yogi becomes self-existent; because it is uncreated, it is "innate" (*sahaja*).
As it has been said: "For intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is uncreated and independent of anything else. By this [and so forth]...

As for what was stated—that "the arising of the non-conceptual from the conceptual occurs because one stands on a path that is not the reality; therefore, one should strive for that reality"—there is no contradiction, for [the statement] "the arisen-order" refers to the superior [practitioner] with respect to the cultivation accompanied by the generation-order (*utpattikrama*). || 15 ||

→ Passion is like great compassion; that which is colored by it is the non-conceptual mind devoid of [ordinary] thought. By means of that, there is the merit of experiencing the bliss of entering the limbs of meditative absorption (*samādhi-aṅga*).
The phrase "not through dispassion" and so forth is clear.
It is because of the state of one who possesses the knowledge of bliss—which is the *mahāmudrā* acting as the means—that [this occurs].

Thus, it is indicated that one who has reached the tenth stage necessarily falls away, just as someone might fall from the peak of the king of mountains even against their will... or like a bird whose wings have not yet grown, or whose wings have been clipped; even if it does not wish to fall midway, it nevertheless falls.

Thus, one who has received instruction from a guru—even if liberation is not yet desired—is indeed fit for liberation because of having firmly grasped the bodhicitta, which is the cause of liberation.
As it is said elsewhere: "In this very life, he attains and reaches nirvāṇa in reality; effortlessly and inevitably, [he does so] in a future birth, like [the ripening of] karma."

The knowledge of the twelve stages is the accumulation of wisdom; the vajraparyaṅka posture is the mind as the accumulation of wisdom, according to the statement: "Beholding the mind within the jewel while in the vastraparyaṅka posture."

Precisely because of the knowledge of bliss that is unobservable within the jewel, there is the radiation of infinite cognitions such as those of a mirror; he says "all," etc., because of the radiation of infinite emanations according to the needs of those to be trained (*vineya*). He is mindful because his hands, feet, eyes, heads, faces, and so forth are everywhere, due to his constant observation of all sentient beings.
Because he abides in the pervasive knowledge that does not turn away from all objects of knowledge,
he is "Great" (mahat) by virtue of the sixteen digits beginning with the bliss of the body (kāyānanda), and so forth, such as Caṇḍa.
The meaning is: by means of conceptual knowledge born from the yoga of *dhāraṇā* and *anusmṛti*.

Because the manifestation [of phenomena] exists as being like an illusion (*māyopama*)—that is, because the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are dependent upon one's own self-mastery (*svādhiṣṭhāna*)—he is "possessed of perception" (*saṃjñī*), meaning he possesses knowledge;
he is a knower of both existence and non-existence because he does not perceive what is false or delusive.
He states the fruit arising from the aforementioned accumulations of merit and wisdom: "All," and so forth.
It is "eternal" (*śāśvata*) because its primordial nature is unchanging, like space;
it is the "dyeing" (*rañjana*) of the channels (*nāḍī*)—which are the forms of wisdom (*prajñā*)—by means of the *bodhicitta* as the method (*upāya*).

Because of the unification of the body and so forth with emptiness, as it is said in the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*: "If I were to perceive anything by means of objects such as direct perception, I might either initiate or cease [action]; since that does not exist, I am beyond reproach."

Dhyāna is of the nature of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); it is the third consecration (*seka*), and the jewel is the fourth. The Victors' gnoses, such as the mirror-like and others, reside in the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Their body is like that of a maiden; just as the bliss of sexual union (*suratasukha*) cannot exist without the seminal drop (*bindu*), so too [the gnosis] cannot exist without [the practice].

Thus, it is clear that such statements as "to be known through one's own experience" and so forth are causes for the delusion of the wind of conceptual construction; as it has been said: "for those whose minds are distracted by various afflictions regarding sense objects."

Due to the force of that [experience], even in deep sleep, there is a turbulent poison of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Because it is of the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is "supreme" (*parama*); and because it is beginningless (*anādi*), it is "original" (*ādya*)—this being due to the elision of the letter 'a'. Through purification by means of the innate (*sahaja*), it becomes the stainless body (*anāsrava-kāya*) and so forth. (17) Even though it is the cause of the states such as waking and the rest, in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), there is worthiness of acceptance (*upādeyatā*) because of the awakening through innate purification; for it is said: "Because of delight. In the union of the *kakkola* (the male organ) and the *padma* (the female organ), the latent impression of hardness arises from the sensation of firmness.
Emptiness itself becomes an entity when it is perfumed by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
just as water becomes like stones through the firm formation of whirlpools; this occurs due to its connection with that which is illuminating.
Its own nature is immovability,
and Akṣobhya is the purification of hatred because of its quality of being undisturbed.

Based on the reading *ira gatāv*, "sukha" refers to the bliss of sexual union (*suratānanda*); that very [bliss] is "rāga" because it is characterized by attachment (*āsaṅga*), and it is "rakta" because it delights the world.
And that form of space, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), is Ratneśa, the Piśuna;

by the passage beginning with "Atharva," he teaches the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*): "The moon possesses the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); possessing equality (*samatā*) along with the seven seed-syllables, it is the sign of one's own deity; it is called 'discernment' (*pratyavekṣaṇa*)," because it is said to be "pure reality" (*śuddhadharmatā*).
Ratnasambhava is so called because his manifestation arises from the sun and the jewel;
"maṇi padme hūṃ" is the mantra;
"dhātu" means that which consists of the five wisdoms.
Specifically, because he is one whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*) after the age of sixteen,

through the vision of the causal signs within the Universal Image (*viśvabimba*), he attains stability and freedom from obscuration; likewise, due to being sealed by the five Buddhas, he possesses a nature comparable to *māyā*.
Likewise,
because all mental activities, when realized as luminous, are of the nature of bliss and arise as untainted (*anāsrava*),
the diamond-jewel itself is the gem; within it is the mass of blissful consciousness.
The Buddha is his own mind; because it is the basis for innate love,
he is born from that— this is the meaning of "from himself."
For it is stated right here: "O Vajra-peak, the excellent lotus is in full bloom; that very thing is Śrī, because it is the locus of non-dual gnosis.

And because of such statements as, "The seed of those who have faith in the Supreme Vehicle is the Mother, Prajñā, for the birth of the Buddha-qualities," the Innate (*sahaja*) is contained within that. 19. "All conceptualization," and so forth.

Faith (*śraddhā*) is the conviction regarding what is possible, the conviction that it can be divided [and yet remains] indivisible; when there is something virtuous, it is clarity; and when there is something possible, it is aspiration. Thus, it is threefold. "Immediately" means at that very moment (*tatkṣaṇam*).
Just as the Son of the Conqueror remains here in the position of a mother and father through his intention for their welfare, maturing the entire world,
so too no ordinary person is considered as affectionate toward themselves as they are toward another person who is deeply beloved and dependent upon them.

"Just as one whose nature is compassion is considered affectionate toward other beings because of his application [of them] to welfare and happiness" (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 8.14–15). Regarding the phrase "that and so forth," the *Amṛtakaṇikodyota* commentary explains that "beginning with night" refers up to "darkness," and "beginning with ignorance" refers up to the end; thus, the six causes are those previously mentioned. This is seen in the explanation of the passage beginning with "one whose self is purified by the ten cognitions" (Nāmasaṃgīti 6.3).

Regarding this, it is said: "Having realized the non-existence of all things and having meditated upon their equality, one should make the mind supportless and free from mental activity, and not think of anything at all. (20–21) The ultimate moon is the luminous clarity; because it acts as the guide for the great mass of sentient beings, it is the "Great Benefactor" (Mahārthakṛt).
It has gone [to its destination].
Having gone by that path which is the *ūrṇā*,
he was led away like an opposing army from the perception of existence.
In that which is beyond description, free from appearances, and non-conceptual,
earth is established in water, water in air, and air in space.

Space is non-abiding within the elements of wind, water, fire, and earth. Through the cultivation of emptiness, one's own being (*ātmabhāva*) becomes the very nature of space; because it is of the nature of bliss, time is the means (*upāya*), which consists of the gnosis of imperishable bliss and has compassion as its essence.
"The wheel of the world has the form of the knowable, while glorious wisdom has emptiness as its essence" (Vimalaprabhā 1.11).
[This occurs] "in the form of innate bliss";
thus, blue is bliss, yellow is bliss, and all that is moving and unmoving is bliss.
"Bliss is existence, the absence of bliss is non-existence; the being that transcends these is supreme bliss"—
thus [it is] the one whose form is the universe, by virtue of having innate nature as its essence.

"One should indeed worship these deities—whether made of wood, stone, or clay—as the very self, as all-buddhahood, and as the solar power (*sauritva*). Even in such passages, this is the intended meaning:
the *mudrā* is the *adhyātma-dharma-mudrā*; by cultivating that through its service, one becomes one who cannot be overcome by the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As it is said: "This host of thieves that is the affliction seeks an opening; having found an opening, it devours and destroys one's companionship and life.
Regarding the word *ṛṣi*: from the root *ṛṣ* meaning "to go," the suffix *ik* is applied according to the rule *kṛṣyādibhyaḥ*.
Through the realization of the ultimate truth, the seer becomes great by attaining the supreme imperishable. || 23 ||
"Body," and so forth,
refers to the cessation of the conceptualization of the drops (*bindu*) and the vital winds (*prāṇa*);
for this very reason, "worldly," and so forth.
The Great Assembly (*mahāsamaya*) is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); through union with that, there is the bliss of luminosity (*prabhāsvara-sukha*).

The mantras are "jewels" (*ratna*) because they are difficult to produce, because they are stainless, and because of their power. Since they have become ornaments for the world, are invisible, and are changeless—just as it is said, "like jewels"—the bodies beginning with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which are the fruit, are without beginning or end.
"The prior limit is not known," so said the Great Sage;
for saṃsāra is indeed without beginning or end, having neither a first nor a last.
"Since it has neither beginning nor end, how could there be a middle?
Therefore, in this regard, the sequences of prior, posterior, and simultaneous do not apply.
Having realized this for the purpose of teaching the Dharma...
"By the three vehicles," and so forth;
it reveals that which is superior to the three vehicles consisting of bliss and the rest.
"Kha-vajra," and so forth.
That which is the element of the void (khadhātu) is a white and red drop; in its center is the meditation on the mandala-circle through subtle yoga.
The Vajrī, possessing the vajras of body, speech, and mind, should remain with the pride of "I am that," like a painting fixed upon a wall-less surface. || 24 ||
"The prior limit is not known," so said the Great Sage.
This *Amṛtakaṇikodyota* commentary is unfailing and fruitful,
for it tastes the suchness (*tathatā*) by means of the bliss of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), thereby gathering in sentient beings.

This very six-limbed object is the firm essence; it is characterized by being unbreakable and indivisible, non-combustible, and indestructible. This emptiness is called "vajra. By means of the meditative absorption (samādhi) resembling that [vajra], there is the cessation of the winds.

By the very *vastrōpama-samādhi* (garment-like samādhi), there is the binding of the mind— that is, the binding of the entire web of conceptual constructions along with their latent tendencies— through the seizing [of the vital essence] by means of the bound *prāṇa*-wind.
Because that [semen] is the seed of awakening (*bodhibīja*), when it is drunk as the imperishable nectar through the adamantine bliss (*vajrasukha*), all the samādhis of bliss arise.
As it is said in the *Saṃvaratantra*: "Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is likewise the mouth.

By means of that which is named Vāsuki—the channel (*śaṅkhinī*) synonymous with the aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*)—the bodhicitta is drawn up from the lower central cavity, reaches the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and through the opening of the *lalanā* by the expansion of the channels, there is the gratification of the aggregates and so forth. || 25 ||

Regarding "the single channel of the heart," since the others will be explained later, it is called "innate bliss" (*sahajānanda*) because of the distinction of the *bodhicitta* to be contained within that form.

By the phrase "through the purity of the lunar steps" (*candrapadaviśuddhayā*), although there is a deficiency of one quarter (*pāda*) here due to a difference in the basis (*ādhāra*), there is an excess of one quarter in the subsequent [section]; thus, no distinction exists in the total number, and their mutual relationship is indicated. *Suviśuddham* (perfectly pure).

Regarding the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), he says: "This wind of the *bhairava* [state], having contracted the mouth of the *rākṣasa*, emits a brilliant light; through that bliss, there is the cessation of conceptual construction.
The distinguished flavor (*viśiṣṭa-rasa*) is the *virama*, and immediately following that is the innate bliss (*sahaja-sukha*). These are synonyms for the 'gate' and the 'means' (*upāya*)."
One does not fear conceptual constructions that are the cause of suffering. || 25 ||
"He terrifies by means of emptiness" refers to the aggregates and so forth; it is precisely through the non-apprehension of these that the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) arise.
By means of its nature as great bliss (*mahāsukha*), having rendered it luminous (*prabhāsvarīkṛtya*), [it is said] "great" (*maha*) and so forth;
for indeed, the great essence (*mahārasa*) is situated even in a single part of the body.
"One should pierce the body, which is satisfied by the fire of desire, on all sides"—this is the intended meaning.

By the power of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) derived from the guru’s instruction, she "bites" (*daṣṭā*) all phenomena; thus, the blazing Caṇḍālī at the navel burns the five Tathāgatas, according to such statements. Because she has ascended upwards and is elevated, she is "terrible" (*karāla*), meaning jagged or formidable.
For this very reason, [the passage] beginning with "What? and ending with "space" refers to the state of having a stable mind within the void.
"By that" refers to the binding of the vital breath;
"a hundred" is an indication for [any number] up to a thousand. || 1 ||
Because it renders that which is called "the Ender" (Antaka) free from appearance,
it is the "yoke-mate" (yuganaddha).
Because it obstructs the attainment of the desired goal for sentient beings by means of the specific state of non-dual bliss, it is an obstacle.

The flow of one's own mind consists of the nets of conceptual construction; by their destruction—that is, by their cessation—one enters the luminosity and shines as the Vajra, because its power is unimpeded.
Its "velocity" is the speed of thought, because it has been brought face-to-face with great bliss.
"Nau" refers to the drop (*bindu*) situated in the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*),
and "HŪṂ" refers to the syllable HŪṂ situated in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*);
when these two are joined, by means of the elimination of even subtle conceptual constructions, it is the "giver of fearlessness."
And the union occurs through the central aperture with the "immediate" [bliss],
which is the great bliss of the oneness of *nāda* and *bindu*.

From the realization of the identity of compassion in the form of apprehension and emptiness, there resounds the great sound (*mahāśabda*), which is the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and consists of unextracted resonance (*anāhṛtadhvani*).
Alternatively, because his speech is like a thunderbolt (*vajra*) due to this resounding,
or because his mind— which has been made into the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)— is an indivisible thunderbolt, he is the "Heart-Vajra" (*hṛdvajra*).
The entire triple world is indeed the mind alone; because it is a mere mental transformation, it is like an illusion.
That which has emptiness-knowledge as its armor is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), for through emptiness it pervades all phenomena.
Its belly is vast, stainless, and resembles the infinite sky, consisting of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). || 2 ||
Regarding "the two apertures":

through the practice of Kaulamukhī at the right ear-aperture of Oḍiyāna, there is bliss; for the sake of the garment (*vastra*), the crown-cakra called Jālandhara is the *kuliśa*, and the aperture is the *kuliśa* because of being the lord (*īśvara*) therein—thus [it is said] "for the garment," and so forth.
The Tathāgatas are united with the innate (*sahaja*), and Mañjuśrī is of that same nature;
thus, by means of innate bliss, he is experienced by the intellect as non-dual. Therefore, he is indivisible, the illumination of the drops of nectar, the essence, and the very heart of them.
Because it is all-pervasive, empty, and unobstructed, it is like space (*nabhas*);
according to etymological derivation, the syllable *sa-* is elided, or alternatively, it is called *nabhi* because it does not come into being (*na bhavati*).
*Acala*: It is called *acala* because it moves together with the innate (*sahaja*), or because it is immovable by opposing factors (*vipakṣa*).
"All," and so forth.

When all the drops (*bindu*) residing in every channel have become unified in a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhūta*) within the *avadhūtī* at the crown of the head—the *uṣṇīṣa* being Mañjuśrī—it is for this reason that the majesty (*āṭopa*) is said to be like that of the goddess Ekajaṭā. Through the perception of true reality (*tathatā*), by means of the experience of sublime bliss and the immutable bodhicitta, there is a pervasion as far as the pores of the skin; thus, she wears a white elephant hide. In this way, she bears the cloth (*paṭa*)—the great bliss, the supple bodhicitta—as if it were a garment. Or, Mañjuśrī is in the form of the illustrious Saṃvara. (3)
"Hā hā" is an imitation of the sound of laughter;
it is "mahāghora" (extremely terrible) because its purpose is to transcend the [ordinary] understanding of what is terrible.
The sound "HOH" is that which terrifies all Māras;
it is the door for entering the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), namely the *vañca* aperture.

The application there is by means of the wrathful gaze, which is called "terrifying" because it produces fear in the ignorant. Through the letter *ha* joined with the eight long vowels beginning with *ā*, there arises laughter and loud, boisterous laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*).

He whose great laughter is the exultation of the mind, a smile of dwelling in happiness in this very life due to the absence of any adversary; he whose great roar, like a thunderbolt, awakens the three worlds through the sound of teaching great bliss. || 4 ||
He whose being (*sattva*) is like a diamond (*vajra*), indestructible, is Vajrasattva;

he is Mahāsattva because, through the power of the constituent of retention (*dhāraṇāṅga*), he consists of the drops (*bindu*) of gnosis that proceed without interruption, beginning with "Awakening" (*bodhi*).
The meaning is that he shines by the radiance of the rays of bodhicitta within the peak of the vajramaṇi;
for this very reason, he is "Great Bliss" (mahāsukha) because his bliss flows effortlessly and is unsurpassed.
Having attained through the application of momentum a non-abiding nirvana whose nature is bliss,
he is characterized by a single inclination toward emptiness regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth.
Regarding "clothing and so forth":
because the wind and mind are ceased, the bodhicitta—which has been ceased by means of the syllable *hūṃ*—enters through its manifestation; thus, it takes the form of the syllable *hūṃ*. (5)

Through the sequence of movement through the four—the right ear, the crest-lock, the head, and the thumb—there is the nature of the four joys and the four meditative absorptions. Having caused [the breath] to enter the *avadhūtī* at the tip of the nose, it is restrained; thus the *avadhūtī* is the "garment" because of its indestructibility, and it is the weapon in the form of an arrow because of its severing of the flow of the breath.

Because it cuts through the afflictions (*kleśa*), gnosis (*jñāna*) is like a sword; and because it enters into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), it is said to be the basis of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
For this very reason...

For knowledge (*jñāna*) is indeed the antidote to ignorance (*avidyā*), and the afflictions (*kleśa*), together with their latent impressions (*savāsanā*), arise from ignorance; therefore, it also cuts away those latent impressions— this is what is meant by "the five," and so forth.

The wind possesses all various colors because it has the colors of the five Tathāgatas; and because it is unbreakable, it is called "vajra. As stated in the *Vajranāpa* with the words beginning "five," when the wind is stabilized, through the practice of successive stages, there arises the capacity for the arising of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the others; once they have arisen, the wind itself becomes their very nature. This breath, situated above, upon the union of the two organs, melts in the fire of great passion (*mahārāga*), exits through the path of the vajra, and falls in the form of a drop (*bindu*) at the tip of the lotus-nose of the Wisdom consort, even upon the earth, possessing the nature of the five elements.

When a practitioner of the generation stage (utpattikrama) meditates on the mandala circle and the subtle yoga, that very [practice] is the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) consisting of exhalation through the left nostril according to the sequence of the four mandalas;
this is its etymological derivation.
2. Face; 3. There is no [lack of] knowledge; 4. It is called the Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti.
It possesses the nature of the five mantras because its essence consists of the five rays of light beginning with Vairocana.
It is the "Great Jewel" because, when the wind becomes stable, it fulfills desired aims like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).

It is called *prāṇa* because it breathes and vitalizes; it is called *āyāma* because the mind is restrained and bound from all sides through the radiation of whichever specific primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is appropriate. Thus, *prāṇāyāma* is the wind.
8. As it has been said: "Wherever the wind is situated, it carries that very nature.

To stabilize that very breath (śvāsa) in the heart, one should meditate upon one's own mantra as the essence of samādhi, and then contemplate the mind (citta) of that [mantra] as consisting of the *nāda* above the *bindu*. [One should likewise contemplate it] at the tip of the nose, in the opening of the olfactory faculty.
Regarding the term *sarṣapī*:
"mustard" refers to the wind (*vāyu*), because it possesses a subtle similarity to a mustard seed.
He says "and that," and so forth, meaning that the winds themselves, consisting of the light rays of the colors of the five Tathāgatas, are what move.
12. On the left, they have the forms of Akṣobhya and the others in the sequence beginning with space;
on the right, they have the forms of Locanā and the others in the sequence beginning with earth.
13. By the word "and so forth," [it includes] fireflies and the like.
Due to the absence of objective entities, it is mere appearance;
due to its imperishability, it is indivisible.
14. Non-dual gnosis, born from the union of wisdom and means, is a single, unified state like a vajra.
Regarding "the pleasure of conceptual construction":
because it generates emission, it is a cause for existence (*bhava*).
As it has been said: "What difference is there between a conceptual construction that is pure or even impure?"
17. Even when being touched, this [fire] burns; even when ignited, it burns in the sandalwood.
18. There is no difference in fire with respect to its capacity to burn, even due to a difference in its fuel. 19. [End of verse]
Thus [ends the section]. 20. 21. (Ārya-mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa 6–7) 22. "Jñāna" and so forth.

By the radiance of gnosis arising from the center of the *vajra* and *maṇi*, there occurs (23) the experience of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). From that, (24) the eye of flesh and so forth becomes formidable, elevated, and distinguished from others.
And for yogins, the head—(25) like the flame of a *vajra*—ascends; thus, the *vajra* of the bodhicitta enters the *kaba*.
He says this very thing with the words beginning with "great" (*maha*) and so forth.

Through the cessation of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths and by the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Guru, there arises an immersion into gnosis (*jñānāveśa*), such as the knowledge of others' minds and so forth; there occurs the trembling of the body and the recitation of mantras by the voice.
And this [state] at the time of initiation is Mañjuśrī himself in the form of gnosis;
thus he says, "The three realms," and so forth.
Because it pervades everything through innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), it is the "Great Penetration" (*mahāveśa*).

Since it is said that "the teaching of the nectar of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is for the sake of abandoning all views," during the fourth arising, the cognitions of bliss proceed uninterruptedly like a stream for one who is inclined toward emptiness; "one hundred" is used as an illustration. Through the attainment of the five eyes, he possesses unimpeded vision in the direct perception of the entire universe.

31. Those channels (*nāḍī*) located within the body that carry semen (*śukra*) and are connected to three and a half million hairs—their "sprout" (32) is the manifestation of its own nature. That itself is his "body," because from the non-conceptual knowledge (*anābhoga-jñāna*), he is the Lord (*nātha*), since [the channels] are exactly seventy-two thousand. 33. Carrying semen, they are like the garments of gnosis (*jñāna-vastra*), emerging continuously like hairs;
they alone are the one supreme possessor of great bliss (*mahāsukhita*). 34. He whose physical form (*vigraha*) is such is described as "one who has such a body."
Because the innate (*sahaja*) is mere gnosis, its body is like space.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In the mouth" (verse 35):

for one who has performed prior service, through union with a woman in her menses, and who possesses the complete collection of conditions, only a meritorious person may thus possess this Gnosis-Body (*jñānakāya*).
36. Regarding "vajrasāra" and so forth:
that channel marked with the vajra is the one through which the movement and return of the *bodhicitta* occur via the apertures of the male organ of the deity.
37. When it undergoes a transformation, the *bodhicitta* suddenly issues forth, devoid of pleasure.
38. Generally,
those which have other natures are of that very nature.
Mukha | syā | 39. 40. The treatise *Amṛtakaṇikodyota* [states]: 41. 42. "The dissolution and enjoyment occur by means of *vikrama*."

The bodhicitta, having dissolved from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), has its domain in Pullīra; in Jālandhara there is enjoyment (*bhoga*); and in Oḍḍiyāna there is dissolution (*laya*). Through this sequence, it circulates through the twenty-four locations beginning with the head and the crest-lock (*śikhā*). By means of these three [stages], there is a garland of the drops (*bindu*) residing in those respective locations.
Because of the awakening to the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaita*) nature of those drops, one is a knower of duality.
"Vajra" refers to unchanging bliss and semen; by that, there is a complete filling and nourishment, and thus one is made capable, adorned, and perfected.
46. Regarding "divya": it is that wherein there is the manifestation (*vikāśa*) of the sound *hā hā*, which is the bliss of Mahāmudrā.
Regarding "nir" and so forth: [it refers to] the state of being free from conceptual elaboration.
47. This means the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*). Regarding "the sky" (*viyat*) and so forth:

the celestial Gaṅgā is the *avadhūtī*; in what kind of opening is she? It is situated in the middle of the tongue and the woman (*lalanā*). 48. [She is] situated in the center of the tongue and the woman.

By the command of the Guru, through the union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds, when the entry of the breath into the central channel (*madhyā*) has been accomplished in the yoga of wisdom and means, at the tip of the jewel, the yogis—who take delight in the experience of non-conceptual bliss through the state of the mind being "no-mind" (*acittatā*)—experience within the center a certain ineffable sound by virtue of immutable bliss. That [sound] is victorious;
it is exalted. That Victor, the *saṃbhogakāya*, triumphs, in whom the world attains identity.

[a] It has proceeded from beginningless time; therefore, because it cannot be perceived as distinct, [it is like] at dawn (52) when the left and right channels are blocked, that which possesses a splendor connected to the twilight, being mixed with the rays of the sun and moon within the *avadhūtī*.

53. It is said: 54. When the disks of the moon and sun have been swallowed in the sky, there is neither day nor night at any time; 55. that twilight exists for yogins at all times within the center of the body, having reached the state of immortality (*amṛtapada*).

56. Just as the moon, its phases exhausted, moves with equal flavor into the solar orb while remaining in the sky; 57. so too, at the time of attainment, when the prāṇa and apāna have ceased, that [state] is clearly obstructed within the body.
Thus:

When the breath flows through the left and right channels and the mind is placed upon the ashes at the tip of the middle channel, the state of nectar within the forehead becomes the *saṃdhyā*. 60. It comes to be so.

Just as the moon, having waned during the dark fortnight, becomes merged into the sun in the sky, so too that *rodha* (obstruction) is clearly experienced at the time of accomplishment (*siddhi*) when the *prāṇa* and *apāna* have become motionless. Furthermore, while the mind is luminous, there is the one, non-dual *nāda*—the essence of gnosis with an imperishable body—which consists of the bliss of sporting in a state of aesthetic flavor (*samarasa*) together with the "Beloved" known as *Mahāmudrā*, whose form is the reflection of the entire universe; this very *nāda* is the *saṃbhogakāya* here, because its nature is speech.

Because even though the vowels beginning with *a* and the consonants beginning with *ka* dissolve back into the *saṃbhogakāya*, the body of that *saṃbhoga* is adorned with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) produced from them; and because it consists of the *āli* (vowels) and *kāli* (consonants), its radiances—the twelvefold scriptural teachings—radiate for the sake of sentient beings. Having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings, they withdraw and enter into the *dharmatā*. Its fruit, characterized by the upward [extension] from the *vairambha* wind below the netherworld (*pātāla*), is such that...
The Lord of the enjoyment ground (*saṃbhogabhūmi*) is the Dharmakāya, which consists of the collection of non-dual mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) of the Great Bliss Sound (*mahāsukhanāda*).
He alone is like a pillar (*stambha*) because of his stability.
Born from that is the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga*), the Vajra-holder (*vajrī*), whose sound is like the unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*) of a divine drum.
By the words "body and so forth," etc.:

having pervaded the intrinsic nature of the eyes and so forth with the bliss-sound (sukhanāda), the vajra—meaning the gnosis of great bliss (mahāsukha)—"resounds," which means it utters internal discourse and experiences [it]. This is the meaning.
Ādarśa 71: There is no "enjoyment" (bhoga) in Oḍiyāna;
[it is attained] through yoga.
74. 75. This is the *Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*. 76. It is described as having the nature of primordial wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) and as the *saṃbhogakāya* whose form is speech.
He is such because his gnosis is imperishable within the wheels beginning with Mahāsukha. 77. He is thus.

78. Because the *bindu*, the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have become unified through these, his resonance (*nāda*) is "pleasing to the mind" (*manojña*).
79. Regarding the passage beginning with "on the garment," etc.:
because the supreme imperishable *bindu* is of the nature of pure bliss (*ānanda-mātra*), it is [described as such].
Regarding "light and so forth":

for one who has previously practiced the yoga of wisdom (prajñā), when the bodhicitta flows from the *brahmarandhra*, because the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) along with its attendants is no longer perceived, a stainless light arises—free from conceptual construction and without objective support—resembling moonbeams.

When the bodhicitta pervades all the joints of the limbs, because the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*) is no longer perceived, there is the appearance of light (*ālokābhāsa*), which resembles the radiance of sunbeams.

When [the mind] has reached the root of the jewel (83), there is the perception of light (*ālokopalabdhi*) due to the non-perception of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
This is the evening twilight, resembling illumination (84). From "light" (*ālokāt*):
the world itself is the triple world; that alone is the one great existence through the *āsphālaka* samādhi (85), because it accomplishes all desired aims.
"Eye," and so forth.
At that time, the very non-perception of the eye and the other [senses] is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Sound is such that it has that very [element] as its ultimate limit (*niṣṭhā*).
"Whose sound is bliss" is thus;
for "the state of being without intrinsic nature" is proclaimed in many senses.
In the midst of that, the Supreme Lord (*vara*) is easily pervaded by the one who extends through the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*).
As it has been said: "Because of taking refuge in the heart, which is moistened by the rays of the flashing [light].
This is because the single channel (*ekanāḍī*) within the heart was previously mentioned.
The remaining [channels] are eighty-nine. Below the seven secretions are three channels for feces, urine, and semen, and the tongue is the channel that carries blood.
The mirror-like wisdom.
93. Existents;
perishable.
94. "Resounding" does not exist.
Āloka | 95. Āsphānaka;
"jñāna" is not present.

96. Discerning Wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna). 97. He speaks of discernment: through the gateway of Amitābha, who consists of the aggregates of perception purified by natural stainlessness, the central channel—suchness—is the inherent nature within the body, due to the metaphorical application of cause and fruit.
By means of the yoga of reality, the deity abides.
99. And reality consists of the four elements beginning with earth, the aggregates, and the five sense faculties.
The five objects multiplied by five [senses] become one hundred through the five cognitions;
thus, there is a thorough knowledge of the body by means of the division into one hundred families (*śatakulaprabheda*).
Furthermore, by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "nāḍikā etc.," the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth is intended.
The supreme, most excellent reality (*tattva*) of those deities is indeed the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*).
In the secret place, the syllable *A* is wisdom (*prajñā*); in great bliss, *HŪṂ* is method (*upāya*).

Their union is *yoga*; through that, by the cessation of all channels (*nāḍī*), there is the non-apprehension of all forms, which is the *avadhūtī*, having shaken off the web of conceptual constructions such as the self and so forth.

The knowledge of the middle way, as well as the conceptualizations of "beginning," "middle," and "end," and the connection that "this is its beginning"— the illumination that occurs therein through non-attention and non-conceptualization is *avadhūtī*.
That very suchness of things that are dependently arisen is selflessness and the absence of intrinsic nature.
To the question "What is that?", he says:
it is the non-apprehension of them as belonging to a self, and that [non-apprehension] exists precisely because of their non-existence.

"That very thing" refers to suchness (*tathatā*), which is the true selflessness (*nairātmya*). It is the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*), the ultimate limit of things as they truly are, and that bliss which has emptiness as its finality—compassion (*karuṇā*) is so called because it "obstructs" (*ruṇaddhi*) that [solitary] bliss, preventing it from being [experienced alone]. Thus, it is compassion.
The body is the drop (bindu), and speech is the wind;
this is because of the teaching on such emptiness as "the manifestation of that" and so forth.
The Māras, such as the afflictions and so forth,
constitute a single joint; "the bull among proponents of emptiness" refers to the sublime bliss experienced through the profundity of emptiness.
The nature of the void, manifesting before one in the mirror-image of the universe,
perceives both the past and the future therein;
yet that [perception] is the void itself, because of the absence of substantiality at that time.
Indeed, it is precisely because of the perception of an entity that a rabbit's horn is not seen;
he states this very point in the verse beginning with "profound," and so forth. || 1 ||

The *dharmodayā* is the lotus; because it is born from that and because it teaches the Dharma, it is the Dharma, as well as the conch. The *sambhoga* consists of the drops of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). The central pericarp of the lotus is the human nose; from the friction [therein], the semen in the form of milk is extracted from the *vajra*. From the enjoyment of the enveloped gnosis (*jñāna*), the form is the innate (*sahaja*) jewel-image, pervading the world like Śrī. *Hetu* (the syllable *he*) means causeless; *ru* means free from discursive thought (*vitarka*); *ke* means not abiding anywhere, because it extends through space like the great ocean—thus I know it.

By the words "Buddhahood," etc., he expresses this meaning: all mundane and supramundane bliss is emitted from that samādhi which consists of it; because it is of the nature of that light of Dharma (*dharmajyotis*), it is the "Great Arana" due to the sound of divine bliss and the essence of Dharma (*dharmarasa*).
Furthermore, because for the Immovable (acyuta) there is no further rebirth, cessation is established in existence and is also Nirvāṇa;
for it would otherwise fall from its foremost state.
As it is said in the *Sekoddeśa*: "The Lord who is the Great Passion is the Immutable; he is Non-abiding Nirvāṇa. Bliss that has not fallen away due to detachment—that is established as Nirvāṇa."

The entire explanation of these [verses] is seen precisely in such scriptures as the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*; it is not based on my own reasoning. For fear of prolixity, I have not written down all of that; let it be understood that this is like the sounding of a celestial drum (*devadundubhi*), because it reveals the treasury of that Dharma, which is bliss and auspiciousness. || 2 ||

Because it is said that "volition arises only with an object," all mind—when taught by the Guru as being established in space—is accompanied by mental factors (*caitasika*) that grasp the essential nature of things; among these, ignorance (*avidyā*) and delusion (*moha*) grasp specific objects such as pleasure and pain.
Through the cessation of the appearance of these, there is no form (*rūpa*) belonging to this [mind] apart from luminosity (*prabhāsvara*); thus, it is "formless" (*arūpa*).
The mental states and mental factors of all [beings] are the *dharmakāya*;

the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are the *rūpakāya*. Due to the unity of these two, having dispelled the afflictions and so forth at the tip of the *vajra*, and having made the sun of wisdom (*prajñā*) one's seat through the process of revelation (*vivṛti*), this innate drop (*sahajabindu*) resides in the heart. By its very nature, it is bliss-emptiness; by virtue of being motionless, it is the drop; and by virtue of pervading the various channels (*nāḍī*), it possesses manifold forms.
Because all phenomena are unperceived in that very single moment of the innate (*sahaja*),
it is "consisting of mind alone" (*manomaya*) and "unattached," and so forth;
for when phenomena do not exist externally, earth and the other elements manifest as the universal image (*viśvabimba*) through self-cognizability, being free from attachment.

His splendor (*śrī*) is seen in the previously mentioned "black line" (*kṛṣṇarekhā*) through the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is the reflection of his own gnosis; thus he is "silver" and "gold.

Just as the moon, though one in the sky, is seen separately in various vessels made of gold and other materials, so too the one Self—indestructible by its very nature—is manifold among living beings, appearing in universal form (*viśvarūpa*), in the form of light, pervading all worlds. || 3 ||
Because it cannot be overcome by conceptual construction, it is invincible;
because of the great sovereignty of the accumulations of merit and gnosis,
mind is the Dharma-body, speech is the Enjoyment-body, and body is the Emanation-body.

The King of these is the Innate (*sahaja*), because of the abiding of the Bodhicitta-vajra within the six wheels according to the sequence of manifestation. *Dharma* is the Clear Light; its *ketu* (banner/sign) is the victory over the afflictions, the ineffable bliss.

Since it is the banner of Dharma, that Innate possesses a "great arising"—an outburst of bliss—by virtue of the fact that the deities, who are the indivisible Great Bliss of the dharmas residing in the [reflected] images, manifest as infinite Buddha-forms (*bimba*) of immeasurable variety. || 4 ||

The three worlds are not one; that innate [bliss] which is about to be described is so because it is free from emission and the like due to its state of having the vital energy drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*).
That very [bliss] is the limb—the body—of Mañjuśrī, who is the cause of the world's arising;
from whom the universe emerges, in whom it delights, and into whom it dissolves again; whose radiance the world shines forth; and whose splendor is the innate bliss-blazing light.
"I praise that Puruṣa, the eternal and inactive Śāstra, the Lord of Beings, for the sake of non-rebirth, whom the wise reach after casting off the darkness of duality.
To the question of how he is to be known by yogins, he says "divine," etc.,
because of the excellence of Mahāmudrā and because Vajrasattva is the eldest of Vairocana and the others.
Regarding "sthavirādayaḥ" and so forth: from the root *sthā*, by adding the suffix *kiraṇ* and the augment *hrasva-vuk*, one who always stands firm is called *sthavira*.
According to the sequence of the *Samādhirāja*, the sixteen digits (*kalā*) increase;

thus, the earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*), and the wind into the mind (*citta*). The mind dissolves into mental factors (*caitasika*), and those into ignorance (*avidyā*); that too then proceeds into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). This is the gradual cessation. Of the mind dissolved into the clear light: it dissolves, it completely dissolves—the consciousness (*cetasa*).
In the three worlds:

thus, from emptiness (*śūnya*) arises the means (*upāya*), and from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) arises the great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*). From the means (*upāya*) is born wisdom (*prajñā*); from that [wisdom] arises fire through wind; from fire arises wind; and from [wind] arises water.

"From water the earth is born; this is the principle regarding the limbs of existence. Through the awakening of such knowledge, that which is luminous (*prabhāsvara*) and beyond the fourth state (*turyātīta*) is its source; because it arises from that, it consists of that. It is the "knowledge of wisdom" (*vidyā*); and because it brings forth living beings through its creative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), it is the Lord of Beings (*prajāpati*).
It is precisely the waning and waxing of the fifteen lunar digits (*kalā*).
There are exactly that many lunar days (tithis), but the sixteenth digit (kalā) is the seed-syllable of the trunk (skandha-bīja) at the portion of the first day of the bright fortnight; however,
from the dark fortnight, it emerges at the time of death.

They are perceived by yogins through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) as being turned upward from the downward course; because there is no cessation of all phenomena due to their innate single essence, they possess the quality of being desirable to all people.

Self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the vision of the three realms within emptiness; from that arises the "inexhaustible" (*asecanaka*), for *sic* means "to flow," and it is "non-flowing" (*akṣara*) because it is immutable.
As before, through the unity of the three bodies (*kāyatrayaikya*), there are the thirty-two major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) such as hands marked with wheels,

and the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) such as the nails and fingers of the Sage being glossy and having four joints; because one easily descends [to these], it is "Possessing Ease" (*sukhāvati*).
That which is named Śukra is the garment of bodhicitta;
because its nature consists in the thorough knowledge of the innate state (sahaja),
its form-body (rūpakāya) has arisen out of compassion for sentient beings.
And that enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) and emanation body (nirmāṇakāya), resplendent with the primary marks and secondary signs,
would not exist without that— namely, the bodhicitta— if one were to abandon bliss.
Because it is of the nature of bliss, that which is named *śukra* (semen) is indeed the arising of bliss; the experience of that belongs to the yogi.

Thus it is said: "The means (*upāya*) has the form of *śukra*, while bliss is the luminous emptiness (*prabhāsvara-śūnya*); the 'beloved woman' (*kāminī*) is not within the sphere of the *śrāvakas* and others, but is the *saṃbhogakāya* of the Bodhisattvas who have entered the [Bodhisattva] stages."

By those who have previously performed service, the state consisting of the five Buddhas—which is a limb of meditative concentration—is perceived through the union of the vajra and the lotus. This entire world has the nature of the five aggregates of appropriation and is devoid of a self;

therefore, it too is a manifestation of mind alone, since from the intermediate state into the mother’s womb, the mind itself, mixed with the semen and blood of the parents, becomes the embodied being.

As it has been said: "Through habituation, the cognition of 'I' arises even toward those belonging to others; one should cultivate this [cognition] even toward the drops of semen and blood [of another].

Thus ends the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*. Furthermore, having abandoned the body at the end, the mind alone—driven by the vital breath—becomes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as is generally stated: "Having abandoned the secure tree of the body, in an instant, the monkey of the mind [leaps away]."
Having described its nature as *saṃsāra*, he now states its nature as *sama*:
"This very one, named Prabhāsvara, divided into infinite varieties of tantras, is perceived according to the dispositions (*āśaya*) of sentient beings. (5)

That by which the world is perceived and understood is the knowledge of the eyes and other senses; through the eye of flesh and so forth, there arises the appearance of forms and other objects within the universal image (*viśvabimba*).

Its quality is the enjoyment of the five objects of desire, and that consists in the immersion of the mind into that image. By means of that very immersion, all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) are severed, thereby eliminating the defects of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Through instruction in this, even the bestower of the fourth initiation becomes fearless regarding *saṃsāra* by virtue of non-abiding *nirvāṇa*.

For it has been said: "The Śrāvakas and others enter Nirvāṇa by transcending existence; however, those for whom there is great compassion remain [in saṃsāra], being dependent on others. Thus, because he is fearless even of suffering due to his indivisible bliss, there is an absence of any opposing factor through non-dual awakening.

Thus it is said: "For the adversary is not of the same nature as that which possesses stains; therefore, the Lord is to be served by those who are well-established in the absence of dualistic grasping."
For fear arises from the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self;
as it has been said: "Because of excessive attachment to that self, even from a slight cause there is fear;
those who have attained [power] bring fear to that very self through old age and death."
And for one who perceives the selflessness of persons and phenomena, there is no [self];
rather, selflessness alone is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Because it conceals reality, it is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), which is the deluded mind.
And that [pleasure], while delightful when not investigated, is in reality nothing at all; thus it becomes the ultimate truth.

This protector does not fall from this state because his defects have been exhausted even while enjoying the five objects of desire. Therefore, his wisdom is established, and his compassion is declared through his abiding in the instruction of pure knowledge for those who are attached to the bliss of emission (*cyuti-sukha*).
For those afflicted by suffering take refuge in a protector, and that [refuge] consists precisely of the appropriated aggregates such as earth and so forth;

yet these [aggregates] have been introduced by him into the essence of the great bliss of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Thus, he is a "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) because he protects the continuum [of beings].
And because the continuum is uninterrupted, it is therefore always of a nature that is not born from the *tanu* [body].
As it has been said: "Ai-u, O Lord, mi-tu," and so forth.
The three worlds are body, speech, and mind; [the name is so called] because of the attainment thereof. ||6||

That which adorns happiness is the lotus (*padma*), meaning the water-lily (*kamala*); because it is always firm, it is the thunderbolt (*vajra*). In their union, due to the excellence of bliss, there is expansion through blossoming.
In the grasping of the pair, because of the lack of falling away, the body is the drop (*bindu*), speech is wind (*vāta*), and mind is conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

The cessation of these occurs at the tip of the jewel; therefore, innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) alone is the mine of jewels, because it is the source of the jewels that are the qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha (*saṃbuddha*). Therein, as stated in the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*, there is no prior state of affliction (*pūrvakleśadaśā*), nor is there the ignorance (*avidyā*) that causes the flow of existence (*bhava*), nor the latencies of affliction (*kleśavāsanā*).
That very [unmanifested state] is the egg-shell and the embryo, the cause of birth for those born from eggs;

and when the latent impression (*vāsanā*), having entered along with [the innate nature], is cut off at its very root, it is said: "When the latent impression is destroyed, one does not fall again," and so forth.
Existence is ignorance; it is the cause of bondage to existence. Its destruction is the luminous gnosis. ||7||

The affliction of defilement (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and grasping (*upādāna*); the affliction of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*) consists of becoming (*bhava*) and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
and the affliction of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*) consists of the eight factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The state of being free from the obscurations of these is like the vision of one who is no longer afflicted by cataracts seeing the hairs seen by one who does have cataracts.

For one who is attached to form and so forth, because of grasping at the aggregates through craving, the aggregates themselves are an ocean; because it is agitated by crocodiles, serpents, and other creatures such as passion (rāga),
its limit is the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha, beginning with the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha).
The meaning is that one attains it;
the fourth is the innate (*sahaja*), which,
through the washing away of impurities, is itself the consecration (*sekha*).
And that [vajra], having opened up, becomes the drop situated in the uṣṇīṣa; it is the awakened vajra whose arising occurs when, by metaphorically applying the name of the result to the cause,
the innate drop (sahaja-bindu) adorns the Buddhas, because it abides as their uṣṇīṣa.
The Blessed Mañjuśrī is of one form with the fruit of the Buddhas, since it is said [in the *Vimalaprabhā*]: "By which he draws forth the mind-born [desire].

Therefore, because it is always the cause of bliss during union with a karmic woman or union with one's own [inner] appearance (*svābhāsa*), the *bindu* must be protected by those practicing celibacy (*brahmacārin*).

Since its protection fulfills the accumulations of merit, wisdom, and ethical conduct, and since one has attained the ten perfections—beginning with generosity—of the Buddhas of the three times, past, present, and future, who set the wheel of Dharma in motion; by this very [protection], the flames of lightning-fire impelled by the *verambha* winds and so forth would melt the wheel of bliss (*sukhacakra*). Thereupon, the moon, having passed through the sequence of the four wheels beginning with the throat, is arrested at the tip of the jewel (*maṇi*). That would be the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), if the garland of drops (*bindumālā*) residing in the throat and other centers bestows bliss by way of non-emission (*acyutatva*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "awake" (*jāgrat*) and so forth:

for transmigrating beings, the *bodhicitta* residing in the body and located in the head is of the nature of the waking state; when dissolved in the breath and located in the throat, it is of the nature of sleep; yet even in both these states, sense objects continue to circulate.

When the mind is motionless, dissolved, located in the heart, and in the form of deep sleep; when it is established in gnosis and has reached the navel, it takes the form of the fourth state (*turya*). Through union with a consort, at the moment of emission, when the *bodhicitta* has melted, that very mind—having ceased its fourfold [states]—becomes the Emanation, Enjoyment, Dharma, and Innate Bodies of the Buddhas, in the sequence beginning with the Emanation Body.

Thus, for those wandering in the saṃsāra of the three realms, the *bodhicitta*—situated within the mind—becomes fourfold according to the states of waking and so forth. That [citta], which bestows imperishable bliss, is pervasive and must be protected by the lord of yogins for the sake of liberation. If the *bindu* is released and falls from its support, where is there liberation?
For when the seed of the yogi’s birth—the supported—is gone, what liberation can there be?
Therefore, the pleasure of death must certainly be abandoned;
for how can there be the blameless attainment of Mahāmudrā for one who is happy? It has been said: "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated."
For one whose semen flows during union with a mudrā, how can there be an increase of bliss? Just as when a bud falls from a tree in spring, how can there be fruit?

He explains that this [bliss] beginning with joy (ānanda) which is to be produced: among all the five objects of desire which are causes of pleasure, the "action-woman" (karmāṅganā) is most excellent, because the three cognitions beginning with *āloka* are perceived right here by one who has performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
He describes the three cognitions: "Āloka," and so forth.
The portion of the night encircled by the rays of the moon is *ānanda* (bliss), which is *āloka* (light).
That which is like the day, illuminated by the rays of the sun, due to its vivid appearance, is *paramānanda* (supreme bliss), which is *ālokābhāsa* (the semblance of light).

"Madhya" (the middle) refers to the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, which— like the crimson twilight— is supremely delightful due to its undifferentiated flavor between night and day; it is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), the attainment of light (*ālokopalabdhi*),
and the conceptualization of embracing and so forth.
That very [state] is subtle and characterized by distinguished, peaceful conceptualization. Thus, "these three appearances are joined with the natures (prakṛtis) in their respective order.

Devoid of these three, the triple appearance consisting of the single flavor of the appearance of great bliss is the innate joy (*sahajānanda*), the moment of awakening (*bodhikṣaṇa*), and the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

Awakening is the clear light, the ultimate reality; it is the personal realization (*pratyātmādhigama*) of all phenomena through the experience of the innate peace that is the intrinsic nature of conventional reality.
Because realization partakes of the aspect of luminosity through identity (*tādātmya*), it is described as such;

thus, conventionally, the consecration of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*) is said to be by means of an external consort (*mudrā*). However, in the ultimate sense, this is not so, because that [realization] is beyond the range of conceptual construction and verbal expression.
Therefore, he says: "Accessible only to yogins" means it is to be personally realized within oneself.

To those who are unable to ascertain the internal reality—the object to be demonstrated by examples—once they have attained the supramundane Great Bliss which is of a single flavor with the Clear Light, he says "naiśam" and so forth. "Vimala" refers to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), emptiness, which he would explain in a state free from the defilement of all superimpositions, such as the existence [of things] and so on.

And at that moment, through the view which serves as an external illustration for awakening, the disciple attains certainty; he realizes the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) in its ultimate form (*paramārtharūpa*),
and that internal bliss (*adhyātmasaukhya*) in its conventional form (*saṃvṛtirūpa*), which is entirely empty and free from the sequence of signs.

The awakening that arises through the practice of the yoga of the "Karmāṅganā" (the woman who is a limb of ritual action) by means of signs such as smoke and so forth— described in the first half-verse— is called the "Parā" (Supreme) [initiation]; the latter half-verse describes the fourth initiation, which is the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Enlightenment is free from the four extremes; at the end of falling away, there is destruction; in the absence of possibility, it is devoid of characteristics;
when there is perception, for one seeking happiness, there would be non-falling. Therefore, the fourth is without intrinsic nature;
thus it is "both."
The fourth [empowerment] is inseparable from great bliss, the lack of intrinsic nature, and non-duality;
it is the cause, while the third empowerment of the master and so forth is the fruit.
Regarding this, the misconceptions of the wise are untenable.

Those who maintain that the goal (*lakṣya*) lies between the ultimate cessation (*paramavirama*) and the intermediate state (*madhya*) rely solely on the phonemes (*vyañjana*). Let them thus establish the correspondence of sounds as being the fruit; however, in their view, this [fourth state] would indeed be the fourth, because it is the fruit of the third.
Furthermore, one must state that the third is the cause of the fourth, but that is illogical: a cause is sought for the sake of a fruit, so if the fruit has already arisen, what is the use of this?
Moreover, regarding the fourth consecration (*seka*), it is said to be for the sake of attaining Mahāmudrā-siddhi; yet, once the fruit has been attained, what purpose would that consecration serve?

Furthermore, if the consecration were to be spoken of even when the fruit is already accomplished, there would be no distinction between the two types of "breaths" (*āśvāsa*). For instance, innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) is the Tathāgata-breath, the third; its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) is the Vajradhara-breath, the fourth.
Furthermore, since both [the first and second] are results,

if one were to accept that the *vajradharāśvāsa* comes first and the *abuddha* comes later in accordance with the statement "the third is the result," it would follow as an absurd conclusion that the result precedes the cause.
That too is stated: "It is established by me precisely because of the statement 'between the supreme [joy] and the cessation [of joy]'";
that is not so, because this sentence has a different meaning altogether, and thus, just as the verse in its true sense has another meaning.

Likewise, even the "object of definition" (*lakṣya*) is something other than what you have stated. Furthermore, it is proper to provide an explanation of the definition—"having observed the object of definition between the supreme and the cessation, make it firm"—in accordance with the object of definition; however, the definition should not be altered to suit the object of definition, because the definition functions only after the object of definition has been perceived.

Furthermore, since the *Samāja* and *Hevajra* are non-different in their essential meaning, there is no distinction in the means (*sādhana*). As for the result, although it is the same, it is said to be fourfold only because of a difference in its specific aspects (*mātra*).

If it is argued that "only three initiations (*seka*) are mentioned therein," [the response is] no; this was stated with the intention that, from a worldly perspective, there are indeed only that many.
Even in the fourth [verse], it was stated to be indistinct; following the third, one must indeed rely upon a teacher to understand it.

Therefore, let others perhaps claim that the third [verse] is the intended meaning (*lakṣya*) by taking it as the ultimate sense according to the literal meaning, without connecting the preceding and following parts; nevertheless, since the fruit is internal through both scripture and reasoning, how can the meaning of the verse be anything other than the fourth? If this is asked, there is no fault; the meaning of the verse is perfectly consistent.

There is no dispute regarding the fact that the *paramavirama* (the supreme cessation) occurs between *ānanda* (bliss) and *sahaja* (the innate). However, the word "in the middle" (*madhye*) should be construed with *paramānanda* (supreme bliss) and *sahaja*, rather than with *ānanda* and *sahaja*. In this interpretation of the intended meaning, the use of the genitive case endings in *paramaviramayoḥ* is not redundant; rather, this is a genitive used in the sense of "disregard," according to the rule: *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare*.

The meaning is as follows: disregarding the intermediate [moments] of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) and supreme joy (*paramānanda*), they regard the fourth as the object to be perceived and make it firm, because it has been explained by the lords of the ten stages, Lokeśvara, Khagarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Yogīndra, Bhūtināropa, and others;
thus, taking it to be "the end of the joy of cessation" (*viramānta*), he explains it with the subsequent half-verse beginning with "this" (*etad*) and so forth:
all this triad of joys is of the nature of the joy of sexual union (*suratānanda*), because it arises from sexual union.
Because this [fourth] is the cause of the innate (*sahaja*),

that triad of blisses— which is the very nature of pleasure— is the means (*upāya*) and the cause; and the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which directly and indirectly experiences those three, is the fruit, being the fourth itself.

He explains the half-verse beginning with "viśiṣṭa" and so forth as the third [stage]; because it involves the destruction of passion (*rāga*), it is not to be adopted, and therefore only the fourth is cultivated.
He then explains the verse beginning with "parama" and so forth.
Supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) is *bhava* (existence) because its nature is the foremost among the afflicted;
the cessation (*virama*) is *nirvāṇa* because its nature is the emission accompanied by conceptualization;
however, the intermediate bliss (*ānanda*) is inferior and base, as it is equivalent to the pleasure of worldly existence.
The fruit is peaceful non-duality, free from conceptual construction, resembling the stainless autumn sky at midday;

it does not manifest as defects such as passion (*rāga*), for since it is of the nature of attachment, it is not perceived as something innate— this is how the passage beginning with "passion" (*rāga*) should be construed.
The cessation [of practice] is not [the goal], because it is not conjoined with the conceptualization of pleasure;
nor is the intermediate [stage],
because it is the most inferior of all.
He explains the second half of the verse beginning with "that" (*tat*) and so forth.

The third [moment] is *virama*, and it is the first of that which has the fourth moment as its beginning; therein he explains the second half starting with "supreme" (*parama*). That *virama* which occurs at the end of the supreme [moment] belongs to that innate (*sahaja*) [bliss] which is in the middle; thus it is caused by *virama*. Non-voidness (*aśūnya*) is compassion (*karuṇā*), and the fruit itself is Heruka.

Having explained the scripture (*āgama*) that appears contradictory [to his own position], he says "But those who... and so forth, citing a scripture that cannot be explained according to the view of the third proponent of the Sahaja (*sahajavādin*).
This is easy to understand.
Terms such as "void" (*śūnya*) and so on are synonyms for bliss (*ānanda*) and the rest.
The first three are the cause, and the fourth is the fruit.
Regarding the phrase "variegated" and so forth: "variegated" means manifold, such as embracing, kissing, and the like.
The maturation (vipāka) is the opposite of that; it is the enjoyment of the knowledge of bliss.
Contemplation (vimarda) is said to be the reflection, "Bliss has been enjoyed by me.
That which is distinct from these three is the extraordinary (vilakṣaṇa), free from both attachment and aversion.
Thus,

"its reversal" means that the enjoyment of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is the opposite of those various [acts] such as embracing. Because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the grasped object and so forth have been attenuated here, it is called "the crushing" (*vimarda*), and so on.
Thinking, "I have experienced bliss," [one recites] the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "Mahāsukhālocanam" (The Vision of Great Bliss), "Vilakṣaṇam" (Distinctive), and so forth;
it is other than the three [joyful states] beginning with *ānanda*.
Attachment (*rāga*) is the opposite of that, while non-attachment (*arāga*) is dispassion (*vairāgya*); he is free from both. "By the Teacher," and so forth.
From the beginning, it is the Ācārya;
from the far-reaching scriptures, it is the Guhya;
because of its preeminent knowledge, it is Prajñā.
And the fourth is so called because it is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

The word "likewise" (*tathā*) means that, by way of its aspect of bliss, it is like the third; these should be understood as being nothing other than Ānanda and the others, distinguished only by different names.
In the *Śrī Kālacakra*, regarding the passage beginning with "kāmā" (*desire*) and so forth: there are four [states] beginning with bliss (*ānanda*).

Each is divided into body, speech, mind, and gnosis (*jñāna*), thus making sixteen. Among these, *kāma* is bodily bliss (*kāyānanda*), *ānanda* is speech, *kampā* (trembling) is mind, and *akṣaraṇa* (non-emission) is gnosis-bliss (*jñānānanda*); this is the first, the single bliss (*eka ānanda*). *Pūrṇā* (fullness) is the body, supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); *paramānanda* is the arising (*udbhava*) of mind, and *śakti* (power) is gnosis-supreme-bliss; this is the second.

The body of the flame is speech; its arising is mind; cessation (*virama*) is speech; the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) is mind; the drop (*bindu*) is gnosis (*jñāna*), and the joy of cessation is the third.

The innate (*sahaja*) is the body of the *oḍu*; the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) is speech; sleep is mind; the resonance (*nāda*) is the gnosis of innate joy; this is the rule for the innate at the end of the sixteen.
As for the lineage of the four mudrās, it is false that it was composed by Mārya Nāgārjuna.
In the *Sekoddeśa*, "the vase" (*kumbha*) and so forth,
as well as "the perishable" (*kṣara*) and so forth, are synonyms for consecration (*sekha*).
Through the purification of the body, it is the vase.
Through the purity of speech, the secret [initiation];
through the purity of mind, the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*);
and the fourth, through the purity of the knowledge of ultimate reality, is the purifier of the body and so forth.
The terms "child" (*bāla*) and so forth are also synonyms.
He describes the sequence of arising: beginning with "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and so on.

Through the touch of the breasts and limbs of the *bhavyā* (the consort), the bodhicitta flows from the *uṣṇīṣa* to the forehead; this flow, which constitutes the experience of physical bliss (*kāyānanda*) and so forth, is the "child," the milk-offering initiation (*payodharābhiṣeka*).

By means of slight oscillation in the secret place, [the drops descend] from the throat to the heart; these are the throat-drop, the heart-drop, and the bindu. Of these, the latter is the innate bindu (*sahaja-bindu*).
Here, they are indeed [so called] because, through luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), they are equal to space.
Having bestowed [this] for the sake of the supreme good, it is the best of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*).
As it has been said: "Even the auspicious vase, the wish-fulfilling tree, and the thought-gem are insentient;
yet even they bring happiness to sentient beings—how much more so [the Buddha], who is embraced by compassion?"
Just as when one inserts a hand into a golden vessel and draws out whatever object one desires, so too is there the accomplishment of desired goals through this Leader who excels that [vessel];
and he performs all those mundane and supramundane benefits for sentient beings effortlessly,
because he teaches the Dharma according to the distinctions of infinite destinies, births, inclinations, and languages.
"Seeking their welfare" means for the sake of whatever happiness sentient beings may have even in future lives;
because he always possesses great bliss, he is affectionate toward all beings, never for even a moment feeling aversion toward them.
Regarding the phrase "knower of the auspicious and inauspicious":
just as there is no measurement of time for iron anywhere, so too,
because the mind of the wise has no latent tendencies (vāsanā) anywhere, it is established that the inauspicious is non-luminous.
One knows that moment of the perfect awakening of great bliss (*mahāsukha-abhisambodhi*) which is the drop situated at the tip of the jewel.
Regarding "action" (*karman*) and so forth: the experience of the body’s nature as bliss is the *kāyasamaya* (body-commitment).

The experience of speech and breath as being of the nature of bliss is the *vāksamaya* (commitment of speech). The experience of a sublime aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) wherein the mind is immersed in bliss, which is the illumination of the drops of nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*), is the *cittasamaya* (commitment of mind).
The experience of non-conceptual great bliss and emptiness by way of the innate (*sahaja*) is the *jñānasamaya* (commitment of gnosis).
"Because it has that nature" means because it has the nature of the four samayas. "Objects" refers to worldly [phenomena] such as form and so forth.
The qualities beginning with the ten powers (daśabala) follow from that, because they are co-nate and pervasive.
Just as iron that has attained the state of gold becomes stainless through fire,
so too the mind becomes increasingly stainless through the fire of passion (rāga).
As it has been said:
"The sense organs of those who possess [the practice], when purified by bliss (*ānanda*) and the other stages, shine forth stainlessly.
Even a wise man might overcome the power of the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters."
"Yet the Buddha does not let the time pass for those who are to be disciplined"—
from this statement, he is one who knows the proper times for attracting, maturing, and liberating [beings].
"Action," and so forth.

Through the *karmamudrā* one attains the state of *bhūcarī*; through the innate consort (*svābhayā*), the state of *khecarī*; and through the divine *samayamudrā*, the accomplishments of *mahāmudrā* which are indeed liberation. He is the one of subtle wisdom (*tanuprajña*). Brahmā is the body, Hara is speech, and Hari is the mind; these three are the Vedas for living beings. You are the syllable *Oṃ*, you are the three letters, you are the moon, the sun, and the fire, and you are the three channels and the [three] qualities (*guṇa*). In the body, the *kaula* is one thing and the *kula* is another; the *Atharvaṇa* consists of the objects and the qualities, having the form of sound (*nāda*). In the midst of that is the Unstruck (*anāhata*), which is devoid of objects, beyond qualities, and imperishable.
Thus it is said. He possesses the qualities of the syllables, the sentient beings, and so forth, and he is a knower of qualities.
He is a knower of the Dharma because of his knowledge of the luminous nature of phenomena (*dharmas*).
He is praiseworthy because he pacifies the world and the afflictions characterized by lack of tranquility.
He is the most auspicious (*māṅgalya*) even among auspicious things such as strength (*bala*) and joy (*ānanda*).

He is the glory (*kīrti*) of glories (*kīrti*) in the auspicious syllable (*bhavye akṣare*). In the state of union (*saṅge*), through the dissolution of the breath (*śvāsa-laya*), there is the dissolution of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-laya*) and the accumulation of all bliss, such as joy (*ānanda*) and so forth, in the fourth state.

// 14 // "Uninterrupted" refers to the experience of the flow of the *dharmatā*. Flowing through the right and left [channels] is the worldly [breath], while that which transcends them flows through the middle. This is the drawing-in (*āyamana*) and entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Through this, by means of the teaching on bliss which takes as its object the ineffable non-dual *dharmatā*, the world is gladdened.
Many, having abandoned their golden beds, lie upon beds of grass.
Those wise ones, satiated with the essence of the Dharma, lay down in happiness.
Regarding the statement "The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti," because of its great majesty, there arises a great delight;
you yourself have declared that it is worthy of practice and worship—beginning with the words "Bodhi," and so forth.

The ultimate reality is emptiness; likewise, there is the sprinkling and purification of the body and so forth by means of constant bliss. Furthermore, there are the powers of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), pervasiveness (vyāpti), irresistible will (prākāmya), and magnification (mahimā).

Mastery (īśitā) and control (vaśitā), as well as the power of determining the course of desires (kāmāvaśāyitā). This same meaning is stated by means of another synonym: subtlety of form (sūkṣmarūpa), lightness of touch (laghusparśa), pervasiveness (vyāpti), reaching (saṃprāpti), luminosity (prakāśa), stability (stheyatva), mastery (vaśitva), and the power of determining desires (kāmāvaśānika).
Thus, because he is the cause of the eight prosperities, he is "prosperity" (*bhūti*).

He is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, and all three of his fetters (*saṃyojana*) are destroyed. Indeed, that Bodhisattva experiences supreme joy, for he possesses the power to shake a hundred world-systems.
Thus it is said.

On the very level of the Joyous (pramuditā), there is spoken of "supreme joy" (prakṛṣṭamoda) and "glory" (yaśas). "Bliss" (sukha) is physical, being free from conceptual construction; "mental well-being" (saumanasya) is mental. He is the Lord (pati) of glory by virtue of those two.
His body is the pure gnosis (viśuddhajñānadeha) resulting from the purification of the afflictions (kleśa), the objects of knowledge (jñeya), meditative attainments (samāpatti), and so forth.
15. He is the most excellent, flowing effortlessly without signs; he is the "Bestower of Boons" (Varada) because of his granting of boons;
he is the supreme due to the preeminence of the union of the two aspects (yuganaddha);
and he is the protector of those who suffer, who are seized by the grasp of conceptual constructions that are the source of all suffering.
Great passion (*mahārāga*) is the innate (*sahaja*).
By means of it, delusion (*moha*) and the other afflictions, when purified, become Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].
