For this very reason, it is said: "Affliction has become a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and cyclic existence has attained the nature of that [enlightenment]."
"Therefore, the Tathāgatas, who possess great skillful means, are indeed inconceivable.
Thus [it is said]. "Latent predisposition" (vāsanā) refers to...
When there is the expansion of the conceptualization of wind and when existence appears,
from whence could the latent impressions of attachment and aversion arise? Therefore, what is the point [in asserting] the superiority of Hari, Hara, and others?
And that preeminence is established by emptiness; thus he says "all," and so forth.
The variety of existence is manifested through natural purity, while the variety of nirvāṇa is manifested through the purity of stainlessness.

This occurs through the power of specific merits associated with various auxiliary factors. As it has been said: "Having entered a void pit, the master of yoga sleeps happily and fearlessly with his movements concealed; by means of subsisting on air, he lives and effects the liberation of the world. Through the binding of the rays of the nectar-drops and the cessation of internal breath, he who is absorbed in the door of the supreme Guru—though bearing the fear of the mongoose—triumphs like a lord of serpents. *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*. The master of yoga, having entered a hollow pit, remains there comfortably and without fear, his footsteps hidden. Sustained by the intake of air, he lives and brings about the liberation of the universe. By restraining the internal breath and dissolving [the mind] at the door of the excellent Guru, he overcomes the fear of the mongoose, just as a lord of serpents triumphs.
Thus:
"from the family" means from the assembly of external and internal adversaries belonging to the family of Āditya; the pure *dharmakāya* is its radiation, which is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
And they have reached every aspect through that emptiness, which destroys conceptual proliferation;
thus he says, "Therefore," and so forth.

Although he pervades the three realms of existence, because his nature is emptiness, he is neither born nor destroyed; since destruction presupposes birth, through his emanation he does not abandon his true purpose even while appearing to undergo birth and other states,
for even in the grasping of birth and so forth, there is no obstruction by karma for him.

Likewise, I too am the Sun-Chariot for sentient beings on the field of karma; I am the one who shows the path of reasoning and destroys their sufferings, whereas Hari, Hara, and others are not, for they are like those blind from birth regarding the vision of emptiness. || 16 ||
Through the power of *dhāraṇā* and by means of *anusmṛti*, [one perceives] Caṇḍālī and the others; thus it is said: "That which is indeed the vision of Caṇḍālī in that subtle space is *anusmṛti*.

For one who has entered the mother’s womb from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the skin and other parts of the body are connected to those of the parents, yet for the yogin they are unobscured.

The dharmas, mutually intermingled like matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*), have a single flavor in emptiness; they possess a state of oneness within all phenomena by virtue of being the supreme immutable drop (*paramākṣarabindu*). As it is said: "As long as the relationship between the support and the supported persists, it proceeds until reaching the state of the immutable; once the mind has attained the state of the immutable, it no longer possesses the characteristics of support and supported. Because of the abandonment of the obscurations of habitual tendencies (*saṃvāsanāvaraṇa*), he is "shaven-headed" (*muṇḍa*) and thus "one who is shaven" (*mauṇḍa*).
By virtue of being a mass (*kūṭa*) of merit and gnosis, the crown (*mukuṭa*) consists of the five Victors; it is a diadem (*phiroṭi*).
Because it consists of the five maṇḍalas of the purified earth and so forth, he has five faces. He possesses the consorts of the five families, Vairocana and the others, such as Ālokā and so forth.
The manifest fruit is the fourth *dharmadhātu*; like the states of waking and so forth, there is a distinction of states due to the difference in appearances.
That which transcends the fourth is the innate (*sahaja*); through its purification, it is the "five thieves" in the crest-jewel, because it possesses the nature of that very form. || 17 ||
Regarding the entry into luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) through the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*),
"mauñja" refers to the wearing of a girdle of *muñja* grass; the purpose therein is indeed the prevention of emission (*cyavana*).

"Truth is Brahman, austerity is Brahman, and the restraint of the senses is Brahman; compassion toward all beings is Brahman—this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa. According to this principle, one whose nature (*śīla*) is to practice *brahman* is a *brahmacārī*;
it is for this very reason [that he is so called].
Having not lived in a household from childhood onwards, but having spent his life in ascetic vows,
[he was] "eternal" and so forth; thus,
even though he was non-dual through his own radiance and so on, the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti* contains the true bindu situated in the secret wheel and other centers.

Above, by means of the gradual cultivation of the dissolution of the breaths outside the channels of the six families (*ṣaṭkulā*), the drawing in of the *bindu* through the vajra-mouth is his great austerity; by which there is the manifestation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and other qualities. Such is his mastery in that austerity, through the reversal of the stages beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), whereby, due to the stability of the *bindu*, body, speech, and mind are purified by great bliss—this indeed is his "bath."

Thus he said: "Do not go to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, nor observe vows, nor practice charity. Listen to everything outside of knowledge according to every doctrine; liberation does not occur even in a hundred births. Thus it is also in the view of others: "The self is a river whose holy waters are self-restraint, which carries truth and has the banks of virtuous conduct; perform your ablution here, O son of Pāṇḍu, for the inner self is not purified by water. Thus says Gautama.

The word *go* denotes a thunderbolt (*vajra*), heaven (*svarga*), a hand (*kara*), a forest (*vana*), and a bull (*balīvarda*); as a masculine noun, it refers to a cow. When it is said that *gotama* is the best among cows, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) to form *gotama*. Conventionally, however, he is a disciple of the sage Gautama, born of the Kapila lineage; by applying the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "his own," he is called *gotama*.
Because it possesses the supreme qualities of a Buddha, it is the foremost among the innate [qualities]. || 18 ||

Because it is said, "Knowledge is Brahman; bliss is the form of Brahman," he says: "Even if you were to enter Pātāla, or traverse the sky and wander through the circle of the directions with unswerving speed, even by such wandering, that stainless Brahman—which is not merged within the self—cannot be touched by one who has not attained cessation (nivṛti). Thus, the syllable *HŪṂ* is the essence of the five Jinas, whose forms are the five vowels: *a, i, ṛ, u, ḷ*.

Taking hold of that resonance (*nāda*), when it dissolves into the *uṣṇīṣa*, one no longer carries conceptual constructions; thus, he is firmly "beyond the external" (*vāhyati*) and is therefore a *brāhmaṇa*.

Furthermore, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the four limbs (*caturaṅga*), the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and the four meditative absorptions (*caturdhyāna*)—these are the means (*upāya*) and the gateways (*mukha*) to him. Thus he is *brahmā*. [The term *vyoman*] refers to space and so forth; in the word *vṛhi*, the suffix *manin* is applied, and there is the addition of the augment *am*.

Brahman itself is the extinction resulting from the cessation of the conceptualization of air; for [the scripture] has itself declared their non-difference through such passages as "Bliss," and so forth—just as in the case of the expression, "The body of the stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*).

Furthermore, it is said: "One who has obtained that [knowledge] may be free from fault in some instances regarding his father, friends, and others, provided that the Veda, which is omniscient with respect to supersensuous objects, is indeed unauthored."
"Having attained the unattained" means that liberation indeed arises from the vision of emptiness;
it is called *mokṣa* because it leads to great bliss (*mahāsukha*) as far as the expanse of space extends.
Thus it is said: "The mind defiled by passion and the like is saṃsāra; its state of being free from that is, in brief, liberation—so declared by the Victors who have abandoned all obscurations.

This concludes the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*. [Regarding the view] that the world consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), others hold that the limbs of liberation consist of *sattva* and the other qualities.

As it is said: "All the phenomena of the world are considered the fuel for the fire of consciousness; having burned them with the flames of correct analytical investigation, it becomes stilled. And: "With the body uncontracted, enduring sensations, his liberation of mind is like the extinguishing of a lamp. Thus, there is the passion of ordinary death, the great passion, and the innate passion—by means of this worldly passion.
It is liberated by innate passion (*sahajarāga*);
it is "reversed" because it is contrary to worldly conventions, and because the innate is opposed by the Buddhists, non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, and others.
How is it that those non-Buddhists (tīrthya), out of hatred for the essential Vajrayāna, are like a physician who would kill with poison—whether black or white—even when combined with medicine?

Just as a medicinal herb is used for inducing perspiration in one who is afraid, so too are the passions (rāga) and afflictions (kleśa) like fires because they cause the burning of hell; scorched by them, they are made to sweat and are fully ripened through the cultivation of "Great Passion" (mahārāga).
The means is great compassion; the sprout is the bodhicitta itself, which has arisen for only a short time and is still very slight, [produced] through fierce actions such as the taking of life.

If, by means of the suffix *kan* in the sense of "slightness," one immediately becomes attached to the taste of sense objects because purity has been reduced to a state of illusion (*māyātva*), then how can that [consciousness], though all-pervasive and bestowing the fruit of meditative absorption, achieve the welfare of the world? The meaning is: it cannot at all.
Some who practice the conduct of the utterly non-proliferated (*atyanta-niṣprapañca-caryā*) awaken after abandoning the five [senses].
However, those who practice the conduct free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-caryā*) perceive them as being experienced and uncontradicted.

On the other hand, those who practice the conduct with conceptual proliferation (*saprapañca-caryā*)—the best of men—intend to distract the minds of beings elsewhere by means of sense objects through the ten types of mental distraction, beginning with "all [objects] are to be grasped. As it is said: "It is not suitable for beings to achieve non-dual knowledge [if their minds are distracted]."
Through the approach of these [deities], there is peaceful nirvāṇa from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
At the entry into the mother’s womb, whatever innate bliss is attained when the father [is present] is experienced together with the female partner through the limb of karma;
by means of that bliss of the dissolution of earth and the other elements, death occurs, and likewise [the state of] conception arises from the cessation of sense objects.

For this very reason, the knowledge of emptiness is Śiva, because he cannot be moved by that which is inauspicious, according to the statement: "The Śivas are so called because they are eternally auspicious.
For this very reason, there is indivisibility.

Because all conceptual constructions have ceased, there is an absence of the grasping at existence and so forth; as it is said: "The exhaustion of the grasping at existence and non-existence is called Nirvāṇa" (in the *Ratnākara*).
Because external entities are not perceived and because there is no objective support, one takes as an object only the emptiness that is without support; thus,
the vision by means of wisdom of the uncreated, self-cognizable universal image is peace,
precisely because it is of the nature of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
All Victors dissolve into the luminous state alone;

he is the "End-maker" because he brings an end to conceptual constructions through wisdom when passion has fallen away. O Noble One, the *Nāmasaṅgīti* is the bliss of a person; the emission of semen is suffering. Through the perfection of non-dual bliss by means of transcending that duality, one reaches the ultimate goal, which is established in the form of that [luminosity].
Just as when extracting the essence, the grain, from rice, the husk and chaff are discarded, so too it is said: "There is no sin greater than dispassion (virāga), and no merit greater than happiness.

When one's own mind is in a state of non-mind (*acittatva*), pleasure and the like are not perceived; because it arises from the scripture of transcendence (*cyuti*) and is born of detachment, it is the Great Passion (*mahārāga*).

Because it is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmatā* is unceasing; that untainted bliss, through the exhaustion of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of the aggregates and so forth, results in the exhaustion of the substratum (*upadhikṣaya*).
This is the beginning of [the description of] that which is called the luminous and delightful reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*). That very *prajñāpāramitā* is the shatterer of all Māras.
Thus, [it is] incomparable because the bliss of the "action-woman" (*karmāṅganā*) and so forth is merely worldly.

Regarding the statement "the sequence of the purification of the mind, beginning with light, is declared as perception," it is said here: "Of all illusions, the illusion of a woman is preeminent. (Anu)

Having thus acted, through the yoga of the non-duality of wisdom and means, having become firm in the very tip of the vajra, one fills the lotus within the bodhicitta. Upon the arising of the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), when there is the non-apprehension of the three lights and so forth— the primordial forms— and due to the cessation of the qualities of nature,
it is unmanifest as a form not of nature, formless, without appearance, and stainless due to the absence of stains such as passion.
Partless and indivisible,
because consciousness is unobstructed like space, it is all-pervading in the form of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Its subtle nature is sovereignty, and because it is the cause of happiness for all sentient beings, it is the seed, the *bodhicitta*.
Because it is non-dual gnosis free from the outflows of desire, existence, views, and ignorance, it is to be personally realized within.
Passion is supreme detachment; cessation is the intermediate state; bliss—these are the impurity of passion.
Purity is suchness; indeed, the purity of all phenomena is held to be suchness.

Because they can be cleared away by the Noble Path, the adventitious passions such as attachment and so forth—the eighty types of hatred—have been vomited out and expelled by him; thus he is "one by whom [hatred] has been cast out.
Furthermore, due to the rejection of all objective supports (*ālambana*), there is an absence of external distraction.
He is "awakened" (*prabuddha*) because his luminous intellect has blossomed through pervasiveness, like a fully opened lotus.
He is "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*) because he possesses self-knowledge that is awakened as the innate nature (*sahaja-rūpa*) through non-differentiation from form and the other [sensory objects],
due to knowing all phenomena contained within the reflection that is non-different from his own gnosis.

“O Protector, you have no conceit, no conceptual construction, and no [linguistic] expression. Because of this statement, [the Buddha is] the All-Knowing One, since he knows that [this teaching] is directed toward those possessed of hatred—[referring to] mental application (*manaskāra*), external engagement, and conduct regarding the limbs of women, and so forth.
For this very reason, due to his great compassion, he is supreme and exalted.
Since the external world does not exist, through reasoning one transcends even that *ālayavijñāna* which consists of the body, objects of enjoyment, and the physical environment;
therefore, this knowledge is beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Those who conceptualize the Buddha—who is beyond conceptual proliferation and imperishable—are all struck down by conceptualization; because he is formless, they do not see the Tathāgata. Thus ends the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*, which is sublime due to its pervasive emanation of the Nirmāṇakāya that delights and is adorned with the primary and secondary marks.

If there were anything non-empty, there might be something empty as well; but since there is nothing whatsoever that is non-empty, how will there be an empty? Thus, "emptiness" is a profound conceptualization of the ultimate truth.
Regarding this, it is said: "The dull-witted person who meditates on emptiness as 'non-arising,' 'empty,' or 'without objective support' does not truly meditate upon it.
Thus, one should neither become discouraged nor be unable to endure [the practice].
Since there is no distinction in the conceptualization regarding the auspicious and the inauspicious, he says:

"Emptiness is said to be characterized by the severance of the continuity of auspicious and inauspicious conceptualizations; emptiness is not considered to be anything other than the intellect. Thus it is stated.

Mental engagement (*manaskāra*) is the mental application (*cittābhoga*); having cast that aside through the realization of the illusion-like nature [of phenomena], there is no mental application toward the enjoyment of sense objects.
"Light" refers to the portion of night; the radiance of daylight is when the rays of the sun are clearly manifest.

These meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), characterized by time, are purified in body and so forth, such as the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and others; the meaning is that one effects entry into their innate state (*sahaja*). || 23 ||
"The prior limit is not known," said the Great Sage;
for saṃsāra is indeed without beginning or end, having neither a first nor a last, and since it has no beginning, how could it have a middle? Or an end?

Therefore, because of the statement, "In this regard, prior, posterior, and simultaneous sequences are not tenable," an entity that is neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, is produced without beginning or end; thus there is neither arising nor cessation,
nor passing away nor death, because all things culminate in emptiness.
These two preceding modes are equal by virtue of emptiness; that is,
the defiled states such as passion and so forth.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and so forth, which are the causes of purity for those engaged in service (*vaiyāvṛtyaka*), are non-existent in reality; thus,
the letter *a* is joined [as a prefix],
signifying *A*, the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*).

The meaning is "the beginningless Buddha. In reality, there are no objects to be awakened to; yet, because he has awakened [to this], he is called "Buddha. Thus, in order to dispel the doubt that those of dull intellect might fail to engage [with the teaching], he says: the Buddha is the bliss consisting of the single-moment perfect awakening previously mentioned and to be described hereafter, which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
As it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti*: "Neither beginning, nor end, nor middle; neither other, nor self—this is that supreme great bliss, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa."

The logical reason based on positive concomitance (*anvaya-hetu*) is refuted by [the evidence of] the action-seal (*karma-mudrā*), the knowledge-seal (*jñāna-mudrā*), and so forth, because it is not perceived at the stage of the fruit;
for his single eye consists of gnosis (*jñānamaya*), since he perceives the entire [reality] as luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Because even the conceptualization of pleasure is abandoned, he is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*) by virtue of having an innate body (*sahajaśarīra*).

Likewise, the ritual consorts (*karmāṅganā*) and so forth are such that they are the formless (*arūpa*) suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the Tathāgata is the bliss-gnosis (*sukhajñāna*), which is the purification of his objective field (*viṣayaviśuddhi*). This is because of the statement beginning with "And if he... (verse 24).

Just as the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśvara) generates joy in the world by the sound of the word *gharma*, so too [does this practice] through the unimpeded exhilaration arising from the consumption of the bliss of the *rakṣa* syllables, which gratifies the continuity of the mind.
Thus, in other cases, there is no cause for non-existence regarding the forms (*ākāra*) and so forth: *hūṃ* at the heart, *oṃ* at the throat, and *huṃ* at the great bliss [center].
Because these [elements] are not common [to others], he is to be honored;
as for the explanation of "the churning-stick" (*manthamanyānam*) and so forth,
it means that which nourishes all the sense organs and the elements such as earth.
Regarding what was said concerning the distancing from the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas and others by means of Mahāmudrā— namely, "he is superior even by way of his far-reaching intellect"—
it is his nature to speak of and to remain steadfast in non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*).

Speak! According to the principle that "for one whose perception is not directly perceived, the vision of an object is not established," and that "the Buddha's omniscience is spoken of only insofar as he follows after such conceptual construction," how much of the Sage of the Śākyas' knowledge can be said to be established? Furthermore, regarding the root *sthā* in the sense of stability: for one who does not perceive [an object] through direct perception, the seeing of an object is not proven; or rather, according to the logic of how far the Śākyamuni pursues that conceptual construction, his omniscience is thus described.

Beyond this, because there is no further reality (*tattva*), it is "supreme" (*variṣṭha*); "innate" (*sahaja*) and so forth refers to its arising within the mental continuum of others and others as well. Through the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the innate nature flashes forth in all things, and so forth. Because of the unity of body and so on within the *avadhūtī*, it is "unconquered" (*aparājita*) due to its non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*).
Alternatively, the relationship of cause and effect follows the sequence beginning with "Because he is the Lord of Speech, he is the best among speakers," and so forth. || 25 ||

Because of his universal auspiciousness, as it is said: "Homage to Samantabhadra, whose form is profound and vast, who has shaken off the web of conceptual construction, and whose radiance pervades everywhere"—
here, "radiance" refers to the teachings.
Regarding this, he says "attachment" and so forth.

Since it is stated that "beings are attached to signs," when there is an absence of an object of apprehension, there is non-dual emptiness; it is not an attachment to non-existence, because the teaching was given for that purpose.

The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated; thus, the retention of happiness is described as being "imperishable" (*akṣara*). It is said: "Even by the arrival of the undesired, one is not shaken"—this is the nature of *muditā* (sympathetic joy), which is "splendor" (*tejas*) and so forth.
The vision of Caṇḍālī that occurs within the body and in the sky is indeed the "recollection" (anusmṛti), because it is said: "From the union with recollection, the circle of light arises.
Since this is a perfect seeing of the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), it is called "Sudarśana" (the Good Vision).
He explains [the term] *sahaja* (innate) with the words beginning with "in the void" (*śūnye*) and so forth,

and [the term] *sakala* (with parts) and so forth; for it is the cause of the origin of the universe, the limit of existence (*bhūtakoti*), and unknowable by others, though it is spoken of as a "universal" (*jāti*) for the sake of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

That very Perfection of Wisdom is the seed of omniscience; because it is born from that, the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*)—such as hands marked with wheels—and the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), which are the manifestations of those marks, such as the *śrīvatsa* and the *svastika*, are present within the mind of a Buddha. *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* (The Elucidation of the Drops of Nectar).
It shines exceedingly because it dispels inner darkness and is thus uncommon to the sun and other luminaries;
he expresses this very point with the words beginning "ananta" (infinite),
for the vision of the four directions is indeed like that of the sun.
This Sahā world-system consists of a single unit composed of four quadrants of one hundred koṭis; it is "light" (*dīpti*) because it is thus illuminated,
and the wrathful kings have "radiant hands" (*bhābhāsura-karāḥ*) because they possess the splendor of the flames of the fire at the end of the aeon.
His splendor consists of that very pervasion;
thus he says: "He who assumes the terrifying form of Vajrabhairava, that glorious Yamāri brought fearlessness to those afraid of Bhairava.
May his awakening, which has conquered the hosts of Māra, lead to your abundant prosperity today! (26)
Regarding the passage beginning with "rāga" (passion) and so forth:

in order to eliminate passion and other such tainted states, he is the teacher of the non-deceptive medicine, as it is said: "We shall praise the supreme physician for the affliction of the great delusion and the defilements."
"To the Omniscient One, who knows the causes of the three realms, for the sake of the destruction of suffering.
Thus it was said: "Belonging to a self," and so forth—just as you [have taught] the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) yourself in the Mahāyāna.
"Likewise, out of compassion, that which was known has been taught to the wise. Thus,
by the "Remover of Arrows"—
the Wind-Lion (Pavanapañcānana)— even those roots of merit accumulated over a long time are destroyed by the thieves of conceptual construction.
As it has been said: "The fear of a multitude of thieves who seize my wealth arises here for me because of the absence of wealth;
since they steal the accumulated merit by means of the defects of vulgar conceptualization, they are like arrows because they cause such suffering."
Regarding what was said [in the verse]: "It is inexpressible"—when the Guru speaks of that state, the disciple does not understand it;
for the nectar of the innate (*sahaja*) is self-evident, and to whom in the entire world can it be described? To whom indeed? Thus it is said.

As for the remaining medicinal substances—such as flowers, fruits, roots, and bark—it is stated regarding those two [the moon and sun] that they are likewise: "They become great trees in the vast forests," and "They become great trees in the vast forests. O Mañjuśrī, the *Nāmasaṅgīti*... [regarding] "with fruit, with afflictions," and so forth.

As it has been said: "The rivers of afflictions, extending as far as their very root in latent impressions (vāsanā), have been conquered by you; and from the very nature of the afflictions, the nectar of immortality has been acquired. (27)

"Because of the statement: 'One who is possessed by the innate (*sahaja*) through the equal flavor (*samarasa*) of body and so forth, [and] from the eye on the forehead, is the Tilaka of the Three Worlds;

self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the vision of the triple world within the void,' the Beloved is the Union (*yuganaddha*), the non-dual gnosis of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-jñāna*); that is the Tathāgata."
The accomplishment of the ultimate reality is "Śrī" (Glory); by virtue of being joined with that, he is "Śrīmān" (the Glorious One).

Because he has expanded into the sky through his own nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which is self-cognized and luminous, the mandala of Vāgīśvara located below—resting upon the earth—is indeed the *uṣṇīṣa*, and so forth.
In the *Kālacakra-vṛtti-ṭīkā*,
regarding the passage beginning with "the great support" (*mahādhāra*) and so forth: by way of the tenfold nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*),
the five mandalas— consisting of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and the others— circulate within the left channel-passage (*vāma-puṭa*).
In the left channel-pouch, there are five forms of the elements beginning with earth;
thus, everything [is accounted for] in one hundred and sixty-two channels.

The twenty-seven constellations (nakṣatras) are the carriers of sixty ghaṭīs; thus, by dividing one thousand six hundred and twenty-two by sixty, the twenty-seven constellations are obtained, because each individual constellation possesses a duration of sixty [ghaṭīs].
In this manner, the purification of the number of deities within the body is brought forth in the *Kālacakra*.

From the cessation of this [central channel], through the cessation of the second and subsequent channels and the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, there arises the manifestation of the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) pervading the ten directions; its limit is the *paramārthabindu* (ultimate drop) itself, which is the Dharma. Because it possesses a great height (*mahān ucchayaḥ*) like a banner (*dhvaja*), he is the "Uṣṇīṣa-Eyed" (*uṣṇīṣanayanaḥ*). The triad of world, body, and so forth, being unified, constitutes the single limb of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Due to the commonality of removing the heat of the afflictions (*kleśatāpa*)—acting as a staff, an umbrella, and the uṣṇīṣa—he is the "Umbrella" (*chatra*). His hair-ends are vast due to their pervasive extension.

Through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which acts as the antidote to hatred, and through the light of the Caṇḍālī, what happiness could obstruct this birth? Thus, by means of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is nourishment; the practitioner of the *bodhicitta* takes their essence as the fruit.
Due to the swaying of the lotus, there is dancing, and likewise, through sovereignty.

The nature [of the Buddha] is like a jewel-handled parasol, because it possesses the perfection of bliss in all its limbs, and because it attains bodily coolness by warding off the burning of conceptual construction within the state of the precious vajra. 29.
Like a jewel-handled parasol.
Because it is free from obscuration through emptiness, he is the Great King of all phenomena; "father" means the sovereign,
and that very phenomenon is emptiness itself— the universal image whose nature is emptiness,
yet which is the existent form of the unified state (*yuganaddha*).

"Mahāyoga" refers to the savoring of the gnosis-body of all the Tathāgatas; for it is said, "The Blessed One Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, is indeed Mahāyoga," because there is no perception of difference and thus the identity of the aggregates and so forth. 30.

By which consecration even those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution are gathered through bliss— the consecration in the tantra consisting of wisdom and means described as "The Illumination of the Drop of Nectar"— it is said that glory (śrī) resides in the consecration within the vajra-jewel alone.

All [the goddesses] beginning with Locanā extend delight (*rati*), and thus they are "jewels" (*ratna*); their lords are the [Buddhas] beginning with Śāśvata; their sovereign is Vajrasattva. Because he brings about the light of gnosis for all, he is the "world" (*loka*)—referring to the Buddhas and others—and as their lord because he is their progenitor, he is the "Vajrin. Furthermore, because he is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is the cause of all phenomena, he is the "Lord" (*pati*).

All Vajradharas—Śāśvata, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya—are the fourth drop, the bodhicitta-vajra. Belonging to all the Buddhas, Mañjuśrī is the "Great Mind" because he is unimpeded; he is the "dissolution in the mind" because his nature is gnosis (*jñāna*). By directly realizing him alone, those [beings] become Buddhas; therefore, Mañjuśrī is the Gnosis-Body (*jñānakāya*) of all the Tathāgatas.

For the body of the Tathāgatas is indeed accumulated from the *dharmadhātu*, and it is clothed in the garment of the *bodhicitta*. Its greatness consists in the immersion within the nectar of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of those bodies and so forth belonging to the Buddhas of the three times; that river filled with such water is the ineffable Sarasvatī. It is called "Bhagavān," or else, by virtue of its emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and its infinite qualities, it is composed of all the Buddhas.

The river Sarasvatī of inconceivable bliss belongs to him; thus his perfection of self-interest (*svārthasaṃpatti*) is described, with the masculine gender and short vowel [of *sarasvatī*] occurring due to Vedic usage (*bhāṣātva*).

On his garment is the sun-dust (*sūryarajas*) of the diamond-jewel (*vajramaṇi*), which is the great light of the jewel of the cognition of Rāhu situated within [the center], pervading the three worlds.
Thus, regarding the stainless radiance of the moon situated upon the *uṣṇīṣa* of that [deity],
he states what was expressed by these two lines beginning with "sūrya": "Therefore, O King, the movement of the lunar nectar must be performed upward within the bliss."

[The state of] Madhu [is located] in the *ūrṇā* lotus of the sun-dust (*arka-rajas*) and the consciousness of Rāhu within the Imperishable (*akṣara*). [The state of] Pūrṇimā is the nectar of the Moon of all Buddhas.

[The state of] Amā is in the secret place (*guhya*) of the sun-dusts, and Kala is in the *uṣṇīṣa* and the jewel (*maṇi*) of those two. Thus, because it is said that "for all embodied beings, the Vajra-word is contrary to the treatises," he states that the Innate (*sahaja*) occurs at the beginning of Cessation (*virama*): "As long as the yogin does not effect the emission of the *bodhicitta*..."

One attains uninterrupted, supreme bliss in the *yoni*. One should constantly meditate upon one's own self as the image of the Buddha conjoined with that very form of bliss, until the semen becomes stable. Thus spoke the mouth of the Guru, beginning with the words "it has rained," and so forth.

When the universal image (*viśvabimba*) has been seen through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and stabilized through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one should daily perform the yoga of restraining the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) by means of breath retention (*kumbhaka*), until the wheel of rays (*raśmicakra*) is perceived. From the aforementioned image, it appears within oneself surrounded by one's own body.

Then, after six months, it becomes devoid of touch, free from the union of the two sense organs, and proceeds as the path-consciousness—the consciousness of the image of emptiness—which is the immutable bliss of equanimity.
For the ascetics who are beginners in the practice of celibacy,

from that moment of awakening in a single instant, there is the first instant that reaches the end of passion and the absence of passion; here, "passion" (rāga) refers to the white side (the waxing phase), and its culmination is the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, characterized by the sixteenth digit.

Non-attachment is black; its beginning is the black fortnight, which has not yet entered [the cycle]. At the moment of perfect awakening (*abhisaṃbodhi*), it increases even for a single instant (*kṣaṇa*). It increases from the number of breaths—counted as two thousand eight hundred—to thirty-six hundred vital energies (*prāṇa*) at the tip of the secret jewel (*vajramaṇi*). Having caused that same number of [breaths] to cease, one reaches the secret lotus (*guhyapadma*); by that, the two stages (*bhūmi*) are attained.
In this way, it reaches the navel, the heart, the throat, and the forehead;
by that, there are four, six, eight, and ten stages, up to the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), which makes twelve.
"By the destruction of all vital breaths"— therefore, it has come into the interior of the flame of Oḍḍiyāna, into the secret place,
between the *virāma* and the *sahaja*, at the navel.
Intent upon the flickering of sleep, within the heart— between knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*)—

that bliss which has come from the forehead in the form of the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, mind, and gnosis during the union of the couple, one should cause that semen-bliss to ascend by means of the guru’s instructions; it increases through the previously mentioned restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and there is nothing surprising in this as it reaches the forehead.

Having thus slain the afflictions (*kleśas*) and the Māras situated on the left and right, and having killed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the excellent yogin enters the empty image (*śūnyatābimba*) of the Lord of Victors (*jinapati*). Then, abiding in the *avadhūtī*, he generates the moment of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) by means of the vase-breath (*kumbhaka*) and increases that bliss; such is the rule.
He explains [the verse] beginning with "that which goes to the end of passion and dispassion" as follows:

And it is said, etc.: the fifteen digits (*kalā*) of the white fortnight are passion (*rāga*); at its end is the black digit, which is dispassion (*virāga*). At the beginning of that [black digit] is the innate (*sahaja*), the assembly (*samāja*) of all elements (*dhātu*), which is called the *saṃvara*.

The vajra and lotus are arisen; such is her cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*). Her element is body, speech, and mind; and through the collision of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*), there is the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*) upon the arising of Caṇḍālī.

Regarding this, it is said: "In the navel-mandala, the Caṇḍālī, with her ten subtle fingers, dances, clapping her hands. The word "body" (*kāya*) and so forth refers to that which holds sixteen, eight, four, and one drop (*bindu*).

"Vacca" means that by means of the shifting flow through the left and right channels, one observes the subtle *bodhicitta* within the lotus and the awakened *vajra-maṇi*, and thus experiences the bliss of *prabhāsvara*.
The root *budh* signifies "to understand"; thus, "buddha" refers to understanding.

Furthermore, "padma" means a lotus born from mud; externally it is a source of pleasure, while internally it is the *bhaga*-lotus. By virtue of this common characteristic (*sādharmya*), the *mahāmudrā* is here [referred to as] the lotus.
"Abandoned by the action-seal (karmamudrā), devoid of the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā),

and arisen from the great seal (mahāmudrā)— the innate (sahaja) is not with another. Because of this statement, "precisely through the perfection of cause and fruit," it consists of all aspects, having the form of the objects existing within the belly of the three realms and the three times.
Thus it is said: "Because he has reached the end of all phenomena.
This refers to his state of being a Tathāgata, which is mentioned as a secondary point (*prāsaṅgika*) because he has directly realized the intrinsic nature of the entire world.
The letter *Va* is the thunderbolt (*vajra*); at its tip is the crescent moon (*ardhacandra*), which is the dust of wisdom (*prajñā-rajas*).
In that context, the *bindu* is the *bodhicitta* endowed with great bliss; the upward ray of light from it is the *nāda*, which is the syllable *vaṃ*. It is said to be the universe.

The enjoyment of the five desires of the syllable is the connection to the radiance of the drop of nectar (*amṛta-kaṇikā*). Because he sustains both *māyā* and the universal *māyā*, he is the *bodhicitta-vajra*; and because he shines as a blazing flame, he is the King.
The four drops located at the *ūrṇā* and other places are the purification of Tārā and the others;
for this very reason, because the great fruit has been attained, he states the fourfold fruit beginning with "the ears," and so forth.
On the forehead is the Vajravatī, sharp because it pierces the four wheels.
As it has been said: "I am the indestructible penetration, because I crush all that is evil; I am the Vajra of all Buddhas, I am the firm Bodhicitta."
In the navel is Mahākhaṅga; in the throat is Viśuddha, because it is the cause of stainlessness;
in the heart is Vipāka, which is distinguished by the ripening of all phenomena into a single essence; and [in the head] is Paramākṣara.
That by which one goes is the *yāna* (vehicle); its greatness consists in cutting through the suffering that has been explained.
Because it is said: "The Great Weapon is Jinajig Vajrasattva because he severs the bonds of existence; the Wisdom-Knowledge of the Buddhas is known as the heart of Jinajig."
And he says that this [Buddha] has emptiness as his form, beginning with the word "Vimala" (Stainless).

His profundity consists in the fact that, although he is a mine of all the jewels of qualities, he is not perceived as having the nature of an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) and so forth; as it is said: "The depth of the salt ocean becomes like the shallowness of a cow's footprint when your unfathomable and boundless intellectual profundity is observed."

As it is said: "Just as the notion of cloth [is absent] at the tip of a gem, and the mind is without mind, so too the object is empty; thus the Buddhas perceive phenomena through their investigation. (36) Because merit precedes giving, it is called "prior," and so forth.

This too is to be understood through the following sequence: "The perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) is said to be the application of the mind toward the renunciation of all possessions at the proper time; therefore, it is indeed the mind itself.
Because they serve as the basis for consciousness, these are known as the stages (bhūmis) of knowledge.
Or [it is called] *viśeṣa* because it possesses the ten ornaments (*daśavibhūṣaṇa*).
Regarding the term "pure" (*viśuddha*) and so forth: all phenomena (*dharma*) are pure by their very nature (*prakṛti-upaśuddhatvāt*).

Because it penetrates them with the mind (*cittena prativedhāt*), its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, its essential knowledge (*svarūpa-jñāna*)—is the "characteristic of mental penetration" (*cittaprativedhalakṣaṇa*).

The non-apprehension of that selflessness, which is its rendering free from appearances, is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the nature of emptiness; because it is unobscured, it is luminous by nature. The Blessed One, whose form is like the moonlight of innate bliss born from that [nature], is thus described. 37.
Through the union of the moon and sun within the *avadhūtī*,
there arises for him a great exertion for the sake of the sign of the innate nature (*sahaja*) of the three realms;
this is the beginning of the *Yoginītantra* and so forth.

"Of that very one" refers to Mañjuśrī. "Beyond that" means after that, because of its non-existence due to obstruction—that is, cessation—it has been said in the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "When the prāṇa and apāna are obstructed, the moon (the drop) is agitated and enters the solar disc; when the vajra is awakened, it flows again by the rays of the solar disc."

Consciousness and gnosis become one with the wind when the moon and sun are indeed obstructed; in this way, in that way, and likewise in various other ways it may come to be, yet there is nothing else whatsoever.
Thus, the gnosis itself is the body of all Buddhas of the three times without exception. (38)

Because it is pure through the complete pacification of all activity on every side, [the text says] "existence" (*bhava*) and so forth; and while such conceptual constructions as "all" and so forth exist,
there are those [states] beginning with "the earth" (*kṣiti*).

While innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) alone exists, from the semen and ovum of the mother and father, the birth of earth and the other elements occurs; from that [arises] the body composed of the five elements (*pañcabhautika*).
Precisely because it is the cause of earth and the rest, even for that which has been born, "the support of the world is by this very form of luminosity" (*prabhāsvara*);
thus he says: "Earth is established in water, water in wind, and wind in space."
"Space is non-abiding within the elements of wind, water, and earth"—
this statement beginning with "all," etc.,
is the seed for those things that will arise through the practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth.
As it is said: "When one has abandoned the innate (*sahaja*) and meditated upon nirvāṇa, that single ultimate reality is realized.
Thus, according to the descriptions of various disciples and so forth, he manifests as the radiation of the wheel of various deities.
By the words beginning with "śukra," the sequence of the fivefold clear realization (pañcākārābhisambodhi) is indicated:
the emanation body is external, while one's own [body] is internal. || 39 ||
Since it is said that "the purity of all phenomena is indeed remembered as suchness," it is pure, empty,
and supreme because it transcends the world.
Because the cessation of the dissolution of bodies is merely a negation and thus non-dual, nevertheless, the nature of the emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) is indeed selflessness;

their reality is non-arising. Their "dharma" is their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), meaning that which is sought or requested, just as [the Buddha] spoke of awakening as "knowledge of things as they truly are": "There is nothing to be removed from this, nor anything at all to be added."
"The real must be seen as it truly is; he who sees the real is liberated. (40)
The moment of death is the fourth [joy] entered into the innate (*sahaja*); even the joys beginning with *ānanda* would be untainted (*anāsrava*),
as in the passage beginning with "the thunderbolt" (*dambholi*).
Because it is said, "One should expand the stable jewel," that which has attained stability is bathed by the bodhicitta heard from the tip of the *vajra*.

From the pure lotus, the innate (*sahaja*) sprout is born; through the movement of the seed, it is nourished by the five elements. That very thing is described as the fourth [empowerment] in the form of a grain; when fully ripened, it becomes manifest. This is not taught even to a scholar, for it is not within their domain; it is known by oneself through merit, as it is said in the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*: "By serving the lineage of gurus."

By virtue of their introductory context, "dharmas" refers to the breaths because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); their cessation within the *avadhūtī* by means of great bliss has been stated: "Through the awakening of the true guru, the wind is restrained by the cessation of the movement of the unblinking eyes."
All phenomena are comprised of the three qualities beginning with *sattva*;
these are nothing other than body, speech, and mind.
Since he experiences them as having the nature of the innate (*sahaja*), he is described in the root text as "the Real" (*bhūta*), and so forth.
Suchness is threefold: stained in ordinary beings, stainless in masters, and immaculate in perfectly awakened ones; it is the state of fruition, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"Meditation upon that" means immersion into it;
"one with supreme intellect" means one whose mind has entered into the jewel. (41)

"Stimite" (in the motionless state) means having withdrawn all discursive thought from every direction, being sprinkled with the nectar of the innate (*sahaja*), resembling the cloudless midday sky of autumn, with all mental impressions (*bhāvollekha*) vanished on all sides; through such meditative absorption (*samādhi*)— namely, the effortless flow of signless absorption (*nirnimittānābhogavāhisamādhi*)— he is the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) whose mind resides within the diamond-jewel (*vajramaṇi*) at the end of the "Immovable" (*acalā*) stage.
Because that [reality] is luminous, it is awakening; its bearer is self-cognizable, and so forth.
For the perfectly awakened ones are fond of the innate (*sahaja*), and since this [bearer] is of that nature, he is their direct witness.

By means of non-referential knowledge (*nirālambajñāna*), some person perceives only the object situated directly in front, and not even that which lies behind it; yet when that [obstructing object] is removed, even something further away becomes visible.
According to this principle—that vision extends as obstacles are removed—the mind, being without support, beholds the infinite.

When the mind, from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) onwards, has rendered the sixfold group beginning with the aggregates free from appearance through the arising of *manobhava*, it performs a discernment of forty-two [points] by means of these seven; thus, this is called the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). || 42 ||
The Wisdom of Discernment.
The knowledge of equality [regarding] "suffering" (as it is).

Regarding the three—pleasant, unpleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which are dependently originated and in reality devoid of both the felt and the feeler, the knowledge that rests upon them as mere consciousness is the "knowledge of their equality. Because they are objects through association, appearing like a closed fist, they are without obscuration. As it has been said: "The aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, objects, organs of action, and activities—each one constitutes the fivefold mandala of existence. By the sequence of the upward gaze, there are five on the left and five joined with the right; by virtue of their transition, O Sage, there is a sevenfold division according to the flow of the wheels."

In the *Bodhyaṅgakusumavyākhyāna*, when the aggregates, elements, and so forth have been consumed, and the flow of the five maṇḍalas has ceased, and when the objects and sense faculties have been obstructed, he is called Ratnasambhava because he arises from the Vajra-jewel;
the meaning is that the fruit, which is the supreme unchanging gnosis (paramākṣarajñāna), is sought through the performance of all desired activities.
Its cause is the innate (*sahaja*).
He says that very thing: "Because it is supreme as the three drops (*bindu*) beginning with bliss, it is the 'Supreme' (*para*).

By means of the emptiness of all phenomena alone, through the cutting off of the latent tendencies of existence (*bhava-vāsanā*), it reveals the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). Since there is nothing other than the [three] bodies and so forth, Mañjuśrī is supreme over them, being of the nature of the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the others.
Because he is the very embodiment of gnosis (jñānakāya), the Lord is not destroyed by fear;
Mahāmudrā is the luminosity, like a lotus because of its delight, and the Innate (sahaja) is that which illuminates it. || 1 ||

How can this one hero fight alone against the afflictions? Because he cuts through the afflictions with the weapon of wisdom for those whose conduct is dominated by passion and the like, he is called a "single hero" (*śūraika*); the inversion of the word order is due to Vedic usage. From delusion alone does the fall, which is itself of the nature of delusion, arise.

And that wisdom (*prajñā*) or intellect (*dhī*), which— by means of the conceptualization of the grasped and so forth— realizes their selflessness and is innate, having abandoned all conceptual constructions, becomes supreme when the mind, due to the causes of afflictions and the like, reaches the state of non-mind (*acittatva*).
The innate cause is semen; it is called "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*) because it is the cause of passion (*śṛṅgāra*).
When it flows downward from the *uṣṇīṣa*, it is mundane; when it moves upward through the reversal [of the flow], it is supramundane.

It is "compassion" (*karuṇā*) by virtue of its nature as the essence of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), for it obstructs (*ruṇaddhi*) pleasure (*kaṃ*)—that is, bliss—due to its quality of non-agitation (*vigateraṇatvāt*).

Through the realization of the emptiness of all phenomena, by virtue of the equality of the beautiful and the ugly, he possesses the aesthetic sentiment of the repulsive (bībhatsa-rasa) through the ornaments of the [four] postures and so forth; he is the bearer of that non-dual great bliss. || 2 ||

From "carrying" (*vahana*) comes "the carrier" (*vaha*); rising like a staff, it is a "staff" (*daṇḍa*) due to the movement through the two nostrils; through its transition and infinity, it is the "parasol" (*chatra*).

Because of its casting into the center of that [parasol], by being deposited in the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), there is "dancing" (*narttana*)—that is, an exhilaration (*ullāsa*)—due to its absorption;
and because of the cessation of internal breath, there is the vastness of the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) of the radiance of non-dual knowledge (*advayajñāna*) from the end.
In the absence of all phenomena, only space exists as the pervasive;
therein lies the manifestation of this luminous gnosis. || 3 ||

The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* states: "At the time of death for all embodied beings, the lunar nectar (*candrāmṛta*) goes downward and the sun (*divākara*) goes upward. To eliminate such defects, the *bodhicitta* which resides at the tip of the *vajra* below the navel is stabilized through an incomparable foundation;

by means of this [stabilization], the supportless form of emptiness is called the "mountain" (*mahīdhara*), because the semen itself is the seed (*bīja*) due to its similarity to the act of holding [the mountain].

Regarding its mandala, which is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), he states the second term— beginning with "Brahma"— to indicate that the state situated therein has been stabilized by this [practice] through an uncommon establishment. This [state] is situated in the *bodhicitta* when the semen, having emerged from the tip of the vajra, reaches as far as the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*).
"One" and so forth—
this is not all that he says; the meaning of that is "the sustainer" and so forth, which is clear,
[referring to] that which consists of the prior arising of *kāmakalā*.

First, at the outset, is the *kāmakalā*, the digit of the first day of the waxing moon; its nature is the arising of the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*). In this regard, it is said that the Blessed One, the Body of Gnosis (*jñānakāya*), who has feet venerated by the three realms and consists of the six elements in the form of the six channels—upward, downward, and transverse—is the white *hūṃ* syllable belonging to the dark fortnight.

Because that which consists of existence is unobscured, he has pervaded both the full moon and the new moon by means of his two feet—which consist of the fifteen voids and compassions, have the nature of the moon and sun, and obstruct the paths of cyclic existence and nirvāṇa.
Thus, the verse beginning with *prāṇāyāma* has been explained in the commentary on the first stanza. (4)

The single breath-bind occurs through the state of emptiness when the left and right breaths do not enter the center; because of the absence of duality, it is the Dharmakāya whose meaning is the non-dual Dharma,
and due to the non-apprehension of all things, there is an absence of attachment.
The drop of meditative concentration equal to space is the great drop, the signless of all visions; because it possesses nothing, it is indestructible.
Thus it is said: "That intrinsic nature which is cultivated through the path is eternal and does not perish."
Established by way of its own nature.
Who is capable of exhausting the power or the lack of power of that which is incurable through the doctrine of eternality?

Thus, because it is said that "supreme sovereignty is attained upon the revolution of the basis of all," the Form Body (*rūpakāya*), consisting of the eight consciousnesses, is perceived; yet its true nature (*dharmatā*) is precisely this [revolution].

As it has been said: "When the Son of the Victor has realized this true nature (*dharmatā*) and is free from conceptual expansion, it appears as a marvel to those blinded by ignorance amidst birth and the rest.
Thus, the mind—which was accumulated through the latencies of all conceptual constructions—is now a non-conceptual, unaccumulated mind.
What does compassion obstruct? It means that it is the continuity of emptiness and compassion. || 5 ||

As it is said: "The ultimate realities are the very non-existence of both external and internal [phenomena], empty by virtue of their luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). Delight in them would cause one to become, in an instant, a single form with heaven, the mortal world, and the underworld.
One cannot be awakened by the conceptualization of self and other. Thus.
The *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti* states "this" (*etad*) and so forth to explain the production of delight: those objects such as form and sound are merely ancient and mundane (*prākṛta*),
and the moments of engagement such as visual consciousness and the rest are likewise [mundane].

The power and vigor of the senses in grasping their objects are themselves the seeds of the afflictions in the form of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); yet for us, the instruction of the true guru is venerable.

By its power, we realize at every moment that this very service is our essence; thus, it is said in experience that these [afflictions] themselves spontaneously touch and flow as the nectar of reality—the continuity of non-conceptual compassion—which is marvelous.
Since the nature of the mind is luminosity, having realized emptiness, there is his delight in the uncontrived nature of phenomena; this is the "limit of both" (*ubhayānta*).
"Existence itself is the end of eternity, for even from annihilation there is no liberation; thus, knowing that false view is the cause of hell, one does not fall [into it].
Existence is said to be supreme bliss" (Hevajra-tantra 1.8.34). According to such statements, passion (*rāga*) is the nature of the manifestation of light.

For one who has transcended the passion for existence (*bhavarāga*) and so forth during the simultaneous entry (*sahajapraveśa*)— due to the perception of that intermediate passion which is the light of dispassion (*virāga*)—

there is for him a great supramundane delight (*lokottarā rati*), because the body and so forth of those who have entered the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), though bearing other names such as "light" (*āloka*), are untainted (*anāsrava*). || 6 ||
Ignorance is the omnipresent affliction; upon its disappearance, there is the disappearance of all obscurations.
For the essence of purified earth and the other elements is indeed the bodhicitta, white like an autumn cloud.
Because it was previously stated [in the passage] beginning with "That very [nature] is the innate (*sahaja*), the thirty-two marks of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)," and so forth,

[it follows that] "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) and so on— up to "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*)— are indeed habitual tendencies, and in the innate state, there is the cessation of all conceptual constructions.
By the statement, "Through the friction of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, because of being mixed with the seminal essence of wisdom (*prajñā-retas*), there is great passion (*mahārāga*);
may I become a consumer of the woman's semen in birth after birth," it indicates the arising of the fourth [empowerment] even without a *karmamudrā*.
The passion (*rāga*) manifested in the mouth of the Blessed One as "innate" (*sahaja*) and so forth was employed;
by that, the arising of ignorance (*ajñāna*) was dispelled for the one whose self is the sole abode of his own [nature].
"Your passion has fallen at the soles of your feet for the very purpose of [inspiring] serene faith. || 7 ||
He speaks of its internal purity with the words beginning "Mahāsukha" and so forth, which are easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "the month is pure" and so forth, it is because one who has a black body possesses a mind of loving-kindness (*maitra*); this is according to the purification (*viśuddhi*) taught in the *Śrī Hevajra*.

"Mahāvyomanīlam" means that the *bodhicitta* is like a blue rod (*daṇḍaka*)—blue within and resembling pure mercury (*pārada*) on the outside—and it is an *indranīla* gem; its "peak" is the great bliss of its own nature (*svarūpa-mahāsukha*), because it is said that the nature of the mind is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).

Its "excellent garment" (*cīra*) is its crest (*cūḍā*), due to the similarity of its upward movement; it is one whose "garment of splendor" (*tejaścīra*) is such that these [flames] are like collyrium (*añjana*) and form a series of breaking waves.
As it is said:
"The fuel of the afflictions is seen by the fire of wisdom like a mere line on a tree"— thus it is maintained.

Because the nature of the crooked [elements] beginning with Nirṛti has been purified, from the crooked [hair], like the tips of great blue locks, the Akṣobhya-s are [emitted] from the uṣṇīṣa; because the vital wind (prāṇavāyu) pervades all limbs and has emerged, it is blue, hence "blue" and so forth. Being himself empty, he "covers" (ruṇaddhi) the garment of bliss; thus Karuṇā is Akṣobhya, and that very Great Bliss (mahāsukha), because it maintains its own characteristic, is Dharma—meaning he takes that as his object as far as space extends. "Earth," and so forth.

Because it is stated that "the earth is indeed in the heart, a connection shining with drops of nectar, square on all sides," [the light] has emerged from the earth of the heart; thus, like a yellow jewel-cluster, it is yellow. Or, because of its yellow color, it possesses the glory of rays like a great sage.
Or, the glory of its rays has arisen, expanding forth from the tip of this great gem of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Alternatively, by the passage beginning with "bliss is the boat" (*sukhaṃ potam*), the colors of the five Jinas are described.
This is the illustration for the verse beginning with "pure," "white," and so forth;
for this very reason, semen (*śukra*) is also fivefold, as it has been said: "It is thin and thick, red, yellow, and blue."
The five-element Śakra is taught as the last [member] of the Cakravartin.

The color of his [the Buddha's] son and of the former [disciples] is yellow; that of the others is red. That of his ministers and so forth is thick, while that of those with incomplete faculties, such as women, those whose wings are severed, and those whose eyes are unripe, is thin. Thus it is said.
Because there is no differentiation due to its all-pervasive luminosity, [one perceives] "I am the world" as the aspect of bliss;
since the entire universe (*jagadviśva*) is a transformation of the five elements, it is the innate form (*sahajarūpa*).

The manifestation of the nature of a Buddha consists precisely in bringing about the state of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāṇām*) being composed of bliss, starting with the realization "I am a Buddha," and so forth. (8)
Because it also generates bliss even for those in the meditative absorption of great bliss (*mahāsukha-samādhi*), he says "innate" (*sahaja*) and so forth;
this is clear.
The miraculous power (*ṛddhi*) is the pervasion of the four bodies of meditative absorption.

"Because it is said: 'In the void, knowledge becomes intermingled, attaining a state of equal flavor (samarasa), imperishable and eternal,' one should always maintain the mindfulness of immersion in the universal image (viśvabimba),
and so forth— just as the burning of iron is extinguished when the [blowpipe] is not seen, and the darkness [is dispelled]."
When the mind has become the Buddha-mind through wisdom, existence perishes.
Because its characteristic is cessation (*nivṛtti*), it is not a [positive] entity (*bhāva*); because it exists as tranquility (*śānti*), it is not a non-entity (*abhāva*).

Regarding the mind (*citta*), gnosis (*jñāna*), non-mind (*acetas*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and liberation (*vimukti*), reality (*tattva*) is equal in both entity and non-entity, according to such statements as: "But if that [cessation] is an entity, then it is this [non-entity]," and so forth. Thus, reality is equal in respect to both existence and non-existence.

Regarding the passage beginning with "hasita" (laughter) and so forth: since the gods of desire (*kāmadeva*) sport by remaining in the states of laughter, hand-holding, embracing in pairs, and sexual union,
the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as *ānanda* arise through the purification of those very states.
As it has been said: "The laughter, the side-long glances, and the beautiful form—these are the *halāhala* poison;
the union with Śrī, Saṃvara, and the rest is the [remedy]."
Through the purification of this, by means of the yoga of Kriyā, Caryā, and Yoga, all these unsurpassed tantras have been revealed by Mañjuśrī. || 9 ||

The six elements, earth and so forth, purified as Vairocana and the others, mixed with great bliss, are seven; alternatively, they are the six tastes, sweet and so forth, which through their maturation and coagulation become the state of "flavor" (*rasatā*);
thus, in this sequence, there are the seven revolutions beginning with blood.

The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti* [states]: because they possess that very nature, the seven drops situated in the tip of the jewel, the wheel, and so forth, are the flowers of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). The exultation of the great bliss produced by them is taught in the *Saṃvara-tantra* and other texts: "One should consume the seven revolutions. The meaning of this is precisely the prevention of their emission.
It is said: "Consciousness and the rest are always on the left; earth and the rest are on the right, in succession."

When the flow of the aggregates beginning with consciousness and the elements beginning with earth has ceased, and the sense objects, faculties, and so forth are restrained, the syllable *HŪṂ*— Vajrasattva— abides in great bliss through the sequence of joy and the rest, and drips down drops;
these [drops] are Amoghasiddhi in the moon at the forehead.
Ratnasambhava is in the sun at the throat;
Amitābha is in the Dharma-wheel at the heart; and Vairocana is seated upon the fire of Caṇḍālī at the navel.

In the secret place that effects the digestion of food, the drop (*bindu*), having become the great sacrificial animal, enters the *rata-kuṇḍa*. It does not go into the channels of feces and so forth by means of the three-pronged [vajra], but rather where the moon is at the tip of the jewel, Akṣobhya is to be consumed through reversal;
the seven-fold whirling drop itself, in due order, bestows the siddhi of moving through the sky.

As for the sequence: through the friction of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, it becomes swooned and removes disease; when "melted" (*jārita*), it removes the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth; through transformation, it grants a state like illusion and the sovereignty over the wheel of the earth.
Having brought about the union of the sense objects and the senses, [the vital breath] when killed bestows the power of moving through the air (*khecaratva*).

When it is repeatedly restrained within the channels through the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of waking, dreaming, and so forth, endowed with qualities such as atomicity (*aṇimā*), it bestows Buddhahood.

Just as mercury bound externally to the body transforms copper and other metals into gold and the like, so too does the essence of knowledge (*jñānarasa*) bring about the accomplishment that removes all suffering.

The semen situated in the wheel of bliss is Brahmā; that very same [semen], when it has entered the secret place, pervades the body with bliss and is thus Viṣṇu. It bestows a vast lifespan until the end of the kalpa. Rāhu is in the middle and above; the breaths in the left and right nostrils are the Moon and Sun. When these, having begun from the middle, fall downward, they grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation. The "falling" and "digestion" (*jāraṇā*) of blood and the other [elements] is the ultimate reality. These alone are the sacrificial animals; external embodied beings such as cows and the like are not to be offered.
He explains what has been described by means of eating, drinking, and so forth: the phrase beginning with "seven births" and so on is easy to understand.
"Sixfold" refers to the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasāḥ*). *Avadhūtī* and *dharmodayā*; therefore, they are the source of all the qualities of a Buddha (*sarvabuddhadharmodayāḥ*).
Upon the cessation of the winds, having reached the respective stages through the state of a Tathāgata, the Tathāgata— beginning with "all" and so forth—
abiding in the stages such as Muditā (Joy) and so forth, is "exalted" and so forth, benefiting existence and acting for the sake of sentient beings.
Through the sequence of the *Samāja* and other tantras, he carries the mandala of space contained within earth and the other elements.

When the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is being taken as the object of focus—according to the instruction beginning with "the intermediate space is the windless wind"—the conceptual winds dissolve, and thus he becomes self-arisen; one who possesses that is "the Self-Arisen One" (*svayaṃbhū*). || 10 ||

"Of all," and so forth; for one engaged in the welfare of sentient beings, "bodhicitta" means that attachment to all sentient beings, great compassion, and delusion regarding what is to be done are not to be prevented.
"Free from attachment" means having emerged from attachment, for a sky-flower does not attach itself anywhere.
Therefore, because it is free from conceptual construction, this mind-born [phenomenon] is like space; thus, by its very nature, sentient beings possess luminosity.
Since whatever deity one has devotion for appears accordingly therein, the "impulse" (java) or speed in the mind is present at that very moment.
As it has been said: "By means of non-reliant gnosis, you behold all fields and indeed the conduct of all sentient beings; O you who are without support, homage be to you! (11)

The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* [states]: The sense faculties, such as the dull [faculties] and so forth, and the practice with conceptual proliferation (*saprapañcacaryā*)—such as the enjoyment of the five objects of desire in various ways like the noble Indrabhūti—are surpassed by the single [practice] which, through wisdom (*prajñā*), is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

Being entirely indifferent and utterly beyond conceptual proliferation, it renders the mind free from appearances (*nirābhāsīkaroti*) by means of the realization of non-selfhood (*anātmya*) regarding all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), whether wholesome or unwholesome.
"By means of the vajra" refers to gnosis;
the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is Vairocana, who is contained within the head.
The mirror-like cognition (ādarśajñāna) is Vairocana; the mirror located therein is Yamāntaka on the right arm. Locanā is the earth element; the eye-faculty is Kṣitigarbha in that very place.
Form is Rūpavajrā in the eyes.
The fifth, the aggregate of consciousness, is Akṣobhya; Acala is the wrathful deity on the right side;
and Maitreya is at the mouth of the Avadhūtī—thus is the entry into the clear light described.
"Arising from the luminous clarity" means that for those aggregates, the very state of arising from the luminous clarity is itself purity; he who bears that [purity] is "pure. || 12 ||

He abides in the excellence of the deliverance of all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Samyaksambuddhas; thus, because he experiences the bliss of selflessness, it is said that those who wish to train even on the level of a Śrāvaka, the level of a Pratyekabuddha, or the level of a Bodhisattva must train in this very Perfection of Wisdom. Therefore, for the sake of favoring those of the various lineages beginning with the Śrāvakas, he stands upon the path of all forms of deliverance.
"Since no phenomenon exists apart from the dharmadhātu, as it has been said, this is the dharma of the body of great bliss. || 13 ||
Ignorance and the rest [are so called] because of covering, planting, leading, grasping, filling, threefold discrimination, experiencing, and drawing forth.

"Because of bondage, because of facing [suffering], and because of the infliction of pain, the world is afflicted. (MAV 1.11–12) The world is afflicted by the obscuration of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) through ignorance (*avidyā*), and so on, up to the infliction of pain by old age and death.

However, upon the arising of knowledge, there is the cessation of ignorance; from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the formative forces, and so on, up to the cessation of birth, which leads to the cessation of old age and death.
And it has been said: "O you who desire liberation, uproot the view of a self (sattvadṛṣṭi).
By means of the *pīṭhas* and so forth, he states the cause of knowledge: the secret *parapīṭha* and the *ātmapīṭha*, which is the wheel of bliss (*sukhacakra*);
the union of these two occurs through the central aperture (*madhyārandhra*).
From that, the innate (sahaja) which is free from objective apprehension and inexpressible is born;
by this much, the pīṭhas and so forth become manifest.
Thus, the channels located in the pīṭhas and other sites are filled with the bodhicitta.
It is said that the "innate cause" consists of the twelve sense bases; namely, the six faculties beginning with the eye and the six objects beginning with form.
Regarding the phrase "by nature" and so forth, even pleasure that arises from the nature of passion becomes suffering through transformation.
Furthermore, because the fourth [truth] consists of the nature of cessation (*cyuti*), the truth of suffering is called "origination" (*samudaya*). As it is said:
"Lust, hatred, and delusion are declared to originate from conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*);
for they arise dependently upon the errors regarding the beautiful and the ugly. Thus it is stated.

The *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: In the entry into the co-emergent (*sahaja*), there is the cessation of the nature of body and so forth, as well as time and so forth; this is "cessation," which is bliss.
Through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), when the mind is without support, that universal image (*viśvabimba*) which shines forth is the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

That which has the non-duality of the four truths—suffering and so forth—as its aspect, and which consists of the eight cognitions regarding the four moments characterized by variety, maturation, destruction, and the distinct [nature], as well as the four fruits of natural outflow, maturation, human effort, and the fruit of purification—that is the Great Nirvāṇa. (14)
Because of the "three qualities" (traiguṇya) which will be explained later, he says "there, the body," etc.;
the differentiation of the hundred families is the non-discrimination of effects previously practiced.
Vajra-recitation is the isolation of speech;
the contemplation of the mind is the isolation of the mind. Its natural outflow is the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The maturation fruit of entering the three natures—the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected—is the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The result of the light, its appearance, the perception thereof, and the human effort of meditative concentration is the *dharmakāya*;
the result of the purification of bliss and so forth is the *jñānakāya*.
These constitute the twelvefold divisions, beginning with the differentiation of the bodies (*kāyaviveka*) and their natural outflows (*niṣyanda*).
Due to the cessation of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) or the cessation of the fire element (tejodhātu),
the sixteen-fold digits (kalās) themselves— arising from the cessation of the semen— are the sixteenfold reality;
the six odd signs beginning with Aries (meṣa) transit into the left nostril.
The six [signs] beginning with Taurus are conjoined with the left channel;

through the cessation of the twelve transits of day and night, there is the attainment of the twelve stages (*bhūmi*). The lunar digits (*kalā*) beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) are of the nature of emission and belong to the realm of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

Having caused [the winds] to enter the *avadhūtī*, there occurs the purification of the consciousness-aggregates (*vijñāna-skandha*) and so forth that flow through the mandalas of space and the other elements, as well as the elemental constituents (*dhātu*) that flow through the mandalas of earth and the others; therein lies the purification of the sense-faculties such as the eyes and the sense-bases (*āyatana*) such as form, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because they are realized in that very aspect.
As it is said: "One is awakened from the night of delusion by means of the breath;
one is awakened through the joy of realization."

Regarding the passage beginning with "sarva," it says: "In every place, from every source, everything, in every way, at all times, and by himself— he sees his own self as established as being entirely composed of the Buddha."
The Supreme [state] arises precisely from the realization of non-duality. || 15 ||

Because of his great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he does not conceptualize even for a single moment the limit of the bodies of the Buddha’s emanations—which are non-dual with the nirvāṇa of all phenomena—and the inhalation and exhalation of this village of existents; rather, by investigating through emptiness at every breath and so forth, he likewise knows the simultaneity of all moments of consciousness. 16.
The passage beginning with "by the method of the various vehicles" is clear;

as for "knowledge," etc., it refers to the Knowledge Body (jñānakāya) that has emerged from the Body Wheel (kāyacakra) located at the forehead and other places; the syllable *ha* signifies the meaning of the syllable *ra*. || 17 ||

Because he has destroyed ignorance, he is the "Eye"; because he is of the nature of the light of wisdom which is its antidote, he is the pure form of those elements—the bones and so forth—which produce the afflictions;
he brings to an end both sinful and meritorious karma through non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpaka-samādhi*);
and as the embodiment of all things, he has crossed over the oceans of the very views of [false] knowledge.

Through the cessation of all inherent natures (*prakṛti*), and since these inherent natures have been explained in the *Cittanidhyapti*, [it is said]: "The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* states: detachment is indeed moderate and likewise intense."
Likewise, the three consisting of the mind’s coming and going, and sorrow.
Discrimination is gentle, as well as moderate fear and extreme fear;
craving is moderate craving and excessive craving, and grasping is likewise.
