The unwholesome, hunger and thirst, sensation, equal sensation, excessive sensation, the moment, and the state of piercing and being pierced.
Discernment is like modesty, compassion arises from affection— these three, along with apprehension,
accumulation, and envy, are proclaimed as the thirty-three innate dispositions of embodied beings that are self-evident. Thus it is said.
Passion, the impassioned, as well as exhilaration, joy, contentment, moderate contentment, extreme contentment, wonder, and laughter; |||
Delightful embracing, as well as fortitude, heroism, pride, enthusiasm, daring, kissing, and sucking;
the powers of the doer and the taker; likewise, the highest daring, middling daring, the fierce, the playful, and even enmity.
Auspiciousness, clarity of speech, truth, falsehood, and likewise certainty;
non-clinging, the state of not giving, weeping, and likewise sexual pleasure.

The shameless, the rogue, the wicked, the deceitful, and the crooked—these are the forty types of characters; as well as those of momentary passion, the momentary, and those born of extreme emptiness.
Forgetfulness, as well as delusion, silence, weariness, laziness, and sluggishness.

"O Śruti, the seven moments of ignorance should be known by yogis. Thus, due to the application of the left and right [channels] toward the object through the suffering of yoga, those very [moments] are difficult to cross because they consist of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Having emerged from them, by means of the "arrow-like" samādhi (*vastrōpama-samādhi*) which uproots the entire web of conceptual constructions, the attainment of pure consciousness alone is designated as "yoga. || 18 ||

Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti: Then, through non-mental engagement with signs, there are the six root afflictions (*kleśa*) beginning with attachment, and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) beginning with anger; these indeed are the defilements (*saṃkleśa*), because they thoroughly and firmly establish the latencies (*vāsanā*) and so forth by way of defiling the mind.
Therefore, in any other interpretation, the compound would be difficult to justify.

By means of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) which serves as its skillful means (*upāya*), and by means of that effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) caused by them, he accomplishes the welfare of the world fruitfully and not in vain. || 19 ||

The meaning [of this] is that it is devoid and free even from such designations as "meditative absorption" (samādhi) and "attainment" (samāpatti). Its apprehension—that is, the act of grasping—is manifestly distinct;
it is the innate (sahaja), which is the object of the minds of all sentient beings insofar as it is to be experienced by those who are capable.

Because of their congenital blindness regarding the vision of emptiness, this [emptiness] is either not the domain of all sentient beings, or it is the movement of the mind and the sphere of experience for all sentient beings, or it is not their movement. 20.

"By way of being the nature of the *dharmadhātu*": because it provides space through the mind which is like the sky, its nature is that of light, according to the statement: "In the center of the heart is the *anāhata*, resembling a blazing lamp."

Since it is said that the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of Subhūti, and the suchness of ordinary beings are one and the same, he has attained equality; thus, for him, all grasping at entities and all objects have ceased in the form of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). For all fortunate ones, the arising of the gnosis of great bliss—which has dawned as the innate (*sahaja*) [bliss] within the mind—brings joy; this is the Blessed One, the untainted delight of supreme immutable bliss. || 21 ||

Furthermore, the two positions of existence and non-existence are not established in reality; for it is said: "Against one who possesses no position such as 'existent,' 'non-existent,' or 'both existent and non-existent,' no criticism can be leveled, even after a long time. Thus, it is established as the nature of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), and it is also the "extreme" (*anta*) in the sense of being the ultimate limit of excellence.
Even while existing as a continuous stream up to the peak of existence (*ābhavam*), it is free from the delusions of a person (*pudgala*), a self (*ātman*), and so forth;
because it is not an object of error regarding imagined phenomena (*kalpitadharma*) and the like, it is of the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
"Worldly," and so forth...
The meaning is: "due to an understanding contrary to the two truths.

Regarding the phrase "by a woman," it means that for one who has performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), the reality of all phenomena, which is to be accomplished through the yoga of wisdom (*prajñā*), is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*).
"Unobscured" because it is purified by the innate nature (sahaja). || 22 ||

The self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the state of one's own reflection, adorned with the characteristics of non-obstruction and so forth, which is the vision of the reflected image of the Buddha-form;

it is the time of that which possesses time, and nothing else. Because its nature is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-rūpa*), the suchness (*tathatā*) equal throughout the three times, it is the "three times.
It specifically cultivates the moments of conceptualization and the moments of breath through great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Because it is said, "By means of yoga, the yogi should remain incessantly," the yogi has realized the reality (*tattva*)—which is non-different from all phenomena—in a single, ineffable, innate moment (*sahajakṣaṇa*).
This is the state of all Buddhas, the Fourth Body (*caturtha-kāya*). || 23 ||
The body is bodiless, clothed in the *bodhicitta*, and is called "body" because it is the practice of bliss; it is "unborn" because it has reached the crest [of realization].
It expands the activity of great bliss to the furthest limit of the *nirmāṇakāya* and the other bodies.

That which has no remainder—that is, nothing left over—because it is the fifth [state] following the fourth, is "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*). That which has the nature of displaying this is the "one who displays it.

It spreads forth bliss itself as a jewel; that by which this jewel-marked banner or flag is held is the "Jewel-Pinnacle" (*Ratnaketu*). Because it is firm at the summit of that great gem, the twelve links beginning with ignorance are the stages of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*). || 24 ||
Equanimity
Regarding the knowledge of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), he explains the performance of duties with the words beginning "of the three times," etc.

Since awakening (*bodhi*) is indeed luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), he says, "You are the father. This refers to what Mañjuśrī said: that the Blessed Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, have been made [manifest] by you.
"Body," and so forth:

"A single entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities. This is the awakening (*bodhi*) of the Buddhas arising from the realization of the body and so on; it is "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing superior to it.

Because it is devoid of being expressible by letters or words, the Lord is "without syllables" (*anakṣara*) and is of the nature of the innate (*sahaja*); and the mantras born from that are: *Oṃ* is inhalation (*praveśa-vāyu*), *Āḥ* is the stabilizing retention (*sthāpaka-kumbhaka*), and *Hūṃ* is exhalation (*niḥsaran-recaka*).

This triad is the Great Mantra Family (*mahāmantrakula*), which is the form of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, purified of body and the rest, and is to be personally realized (*svasaṃvedya*) by him. || 1 ||
The mantra that effects pacification and so forth consists of phonemes;
the *bindu* is Akṣobhya, compassion is the *nāda*, and Vajrasattva is wisdom.
The meaning is that the mantra, which has become unified with that [wisdom] and whose nature is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), is what is sought.

The meaning of Mahāmudrā is the innate (*sahaja*). Through the [vowels] beginning with *Ā*, there is the gathering of each respective group; by those [vowels], there is the dissolution of the vowels and consonants (*āli-kāli*), or by those two, the dissolution of the three [syllables] and the ten winds—which are the nature of the ten [groups]—into the body through the central channel (*madhyāvāha*).
"Ultimate reality" (paramārtha) is emptiness (śūnyatā); "body" is the drop (bindu), "speech" is the breath-wind, and "mind" is the mental faculty (manas).
The protector of these four—the fourth—is caused by merit and gnosis;
by means of the passage beginning with "the aggregate of gnosis," he explains the term "the five-syllabled great emptiness."

In the *Āryamañjuśrī-vyākaraṇa*, the five syllables of the *pratyāhāra*—*a*, *i*, *ṛ*, *u*, and *luṃ*—are the source from which the deities of the glorious *Kālacakra* maṇḍala arise. Above that, the syllable *aḥ*, born from the *vastra* (garment), is Akṣobhya, who is green (*harita*). The modifications consisting of the *bindu*, *visarga*, short, long, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *yaṇādeśa* belong to this very [syllable]. Therein, the syllable *a*, born from the purity of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), is the unarisen (*ajāta*) Vajradhātvīśvarī, who is green. Below, the syllable *aṃ*, born from the purity of the gnosis aggregate (*jñānaskandha*), is Vajrasattva, who is blue (*nīla*). The syllable *aḥ*, born from the purity of the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*), is Prajñāpāramitā, who is blue.
For one who stands before Yama, there is the embracing of another’s family and so forth; all this is purified in the center of the wheel of the glorious Kālacakra.
As it has been said: "I praise that glorious Kālacakra, the father of the world, whose body is entirely pure and joined with the Mothers, and who resides in the center of the wheel. Thus it is said.

On the third enclosure band of the mind-maṇḍala, to the left of the eastern gate, is Samantabhadra, born from the syllable *Aṃ* and purified by the mind-faculty; to the left of the western gate is Dharmadhātuvastā, born from the syllable *A* and purified by the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and to the left of the southern gate is Vajrapāṇi, born from the syllable *A* and purified by the ear-faculty.
To the left of the northern gate is Śabdavajrā, pure sound, born from the syllable *A*.

Above the body-maṇḍala is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, whose form consists of divine sense-faculties arisen from *Hūṃ* and *Vaṣṭ*. His consort is Prajñā; she holds a scissor (*kartarī*) and a skull-cup (*haraṭaḥ*). She is the manifestation of the radiance of the nectar at the center, appearing intensely blue in the form of the emission of semen due to the embrace of the supreme family.
Aghora is the son of Hava, whose nature is Bhaga;
Sumbha is his Prajñā. By the logic of the *makuhā* [mantra] and others, the letter *ha* is also understood as being present in the form of *ka-ti-ja*, which consists of the discharge of urine.

However, through the guru’s instruction, when the eye of flesh and so forth arises as unobstructed and the like, there occurs the vision of the deities and other forms residing within the universal image (*viśvabimba*) due to the non-perception of ordinary objects;
as it has been said: "What is that which obstructs bliss? It is emptiness—the supreme knowledge of compassion—which is the vision of all phenomena like a reflection."
In that regard, because there is no differentiation and because of the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), he explains the extraction of the letter *va*: "The line," and so forth.

This is the conventional designation (*saṃketa*) for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). The syllable *i*, born from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and pure, is Amoghasiddhi in the eastern square.

Their transformations or those born from them are as follows: the wind element (vāyu-dhātu) is Tā, located in the fire-pitcher (agnikoṣṭha) of the mind-maṇḍala on the third row to the left of the eastern gate; Eka-raja is the nose-faculty (ghrāṇendriya), Khagarbha; Ai-ja is the touch-vajra (sparśavajrā). Ho.
At the eastern gate is Vighnāntaka, who has the form of the faculty of speech;

at the western gate of the body-maṇḍala is Mahābala, whose wife is Vajraśṛṅkhalā, born from Viṭsrāvaśuddhā and having the form of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha); and in the southern cell is Ratnasambhava, born from the syllable *ṛ*.
The syllable *Ṛ*, differentiated as the fire element (*tejodhātu*) and white in color, born from *Ṛ*,

is in the south-western quadrant (*nirṛtikoṣṭha*) on the third row of the mind-maṇḍala; on the left side of the southern gate is Kṣitigarbha, whose form arises from the syllable *A* and represents the eye faculty, while Rasavajrā, born from the syllable *Ā*, is in the south-west.
At the southern gate is Prajñāntaka, whose nature consists of passion (*rajas*) and the hand;
at the northern gate of the body-maṇḍala is Bhr̥kuṭī, the wife of Acala born from the syllable *va*, who is the embodiment of the movement of royal splendor.
The syllable *ṛ*, representing the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and having the form of the syllable *u*, is Amitābha in the northern cell;
Māmakī, born from the earth element and having the form of the water element, is in the northeast cell;
and the essence of the tongue, belonging to the third row of the mind-maṇḍala, is in the right side of the northern gate.
From the syllable *ukāra* arises Lokeśa; from *aij* arises Rūpavajrā in the northeast at the northern gate; from *vaṃ* arises Pādendriya; and from *jaḥ* arises Padmāntaka.

At the southern gate of the body-maṇḍala is Cundā, the wife of Ṭakkirāja, born from the syllable VĀK; and in the western chamber is Vairocana, whose intrinsic nature is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), born from the syllable KĀRA.

Lavikārā, however, is in the wind-vault, having the form of the earth element; she is born from *lu*, is Locanā, and is on the third cloth of the mind-maṇḍala, on the right side of the western gate, as the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Viṣkambhī is born from *alkāra*; Gandhavajrā is born from *āḷkāra* [and belongs to] wind.
At the western gate is Yamāntaka, who is of the nature of the anus and whose seed-syllable is *laṃ*.
At the eastern gate of the body-maṇḍala is Nīladaṇḍa, whose wife is Mārīcī; she is of the nature of speech (*ālāpa*) and her seed-syllable is *lā*.

Because she is free from the ordinary object of support (*ālamba*), she consists of non-referential compassion (*nirālambakaruṇā*); because she is mere appearance (*pratibhāsamātra*), she transcends the nature of atoms (*paramāṇudharmatātīta*).
Thus, the syllable *vaṃ* has the form of the moon on the forehead;
by the words "resting upon that" and so forth, he explains the term "the six-syllabled [mantra] consisting of the bindu and the void.
Four finger-breadths below the navel is the *dharmodayā*.

In that regard, it is stated in the *Bṛhat-Kāśmīra-pañjikā* that within the six-spoked wheel (*ṣaḍāra-cakra*) consisting of the six channels (*ṣaṇ-nāḍī*), these beings such as Vajrasattva and the others are each of six types;

thus, the sixfold nature of each one is exactly as stated there. Furthermore, in the *Ārya-mañjuśrī-nāma-saṅgīti*, in the section titled "The Five Syllables" (*pañcākṣara-ākhyāna*), [the text] extracts the letter *E*, which is calculated according to the form of the sun through the distinction between the families (*kula*) and those belonging to the families (*kulī*).

Having inserted the letters from the form of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and so forth up to the five groups of five letters beginning with *ka*, and having added the six letters *ha ya ra va la* and the letter *kṣa*, [one obtains] the sixfold nature (*ṣat-tvaṃ*) along with the *savarga* and the *mātrā*: *sa pa ṣa śa ka*. 2. *ga* reads "mukhena"].
