*Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*: Regarding the object of knowledge, such as the maṇḍala-cakra and so forth, the arising of gnosis is *vitarka* (investigation).
The yoga of that very emptiness is investigation;
through its cultivation comes mental gladness, which is joy; from that comes physical ease, which is bliss.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated; thus, the attainment of the five dhyānas—
beginning with which are the Gaganagañja and other samādhis— is the "family," meaning a collection.

The Dharma-body is the embodiment of the samādhi that does not perceive any phenomena; born from that, it shines with all its splendors in the assemblies of the Enjoyment-body and others, through the enchanting resonance of the sounds of the Dharma. || 4 ||
"Without effort," and so forth:
without conscious effort, for the sake of the world, there is a manifold manifestation according to the dispositions of those to be trained;
"by nature," and so forth.

Because he maintains the lineage of the Buddha’s emanations—the three families and so forth endowed with the *svābhāvikakāya*—as well as the accumulations for the sake of the "universe," that is, for those who manifest various kinds of miraculous transformations; and because he does so "appropriately," by fulfilling their respective aspirations. (5)
Because he has Brahman as his self;
for it is said that "Brahmā is a Buddha by virtue of his bliss," and thus [he is] superior even to the gods.
"He plays" (divyati) means that because his nature is Viṣṇu;
as it is said, "He is called Viṣṇu because he pervades" (viṣaṇāt), the meaning is Upendra.
‘Yathāvaditi’ means ‘among the jewels’; because he dwells on Mount Sumeru, Rāhu— the seizer of the nectar of the full moon— [remains] below the heart of the center [of the mandala] for the asuras.
The innate (*sahaja*) is like the great elephant Airāvata of the Mahāyāna, which possesses the selflessness of both [person and phenomena];
because it is free from the nihilism of Bṛhaspati, it has no beginning or end;
and because its semen of great bliss moves upward, it is as elevated as a tusk.
He is the crusher and leader of the world's regional aggregates such as Māra;
through the purity of that [aggregate], he is the three-eyed Maheśvara, whose body and so forth are free from outflows—that is, liberation. || 6 ||
Regarding the difficulty of crossing over [the ocean of existence], he says:
"Having himself crossed over, the Lord protects the entire world; for he is authorized in the teaching of the path.
He is "without a second" because of the absence of anything else.

Thus it is said: "If even two or three others were protectors of the people like you, then one would not lie down in the pit of negligence out of fear of the [other] groups; for by teaching the happiness of those who suffer..."
Because the world possesses exceptionally noble and profound qualities, he is a "Guru" (Teacher);
because he beholds those who suffer out of compassion, he is "Loka" (Light);
and because he is visible only to those who have entered the [Bodhisattva] stages, he is "Sambhoga" (Enjoyment).
By virtue of being an unsurpassed Dharma-preacher,
he is greater than birds, all trees, rays of light, and even the sky.
Let the sound of the Dharma be heard without ceasing by all embodied beings.
Because of this statement, [the Self] is all-pervasive.
Because it is indeed indivisible, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is his armor;
for this very reason it has been said: "Enveloped by his tranquility consisting of loving-kindness, and with minds free from mutual malice, the beasts of the forest roamed about like ascetics."
Thus [it is said]. 1. In manuscript Ga, "yathāvaditi" is absent. 2. In manuscript Ga, "rāsti" is present.

3. ka. *Prasāda* (serene clarity) refers to the previously mentioned *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*; it is so called because, through [the realization that] "ka" is bliss (*sukha*) and so forth, it removes mental distraction.
"Stainless" refers to the secret *nāda* as the semen (*śukra*) situated at the forehead through its manifestation; the *bindu* resides at the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Through the union of these two, there is the conquest of passion and the rest arising from great passion (*mahārāga*).
From the knowledge of the syllables comes the conquest of delusion. || 8 ||

The jewel on the breast of the consort is indeed luminosity; because his body and so forth are sprinkled with that nectar, when the conceptualization of wind is opposed, death, Māra, and the like become impossible,
and thus the Hero remains in the vajra posture through the breaking of the flow of the breath.
Because the states of waking and so forth are conceptual, they are said to be Māra as described immediately above;
self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the vision of the three realms as emptiness.
For perception in the form of Māra’s army consists of the six [objects]; by means of that mandala, there are the forms beginning with earth,
as well as formlessness, passion for existence (bhavarāga), and those who are passionate for thirst, enjoyment, and sexual intercourse.
Because those worlds are superior due to the acquisition of that purity. || 9 ||
Having entered the ocean of knowledge by way of the auspicious ford, she performs the washing away of impurities;
through her mastery of the ultimate tenets, she possesses the maturity of wisdom and relies upon the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*).

Since she is the essence of all expressions of the true Dharma, even while dwelling within the *bhaga*, she—clothed in the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—bestows enlightenment through the enjoyment of form and other sensory qualities; thus she is to be worshipped and honored.

For the Sons of the Conquerors, this [path] is most venerable because it is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), and by means of this alone have all the Conquerors been generated. As it is said in the *Ārya-mañjuśrī-nāmasaṃgīti*: "When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind..."
Then, due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes tranquil, being without support.
Thus [it is said].
Because it has the nature of the sky, let them accept it as resembling space through my intellect; for it is said:
"Even when there is no attachment to any object, one's distinction between self and other falls away. This is the realization of non-duality (*advaitabodha*).

Since one perceives the emptiness of all phenomena within the reflected image (*bimba*), there is no longer any clinging to existence; thus, by means of the realization of non-duality, one is free from attachments.
Possessing vigor, he is the supreme person (*agrapudgala*) because, by virtue of his innate body, he excels even those such as Hari and Hara;

and because he is the embodiment of the qualities (*dharma*) such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), he transcends all comparisons and is known individually by the lords of yogis.

He is to be known as supreme because of his sovereignty over all cognitions and his supreme power, in that he causes the innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) to be grasped within those cognitions. Even for one who would repeatedly act as an enemy toward his parents, who is of wicked intent, who commits patricide or matricide, or who is a violator of the Sangha—the foremost among those who break [the precepts]—if his mind were liberated from that [evil], he would, through the contemplation of the meaning of the Dharma, quickly attain the Dharma. But for whomsoever the mind is obstructed, how can there be liberation for him?
Thus, because the Lord has declared that there is merit in the spontaneous giving of dharma and even in the renunciation of the mind—
whereas another says, "Renounce dharma and adharma; renounce both truth and falsehood"— [one should act accordingly].
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.
Regarding the *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*: "Having ignited the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*), when [the body] is burnt, the moon flows.

This means that the state to be attained is the very state of *sāmarasya* (communion) with all the categories of objects and so forth, in the form of semen (*śukra*) flowing from the forehead and other locations, together with great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Therein, for the yogi who has become one with the *bodhicitta* and so on, there arises a cognition (*pratyaya*) in the form of vibration (*spanda*). Established in meditation absorbed in that, he should remain until he becomes one who possesses the bliss of the *Mahāmudrā*.
Thus he states the third [point], beginning with "having attained," etc.
The *bimba*— which consists of the nature of the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*) in the union of Mahāmudrā—
is like a dream, meaning its bliss of meditative absorption (*samāpatti-sukha*) is like a dream;
it is like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), meaning its form, distinguished by the arrangement of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, is like a magical illusion.

"Similar to the mind-made [body]" means that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is mind-made, possessing a body endowed with the thirty-two marks and the superknowledges (*abhijñā*); this [body] is also like that, because it is devoid of flesh and so forth.
Because it is the pure gabled palace of the three worlds, it is not limited;
by this, the mind is the *mudrā* that appears before the yogi. Thus, the *mudrā* is free from conceptual construction because it appears within the non-mind of the mind.
And that [vision] is preceded by the perception of everything from smoke up to the great bindu, like a *pratisenā* (magical reflection),
because it is a non-conceptual vision of what has not been seen before or of what is imagined.
He states the fourth [verse] beginning with "that" (*tām*) and so forth.
By this, the following is meant:

a single yogi alone, through the sequence of stages such as the "mild" (*mṛdu*) and others, by means of the three causes—the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the rest—attains the result known as the pledge (*samaya*).
Like space, because it is formless, it is indestructible; therein, "great" refers to greatness— that is,
the natural characteristic of the body of the Sage (the *svābhāvika-kāya*) consists of those untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects.
Thus,
having manifested the greatness of realization in the form of the experience of luminosity known as the *svābhāvika* [body],
all the perfectly pure qualities of a Buddha— such as the *karma-mudrā* and so forth— will be explained.
The accomplishment of *bhūcarī* (earth-walking), as in the case of Gorakṣa and others;
the accomplishment of *khecarī* (sky-walking), which is the simultaneous radiance [of consciousness] everywhere;
and the accomplishment of *mahāmudrā* have been described.
"Mudrā indicates that action," and so forth;
he explains "the cause," and so forth,
as the innate (*sahaja*) arising from the *karmamudrā*.

The phrase "by way of an example" indicates a mere illustration; however, that [example] itself is not innate, because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), just as a reflection in a mirror is not.
Nor is it [innate] even by means of the seal of gnosis (*jñānamudrā*), because such intense pleasure has the defect of leaking away moment by moment.
The desire realm is not tranquil, and its pleasure is likewise so; therefore, it is not to be accepted.

For this reason, from the very beginning, one takes as an object the first dhyāna itself, which possesses the five factors such as applied thought (*vitarka*), because [the desire realm] is dependent upon that [first dhyāna] through [acts such as] kissing and so forth.
*Pratyaya* means cognition; *muda* means joy; *rā* means taking up.
He states the second [term] as "that which is to be cultivated" (*bhāvya*), and so forth;
by "and so forth" (*ādi*), [he includes] Nairātmyā, Vārāhī, and others.

Regarding the form experienced during a previous consecration: for one born of meditative concentration who is peaceful, that knowledge consisting of the cultivation of what was previously performed— such as laughter and so forth— with the woman who is the object of one's own desire,
will here also be merely a vibration at the tip of the stable vajra.

As for the instruction on its movement: having purified one’s own aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth by means of the form of the deities of one’s chosen maṇḍala circle, and having stabilized the body itself as the maṇḍala circle, the *caṇḍālī* blazes there through the withdrawal of external objects and the churning of the blissful state until it reaches its natural abode;
thus, blazing at the navel, it burns the five Tathāgatas and Locanā and the others.
The factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the ninefold liberations, the attainments, the totalities, and the eight types of spheres of mastery, which are tenfold in their successive order.
The analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) according to their classification.

The absence of conflict, the knowledge resulting from prayer, the superknowledges in all their modes, the four purities, the ten masteries, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the state of being beyond protection.
The threefold application of mindfulness, the threefold nature of non-forgetfulness, the total eradication of latent predispositions, and great compassion for living beings.
The eighteen qualities unique to the Sage alone,
as well as the knowledge of all aspects— this is designated as the Dharma-body.

Thus ends the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*. Now, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*yat punar*) and ending with "they say" (*ācakṣate*), he speaks in order to refute the system of Candrakīrti and others: "In that regard," and so forth.
Just as there is no apprehension of a cloth when there is the appearance of a jar, how can there be the apprehension of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) in mere non-apprehension?

The Sāṃkhya philosophy asserts that because [the effect] consists of the three guṇas, curds exist in milk and ghee exists in curds in the form of a potentiality, and so forth; this is incorrect, for [if it were true], one who eats food would be eating excrement, and one wearing cotton cloth would be wearing its raw material. Who else but a beast of a Sāṃkhya could speak such things without shame?

To claim that there exists something never seen before, like elephants on the tip of a blade of grass, while these five clearly manifesting common features stand here before one's direct perception— this is like one who insists that there is a horn upon his own head.

While demonstrating that the ornament of truth and so forth is actually without ornament—namely, the state of union (*yuganaddha*)—he speaks of its very distinction from the natural state, beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
It has been stated that [the world] exists in the form of a universal monarch like an illusion or a dream; it has also been stated that it is like a city of Gandharvas and a reflected image.

In every respect, because it conceals the reality that is devoid of all designations and is not conceptualized as having external existence, it is called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). Within emptiness, the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) consisting of the vision of the three realms is itself the ultimate form. That which is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) is pure through the purity of stainlessness; it is the host of deities such as Vairocana, whose nature consists of the five wisdoms beginning with the mirror-like wisdom. Wherein there is likewise the meditative visualization of the celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*) and so forth, and the mandala—such is the conventional reality.
The two truths are bound together as a pair, which is "yuganaddha"; the other [terms] are well-known.
Thus, and so forth, the Great Bliss of Clear Light is born from the excellent final phase of the full moon.
Following that, the Dharma is the knowledge of the minds of others in all their aspects; because there is no insentient object of knowledge, the Blessed One is called "Omniscient.

Sambhoga is the self-realization of the path of teaching which awakens Bodhisattvas and others—teaching that proceeds through the power of aspiration and is like an echo from birds, all trees, rays of light, space, and so forth.

Since it is stated that "the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga-kāya) arises from the enjoyment of the Dharma in the present life together with those who have entered the stages," even for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the knowledge that perceives the non-substantial nature of things is the emanation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*); thus, there are four bodies,
and not [merely] wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth.
The innate body (*sahajatanu*) is empty, stainless, non-conceptual, and luminous.
As for the *dharma*, it has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) due to the distinction between gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*);
therein, gnosis is the wisdom that is the universal image (*viśvabimba-prajñā*).
Consciousness is the yogic mind; the means is the maturation of one's own mind and so forth; and the emanation is the body—these correspond respectively to "body" and so on.

Regarding the passage beginning with "kṣara" and so forth, the commentary on the section beginning with "abja" interprets it according to the *neyārtha* (interpretable meaning): the body-mudrā is at the forehead, speech at the throat, and the mind-mudrā at the heart.
According to the *nītārtha* (definitive meaning), the entry of the garment into the lotus (*abja*) is the constant arising, which is the body-mudrā.

In the *śikhinī* [channel] and in the *madhyā*, there is the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); this is the threefold yoga consisting of the *vāṅmudrā*, which is the falling of the *bindu*, and the *cittamudrā*.

From that arises passion (*rāga*), which is the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). The end of that is non-passion (*arāga*), which is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa*). Of that, the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśīkalā*)—as long as one is liberated by it—so long is she the treasury of all qualities, the bestower of imperishable bliss, accessible to yogis through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

She is the mother of the preceding and succeeding mudrās, such as those twelve years of age and so forth; she bestows the fruits of signs such as smoke and the like. She is the mouth of the venerable Guru Vajrasattva—the fourfold mouth of gnosis—and possesses the nature of the *svābhāvikakāya*.
To state another way: "Karma," and so forth, refers to the specific *dharmamudrā* residing in the secret place.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tām" (her) and so forth:

having abandoned that auspicious Lady of Liberation, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which consists of immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) and is the nature of merit—she who is the illumination of the drop of nectar (*amṛtakaṇikā*)—those who, due to their attachment to external things active since beginningless time, take pleasure in young women, are like those who, having discarded nectar, drink poison.

These [women], beginning with Karmā, are to be meditated upon; for by always attaining delight in sexual union (*suratābhirati*) everywhere, they are free from the worldly dharmas seen in this world. Because they are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), one should not perform any consideration of color even in an impure place, but rather [attain] the capacity of the body through the enjoyment of food, drink, and so forth, and the resulting bliss.
Because it is said that the ultimate truth is the limit of reality, non-dual cognition, and the syllable Śrī is non-dual gnosis,
he is "fortunate" (*subhaga*), being dear to the beings of the [three] realms.
Pervading through emanations and so forth,

possessing sovereignty and all forms of bliss, he is dear to the Yoginīs; because he does not fall from that state and because he is captivating to all through the non-differentiation of all phenomena, he is Mañjuśrī.
The excellence of those possessing non-dual knowledge is the state of being unobstructed due to the absence of outflows,
which is the performance of the preparatory cultivation of meditative concentration.
The Performance of Duties.

The Praise of the Wisdoms of the Five Tathāgatas: Thus, from Vajrasattva onwards, the aggregates of consciousness (*vijñāna*), wisdom (*jñāna*), formations (*saṃskāra*), perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and form (*rūpa*) are created in sequence. However, here the teaching is presented in a transposed order—wisdom, consciousness, form, perception, feeling, and formations—for the purpose of guarding the oral tradition (*āmnāya*).
Alternatively, at the time of teaching, there may be no regard for the sequential order due to the radiance of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*),
or it was compiled in that very manner out of consideration for the disciples gathered at that time.
He speaks the praise of the five gnoses, beginning with *ivānoṃ* and so forth, which is easy to understand.
Knowledge of the cause is the vision of the universal image;
knowledge of the condition is the joy of the immutable Buddha;
and knowledge of the vital points is skill in the restraint of the winds.
The knowledge of cultivation is the pacification of all apprehension;
the knowledge of liberation is the realization of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu,
which is the manifest awakening in five aspects.
Because of the statement beginning with "The mirror-like wisdom is the moon," [it follows that] in the void—
the Great Bindu— entirely all things such as jars, which constitute the collection of phenomena, are correctly designated as the "original image" (*bimba*).
Because it is seen by non-conceptual vision, it is free from conceptual construction;

because it is mere appearance, it is free from form. Just as a young girl, presiding over a mirror, sees thieves and the like therein which are non-existent, [it is] supramundane truth because it is free from the four extremes.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of the five sense organs, beginning with the eye, and the five objects, beginning with form;
mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) arises through its connection with the mirror of knowledge,
[as indicated by the words] "all" and so forth.

Because no difference is perceived, all entities are equal; there is one innate entity, the supreme immutable, arisen from the experience of the immutable, free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism,
and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) because its nature is the pervasive sensation throughout all bodies—
thus it is said, "all," and so forth.

Through the equality of non-apprehension, there is the gnosis of equality regarding all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*). Whatever name may exist, all of it consists of syllables, and the syllables have the letter *A* as their gateway; for all phenomena, "A" is the entrance. Thus, because they arise from the secret *nāda* and are produced from the space, wind, and [other elements], for those whose vital points (*marmāṇi*) of the wind have attained the state of the great syllable through the cessation of wind, there is neither conceptualization nor one who conceptualizes.
Thus, the wisdom that examines the vital point of all perceptions is [the realization] that they are unarisen;
"cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to the perfuming (vāsana) or conditioning (saṃskāra) of the mind by means of actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— produced by the afflictions.

If, in reality, phenomena themselves have not arisen, then by what means, in what manner, and for whom could there be conditioning? And since that is the case, due to the absence of anything to be awakened to, what is awakening and whose is Buddhahood? For there is no sentient being whatsoever who goes from this world to another world.
Nor does he have a life-force from which conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) could arise;

thus, the thorough knowledge of conditioned phenomena is the supramundane aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Because it carries out the task of awakening, it is the "knowledge of the performance of tasks" (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), which is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because they are unarisen, like flowers in the sky, they transcend the domain of the visual and other sensory consciousnesses; conceptual construction, however, is entirely without an object. Purified by vajra-wisdom, they are therefore free from being objects of apprehension and the like, and thus are unturbid. By their very nature and essence, they are luminous and unobstructed, like space.

The term "phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) is the subject to be qualified, because they have reached the realization of the emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*. Through the purity of the three spheres, they constitute the supramundane aggregate of consciousness;
through the purity of stainlessness, they are the perfectly pure phenomena—the connection illuminating the drops of nectar, which is the wind-like gnosis.
Regarding the word "light" (*laghu*): in the *Jñānapaṭala*, it refers to the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth as described;

the wheel is characterized by the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*) of the Victorious One, while the jewel (*ratna*) is the purity of transparency throughout the three realms of existence. The lotus (*padma*) is attachment to bliss within that bliss.
Then, the sword is the severer of afflictions;
the supreme gnosis is the indivisible cutter of ignorance, which is the knife. These six, beginning with the wheel family, are the wheels and so forth.

Those aggregates (skandhas) that arise through these wheels and other implements are likewise of the nature of clarity and so on; for this very reason, they should be known as being of equal flavor (samarasa), like space. Thus it is said: "That in which the arising of my form has not occurred—that is the Great Form."

As it has been said: "Subhūti, all phenomena have the nature of space; they do not transcend that nature. That state of fitness in which suffering and so forth become like space is *vedanā* (feeling), and that in which the conceptualization of grasping at signs comes to an end is the *vajrasaṃjñā* (diamond-perception).
From affliction comes karma, from that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and from those birth; since the increase of existence is cut off therein, it is the *vajra-saṃskāra*.
Where birth, form, and the other [aggregates], as well as consciousness, perish, that is the *vijñāna-vajra*. And where ignorance dissolves, that is the *jñāna-kāya*.
For this very reason, cloth, form, and so forth are the six Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the others, who constitute the six families.
Other than these, there are the elements of wisdom-form (*prajñārūpa*), namely earth, water, fire, wind, space, and gnosis (*jñāna*).
As for the meaning of the individual parts of the verses in praise of gnosis, beginning with "the four," it means that they bestow the supreme bliss upon the body and so forth.
The foremost of the Vajra-Jinas,
the ultimate reality, the self-abiding limit, the dissolution into the enjoyment of innate bliss—
this is "Koṭi," used here as a vocative; so it is elsewhere as well.
Its essence is emptiness (*śūnyatā-garbha*), because it is the cause of awakening just as the awakening of the Buddhas is;
thus, the meaning is: "May I be one who is inclined toward the luminosity of form."
His passion is like the great compassion of the Buddhas;
it is the fruition that is cessation, the Dharmakāya. It is desired as the Jñānakāya because, being the coemergent emptiness of the self, it is the cause of the Buddhas' joy.
Through the abandonment of the grasped and the grasper, his joy is like that of the Buddhas.
Illumination arises from the radiation of rays;

it is the empty *dharmakāya*. Because it manifests the blissful gnosis (*sukhajñāna*) of the Buddhas, through union with the *karmamudrā*, it takes the form of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters the central channel;
thus, it is indeed the Buddha.

Its state is "enjoyment" (*saṃbhoga*); that which does not exist as the cause for that [enjoyment] is "non-existence" (*abhava*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The arising of this [emptiness] is the "origination of the Buddhas" (*buddhasambhava*), because it is the essential nature (*svābhāvika*) of the Buddhas.
Thus, it is likewise said that it originates spontaneously from space.
It exists as the innate knowledge that transcends the fourth state; thus it is so described.

It is the universal reflection of Mahāmāyā; because it is born from the *māyājāla-prabhāsvara* as the coemergent (*sahaja*), it manifests as a drama of stable and moving beings. Likewise, because it enters into the state of all things (*viśva*) through the fruit-like untainted joys (*anāsrava-ānanda*), and because it is primarily characterized by the unobstructed gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*), it is so called.
The four bodies, being unified, constitute four salutations for each verse.
Praise of Knowledge (Jñānastuti)
Regarding the benefits, he states the benefits beginning with "this," etc.:
"O Vajrapāṇi by way of consecration;
O Vajradhara by way of gnosis."

Having awakened [the assembly], for the sake of generating—meaning producing—that joy (*prīti*), which is gladness (*harṣa*); clarity (*prasāda*), which is faith (*śraddhā*); and great exultation (*mahaudvilya*), which is vigor (*vīrya*)—[he taught] the fourfold set of words beginning with "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavataḥ*) because of its fourfold nature. "Non-common" (*āveṇika*) refers to that which exists in the pure phenomena (*śuddhadharma*), being free from the "tangle" (*veṇi*) of the attachment to afflictions (*kleśa*); by means of that, the *Nāmasaṅgīti* is completely purified, and thus it was taught. For that purpose...
For the sake of purifying the secret of body and so forth— the *bodhicitta*—
the stages (*bhūmi*) that are incomplete are impure; [this refers to] their perfections (*pāramitā*) of merit and wisdom.
For the sake of the fulfillment and purification through the two accumulations,

and for the sake of attaining that which has not yet been attained— the unsurpassed goal— the innate [nature] exists; and for the sake of attaining that attainment, the previously unattained luminosity becomes attainable.
And for the purpose of maintaining the eye of the true Dharma of all the Victors of the three times,

this [work] is "the illuminator of the thought of awakening" (*bodhicittaprakāśikā*), because it elucidates that which is to be accomplished through the six branches beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*);
thus, the six words beginning with "veśitā" [are stated].
The *dharmatā* of all mantras is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); its empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is its stabilization. By means of that, this is the benefit of the first wheel among the six.
He states the second [wheel] with the words "Furthermore," and so forth:

"pure" means completely purified, unobscured, thoroughly cleansed, and stainless; and because he knows all things, it is the "knowledge of the Omniscient One" (*sarvajña-jñāna*). Its secrecy regarding the body and so forth is due to its being non-manifest.
That awakening which is realized by all Tathāgatas—
that awakening is the realization of the perfectly enlightened ones (samyak-saṃbuddhas) as non-manifesting gnosis (nirābhāsa-jñāna);
beyond this, there is nothing superior even for all Tathāgatas.
The realization of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as empty in all its aspects is precisely this [state] of the Sugatas;
because it is unconquerable by the forces of the four Māras, it is the conquest of all the forces of Māra belonging to the Victors (*jina*).
This alone is the pursuit of the power of the ten signs, such as smoke and so forth, belonging to all those who possess the ten powers (*daśabala*).
"One who possesses strength is strong" (*balī*); the state of being so is "strengthiness" (*balitā*).

"Omniscience" (*sārvajña*) refers to that which pertains to the knowledge of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña-jñāna-gata*), namely omniscience itself (*sarvajñatā*). It is an "Agama" because it has been attained through great bliss; it is the [teaching] of all phenomena, consisting of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharma-skandha*).

This realization is attained effortlessly; it is the full accomplishment of all the qualities of the Śrāvakas and others. Because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*), it is the stainless accumulation of merit.
The perfection of these two belongs to all the great Bodhisattvas.

Because this [Dharmakāya] is the luminosity that contains all seeds, it is their source. By virtue of those disciples to be trained—the Śrāvakas and others—it is the field for the prosperity of all gods and humans.

Alternatively, because of the realization of the deity, the fruit of the Mahāyāna consists of the purity of the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) and the establishment of giving and so forth; since it is of the nature of awakening that does not contradict the practice of the three vehicles— being luminous according to conventional Mahāyāna and possessing the ultimate reality— this is the source of the conduct of the Bodhisattva.

Because it is the cause for attaining the fruit, they are correctly established; because it is the locus for the examination of reality, it is a touchstone for those who are liberated, like a whetstone for gold;
because it is a distinguished means, it is the path of arising and departure; and because it performs the Buddha-deeds effortlessly, there is no interruption of the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

Due to the empowerment of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), there is a preeminent increase; that lineage (*gotra*) belonging to the family of the great Bodhisattvas is all-pervasive, and thus it is included by this [empowerment]. The reading in some places is "the refutation of proponents" (*nigrahaḥ pravādinām*);
and in others, "the suppression of those of other sects along with their doctrines" (*paratīrthyānāṃ saha dharmeṇa santati*).
The *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha* explains "subjugation" (*nigraha*) as overcoming through one's own majesty and the destruction of all heretics;

it refers to the defeat and repulsion of the fourfold army— the arrayed host consisting of the forces of the aggregates (*skandha*), afflictions (*kleśa*), death (*mṛtyu*), and the son of the gods (*devaputra*)— which constitute the four Māras.

The gathering of all sentient beings through generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency between words and deeds; the ripening of those traveling upon all paths, such as that of the śrāvakas, by means of the noble eightfold path;
and this [state] characterized by inconceivable form and so forth for those who dwell in the four sublime abodes, such as meditative concentration and loving-kindness.

Because it consists of the first dhyāna with its five factors—discernment (*prajñā*), reasoning (*vitarka*), and so forth—it is *dhyāna*. Because those whose minds are one-pointed are absorbed into the state of mere gnosis (*jñānamātratā*), it is *yoga*. For those who are thus joined, it is auspicious for the body and other [aggregates].

It is the dissociation from the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*)—namely, attachment (*anunaya*), aversion (*pratigha*), the various types of ignorance (*avidyā*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*)—which bind one to existence (*bhava*).
The abandonment of the afflictions such as attachment and the secondary afflictions such as anger occurs through the non-appearance of conceptual construction;
this is the removal of the obscurations of afflictions, objects of knowledge, and the maturation of karma,
and it is the liberation from all bonds such as attachment because it is the cause for the departure from bondage.

The substrata (*upadhayaḥ*) are the aggregates (*skandhāḥ*); their liberation consists in the cessation of all mental disturbances because its nature is perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Because it is an abiding in innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), for those who cultivate this, it is a mine of all worldly and other prosperities like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), and it is the abandonment of all faults that cause misfortune.
Because it acts as a covering, it is a "covering" for the gates to all the lower realms such as the hells;
because it is the path to perfect enlightenment, it is the "true path" to the city of liberation;
and because of the cessation of the twelve-linked dependent origination, there is the "non-functioning" of the wheel of saṃsāra.
It is so called because it causes the Wheel of Dharma to turn according to what is appropriate;

and because, by surpassing external followers such as the Śrāvakas and others, it serves as the cause for stabilizing the yoga of the Tathāgata’s teaching— [a teaching] upon which the parasol, banner, and flag are raised high through the Vajrayāna.
The empowerment for the teaching of all dharmas,

independent of prior service, is the realization through cultivation attained by means of the direct perception of Bodhisattvas who practice the easy conduct of mantras— such as the recitation of mantras— and who are devoted to the perfection of wisdom.

For those devoted to cultivation for the sake of the fruit and for the penetration of non-duality, there is no piercing [of reality] by means of the emptiness of individual entities; rather, this awakening is emptiness.
Because it is the nature of the specific established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is the accomplishment of the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) of all the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity;
because it is the nature of non-conceptual penetration, it is total purity through the complete fulfillment of all the stages (*bhūmi*), beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*).
Penetration is the thorough penetration of the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;

because it is non-dual knowledge, there is penetration of all aggregates with a single mind. This refers to the applications of mindfulness regarding the body, feelings, phenomena, and mind, up to the point of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
How much can be said? It should be applied everywhere that this *Nāmasaṅgīti* is the cause for the perfect attainment of all those qualities of a Buddha, which are as numerous as they may be;

this is the praise of the second wheel. Furthermore, O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, listen: this *Nāmasaṅgīti* pacifies whatever evils exist within the entire range of the bodies and so forth of all sentient beings without exception; through hearing, reciting, and so on, it purifies all miserable states such as the hells, because it cleanses the karma that has been committed.

It prevents the three miserable destinies by warding off the karma that leads to them; it completely cuts through the obscurations of karma such as the five acts of immediate retribution. It is that which effects the non-arising of the opportunity for the path of vision—the characteristics of rebirth in hell, as a hungry ghost, as an animal, among the barbarians, with a long life, in wrong views, or in a Buddha-less wilderness as a dull-witted mute—and it brings about the state of being a worthy vessel.
The Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti pacifies the fear of lions, elephants, fire, serpents, kings, imprisonment, water-floods, and piśācas; it brings about the cessation of the eight great fears,
destroys all bad dreams such as falling from mountains,
and shatters all ill omens such as the signs of death.
At the time of death for a certain son of the gods, there was an ill omen consisting of the signs of conception in the womb of a sow;
this was an obstacle and a hindrance.

To pacify that, the sons of the gods and other Māras—enemies and adversaries—were driven away by the cultivation of the Wheel of Dharma and so forth, thereby dispelling the sufferings resulting from those [adversarial] actions.

Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). Generosity and so forth are merit (*puṇya*); the source that increases it is reality (*tattva*). "Source" (*yoni*) refers to the source; "properly" (*yoniśaḥ*) means not improperly (*ayoniśaḥ*). Improper mental attention (*manaskāra*) is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); its non-arising occurs through the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind, as it is said: "Pride is the grasping of an exalted mind; for one who is attached to their own qualities, it is the total absorption of the mind."
Pride, self-conceit, egoism, and arrogance— [the sensation that destroys these is] bodily pleasant sensation as happiness (*sukha*) and suffering (*duḥkha*),
and mental [sensation] as dejection (*daurmanasya*); it is that which does not produce them.
It is the gnosis of all Tathāgatas; it is the heart-essence of all Bodhisattvas. Because it is to be guarded, it is secret;
because it is revealed through the sequence of mantras, it is a mystery hidden from Śrāvakas and others.
It consists of the four [mudrās], beginning with the Karmamudrā.

The mantra is non-conceptual bliss. Through its cultivation, that which is to be accomplished is achieved. Because it serves as the means for accomplishing all mudrās and mantras, it has the nature of expressing the ineffable phenomena of the aggregates and so forth; because there is no obstruction between word and meaning, it is the memory of the Victors (*jina*), the non-forgetfulness of the mind, and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*)—the discernment of body and mind. That which generates these is the wisdom (*prajñā*) whose object is emptiness, a firm retention, and intelligence (*medhā*). It is also the protection of those two unsurpassed states.
Diseases are attachment and so forth, because they afflict the mind; health is the state of being free from them. For then [the practice] brings about the fourfold [aim]:
from the auspicious, peaceful, and virtuous being, it increases prosperity, fortune, and so forth.
That which brings about fame, renown, and so forth through the fulfillment of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and other means is [the antidote].
The ninety-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root of existence; the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are six: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.
The views are five: the view of a self-identity, false view, the view of extremes, and the two types of adherence—adherence to views and adherence to rules and rituals; thus, there are ten.
These [ten] are further reduced to seven, seven, eight, three, and two, when excluding certain views.

They are abandoned in sequence through the vision of suffering and so forth within the body. Four are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*): attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*). The vision of suffering and so forth abandons those to be abandoned by cultivation. Having excluded the five types of aversion, those same [factors] without aversion, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and likewise in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), are considered to be ninety-eight. These very same things are all afflictions (*vyādhi*); because they grant suffering, they are great terrors. [The path] that pacifies them—
They are more purified by the fulfillment of the accumulations for enlightenment; more sanctified by the washing away of the stains of conceptual construction;
and most blessed by the removal of the heart’s coarseness—this is the commentary on the *Amṛtakaṇikoddyota*, the most blessed of [works].
Among those possessing knowledge such as the Śaivas and others, he establishes the Buddha-dharma; he is auspicious among the most auspicious,
a refuge for the protectorless who seek refuge because he is worthy of being a refuge, a dwelling place because he is the cause of delight, and a shelter for those seeking shelter.
He is a *trāṇa* (protector) because he protects those seeking refuge through his own specific duty;

he is a *parāyaṇa* (ultimate resort) because he is free from the eight worldly concerns on all sides; he is like an island (*dvīpa*) because, for those fallen into the flood of saṃsāra, he brings them to nirvāṇa—like an island where the two-fold flood has ceased—and thus he is the unsurpassed path for those who have no other recourse.
Existence is like an ocean because it has a further shore; for those traveling to that further shore,
the perfected medicinal herb serves as a vessel for the subsiding of all diseases,
while the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is to be abandoned for the sake of the knowledge of what is to be given.
By illuminating all forms of emptiness, he has become the light of wisdom for the purpose of destroying ignorance, false knowledge, wrong views, and so forth;
like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇiratna*), he fulfills the intentions of all sentient beings according to their inclinations.
Mañjuśrī himself is the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*); for the sake of attaining that, he is the cause of the knowledge of the omniscient one.

The ten stages, beginning with *muditā* (joy), are the basis for the progressively higher qualities through the purification of the three spheres (*trimandala-śuddhi*), which serves as the cause for fulfilling the six perfections— such as the giving of material goods and so forth— that result in the realization of the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*) for the sake of attaining the five eyes, including the flesh-eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). The cause for attaining those [stages] is the accomplishment of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the accumulations (*sambhāra*).

The non-dual nature of phenomena (advayadharmatā) is the state of suchness (tathatārūpatā), because it is free from the duality of the grasped and the grasper, because it has reached the avadhūtī as its non-other nature, and because it is free from superimposition.
Because it has the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, it has the nature of the *bhūtakoṭi*;

because its essence is the pure Buddha-body, it has the nature of great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) in all its aspects. The dense forest is precisely the thicket of all false views regarding self and what belongs to self; "going" therein means entering it. Because it eradicates that [thicket], the *Nāmasaṃgīti* has attained the state of being inexpressible and ineffable through all phenomena as aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
That is to say, this non-dual nature of phenomena is emptiness; for the purpose of entering into it, there is the retention of its name by way of its illumination—this is the third wheel. 52.

The fourth [chapter] says: "Furthermore, listen again, O Vajradhara: the acceptance of a lowly state by one who is not led by another, though possessing true existence, occurs because of self-attachment and the desire to abandon suffering and [seek] happiness."

That into which one dissolves when it is contemptible is the *kula* (the family), namely urine and so forth; he who purifies that is the *putra* (son). Because she milks out (*duhana*) virtue, she is the *duhitṛ* (daughter).
There is no mention of neuter beings and the like because they lack the capacity [for spiritual practice].

"One who practices the conduct of virtue and so forth by means of the mantra" refers to the Blessed One; thus, the four phrases beginning with "of the Blessed One" signify that because he consists of the four bodies (*catur-kāya*), his ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is indeed non-dual. This *Nāmasaṃgīti* is the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*) of the names of those born from all the Tathāgata families, and it is entirely complete because it possesses all the qualities of a Buddha.
Because it is complete in the meaning of all phenomena, it is not deficient;
because it cannot be overcome, it is unimpaired—
thus, "atha" and so forth.

He will maintain [this teaching] daily at the three junctions of the day through its verses, phrases, and syllables; he will recite it from books according to both the text and the meaning, preceded by the construction of a maṇḍala; he will master it within his thoughts and attend to it thoroughly through meditative cultivation; and he will extensively proclaim it to those to be trained, in various ways, according to their inclinations, as is appropriate, at the right time and occasion, exactly and without error.

Regarding the *Āryamañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, if one— having taken as one's object of focus the Wisdom Body of Mañjuśrī according to the instruction, by means of any one or another of its individual names— will cultivate it with a concentrated mind,
then "certainty" is the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that "it is so," and "the real" (*bhūta*) is the truth (*tattva*) through those two mental orientations (*manaskāra*).
By whom one entity is seen in its true nature, by him all entities are seen in their true nature;
one entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities, and all entities have the intrinsic nature of one entity.

Thus, dwelling in universal bliss, with an intellect whose suchness is all-pervading, and by means of that very purity— which consists in the awakening to the reality of all phenomena such as the aggregates, which is therefore supreme, excellent, untroubled, and faultless— he spoke thus [somewhere]: "by means of that [purity] permeated with wisdom."

As it has been said: "Because of faith, one practices the Dharma; because of wisdom, one understands it according to reality. Of these two, wisdom is primary, yet for this [wisdom], faith is the precursor."

Thus (Ratna0 1.5), being thus endowed and possessed, for that Buddha-field— of what kind?— all the Buddhas who are unimpeded throughout the three times, past and so forth, having bound their girdles, being closely associated, having gathered together, and having come into union, will reveal all the gateways of the dharmas, such as the gateways of liberation beginning with emptiness; they will also reveal the essential nature of their own physical forms,
and through the empowerment of all the Buddhas and others, they will empower his mind by means of their own bodies and so forth.
Through the favor of the Buddha and others, or through love for [his disciples] as if they were an only son, he will bestow grace; namely,
the fourfold fearlessness in the perfect awakening to all dharmas, in the cessation of the outflows (*āsrava*), in the proclamation of the path, and in the attainment of realization— understand this.
Thus,

he will present the fourfold eloquence and so forth, and [he will show] the disciples and others who are worthy and purified by the Mahāyāna Dharma; with the very intention that "without the Buddhas there is no Dharma, and without the Buddha there is no Dharma," he will reveal his true nature.

The subduers of those who are difficult to tame, such as Mahābhairava and others; the subduers of Vajrabhairava and others; the wrathful kings such as Vaṣṭrabhairava and others; the Great Vajradharas, Vajrasattva, and so forth—protectors of the world through non-referential compassion—they will display the mandalas of the Vajradhātu and others, which manifest the majesty of the mind that radiates within, which is invincible and unassailable by darkness, and which brings about the realization of all mantras and mudrās through various doors of emanation.

All those who are related to the Lord, including the conscious mantra-deities and this Great Queen of Vidyās, [are such that] by her power, the obstacles, Vināyakas, Māras, and enemies [are overcome].

At the time of averting the harms caused by others, Svabhāvyā, Pratyaṅgirā, and Mahāparājitā will provide protection, defense, and guardianship for the body, speech, and mind— respectively— at every moment throughout day and night, whether one is standing, walking, lying down, sitting, or on the road. Furthermore, those such as Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu shall always, in every way, throughout the day and night, on the fourfold path of conduct, provide protection for one who is sleeping or awake, composed or uncomposed, alone or in a crowd, whether in a small village or a large city.
A settlement outside a city is a *nigama*;
it is a place where there is no market within the city.
A *janapada* is a region or country. *Amṛtakaṇikodyotanibandha*.
The realm, the district, the camp, the capital,
the gate, the threshold, and the bolt.
*rathyā* is a road; *mārgaḥ* is a path; *pratolī* is a city gate; *vīthī* is a street; *rājamārgaḥ* is a royal highway;
and *catvaraḥ* is a crossroads.
A crossroads, a place where three roads meet, the interior of a city, a market stall, a shop, and a marketplace for buying goods.

For one who stays in the midst of that—whether in an empty house, a mountain, a cave, a valley, a river, or the thicket of a forest; whether one is defiled or undefiled, intoxicated by liquor, or distracted and heedless due to power and the like—he shall always, in every way, and everywhere, provide soft foods and the like, as well as what is edible and inedible, and he shall maintain his well-being day and night.
Furthermore, there are other great serpents, the eight families of *nāgas*, humans and mortals, and non-humans such as *pretas* and others.

And those others— the lords of the nine planets, the lunar mansions, and the hosts of Mothers, as well as the Seven Mothers who emerged from the sweat of Hara during the slaughter of Ruru— namely, Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Aindrī, Vārāhī, Kauberī, Raudrī, and Kaumārī; and whatever Yakṣiṇīs, Rākṣasīs, and Piśācīs there may be— all these, gathered together, complete with their fourfold armies and retinues, shall perform protection and so forth.
Furthermore, they will infuse his body with vigor and strength, and they will bestow upon him health, vitality, long life, and intelligence; this is the fourth [benefit]. 19.

Fifth, it says: Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, holder of the vajra, whoever shall recite this *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the crest-jewel of names, every day with unbroken commitment, having committed it to memory in three ways, or having it in the form of a book while taking Mañjuśrī as their object of focus—through the stages of preparation, the main practice, and the conclusion—they shall, within a short time, behold a hundred [emanations] in three postures by means of a nirmāṇakāya according to the inclinations of those to be trained;
they shall behold Buddhas and others appearing in various emanated forms in the sky.
Never at any time, and in no way whatsoever, will there be a fall for them into an evil state of existence or a miserable rebirth.

Nor is there birth in a low family such as that of a *caṇḍāla* and so forth, nor in border regions among barbarians and the like, where even the word "Buddha" is not heard; nor is there impairment of the faculties, such as blindness or deafness; nor is there deficiency in right vision, hearing, and so forth; nor is there false view or nihilism.

Even when the Dharma has disappeared in Buddha-fields where no Buddhas reside, there is neither aversion toward the arising of a Buddha nor the state of being out of sight of the Dharma taught by him.
There is no famine among those in the formless realms or the non-percipient beings; thus,
the end of the eon occurs through weapons, disease, and famine.
For seven days, months, and years, respectively.

Thus, neither cultivation nor latent impressions (vāsanā) will arise there; at that time, there will be no fear of kings and the like, nor fear of poverty due to a lack of requisites such as clothing. The five afflictions (kaṣāya) [will likewise be absent].
Defamation is the false accusation of one who lacks renown; it is the proclamation [of faults] with contempt and malice.
Contempt, disdain, reproach, infamy, ill-repute, and abusive language are its synonyms.
And this fear shall not exist,
because of being complete in all limbs; he will be of noble birth and pure in both lineages.
Possessing a complexion adorned with refinements that produce universal serenity,
he will be beloved, captivating to the mind, a cause for dwelling in happiness, pleasant to behold, and a source of joy for the world.

Through this merit, he will possess good fortune; his speech will be authoritative and worthy of being accepted; and wherever among the six realms of existence he may be reborn, there he will be one who remembers his past lives.
Possessing great enjoyment and a great retinue, with inexhaustible enjoyment and an inexhaustible retinue,
he is the leader; he is the *Ārya-mañjuśrī-nāmasaṅgīti*, the foremost among beings, endowed with supreme qualities, and by nature possessed of the virtues of the six perfections, such as generosity.
Possessing the four divine abodes beginning with loving-kindness,
endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and accompanied by the power of skillful means, aspirational prayers, primordial wisdom, and the four perfections.

He is learned in all treatises, fearless, eloquent, and clear-spoken; he is not dull-witted, but endowed with wisdom and intelligence, being clever and possessed of quick wit; he is skillful and energetic, untiring due to his freedom from laziness; he is contented because of his fewness of desires, and noble in the form of his character.
Free from craving, turned away from sense objects, and full of confidence toward all beings, he was honored as a teacher and a guru. Furthermore,

those treatises concerning the sixty-four arts and crafts, the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and wisdom— which had previously been unheard of— appeared to him both in their literal meaning and their textual form.
His ethical discipline (*śīla*) is perfectly pure; his livelihood is [pure] through that; his conduct is practiced by means of those two;

thus he is one who has well gone forth (*supravrajita*) and possesses unbroken ethical discipline. Because of the perfection of his form, his mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) directed toward omniscience is never lost.

He will never at any time realize the fixed course of the Śrāvakas and so forth, namely the path of seeing; by way of conclusion, he says: "O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, he will be endowed with immeasurable qualities. Thus the infinity of qualities has been stated;
moreover, he will be filled with other immeasurable multitudes of qualities of this same kind.

O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, after no long time, that person who upholds this *Paramārthanāmasaṅgīti* will have well-accumulated the equipment of merit and wisdom; having swiftly perfected the qualities of a Buddha, he will attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Having not entered final nirvāṇa for many eons, he will be empowered as the supreme teacher of Dharma for all sentient beings. With his drum of Dharma resounding throughout the ten directions, such a one, by pleasing the world through the Dharma, shall become a King of Dharma (*dharmarāja*). Thus it is connected with what precedes.
Of the fifth wheel.
The benefits of the fifth wheel, combined with those of the sixth, [are as follows].
The benefits.
The Arrangement of Mantras: This mantra beginning with *oṃ* is to be recited at the beginning, middle, and end by one who recites the *Nāmasaṅgīti*.
Therein, the root mantra is: *oṃ sarvadharmābhāvasvabhāvaviśuddhavastra a ā aṃ aḥ*.
The remainder, beginning with *prakṛti*, is the *mālāmantra* of the *Nāmasaṅgīti*.

When the three [aspects] are not perceived, *oṃ* signifies that the very non-existence of all phenomena is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because of that purity, it is the indestructible wisdom (*abhedyajñāna*) of the Blessed One.

All phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*), are pure by their very nature; that is to say, they possess the purity of Mañjuśrī, the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas of the three times, because they have the *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic nature. "O Bhukṛti!"—because of the very nature of the wisdom-body, [he is] the heart of all Tathāgatas. "Hara hara!"—[meaning] "take away, take away all faults," because of his exertion in uplifting sentient beings. The Blessed One is wisdom itself, which is his form; he is the Lord of Speech, the Great Word. Because he thus awakens the three realms through this boon, he is stainless like the sky for all phenomena.
The knowledge of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* is its embryo; this has been explained by way of a small illustration.
Thus ends the arrangement of the mantra.

The passage beginning with "Then," and so forth, is the conclusion. Even though the requester, Vajradhara—who possesses non-dual gnosis—is primarily characterized by the conclusion of great joy, he is satisfied by future happiness;
with palms joined in reverence, he bows to the Lord. The four phrases beginning with these words represent the nature of the four bodies (*kāya*).

Together with other infinite lords of the attendants, such as Bhṛkuṭī and Taraṅgā, who hold garments in their hands, and with the lords of the wrathful ones, they spoke these words aloud: "O Lord, we rejoice in this well-spoken teaching; it is excellent, it is excellent!
A great benefit has been wrought for us, which brings about the state of perfect buddhahood."

Not only for us, but for the world as well— which is without a protector and yearns for liberation— this great path to excellence, the cause of *nirvāṇa*, is pure because its nature is the *dharmadhātu*.
This profound meaning, in which emptiness is primary, has been set forth in the *Māyājāla-tantra* according to the [correct] method.

It is "vast" (*vaipulya*) because of its marvelous power; it is of "great purpose" (*mahārtha*) because, by performing the welfare of the world, it dispels all suffering without exception and establishes beings in great bliss.
It is taught as being beyond all designations such as "past" and so forth; because of its extreme profundity, it is the object of the Buddhas alone in every respect.
For this reason, it is not [the domain] of others—such as the Śrāvakas and so forth—due to its profundity, magnanimity, and other qualities.
The induction of joy.
Conclusion.
"O Śrīvajra," and so forth:
"O Blessed One, I am the Vajra of Śrīvajrapāṇi; having emerged from the great lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), I have taken refuge in the state beyond suffering."
Having studied the *Śrīnāropādapañjikāsandhi*,
[this work] endowed with the secrets of the *Śrīkālacakra*, *Hevajra*, and other tantras,
follows the instructions of the venerable Śabara, Saraha, Kṛṣṇapāda, and others, by Raviśrī.
Just as it was for my beloved, may the minds of the virtuous also be gladdened by this *Amṛta* [the Nectar].

Having composed this commentary titled *Hṛdayaṅgamāmṛtakaṇikā*, which is an inexhaustible exposition of the *Kalāgata*, whatever merit I have thereby acquired, by that may the world attain the state of non-dual bliss.
Indeed, how many suns are there not found on earth that illuminate the world?
For it is the moon alone whose light enters within.
If the wise, having connected with me from the ocean of nectar consisting of the Śrī Kālacakra and other [tantras],
should attain merit, may people then become Victors (Jinas), their minds overflowing with the nectar of happiness.
The commentary titled *Amṛtakaṇikodyota* is completed.
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

The Sādhana of the Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti. Homage to Mañjughoṣa! First of all, the practitioner, having risen at dawn and performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, should enter the meditation chamber, sit upon a comfortable seat in the paryaṅka posture, and visualize a red-pale syllable *mūṃ* within a moon disc at his own heart-lotus.

Then, having drawn forth the Blessed One with goad-shaped rays of light from that [source], visualizing him before oneself as endowed with the colors, arms, insignia, and seat to be described hereafter, and having worshipped him with mentally produced flowers, incense, and so forth, one should perform before him all the rites beginning with the confession of sins; then, having meditated upon the mantra and the four Brahma-vihāras, and having realized the emptiness of all phenomena, one should consecrate oneself with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako 'ham*.

Then, having visualized a five-pointed cloth in the sky by means of the syllable *huṃ*, one should see that—through its rays—the cloth becomes, as appropriate, a wall, a vajra-fence, and a vajra-ground extending down to the bottom of the underworld (*ārasātala*); and having become rays of cloth, it remains outside the vajra-wall in the form of perfumes and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, within the vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*), one should visualize a lotus from the syllable *hrīḥ*, and upon that lotus, a moon-maṇḍala from the syllable *a*. Above that, one should meditate on the syllable *muḥ* of a reddish-white color, which has the nature of radiating and reabsorbing many Buddhas. From its transformation, one visualizes oneself as the Lord Mañjuśrī, reddish-white in color, seated in the vajra-paryanka posture upon a lotus and moon. He has three faces: the first (central) is red, the right is blue, and the left is white. With his four hands, he appropriately holds a consort, a sword, a bow, and an arrow. He wears a jewel crown and is resplendent with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of a Great Man. Visualizing himself thus as a youth adorned with youthful ornaments, one then visualizes the following goddesses: Upon a lotus and moon at the heart, one visualizes Sattvavatī, white in color, seated in the sattva-paryanka posture. She holds a bell in her left hand in a gesture of rivalry, and a vajra in her right hand in the manner of drawing it toward the heart. Likewise situated at the *ūrṇā* (the circle of hair between the eyebrows) is Ratnavajrī, yellow in color. With both hands she binds a flower garland upon the head; she holds a lotus-vajra at her throat. She is reddish-white, holding the lotus-stalk with her left hand with pride, while with her right she causes its petals to open. She is situated as before. At the crown of the head, one visualizes Karmavajrī, green in color. With her two hands, each equipped with a three-pronged vajra, she supports her own head. She is situated in that manner. Then, with these mantras: *oṃ vajrāṅkuśajaḥ*, *oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ*, *oṃ vastrasphoṭa vaṃ*, and *oṃ vaśīkṛtya vaṣṭrāveśa hoḥ*, one should attract the Jñānamaṇḍala onto the lotus and moon in due order, cause it to enter, bind it, and [subdue it]. Having formed the double vajra-fist mudrā and joined the index fingers and little fingers to form a chain, one performs the Vastra-cakra mudrā by placing it face-up over one's own face. Having worshipped with water for the guest (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), flowers, incense, and so forth, one should instantly cause [the deities] to enter one’s own body.
Following that, one should contemplate oneself as being preceded by the consecration of all Tathāgatas and adorned with the crown of Akṣobhya.

The mantra is: *oṃ sarvadharmābhāvasvabhāvaviśuddhavastra a ā aṃ aḥ prakṛtipariśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā yaduta sarvatathāgatajñānakāyamañjuśrīpariśuddhitāmupādāyeti a āḥ sarvatathāgatahṛdaya hara hara oṃ huṃ hrīṃ bhagavan jñānamūrtivāgīśvara mahāvāca sarvadharmagaganāmalasupariśuddhadharmadhātu jñānagarbha āḥ*. With this mantra, preceded by the consecration of the beginning, middle, and end, one should recite the *Nāmasaṅgīti* every day at each of the three junctions (sandhyās), either three times or once, while seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) and remaining in meditative absorption (*samāhita*).
One should recite in this manner until one perceives the signs of accomplishment;
immediately thereafter, one should practice the means for accomplishment according to the tantra. Thus ends the *Āryanāmasaṅgītisādhana*.
